A Russian film has emerged as the winner of the prestigious BBC World Prize.
The film, titled "The Silent Revolution," captivated audiences and judges alike with its powerful storytelling and thought-provoking themes.


Directed by acclaimed Russian filmmaker Ivan Petrov, "The Silent Revolution" tells the story of a group of young activists who challenge the oppressive regime in their country.
The film explores themes of freedom, resistance, and the power of unity in the face of adversity.


The BBC World Prize is an annual award that recognizes outstanding films from around the globe.
It aims to celebrate diversity and promote cultural exchange through the medium of film.
This year, the competition received a record number of entries from over 50 countries, making the victory for "The Silent Revolution" even more significant.


The judges praised the film for its exceptional cinematography, compelling performances, and its ability to shed light on important social and political issues.
They commended Petrov for his masterful storytelling and his ability to create a gripping narrative that resonates with audiences worldwide.


"The Silent Revolution" has already garnered critical acclaim at various international film festivals, and its win at the BBC World Prize further solidifies its status as a must-see film.

Smartphones have become an integral part of our lives, serving as a constant companion and a gateway to the digital world.
With each passing year, these pocket-sized devices continue to evolve, offering an array of features and capabilities that were once unimaginable.
The future of technology is indeed in our pockets.


Gone are the days when phones were merely used for making calls and sending text messages.
Today's smartphones are powerhouses, capable of performing a multitude of tasks.
From browsing the internet and checking emails to streaming videos and playing games, these devices have transformed into mini-computers that fit snugly in our pockets.


One of the most significant advancements in smartphone technology is the integration of artificial intelligence (AI).
AI-powered virtual assistants like Siri, Google Assistant, and Alexa have become our personal helpers, ready to answer questions, set reminders, and even control smart home devices with just a voice command.
These virtual assistants continue to improve, becoming more intuitive and understanding our needs better than ever before.


Another area where smartphones are making strides is in the realm of photography.

A new study has found that Muslim individuals are more likely to be stopped and searched by police in the UK compared to their non-Muslim counterparts.
The research, conducted by the University of Oxford, analyzed data from over 1.5 million stop and search incidents between 2019 and 2020.


According to the findings, Muslim individuals were 2.5 times more likely to be stopped and searched by police compared to individuals from other religious backgrounds.
The study also revealed that Muslim women were disproportionately targeted, with a 93% higher chance of being stopped and searched compared to non-Muslim women.


The researchers suggest that these disparities in stop and search practices could be attributed to unconscious bias and stereotypes held by police officers.
They argue that these biases may lead to a disproportionate focus on Muslim individuals, resulting in a higher likelihood of being stopped and searched.


The study also highlighted regional variations in stop and search rates.
Muslim individuals in London were found to be six times more likely to be stopped and searched compared to non-Muslim individuals, while in the West Midlands, the figure was four times higher.


These findings raise concerns about the potential impact of such practices on community relations and trust in the police force.
The researchers argue that the over-policing of Muslim individuals can lead to feelings of alienation and marginalization within these communities.

The European Union (EU) has announced plans to increase its development aid budget in an effort to fuel global development and tackle poverty.
The move comes as part of the EU's commitment to the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), which aim to eradicate poverty, promote sustainable economic growth, and address social and environmental challenges by 2030.


The EU has pledged to allocate 0.7% of its gross national income (GNI) to development aid by 2030, a target set by the UN.
This would represent a significant increase from the current level of 0.47% of GNI.
The EU's development aid budget is one of the largest in the world, and the increase in funding is expected to have a substantial impact on global development efforts.


The additional funding will be used to support a wide range of initiatives, including education, healthcare, infrastructure development, and climate change mitigation.
The EU aims to prioritize the most vulnerable countries and regions, particularly those affected by conflict, natural disasters, and extreme poverty.


In addition to increasing its financial commitment, the EU also plans to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of its development aid.
This includes strengthening coordination and cooperation with partner countries, international organizations, and civil society.
The EU will also focus on promoting good governance, human rights, and gender equality in its development efforts.

The party argues that extended drinking hours have led to an increase in alcohol-related crime and disorder, putting a strain on emergency services and local communities.

They argue that the legislation has failed to deliver the promised benefits and has instead created a culture of excessive drinking and antisocial behavior.


According to the party, the extended drinking hours have resulted in a significant rise in alcohol-related violence, particularly in city centers and town centers.
They claim that the police and ambulance services are being stretched to their limits, dealing with the consequences of excessive drinking.


The Conservative Party is now calling for a review of the licensing laws to address these concerns.
They propose introducing stricter regulations on opening hours and a more robust enforcement of licensing conditions.
They also suggest giving local authorities more power to refuse or revoke licenses in areas where there is a high concentration of alcohol-related crime.


Critics argue that the Tories' stance on 24-hour drinking is overly simplistic and fails to address the underlying issues of alcohol abuse and addiction.

Parents and grandparents are increasingly turning to financial gifts as a way to support their children's future.
According to a recent survey, more than half of parents in the UK have given or plan to give a financial gift to their children.
This trend is driven by a desire to help children get a head start in life, whether it's for education, buying a home, or starting a business.


One of the main advantages of giving financial gifts to children is the potential for long-term financial security.
By starting early, parents can help their children build a solid financial foundation that will benefit them throughout their lives.
This can include setting up a savings account, investing in stocks or bonds, or even contributing to a pension fund.
By instilling good financial habits from a young age, parents can empower their children to make smart financial decisions in the future.


Another benefit of financial gifts is the opportunity to teach children about money management.
By involving children in the decision-making process, parents can help them understand the value of money and the importance of saving and investing.
This hands-on experience can be invaluable in preparing children for the financial challenges they will face as adults.

Former United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon has criticized the United States for its response to the devastating tsunami that struck Southeast Asia in 2004.
In a recent interview, Ban Ki-moon accused the US of providing insufficient aid and failing to take decisive action in the aftermath of the disaster.


The tsunami, triggered by a massive undersea earthquake, claimed the lives of over 230,000 people across 14 countries.
It caused widespread destruction, leaving millions homeless and in desperate need of assistance.
While many nations rallied to provide aid and support, Ban Ki-moon believes the US fell short in its response.


According to Ban Ki-moon, the US government's initial pledge of $35 million in aid was far from adequate given the scale of the disaster.
He argued that the US, as a global superpower, had a moral obligation to do more to alleviate the suffering of those affected.
Ban Ki-moon also criticized the slow deployment of US military assets, which he claimed could have played a crucial role in delivering aid and providing relief to the affected areas.


The former UN Secretary-General's comments come as the world reflects on the 17th anniversary of the devastating tsunami.
The disaster served as a wake-up call for the international community, highlighting the need for improved disaster preparedness and response mechanisms.

It suggests that China's actions were driven by a desire to reduce its dependence on Middle Eastern oil and establish a stronger foothold in Russia's energy sector.


The revelations come at a time of heightened tensions between Russia and the West, with the report likely to further strain relations between Moscow and Beijing.

The UK's highest court, the House of Lords, has ruled that the government's policy of detaining foreign terror suspects indefinitely without trial is unlawful.
The ruling is a major blow to the government's anti-terrorism measures and has sparked a heated debate about civil liberties and national security.


The case was brought by nine foreign nationals who have been held in detention for several years under the controversial policy.
They argued that their indefinite detention without trial violated their human rights and amounted to arbitrary detention.


In a unanimous decision, the Law Lords ruled that the government's policy breached the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits arbitrary detention.
They also found that the policy was discriminatory, as it only applied to foreign nationals and not to British citizens suspected of terrorism.


The ruling has been hailed as a victory for civil liberties and the rule of law.
Human rights groups have long criticized the government's policy, arguing that it undermines fundamental rights and does little to enhance national security.


However, the government has expressed disappointment with the ruling, warning that it could hamper efforts to combat terrorism.
Home Secretary John Reid said that the ruling would make it more difficult to deport foreign terror suspects and could lead to their release into the community.

Residents of Beijing are expressing their frustration and anger over the soaring parking fees in the city.
The cost of parking in the Chinese capital has skyrocketed in recent years, leaving many residents feeling burdened and financially strained.


Beijing, known for its congested streets and limited parking spaces, has seen a significant increase in parking fees as the city aims to reduce traffic congestion and encourage the use of public transportation.
However, this move has not been well-received by the city's residents, who argue that the high fees are unfair and unreasonable.


Many Beijingers rely on their cars for daily commuting and find it increasingly difficult to afford the exorbitant parking fees.
Some residents have reported spending a significant portion of their monthly income on parking alone, which has led to growing frustration and resentment towards the local government.


The issue has sparked heated debates on social media platforms, with many residents sharing their personal experiences and expressing their dissatisfaction.
Some have even called for a boycott of paid parking lots in protest against the high fees.


In response to the mounting criticism, local authorities have defended the increased parking fees, stating that they are necessary to manage the city's limited parking resources and reduce traffic congestion.
They argue that the fees are aimed at discouraging car usage and promoting the use of public transportation, which is seen as a more sustainable and efficient way to navigate the city.

A landmark court case is currently underway, with potentially far-reaching implications for the future of file-sharing.
The case, which is being heard by the highest court in the land, has brought into question the legality of sharing copyrighted material online.


The court is considering whether file-sharing platforms should be held responsible for the actions of their users.
The case has been brought by a group of major music labels, who argue that file-sharing platforms have facilitated widespread copyright infringement and should be held accountable.


File-sharing has long been a contentious issue, with proponents arguing that it allows for the free exchange of information and promotes creativity and innovation.
However, critics argue that it undermines the rights of content creators and deprives them of their rightful income.


The outcome of this case could have significant implications for the future of file-sharing.
If the court rules in favor of the music labels, it could pave the way for increased regulation and stricter enforcement of copyright laws.
This could mean that file-sharing platforms would be required to implement measures to prevent copyright infringement, such as filtering or blocking certain content.


On the other hand, if the court rules in favor of the file-sharing platforms, it could set a precedent that would make it more difficult for copyright holders to take legal action against those who share their content online.

The San Jose Open saw some of the biggest names in tennis breeze through their opening matches, as the tournament got underway in California. 


World number one Novak Djokovic wasted no time in dispatching his opponent, American Bjorn Fratangelo, in straight sets.
Djokovic, who is aiming to win his fifth title in San Jose, looked in fine form as he cruised to a 6-2, 6-2 victory. 


In the women's draw, top seed Serena Williams also had a comfortable start to her campaign.
The 23-time Grand Slam champion defeated German Laura Siegemund 6-3, 6-2 in just over an hour.
Williams, who is making her return to competitive tennis after giving birth to her daughter, showed no signs of rustiness as she dominated the match from start to finish. 


Another big name to progress was Australian Open champion Naomi Osaka.
The Japanese star, who is currently ranked number two in the world, defeated American Madison Brengle 6-3, 6-4.
Osaka, who is known for her powerful groundstrokes, showcased her skills as she overcame a determined Brengle to secure her place in the next round. 


However, not all the big guns had it easy.

Asian stock markets have defied expectations and risen in the wake of last week's earthquake in Japan as investors looked through the current turmoil and focused on the longer term prospects.


Japan's Nikkei index closed up 1.2% after falling as much as 2.5% earlier in the day.


In neighbouring South Korea the Kospi index rose 1.1%.


In Australia, the ASX/200 closed up 1.4%.


In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng index ended the morning 0.3% higher.


And in China, where markets were closed on Friday for a public holiday, the CSI 300 index of the largest listed companies in Shanghai and Shenzhen rose 1.4% on Monday.


The resilience of Asian markets is in stark contrast to the reaction to the earthquake seven years ago.


After the earthquake in Tohoku, northern Japan, in March 2011, markets were jittery for months, said Yoshikiyo Shimamine, chief strategist at Daiwa Securities.


Back then, market participants were worried about the impact on the world's third biggest economy.
This time, they are more worried about the rest of the world, given the strong economic ties between Japan and its Asian neighbours.

Barclays has reported a sharp rise in first-half profits, boosted by the release of pandemic-related provisions and strong trading.


The FTSE 100 bank said pre-tax profits doubled to £5.9bn ($7.5bn) in the six months to 30 June, compared with £2.5bn a year earlier.


Barclays - which is due to announce a shake-up of its management later on Thursday - said it would resume its share buyback programme.


The lender added that it now expected to pay a dividend for the first half of the year, as well as a "modest" interim payout in the third quarter.


Its performance was in sharp contrast to rivals HSBC and Lloyds, which reported falls in first-half profits earlier this week.


Barclays' profits were boosted by the release of £1.4bn from reserves that were set aside during the pandemic in case of increased loan losses.


The bank said it now expected to pay a dividend of 6p per share for the full year, and added that it would consider a "modest" interim payment in the third quarter.


John Cronin, an analyst at Goodbody, said the bank had delivered a "solid" set of results.


"Barclays' performance this year has been underpinned by its investment banking division, with M&A advisory thriving in the first half of the year," he said.


However, Mr Cronin added that the bank's retail arm - which includes its UK operations - continued to be "challenged".

Fiat is considering floating 10% of its iconic supercar brand Ferrari, in what would be the Italian car maker's latest effort to trim its debt. 


The proposal could value Ferrari, known for its sleek sports cars, at between $7.6bn and $10bn, and follows a failed attempt in 2008 to sell Ferrari outright. 


Fiat and Ferrari are both controlled by the Agnelli family's Exor investment vehicle. 


At the end of March, Fiat said it planned to spin off Ferrari within two years, and list it in New York. 


The group had also been considering floating part of its automotive business on the Milan stock exchange, but said in April that a listing of Ferrari would "create greater value" for the group. 


Fiat said in a statement on Saturday that "various options" for Ferrari's IPO were "being analysed". 


"A decision in principle is expected to be made in the next few months," it said. 


The spin-off of Ferrari would be the latest in a series of moves by Fiat to raise money and cut debt built up by its unsuccessful takeover of Chrysler Group. 


The US car maker has not yet returned to profit, and Fiat has had to pump money into the company. 


In an earlier effort to reduce debt, Fiat sold a 19% stake in Ferrari in an IPO in October 2015.

text:
Microsoft has launched a new version of its Windows operating system in India, aimed at curbing software piracy.


Windows 10 "Core", as it has been named, is an edition of Windows 10 that contains minimal features.
While users will be able to run apps, they will not be able to access Microsoft's Windows Store to download programmes.


The move aims to offer a low-cost alternative to Windows, making it easier for Microsoft to compete with cheap pirated versions of its software, which are widely used in the country.


It also hopes the new version will encourage users of pirated Windows to move towards legal versions, by offering a more affordable option.


"It has always been our endeavour to ensure that customers have the best possible experience on our platform, and as a part of this, we are bringing the Windows 10 'Core' edition to India," said Bhaskar Pramanik, chairman of Microsoft India.


"This edition offers a no-frills Windows 10 experience to our customers at an affordable price, and we believe this edition will be attractive to both desktop and mobile customers in the country."


The Indian computer market is currently dominated by software pirates, who buy a single copy of Windows and install it on multiple computers, rather than buying separate licences for each.


According to industry body National Association of Software and Services Companies (Nasscom), the rate of software piracy in India in 2016 was more than 59%, costing the country more than $1.7bn (£1.2bn) in lost revenue.


Microsoft has launched several initiatives in India to curb the practice.

text:
High fuel costs are hitting US airlines, as they struggle to buy enough fuel to meet demand.


The head of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Billy Nolen, says the aviation industry is "in crisis" because of the high price of jet fuel.


Five major US airlines have filed paperwork indicating they may have to cancel flights this summer because they cannot afford to buy enough fuel.


The FAA said it will not allow US airlines to ignore safety rules to save fuel.


US airlines reacted with anger to Mr Nolen's comments, saying the FAA should be focusing on safety, not commenting on the economic situation.


American Airlines' chief executive, Gerard Arpey, said the FAA's comments were "unfortunate and inappropriate".


Fuel prices are a major concern for airlines, because they account for up to one-third of operating costs.


The five airlines that have said they may have to cancel flights are American, Continental, Delta, Northwest and United.


But all of them say they are working to find a solution to the problem.


The International Air Transport Association (Iata), which represents airlines worldwide, said this week that high fuel costs could lead to higher air fares.

The UK economy grew faster than expected in the October-to-December quarter, despite worries about higher interest rates and falling consumer confidence.


Official data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed that economic growth accelerated to 0.2% in the final month of 2022, above analysts' forecasts of 0.1%.


For the whole quarter, economists had expected 0.2% growth, but official figures showed that the economy expanded by 0.3%.


It comes after the UK economy contracted in the third quarter as households cut back on spending.


The ONS said that warmer weather helped generate 0.3% growth in construction in the fourth quarter, while a weaker pound helped manufacturing to expand by the same amount.


However, retailers continued to struggle as sales fell by 0.5% in December, the biggest fall since January 2021.


Chancellor Jeremy Hunt said: "Today's GDP data shows that the fundamentals of our economy are strong with solid consumer spending and a resilient construction sector supporting growth, despite global challenges.


"However, I am not immune to the pressures facing households around the UK with the cost of living, and we are taking decisive action to support people in getting through the winter, with further support to come at the next Budget."


But the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) warned that the cost of living crisis and soaring inflation was likely to drag on the UK's economic growth in 2023.


Suren Thiru, head of economics at the BCC, said: "The UK's economic growth surge at the end of 2022 was driven by the vagaries of the weather, the NHS backlog and the Omicron wave, rather than underlying strength.

Xstrata has "snubbed" its biggest shareholder by rejecting a £2.7bn ($4.5bn) takeover bid, mining group Xstrata's management has said.


Xstrata's board said the offer from commodities trader Glencore did not reflect the company's worth and was not in the best interests of shareholders.


It described the bid as "opportunistic" following Xstrata's fall in value since October.


Glencore, which already owns 33% of Xstrata, had made an all-share offer equivalent to 430p per share.


Xstrata said the offer "significantly undervalued" the company.


"The board of Xstrata believes that the offer does not adequately reflect the long-term value and prospects of Xstrata and is therefore not in the best interests of Xstrata shareholders as a whole," the company said in a statement.


"Shareholders should have the opportunity to participate in the continued strong performance of Xstrata.
"

Xstrata also said the offer would have meant its shareholders owning just 34% of the combined group.


Glencore's offer came after Xstrata's value was hit by uncertainty over the future of its biggest mine in Spain, Los Llanos.


The mine's future was thrown into doubt after the regional government in Spain said it planned to revoke its licence following protests from local residents over the environmental impact.

The government will introduce laws to force tech firms to help police investigations, home secretary David Blunkett will say.


In a speech to the Police Superintendents' Association, he will argue that "evasive" behaviour by some companies hampers criminal investigations.


Mr Blunkett will add that a "consent regime" - rules aimed at protecting civilians - will be among the new laws.


The proposed legislation will form part of the government's anti-terrorism strategy, due out next month.


The speech will be the latest in a series of initiatives aimed at boosting Britain's anti-terror measures ahead of the G8 summit in Scotland next month.


The summit, to be held in Gleneagles, will bring together the leaders of the world's eight richest countries, along with leaders from five developing nations.


The meeting will be a security operation on a huge scale, probably the biggest in Britain this century. 


Mr Blunkett will say later: "We are undertaking the most substantial overhaul of police powers in a generation. 


"New legislation will make it a requirement, not an option, for communications companies to provide assistance to the police and security services in the investigation of crime.
"

He will argue that the "biggest obstacle" to effective police work is the "evasive behaviour" of communications companies.

Tim Henman has overcome a stern test from Greg Rusedski to reach the quarter-finals of the Nasdaq-100 Open in Miami.


The British number one, 29, beat the Canadian wildcard 6-7 6-4 6-3 in their third-round match.


Rusedski, ranked 81 in the world, broke Henman's serve in the opening game of the match and took the first set on a tie-break.


But Henman, the 11th seed, fought back to win in two hours and 20 minutes.


He will now face Spain's Carlos Moya, the Australian Open champion, in the last eight.


Moya, seeded 16th, saw off Dutchman Sjeng Schalken 6-3 6-4.


"Greg's a great competitor, it was a high-quality match and I'm very pleased to get through," said Henman.


"I had to play aggressively to have a chance and it was important to make him play one more shot.
"

The writing was on the wall for Rusedski early in the third set when he double-faulted to hand Henman a break and trail 2-1.


Henman moved 4-2 up with a rasping cross-court winner and although Rusedski broke back immediately, the Briton broke again to take victory.

Saxophone player and composer Ornette Coleman's personalised alto saxophone is being sold at auction.


The instrument, which is expected to sell for up to $35,000 (£26,000), was played by Coleman at New York's legendary Birdland club in the early 1960s.


It will be part of a sale of more than 500 items of music memorabilia in California on 16 November.


The sale includes guitars once owned by Bob Dylan and Tom Waits, and a violin played by Itzhak Perlman.


Coleman's saxophone heads to auction

The saxophone has a copper neck and is engraved with the musician's name and the inscription: "Property of Ornette Coleman, The Pioneer Of Harmolodic Music, The Greatest Composer In The World.
"

London-based auctioneers Bonhams, which is managing the sale, described the instrument as "a true piece of jazz history".


"This is a superb example of the saxophone custom-built for Ornette Coleman by mouthpiece maker and instrument technician Ronald Van Der Waals in 1961," it added.


Ornette Coleman was an American jazz saxophonist and composer who was widely recognised as an influential figure in the history of jazz.
He received numerous awards, including a Pulitzer Prize for Music in 2007, and was inducted into the Downbeat Jazz Hall of Fame in 1989.


The sale at Bonhams in Los Angeles also includes a guitar owned and played by Bob Dylan during the recording of his 1975 album Blood On The Tracks.

Quartet of British athletes chosen for prestigious awards - including one who missed out on going to Tokyo - after helping to ramp up awareness of mental health issues.


Straight after the closing ceremony of the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, 4x100m medley relay bronze medallist Freya Anderson and her fellow British athletes were on a flight back home.


But instead of it being a moment to relax after an intense Olympic campaign, for three of them it was the start of a busy summer of events.


Along with relay teammates Anna Hopkin, who won an individual silver medal in the process, and boys' 100m freestyle champion Tom Dean, Anderson was chosen to be an MBE in the Queen's Birthday Honours list.


And the three relay swimmers, plus Dean's brother, Edward, were also named in the New Year Honours list.


The honours are in recognition of their swim in the final of the 4x100m medley relay in Tokyo, when they took a knee on the starting block before swimming their laps in a show of support for the Black Lives Matter movement.


They have also been recognised for their work raising awareness of mental health issues - a cause all four swimmers say they are "proud" to have been able to help.


"It was really nice to be recognised for using our platform, especially in the context of the Olympics where it reaches so many more people," says Anderson, 21, who was named female world swimmer of the year in November.


"A lot of people have said they have been affected by it, which is amazing to hear.


"We have been able to use our voices, and it has definitely opened my eyes to how big a step we have taken.

Young people know "little" about politics and "could not point to the UK on a map", according to a study of 16- to 25-year-olds.


The study, by pollster Ipsos MORI, also found that fewer than half could name the prime minister - and more believed Boris Johnson was a fictional character than a real one.


Only a third of those surveyed felt "positive" about politics and current levels of political engagement.


Ipsos MORI's head of political research, Emily Gray, said it was "reassuring" that many knew "how they would vote" in an election.


The study was based on interviews with 1,969 British adults aged 16-75, conducted online between 30 May and 3 June.


How well do you think you know politics?


Question: Who is the prime minister?


Answer: The prime minister is the head of the government of a sovereign state, such as the United Kingdom.
The prime minister makes the key decisions, and sets the political agenda.
Right now, the UK prime minister is Boris Johnson.

China's economic growth slowed in 2022, but the fourth-biggest economy in the world still managed to exceed analysts' expectations.


Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 2.9% in the last 11 months of the year, which was better than many forecasts.


The figure was heavily skewed by the rapid recovery in 2020 and the size of the country's Covid lockdown in 2022.

 
Expansion in the third quarter of 2022 slowed to 3.9% from 7.9% in the same period a year earlier.
In the second quarter, it slowed to 0.4% from 8.1% a year earlier.


The pandemic and lockdown disrupted manufacturing and supply chains throughout 2022.
But China's economy recovered rapidly after the lockdowns were lifted in December.


"The Chinese economy stabilized after the Covid outbreak," said Julian Evans-Pritchard, chief China economist at Capital Economics.
"But the recovery is losing steam fast.
The main weakness is the property sector, where activity has hit rock bottom.

text:
The NHS is likely to need more reform, particularly in increasing the number of staff and efficiency of care, says former health minister Stephen Dorrell.


Mr Dorrell, who was speaking at the NHS Confederation conference, also said the health service had managed to avoid the worst of the economic crisis.


And he warned that any attempt to meet rising demand with limited resources would inevitably lead to worse outcomes and increasing inequity.


His comments came as latest figures showed the NHS in England had missed its A&E target for the 22nd consecutive month in February.


Just 89.4% of patients were seen within four hours - well below the 95% target.


Mr Dorrell, who was health secretary between 1995 and 1997, now chairs the Health Select Committee.


And he used his Confed speech in Liverpool to issue a warning that the "easy" decisions on the NHS had already been taken - and that tougher choices were to come.


There was a danger that the health service would "slide into becoming a national religion" whose followers believed it was "beyond criticism", he added.


In his widest-ranging speech to the NHS since leaving the Department of Health last summer, Mr Milburn said the health service had enjoyed its "best ever" winter.


But he added that it had not been "plain sailing" and that there were still huge pressures on A&E departments.

text:
Rank set to sell off film unit

Rank, the entertainment group, is preparing to sell its film-making unit, which includes the Hammer Films horror brand, in a move which marks the end of an era for one of Britain's best-known companies.


The decision to sell comes after Rank failed to find a buyer for its leisure business, which includes the Odeon, UCI and Rank Vue cinema chains, and the Mecca bingo and casinos operations.


Last month, the company said it was in talks with a small number of potential buyers for the leisure business, which contributed revenues of £1.46bn to Rank in 2005.


But today it confirmed it had decided to split its film and leisure businesses, and said it had received several approaches for its film unit.


The Rank Group's film operations include production companies Hammer Films and Rank Film Distributors, and cinema chain Screen International.


The company has produced hundreds of films, including the popular "Carry On..." comedy films, and developed the Hammer House of Horror brand, famous for its ghoulish depictions of famous figures such as Dracula.


The company said in a statement that its film unit was "non-core" and had been "exploring opportunities to maximise value from this division".


It said it had received a number of approaches and was "currently considering these in the context of a sale of the whole division".


Rank's decision to sell its film unit comes just weeks after its rival, MGM, was bought by a group of investors including Sony and Comcast.


The BBC's media correspondent, Torin Douglas, said Rank had been in a strong position ahead of the sale of its leisure business, but added the failure to find a buyer had "thrown into doubt plans to spin-off the film business".

Intel has built a breakthrough new laser that could finally help bring extreme high-speed internet access to your home.


The chip maker has demonstrated a technology called "terabit silicon laser" that can transmit data at a staggering rate of 1.02 terabits per second over a distance of 2km (1.24 miles).


That's 50 times faster than the fastest fibre optics connection available today and speeds that even quantum computing cannot hope to match.


The silicon laser could be used to upgrade the infrastructure of internet service providers (ISPs) to enable speeds of up to 1.6 terabits per second downstream from ISPs to homes.


Thereafter, the speed of data transmission would be dependent on the equipment inside consumers' homes.


Today, most homes in the UK have a broadband speed of 36Mbps, while those lucky enough to live in areas covered by Virgin Media's cable service can receive speeds of up to 1Gbps - less than 0.2% of the speed that the new silicon laser is capable of.


The technology relies on a new type of laser etching that allows data to be processed and transmitted using light, rather than electrical pulses.


Justin Rattner, Intel's chief technology officer, said: "For the data centre market, where optical interconnects are beginning to reach their limits, the terabit silicon laser demonstrates how scalable and compact optical I/O can be for future high-performance computing platforms."


He added that the technology could be used to connect computers within a data centre, connecting data centres themselves and providing internet access.


The silicon laser could also be used to provide the infrastructure for 5G networks and high-speed autonomous vehicles.

Oil company Yukos has lost its bankruptcy battle in a US court, leaving its former owners with nothing.


The former Russian oil giant had been appealing against a court ruling last year that cleared the way for its assets to be sold off to pay off debt.


The Texas court rejected the appeal, saying Yukos had filed too late and failed to provide sufficient evidence.


Former Yukos shareholders including its former chief executive Mikhail Khodorkovsky had hoped to share in the proceeds.


They were jailed in Russia but have since been released.


The case dates back to 2004 when Yukos was broken up and its main production unit was sold to state-owned gas giant Gazprom for $9.35bn (£5.8bn).


The company was placed into bankruptcy protection, with its main assets sold to a company called Baikal Finance Group.


Last year, a US court ruled that the sale of Yukos' main production unit could go ahead, clearing the way for its assets to be sold off to pay off debt.


Yukos had argued that the sale was merely an attempt by the Russian government to seize its assets and that it was politically motivated.


However, the US court rejected this argument, saying that there was "sufficient evidence" that Yukos had filed its appeal too late.

The BBC's John Simpson in Shanghai says that, despite the warming of relations between the two countries, the Chinese are still very wary of foreign companies.


And although Shanghai Automotive has been praised by British Prime Minister Tony Blair for its rescue of Rover, the Chinese company may now have second thoughts.


"It is understood that SAIC's due diligence inspections have discovered that MG Rover's books are in far worse condition than they had previously thought," says the Reuters news agency.


"That means SAIC would have to pay far less than the previously agreed $230m for Rover, and it may even try to walk away from the deal."


The Chinese company's decision has taken MG Rover's directors by surprise.


The two sides had been due to finalise the details of their partnership on Monday, and the deal had been approved by the British government.


Now, it seems likely that the Shanghai Automotive delegation will fly home without agreeing a deal.


MG Rover, which makes the MG and Rover cars, went into administration last April after more than a decade of losses.


The company's administrators, Deloitte, have been trying to find a buyer for the company's assets since then.


They selected Shanghai Automotive as their preferred bidder last month, and the two sides initially agreed a price of $230m.

text:
Britain's former prime minister Tony Blair has rejected accusations that he deliberately took the country to war in Iraq on the basis of false evidence.


The former Labour leader told the BBC's Andrew Marr the decision to invade had been based on "solid intelligence".


He said he would "never have done anything to harm" the UK and people should be "relaxed" about the decision.


The ex-PM made the comments in his first BBC TV interview since leaving office.


Mr Blair - who was prime minister from 1997 to 2007 - said he did not "believe in retrospective decision-making".


And he defended his decision to join the US-led invasion, which began in March 2003, insisting that "the world is a better place" as a result.


The interview - recorded on Friday in London and broadcast on Sunday - came ahead of the publication of a heavily critical report into the UK's role in the Iraq war.


The report by Sir John Chilcott, a retired civil servant, is due to be published on 6 July after years of scrutiny of more than 150,000 official documents.


Sir John's 4,000-page report is expected to criticise Mr Blair's decision to join the US-led invasion, as well as the planning and execution of the war.


The ex-PM has always defended his decision to join the invasion, saying he did so to rid the world of a "monster" - Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein.

text:
Local councils must do more to find sites for gypsies and travellers who live on the roadside, the government says.


Communities Secretary Eric Pickles has warned that the "current situation is unacceptable".


He said he would give councils until the end of March to draw up plans.


It follows a court ruling which said that councils had a legal duty to provide more sites.


The government said it would appeal against that decision.


Mr Pickles said he agreed with the sentiment of the court ruling but added that it was important for councils to take into account the needs of settled communities.


"Councils should not shy away from doing the right thing by engaging with travelling communities and finding sites that work for residents, travellers and the local area," he said.


"But they should also be mindful that courts exist to interpret the law, not make it.
That is the role of parliament and I will seek to clarify the law to ensure all communities are treated equally under the planning system."


The announcement came as the government published its response to a consultation on the issue.

text:
Industrial revival hope for Japan

Japan's once-booming manufacturing industry has been on the decline for nearly 30 years.
But could "smart factories" help it stage a comeback?


Akio Toyoda is proud of the car he is about to show me.
It is not yet another hybrid, or an electric vehicle, but a petrol-engine sports utility vehicle (SUV).


"I love SUVs, because people who like SUVs are people who like to have fun," says the chief executive of Toyota, the world's largest car maker.


"This is a car that brings together the know-how and the technology of Toyota engines, and Toyota teamwork.
"

The new Toyota Highlander SUV will soon be making its way to car dealerships in the US and elsewhere.
It is one of dozens of models Toyota hopes will revive its fortunes in global car markets.


Toyota has invested billions of dollars in new plants and equipment in the US and Asia.
It has also raised wages and streamlined production lines.

text:
Judge rules against former Brexit minister, who earned £600k from TalkTV and Telegraph columns

The BBC can reveal the Conservative MP was paid £122,000 for a column in the Telegraph and £475,000 from TalkTV. 

The MP for Forest of Dean, who was justice secretary between September 2022 and July this year, has had a column in the Telegraph since November 2016. 


According to accounts filed with the House of Commons, his earnings from the newspaper increased from £75,000 in 2019 to £122,000 in 2020. 


Mr. Hague's earnings from his TalkTV contract were revealed in a document filed at Companies House. 


According to the document, filed on 30 November, the channel agreed to pay the former foreign secretary £475,000 "for the provision of services as a presenter on TalkTV's current affairs programming". 


The document said the services would be provided for two and a half hours a week across a year, but it did not say how much Mr. Hague was paid upfront. 


The details emerged in a ruling published on Friday by Judge Mark Pelling, who is sitting at the High Court in London. 


He ruled against Mr. Hague, who had tried to stop the BBC from reporting how much he earned from the two outlets. 


The judge said the MP had not proved there was a "real and not fanciful risk" of violence or intimidation if the information was made public. 

The ruling comes after a former adviser to Boris Johnson, Dominic Cummings, claimed last month that Mr. Hague had "sold out" by taking money for political commentary.

The friendly matches that litter the football calendar might seem innocuous enough but they are "threatening the health of the game", according to FIFA's head of global football development, Arsène Wenger.


In a frank interview with BBC Sport, the former Arsenal manager said friendlies were "killing the game".


He added that he wanted to see them replaced with proper competitions for young players.


Wenger's views chime with those of many in the game - but how might his proposal work in practice?

Are friendlies really a problem?


There are plenty of people within football who believe that the sport has become oversaturated, that there are too many games and too many meaningless matches.


Wenger, who was appointed by FIFA in August, believes that the international break is particularly damaging to the game.


He said: "In the international break there are too many friendlies.
You hurt the credibility of the competition because people think it is not serious.


"You play a friendly in Switzerland, in Norway, in Finland - for nothing.
The audience is not interested, the players don't really focus on it.

Wales coach Warren Gatland has criticised England's Paul Grewcock for making a legal joke about the 'granny rule' prior to Saturday's Six Nations opener in Cardiff.
The official Rugby Football Union website carried a story entitled 'England plot granny rule twist to confuse Wales'.
It has since been removed but the Welsh camp were still aware of its contents when they arrived in Cardiff on Tuesday.
"It's not the professionalism that we've come to expect from the RFU," said Gatland.
"It's not the correct thing to say in relation to a woman's age and it's not the right thing to do.
"I don't know what their reasoning was for doing it
but it's not the professionalism that international rugby expects and it's not something we're used to from the RFU.
"I don't know what their reasoning is for releasing a statement like that
but it's not acceptable."
In 2003 World Cup final referee Andre Watson cited the 'granny rule' when sending off Wales' Richard Hibbard for a dangerous tackle on Australia's Elton Flatley.

GM pays $2bn to evade Fiat buyout

Detroit carmaker General Motors has made a payment of more than $2bn (£1.3bn) to a joint venture with tyremaker Bridgestone to settle a dispute with Fiat.


The payment ends a contentious relationship between GM and Fiat Chrysler, and clears the way for the Italian-American carmaker to merge with France's Renault.


The two firms have been locked in a battle for more than a year.


In a joint statement, GM and Bridgestone - which makes Firestone tyres - said they would also end their 15-year old alliance in Russia and other countries.


GM has been trying to escape from its partnership with Fiat, which pays royalties to the Detroit carmaker for technology used in their vehicles.


Last summer, GM offered to pay $2bn to buy out its partner, but Fiat replied with a $1.3bn counter-offer to buy out GM.


The dispute attracted attention after GM accused Fiat of bribing officials in the Mexican city of Toluca to obtain favours.


Fiat denied the allegations, but last month, the former attorney general for the state of Mexico indicted Fiat for the alleged bribes.


The carmaker said it would "vigorously" fight the charges, and on Saturday, it filed a lawsuit in the US demanding documents from GM related to the case.


In a statement, Fiat said it welcomed the end of the dispute with GM, but said the payment was "totally unacceptable".

In a joint statement, GM and Bridgestone - which makes Firestone tyres - said they would also end their 15-year old alliance in Russia and other countries.


GM has been trying to escape from its partnership with Fiat, which pays royalties to the Detroit carmaker for technology used in their vehicles.


Last summer, GM offered to pay $2bn to buy out its partner, but Fiat replied with a $1.3bn counter-offer to buy out GM.


The dispute attracted attention after GM accused Fiat of bribing officials in the Mexican city of Toluca to obtain favours.


Fiat denied the allegations, but last month, the former attorney general for the state of Mexico indicted Fiat for the alleged bribes.


The carmaker said it would "vigorously" fight the charges, and on Saturday, it filed a lawsuit in the US demanding documents from GM related to the case.


In a statement, Fiat said it welcomed the end of the dispute with GM, but said the payment was "totally unacceptable".

Mourinho was charged with misconduct for allegedly poking Southampton's assistant manager, Eric Steele, in the eye during the game on 1 October.


He was also accused of violating the FA's rule that managers and coaches are not allowed to leave their area.


An independent regulatory commission found that Mourinho had breached the FA's rules, but decided that no punishment was necessary.


"The commission decided that the breach was inadvertent and intended no malice," said an FA statement.


Mourinho welcomed the decision, saying he had been confident that he would not be punished.


"I'm happy with the decision.
I knew from the beginning that I would not be punished," he said.


"I didn't make a gesture of violence.
I reproach myself a little bit for not being more careful with the technical area, because I know that the rules are different in England from the rest of Europe.

The BBC has apologized to Ms. Wells for any shortcomings in its response.


A spokesman for the broadcaster said it had "supported Grace and taken advice from experts on how we could have done better".


"We are genuinely sorry for any shortcomings in our response and we will continue to support Grace," the spokesman added.


In addition to her lawsuit against the BBC, Ms. Wells has also filed a lawsuit against Mr. Medavoy and his wife for alleged sexual assault, harassment, and wrongful termination.


Mr. Medavoy, who was accused by a number of women of sexually assaulting them, died in October last year. 


His wife, Lady Carolyn Medavoy, has denied all the allegations against her.


Several other women have filed lawsuits against the Medavoys, including actress Scarlett Johansson and former Olympic skier Lindsey Vonn.

text:
Continental warned on Thursday it may run out of cash as the German automotive supplier continued to struggle with a global shortage of semiconductors, which has led to a sharp fall in production.


The news weighed on Continental's shares, which were down 6.5% in early trade, wiping off about €1.6bn ($1.8bn) of the company's market value.


Chief Financial Officer Wolfgang Schäfer said Continental had seen a significant recovery in its operations in the second quarter as lockdowns were eased, including in key markets such as China.


But he said that recovery had stalled in the third quarter due to the shortage of semiconductors, as well as rising costs and supply chain problems that were causing delays in production.


"We currently expect that we will generate positive cash flow in the third quarter, but that this will be significantly lower than in the second quarter," Schäfer said.


"We are doing everything in our power to ensure that Continental does not run out of cash.
At the same time, we are making advances in securing additional financing for the company.
"

 Continental, which is due to report third-quarter results on Oct. 28, had cash and cash equivalents of €4.3bn ($4.9bn) at the end of June.


The automotive industry has been hit by a global shortage of semiconductors, which are key components in electronic devices used in cars, including power steering and cruise control systems.


The problem has led major carmakers such as Volkswagen, Toyota and General Motors to cut production and warn of a significant hit to their sales and profits.

The Mac Mini is an unusual computer.
There's nothing else quite like it on the market - no other device packs as much power as it does into such a small and affordable package.


It's not a laptop, but a desktop computer, albeit a very small one.
You can hook it up to a separate monitor, keyboard and mouse, and it connects to the internet in the same way as a normal desktop machine.


The Mac Mini comes with Apple's M2 processor, which is an upgrade on the M1 chip that powered the previous version.
It's a significant step up in performance, and helps the Mac Mini compete with cheaper PCs.


It is, however, the price that is the most impressive thing about the Mac Mini.
The model we tested costs $599 (£569), which is less than many PCs, and considerably less than most Macs.


The Mac Mini comes with a lot of power for the price.
Our test model had 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, which is double what it had in the previous version.

Manchester United co-chairman Avie Glazer has apologised for the club's poor season and admitted fans' protests had been "difficult to witness".


The Old Trafford crowd protested against the Glazer family throughout United's final home game of the season against Brentford on Tuesday.


Supporters also stopped traffic on the M6 motorway and outside the ground before the game, while thousands more voiced their opposition to the Americans in a boisterous atmosphere throughout the 1-1 draw.


The Glazers, who completed a leveraged takeover of United in 2005, have seen the club's debt rise to well over £1bn.


They have also been accused of not investing in the team, with United's last Premier League title coming in 2013.


A United statement released before the Brentford game said the club "heard" the fans' protests "loud and clear" and acknowledged the need for a "stronger and closer relationship" with supporters.


That move appeared to be an attempt to head off a vote of no confidence in the directors by the Manchester United Supporters Trust (MUST), which gave its support to the protests.


But Avram Glazer, who was at the game on Tuesday, has now gone further in a statement released to the Manchester Evening News.


He said: "You expressed your dissatisfaction with the management of the club - and we hear you.


"You voiced your frustration with our ownership - and we hear you.

The Teesiders are now set for a Europa League last-32 tie at home to Sparta Prague or Rapid Vienna.


"The attitude, application and desire of the players has been first class in Europe," said McClaren.


"We said before the game we'd need all those things and a bit of luck, and we got it," the Boro boss added.


McClaren's side survived a Roma fightback in the last 20 minutes to secure their place in Friday's draw with two goals from Brazilian forward Afonso Alves and one from central defender Emanuel Pogatetz.


The Romans, who had forward Francesco Tottesco sent off on 70 minutes for a second bookable offence, pulled a goal back through Daniele De Rossi's penalty seven minutes from time but Boro held on.


"We talked before the game about having the courage to get on the ball and pass it, and not be frightened of them," said McClaren, whose side had 67% of possession.


"We played some excellent football at times.
The players have executed the game plan superbly.


"We had to withstand a lot of pressure in the last 20 minutes

text:
The political blogosphere has always been a crowded place,
but never more so than at the moment.


As the US gears up for November's presidential election,
would-be candidates are fighting for every scrap of
coverage they can get.


So it is interesting that one site,
Politicalwire.com, should have attracted 700,000
visitors since it launched in June.


Its secret weapon?
A set of blog awards.


Politicalwire's 50 Most Influential Blogs Awards
has become a must-stop for political
wonks, activists and journalists looking to
keep tabs on the online conversation.


"There are a lot of political blogs out there
and this is a good way to separate the
wheat from the chaff, so to speak,"
says Political Wire editor-in-chief
Marc Ambinder.


"A lot of political journalists
are using it as a tool to find
interesting things that they might
want to write about.
"

The award winners are decided by a panel of
eight judges, all veteran political
reporters and bloggers.


They include Janine Warner,
editor of RollCall.com,
a site covering Capitol Hill;
Glenn Thrush, who covers politics
for the Newsday newspaper
in New York; and Susan
Gerard, editor of the HotAir
blog, who served as
a foreign policy adviser to
John McCain's 2000 presidential
campaign.

A judge has fined US agrochemical giant Monsanto $1.5m for bribing Argentine officials.


Monsanto pleaded guilty to the bribery charges in March.


US District Judge Jeffery White also fined the company's former head of global sustainability, Hugh Grant, $78,000 for his role in the scheme.


According to the Justice Department, Grant authorized a $50,000 bribe to an official in Argentina's agriculture ministry in order to preserve commercial permits for Monsanto.


The company also admitted to transferring $200,000 to a former official in Argentina's environmental and sustainable development ministry.


"Monsanto chose to illegally bribe foreign officials instead of complying with antitrust laws," said Assistant Attorney General Brian Benczkowski.


"This behaviour threatens our system of international law and commerce and we will hold accountable companies that corrupt the integrity of foreign elections and democratic institutions."


In a statement, Monsanto said it took "full responsibility" for its employees' actions and said the fines would not be passed on to its customers.


"This resolution with the DOJ concludes this investigation," the company said.


"Monsanto strongly opposes bribery of any government official and has taken steps to ensure that such behaviour does not occur.

It sounds like a device straight out of a spy movie, but its makers say it is the future of mobile phones.


The Mobifone is a mobile phone with a difference - it has no screen or keypad.


Instead, it uses "eye music" - a system where the user glances at symbols on the lid to open messages, select music and pick up calls.


South Korean firm Pantech has developed the device, which goes on sale there this week.


The phone recognises up to 2,000 different glance actions - such as quick sideways glances, prolonged eye contact and blinking.


Pantech is one of South Korea's biggest mobile phone makers and launched the device at the CES technology show in Las Vegas this week.


The firm's CEO, Lee Jong-seok, said the device had been four years in the making and was a world first.


"This is the world's first eye-controlled mobile phone.
There are other eye-controlled computers but they don't have the mobility of a mobile phone," he said.


"The phone's lid becomes a new kind of mobile interface.

Steve Coogan's comic character Alan Partridge returns in a new sitcom, Alpha Papa.


The actor chats to BBC entertainment correspondent Gordon Smart about reviving his most famous alter-ego.


Steve Coogan's most famous comic creation, Alan Partridge, is back on the small screen after an absence of more than a decade.


The sitcom Alpha Papa, begins on BBC One on 7 August and features Partridge as a middle-aged manager at a small independent radio station in Norwich who becomes trapped inside the building with a group of colleagues when a disgruntled former employee takes them hostage.


Coogan, 49, spoke to BBC entertainment correspondent Gordon Smart about bringing back his most famous alter-ego and working with his friend and co-writer Neil Gibbons on the project.


Gordon Smart:
Steve, it's 12 years since we last saw Alan Partridge on screen in the movie Alan Partridge: Alpha Papa.
Why now for his return?

Steve Coogan:
Well, Neil [ Gibbons] and I had talked about it for ages and actually went through the process of writing it and then we stopped because we weren't happy with it
and I was doing other things.

Apple has been accused of "double standards" over its refusal to help the UK police unlock an iPhone as part of a murder investigation.


The tech giant has been contacted by officers investigating the murder of Lucci Smith, an aspiring model and actress, in London in 2015.


The model's iPhone 6s is being held by detectives, but Apple has not responded to their request to unlock the device.


The company previously refused an appeal by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) to unlock the iPhone of the man who carried out a mass shooting in California in 2015.


Apple chief executive Tim Cook argued that the company had a responsibility to protect the privacy of its customers.


Now, the company is being criticized for applying different standards to its US and UK operations.


Police and prosecutors in the UK have made a series of appeals to Apple for help in unlocking phones, with no response.


Det Ch Supt Paul Brogden of the Metropolitan Police said the force had been unable to access the device in the Lucci Smith investigation, or to "gain any assistance from Apple Inc".


"As we have requested assistance from Apple on a number of occasions, without success, we have commenced the process of seeking a court order," he said.


"We have pursued all possible forensic options within our control before we take this action.

The role of a controversial "fee factor" in possible student fee increases has been played down by the universities minister.


Chris Skidmore said the figure - used to calculate tuition fee increases - was not a "magic number" and that a government green paper on fee increases would not be "led by" the figure.


He said it was "a total myth" that the fee factor - which stands at 3% - would be used to raise fees every year.


The minister said it was "not a decision" for him to take on fee levels.


Speaking to the BBC, he added that it was for universities to decide what they thought was "reasonable" in terms of fee levels, and that he wanted a debate with the sector on what those levels should be.


The green paper on the future of university fees in England will be published later this month.


It comes after universities were accused of using the fee factor - the maximum fee increase universities can impose - to suggest they could raise fees by as much as £250 per year from 2022.


Several universities - including some of the most prestigious in the country - have announced increases in tuition fees for the 2022/23 academic year using the fee factor, with some setting hikes of up to 6.5%. 


These increases are well in excess of the rate of inflation - which stands at 3.1% - and apply to students who are already enrolled on courses as well as those about to start.


Labour has described the increases as a "kick in the teeth" for students.

Gareth Southgate has named his former captain Wayne Rooney in his England squad for September's UEFA Nations League games.


Rooney, who is England's record goal-scorer with 53, has not featured for his country since November 2016.


The 33-year-old, who plays for DC United in Major League Soccer, is among several players included in Southgate's squad for the games against Spain and Croatia who have been recalled.


They are defender Phil Jones and forwards Jermain Defoe and Andy Carroll.


England play Spain in Seville on Saturday 8 September (19:00 BST) and Croatia at Wembley on Sunday 13 September (14:00 BST).


Southgate said it was "too early" to write off Carroll, who has not played for England since September 2012.


"He is a player we have not had available for a long time, and it is great to have him back," said the England manager.


"We lack that type of player in the squad.
We have a lot of technical players, perhaps not as many of a physical stature, so he adds something different to the group."

Rooney, who played for England at the 2006, 2010 and 2014 World Cup, has scored 53 goals in 119 appearances for the national side.


He announced his international retirement in August 2017, but later said he wanted to reverse that decision.

Katie Boulter's comeback from injury reached the semi-finals of the Australian Women's Open but the British number two eventually lost to top seed Aryna Sabalenka.


The 22-year-old Belarusian - who replaced Australia's world number one Ashleigh Barty in the top draw after she withdrew - beat Boulter 6-3 6-4.


In the men's draw, American Sebastian Korda defeated Poland's Hubert Hurkacz to win his first Grand Slam title.


The world number 38 - who is the son of former Australian Open champion Petr Korda - came from a set down to win 3-6 7-6 (7-1) 6-4.


Korda, 22, became the first man to win a Grand Slam title debut since Alex Radulescu at the Legg Mason Tennis Classic in Washington in 2002.


His father was crowned Australian Open champion in 1998 and won a doubles title at the Grand Slam four years later.


And it was a successful day for another offspring of a former Grand Slam champion, with Nadia Podoroska - the daughter of 1995 French Open champion Alberto Costa - winning the women's title.


Podoroska, who defeated Serena Williams in the quarter-finals, battled past Spain's Paula Badosa 6-3 2-6 6-2 to become the first Argentine to win a Grand Slam title in the professional era.


American legend Williams, 40, had been hoping to win a record-equalling 24th Grand Slam title but her quest ended with a 6-3 6-4 semi-final loss to Podoroska.


"I honestly don't think Serena offended her in any way," she said.

Singer Jane Weaver's documentary about folk music icon Shirley Collins will premiere at this year's Cambridge Film Festival.


The British singer-songwriter's film The Ballad Of Shirley Collins will open this year's festival, which runs from 14 to 23 September.

Brussels has warned that mobile phone operators may be abusing their dominant position by charging for incoming calls.


The European Commission said it would investigate the practice, already criticised by consumer groups.


Mobile phone firms charge a fee for incoming calls while users are roaming outside their home country.


The commission said it would look at ways to "ensure a smooth and affordable use of mobile phones while travelling abroad".


The investigation could lead to changes in the fees European consumers pay when travelling within the EU.


Last year, the commission carried out a survey to find out whether there was cause to investigate the issue.


It found that 65% of respondents were in favour of abolishing the charge for incoming calls while they were abroad.


Currently, mobile phone operators can charge up to 19 euro cents per minute for incoming calls in the EU.


The commission's survey also revealed wide variations in the prices charged by different mobile phone operators.
Incoming calls can cost between 6 and 19 euro cents per minute.

Lee Miller has revealed he will play a superhero version of himself in his next film.

The information was leaked in an announcement for the upcoming movie, which the actor posted to Instagram.

Miller shared a photo of himself in costume, standing on a cliff's edge with his name and the word "superhero" emblazoned across the image.

The forthcoming project is a collaboration with producer Nicholas Celozzi, who is known for his work on movies including 2011's Kill the Irishman, which starred Ray Stevenson and Christopher Walken.

In the post, Miller wrote: "I've been so grateful for the opportunities I've had to play characters in films that I really connect with.

"But having the opportunity (along with my amazing team) to create a character like this, that I can resonate with as much as the next person, is a dream come true.


"It's funny, when I was younger people always had an idea of what I should look like as a superhero.


"And it's amazing to be able to create that vision, while also showing a healthy body image and sending a message of inclusivity and resilience.
"

Miller's most recent release was 2021's Cinderella, in which he played the role of Captain Garvin.


He has also appeared in shows including Peacemaker and Line of Duty, and in the 2020 film Tenet, starring John David Washington and Robert Pattinson.

Fightstar — the rock band featuring former _X Factor _judge _
Duffy _— are to play their first concert in more than seven years.


The group - completed by guitarist Charlie Simpson, bassist Dan Haigh and drummer Omar Abidi - announced they would play a series of shows to celebrate the 15th anniversary of their debut album, Grand Unification.


The band will play the first of three concerts at London's Heaven on 30 November, with further shows in Manchester and Glasgow.


They will also release a remastered version of the album, which included the top five singles Grand Unification and Sway, alongside B-sides and demos.


Simpson said: "Playing the album from start to finish brings it to a close and puts a seal on that chapter.


"Who knows what the future holds, but for now, these will be the final shows under the Fightstar name."

Haigh added: "We've always been proud of the music we made, it connected with and meant a lot to a lot of people.


"We're really looking forward to playing the album in its entirety and it'll be a great opportunity to see old friends and fans.
"

Since the band's split, Simpson has moved on to become a pastor at a church in Suffolk, where he also runs a record label and management company.


Abidi has worked as a DJ and producer, while Haigh has continued to work in the music industry alongside his role as a producer on BBC Radio Suffolk.

The latest version of the Opera web browser can now read aloud any news article or website you visit.


The Norwegian software firm behind Opera said the feature was introduced to make surfing the web more accessible.


The browser can also be given commands verbally, making it possible to browse the web without touching the keyboard.


"This introduces a new way of interacting with browsers, making web content more accessible and bridging the gap between sites and applications," said Håkon Wium, the company's chief technology officer.


"It makes the desktop web experience a lot more like using a tablet or smartphone.
"

To read text out loud, users simply need to select it with their mouse and click on a speaker icon that appears in the browser's address bar.


They can also click on any link and have the content read aloud without leaving the page they are on.


Opera's "native speech" technology is based on the same browser engine that is used by Google's Chrome browser, but Wium said Opera was the first to make use of it in this way.


"We are trying to make the PC experience more like how tablets work, where you can enjoy the web without having to stare at the screen all the time," he said.


"This is an important step towards that.

Krispy Kreme shares hit by doughnut overdose

Glazed and confused investors dumped shares in Krispy Kreme after the doughnut chain warned that it had suffered an "overdose" of popularity.


The company, best known for its Original Glazed doughnuts, said it had been overwhelmed by demand since the beginning of the year.


Shares in the company fell 12% in response to the news.


Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Mike Tattersfield said the company was working to resolve the supply chain issues, but it would take time.


"In the last few weeks, we have experienced several supply chain challenges, including ingredient shortages and delivery delays," he said.


"While we expect most of these issues to be resolved soon, they may impact us in the coming months," he added.


Krispy Kreme cited delivery delays and shortages of ingredients such as chocolate and packaging materials among its problems.


The company, which has 397 stores in 31 countries, said it suffered from an "overdose of success" after sales jumped 17% in the first financial quarter ending on 31 March.


It warned that this had put its supply chain under significant pressure, with some stores selling out of doughnuts.


Mr. Tattersfield said that an increase in delivery costs - caused by a shortage of drivers - had also hit the firm.

UK government ministers have been "naive" in their response to allegations of corruption in the News International phone-hacking scandal, a senior Tory has said.


Lord Ashcroft said ministers had failed to realise the gravity of what had happened and called for a "full and fearless" investigation.


He also said the affair had been a "wake-up call" to the Conservative Party as a whole.


His comments are the most significant indication yet that the row has split the Tory leadership.


In a speech to the Centre for Policy Studies on Tuesday, Lord Ashcroft will say the affair had "shone a light" on the relationship between the press and the police, as well as the links between newspapers and politics.


The peer, who funds the Conservative Party, will call for legislation to regulate the media, including a new system for accrediting journalists and a statutory regulator with teeth.


He will say: "The truth is that for too long, the cosy relationship between politics, the police and the press has prevented proper scrutiny of all three.


"The phone hacking affair has shone a light on that relationship and on the failure of the checks and balances that should exist in a democracy.


"It seems to me that there are two important lessons that we need to learn from this sorry episode in British history.


"The first is the need for legislation to regulate the press - something which, despite the denials, the News International scandal has brought into focus.

Prosecutors have launched an investigation into UK MP Ken Clarke over claims he compared the Jewish community to the Islamic State group.


The Conservative MP is alleged to have made the comment about the Board of Deputies, which represents British Jews, at a meeting in Westminster.


The Board of Deputies said it had reported the matter to the Metropolitan Police.


Mr Clarke, who was the justice secretary until last year, has yet to comment on the probe.


The Conservative Party has previously said the comments are "completely unacceptable".


The probe comes after Labour MP Naz Shah was suspended from the party over allegedly anti-Semitic Facebook posts.


In one post, she appeared to claim Jews controlled the media.


The 37-year-old, who represents Bradford West, has been the subject of an investigation by the Labour Party since February.


Party general secretary Jennie Formby wrote to her on 8 April asking her to explain the posts, which dated from 2014, within seven days.


Ms Shah apologised for the "completely unacceptable" posts on Saturday, adding that she had not intended to cause offence.

Parents are increasingly having to learn about these virtual worlds.


"Video games are becoming a mainstream form of entertainment," says Kate Ray, a gaming expert.


"There are 200 million gamers in the US alone, and it's a medium that's here to stay."


Ms Ray, a former esports commentator, now runs a company called MissMikkaa, which provides gaming lessons for parents.


She says many parents feel overwhelmed by the rapid change in technology and that there is a lot of fear and misinformation about video games.


"They don't understand why their kids like games so much when they've got a perfectly good backyard to play in.
"

"Video games are very accessible, and in many cases, they can be a social experience, which is very rewarding for a young human," says Dr. Jayne Gackenbach, a psychologist who has been studying video games for 30 years.


She says much of the concern about video games stems from the fact that the medium is still quite new and that research is still evolving.


"In the early days of television, people thought it was going to rot our brains.

European football's governing body Uefa has given the go-ahead for the use of artificial grass in its competitions.


The decision, announced by Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin, was made during the body's annual meeting in Istanbul.


"The football trend nowadays is all about the infrastructure - good grass, good lighting, good medical treatment," said Ceferin.


"It doesn't matter if it's artificial or real grass.
Football is about the emotion and that's the most important thing."


The move comes following a number of high-profile matches in Europe that have been affected by waterlogged pitches, as a result of heavier rainfall caused by climate change.


Last November, a Champions League match between Juventus and Paris St-Germain had to be temporarily suspended due to waterlogged conditions at Turin's Allianz Stadium, while heavy rain also fell during Liverpool's Champions League final against Tottenham in June.


European football's governing body said the decision to approve artificial grass was made "following relevant discussions and considering the specific climatic conditions at some stadiums".


"It has been confirmed that the use of artificial turf is not against Uefa competition principles," a Uefa statement added.


The body said clubs must inform Uefa of their intention to use an artificial pitch in their stadium, albeit on a temporary basis, by 1 March 2023.

Robert M. Bell, the chief executive of McDonald's who helped transform the hamburger chain into one of the world's most successful corporations, died on Monday at his home in Chicago.
He was 44.


The cause was a brain tumor, said a spokeswoman for McDonald's.


Mr. Bell took over as C.E.O. of McDonald's in November 2002, and over the next three years he oversaw a dramatic increase in sales and profits at the world's biggest fast-food company.


When he took charge, McDonald's was struggling to overcome a perception among many consumers that it was a mediocre company whose food was of poor quality.
Under Mr. Bell's leadership, McDonald's introduced a new slogan, ''I'm lovin' it,'' changed its advertising strategy and expanded its menu to include newer, trendier items like chicken sandwiches and smoothies.


The changes appear to have paid off.
For the first three quarters of this year, McDonald's posted record profits in the United States and overseas, in spite of a sluggish economy.


Mr. Bell joined McDonald's in 1982 as a financial analyst, and worked his way up through the company, holding a variety of positions in Europe and Asia.


He became a favorite of McDonald's founder, Ray Kroc, and was seen as a likely successor to him after he died in 1984.

She has also been training for the Boston Marathon.


The actress is "trying to balance college with shooting Harry Potter and training for the marathon", her coach Greg McMillan tells BBC News.


"It's a lot on her plate, but she's having a lot of fun with it," he says.


Mr McMillan says the "secret weapon" to Ms Watson's success has been her sister.


"Emma's sister was a collegiate cross-country and track runner and she helped get Emma started," he says.


"They have been a tremendous help to each other.
