MPs' murder sentence concern

MPs have questioned the judge's decision to hand down a life sentence to a man who murdered an MP.


WA Corke, who killed Jo Cox, was given a minimum term of 35 years in December.


The Sentencing Council said it will examine whether the sentencing guidelines for murder are "fit for purpose".


Its statement came after a number of MPs raised concerns over the "vague" and "incomprehensible" law.


The Labour MP for Batley and Spen, who was pregnant, was attacked by Corke in Birstall in June 2016.


He was charged with her murder and the murder of Labour councillor Bernard Carter outside a library in Birstall.


At the time of the attack, Corke gave his name as "Death to Traitors, Freedom for Britain", which was also written on his baseball bat.


He was sentenced to life imprisonment with a minimum term of 35 years, which is variable and can be increased or decreased depending on behaviour.


The judge said the minimum term would have been 30 years but it was increased because the murder was "a terrorist act" and carried out "in pursuance of extremist ideology".


On Friday, Labour MP Yvette Cooper, who chairs the Home Affairs Select Committee, tabled a debate on the sentencing guidelines for murder, calling them "vague and incomprehensible".

Art school is a glamorous notion.
Just think of all those talented, creative, and interesting people gathering in one place to learn and grow together.
There's lots of bubbly creativity and probably lots of people passing around a joint or two.


It is therefore surprising to learn that Franz Ferdinand's Alex Kapranos hated it.
"It was the worst time of my life," he says.
"It was three years of feeling like a fish out of water.
It was punishing.
I was totally unprepared for it.
"

This is not how it's supposed to be.
But then, Franz Ferdinand aren't supposed to be one of the world's biggest bands, selling millions of records and filling arenas.

Yahoo celebrates a decade online

Yahoo has celebrated its first 10 years of existence by throwing a party for its 1,000-strong staff and sending its founders on a world tour to thank users for their support.


The event culminated with a "birthday blast" at Yahoo's Sunnyvale headquarters, with employees donning costumes and singing company songs.


"It feels like we're sending a teenager off to college," co-founder David Filo told staff at the celebration.


Yahoo has grown from a simple list of David Filo's favourite websites to a global network of sites offering news, sport and email.


Mr Filo, chief technology officer, and Jerry Yang, chief executive, sent their birthday greetings from a list of countries where Yahoo has sites.


These include the UK, Japan, China, Canada and Australia.


In an interview posted on Yahoo's website, Mr Filo said the company had grown far beyond his expectations.


"When we started this thing, we really did not have a vision of where it would go," he said.


"Certainly things have changed a lot in the last couple of years, but it's been fun.
I've enjoyed it.

The manufacturing recovery is slowing, according to a new survey, which also shows that the number of firms reporting rising costs is at a record high.


The monthly survey by the CBI trade body found that its measure of manufacturing output slowed "significantly" in December, with firms reporting that uncertainty about the outlook had increased.


Orders books were described as "solid" by firms, the survey found, but added that they were "nowhere near" pre-pandemic levels.


In addition, the number of firms reporting rising costs reached a record high in December, according to the CBI.
It said that firms expected inflationary pressures to weaken, but "only slightly" over the next three months.


Rain Newton-Smith, the chief economist at the CBI, said that while output growth slowed in December, "that doesn't mean the manufacturing recovery is stalling".


"Output growth remains robust and firms are increasingly confident that conditions will improve in the year ahead," she said.


"But rocketing inflation and persistent supply chain disruption mean that Brexit is still a big drag on the sector.


"To overcome this, the government must do whatever it can to smooth relations with the EU, including exploring options for customs cooperation to help tackle the mountain of red tape exporters still face.

US oil firm Kosmos Energy has admitted bribing ministers in the West African nation of Benin.


The Dallas-based company said it had paid $100,000 to Beninese customs and tax officials to obtain improper tax reductions.


In a filing to a US government agency, Kosmos said the payments had been made between 2007 and 2011.


Kosmos acquired an offshore oil block in Benin in 2008.
It did not reveal its findings in the filing, made to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).


The company said it had launched an internal investigation into the payments after Benin issued an arrest warrant for its country manager in May.


It said the manager, who was not named, had admitted making the payments.


Kosmos said it was cooperating with Beninese authorities, and that it had alerted the US Department of Justice and the SEC.


It added that it was withdrawing as a defendant from a civil suit launched by Beninois citizens in the US in 2015.


The suit, filed in Texas, alleged that Kosmos and oil firm Addax Petroleum Corp had paid more than $110m in bribes to Beninese officials.

text:
Chancellor Rishi Sunak has been criticised for "paying people to do nothing" after it was revealed the UK's unemployment rate could rise to 5% despite the budget's focus on jobs.


The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) - the government's official forecaster - said the labour market had held up better than expected, despite end of the furlough scheme.


But it said that with the scheme gone, unemployment would rise to 4.4% next year, up from 3.9% now, and peak at 5% in 2024.


Unemployment benefits were increased by the government in the last budget, while the decision to raise corporation tax will make larger companies contribute more to the public finances.


But Labour, unions and some Conservative MPs have criticised the chancellor for not doing more to help people who will lose their jobs, with the UK's unemployment rate still among the lowest in Europe.


"The chancellor's prediction that the end of furlough will lead to a surge in unemployment has proved utterly false," said shadow chancellor Rachel Reeves.


"He needs to come to Parliament on Monday and explain why he ignored warnings from businesses, unions and many of his own backbenchers.
"

General Secretary of the Trades Union Congress (TUC) Frances O'Grady said: "The chancellor has been asleep at the wheel while British workers have been hit by an unemployment time bomb.


"Unless he takes action, we are heading for a jobs crisis that could leave one million fewer people in work by the end of 2024.
"

The OBR also warned that the UK's inflation rate was set to climb to 7.1% in April, up from the forecast made in October of 6% - and that the price of goods would continue to rise as the Ukraine war affects commodity prices, and customers face higher energy bills.

Apple has forced prominent blogs to reveal their sources for stories critical of the company, according to journalists who say they were summoned to meetings at the tech giant's California headquarters.


The move is a departure from Apple's previous position on confidential sources, and underscores the changing relationship between journalists and the companies they cover.


Journalists from Forbes, Bloomberg, and VentureBeat reported being contacted by Apple and asked to turn over information about anonymous sources cited in their stories.


All three publications have run articles in recent months detailing parts of Apple's plans to enter the metaverse, the virtual world where people can interact with each other and with software applications.


Apple declined to comment.


Forbes reporter Aaron Tilley said it was the first time in his career that a company had sought to learn the identities of his anonymous sources.


He said Apple representatives requested a list of everyone who had spoken to him about the story, including freelancers and analysts.


"They wanted to know who my sources were for a September story about Apple's virtual reality plans, and they specifically wanted to know who said Apple was developing a standalone VR headset for 2022," Tilley said.


"I declined to provide any sources.
Ultimately, I think standalone headsets are going to be a big part of Apple's VR plans, so I'd like to keep my sources for that story.

Frank Lampard scores against his former club as England beat Romania 2-0 in a friendly at Wembley.


The England manager described his side's performance as "workmanlike" but said the win proved they could get the job done.


Hodgson said he took "full responsibility" for England's poor showing at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, where they lost to Italy, Uruguay and Costa Rica in the group stage.


"I don't think there is any doubt that in previous games leading up to the World Cup, and in the World Cup, we didn't play as well as we are capable of," he said.


"I include myself in that because I am in charge of the team.
It is up to me to make the team play as well as it can and, certainly in the last two years, I haven't always been able to get that across.
"

England were criticised for their negative approach in Brazil, but Hodgson said a more positive brand of football would not have guaranteed success.


"Over the last two years we have tried to be more positive, we have tried to play higher up the pitch, and in the main we have been pretty successful," he added.


"But the negative approach that was seen in the World Cup wasn't something that I agreed with or wanted.


"I don't think it would have made us a better team and it certainly wouldn't have guaranteed us success at the World Cup.

text:
Ask Jeeves has launched a new service which offers small businesses affordable and simple internet advertising.


The company said its new service, Ask Ad Solutions, fills a gap in the market.


"Many small and medium sized businesses have been left behind by the complexities and costs associated with online advertising," said Greg Sterling from the Interactive Advertising Bureau.


"While search engines, online directories and other web sites offer a range of advertising options, they are still difficult and too expensive for many small businesses," he added.


Ask Jeeves said it had developed its new service after research revealed many small businesses felt "left out" of online advertising.


"We saw a need to streamline and simplify the process, making it easy and cost-effective for local businesses to tap into the power of internet search and attract new customers," said Brian McAndrews, chief executive of Ask Jeeves.


"We believe this service will be particularly appealing to the vast majority of local businesses that do not have websites," he added.


Ask Ad Solutions allows businesses to create and place ads on the Ask Jeeves website, and appears alongside search results when users look for a particular product or service in a specific region.


The ads can be updated daily, to feature special offers or to announce new services.


Mr Sterling said small businesses had been "underserved" by the online advertising industry.

Petrol and diesel duty will be frozen for the remainder of 2022/23, the Chancellor has said.


Rishi Sunak told MPs that the measure would help cut costs for motorists.
It follows a similar freeze in January, which the chancellor said would save average car drivers £1,900 over the next 12 months.


The announcement was among a series of measures in the chancellor's spring statement, which also included an end to the public sector pay freeze and an increase in the minimum wage.


Labour said the measures did not go far enough to help working people, while the Liberal Democrats said the chancellor had "failed on housing".


The spring statement is a mid-year update on the state of the economy and the government's plans for taxes and spending.


Mr Sunak said the decision to freeze fuel duty would save drivers £5 per tank, or around £100 per year.
It means the price of petrol and diesel will remain at £1.71 and £1.81 per litre respectively.


The chancellor said the government had made decisions that would affect "every household in the country" and announced a "new age of optimism".

'Not enough'

Shadow chancellor Rachel Reeves said the chancellor had "failed on housing and childcare".


She added: "Working people across the country will not be convinced by this statement, because although Rishi Sunak has pointed in the right direction, he has not gone far enough.

The richest man in Russia has sold his last remaining shares in Yukos, the oil company he ran before he was jailed on fraud and tax charges.


Mikhail Khodorkovsky's resignation from the board of Yukos' main production unit was revealed a day after a court ruled that the taxman could auction off the company to recover a $30.8bn (£15.6bn) tax bill.


The sale of Yukos could well be the biggest in Russia's history, and has sparked fears of widespread job losses.


Mr Khodorkovsky's prison sentence ends in August 2014.


He said his decision to quit the Yukos Production unit was for "personal reasons".


"I intend to focus on my political and public activities," he said in a statement released by the Open Russia foundation, which he chairs.


Mr Khodorkovsky added that he believed that his departure from the company would benefit "both the company and our common cause".


Open Russia, set up by Mr Khodorkovsky last year, describes itself as a public organisation working to promote open governance, education and culture.


Mr Khodorkovsky's resignation came on the day that Yukos' bankruptcy committee met for the first time to try to work out how to pay off half of the massive tax bill.


The committee includes three representatives each from the tax authorities and Yukos, and one independent chairman.

Britain's Holmes selected for double bid

Holmes was already assured of a place in next month's World Championships in Beijing after winning the 1,500m and 5,000m at the British Championships in July.


The 26-year-old, who was a late addition to the British team for London, will now bid to repeat Sir Mo Farah's feat of winning both the 5,000m and 10,000m at successive Games.


"It shows the strength in depth now in British distance running," said Holmes.


"It's amazing to be given the chance to compete in both events in Beijing.
It was a no-brainer for me to take that opportunity.
"

Holmes' selection was confirmed at a British Athletics selection meeting in Birmingham on Saturday.


The double victory in London made Holmes only the third man to win both events at a single Games, after Farah and Finland's Lasse Viren, who achieved the feat in 1972 and 1976.


In Beijing, Holmes will aim to improve on his fifth-place finish in the 5,000m and challenge for a medal in the 10,000m.

"I think I've got as good a chance as anybody in the 10,000m," said Holmes.


"I've got a good shot at a medal in that and I'm going to go into it trying to win.


"Hopefully I can squeeze under 13 minutes in the 5,000m. That's the aim.

"It's amazing to be given the chance to compete in both events in Beijing.
It was a no-brainer for me to take that opportunity.
"

Holmes' selection was confirmed at a British Athletics selection meeting in Birmingham on Saturday.


The double victory in London made Holmes only the third man to win both events at a single Games, after Farah and Finland's Lasse Viren, who achieved the feat in 1972 and 1976.


In Beijing, Holmes will aim to improve on his fifth-place finish in the 5,000m and challenge for a medal in the 10,000m.

"I think I've got as good a chance as anybody in the 10,000m," said Holmes.


"I've got a good shot at a medal in that and I'm going to go into it trying to win.


"Hopefully I can squeeze under 13 minutes in the 5,000m. That's the aim.

Mitsubishi Motors has confirmed that it is in talks with Peugeot SA about a possible merger.


The Japanese car maker said it has asked Peugeot - which is itself preparing to merge with Fiat Chrysler - to "jointly study" a merger plan.


A merger between Mitsubishi and Peugeot would create the world's fourth-largest auto maker by sales, behind Volkswagen, Toyota and Renault-Nissan.


In a statement, Mitsubishi said the two companies plan to hold talks "from a long-term perspective".


Last month, Peugeot revealed that it was in talks to buy Fiat Chrysler, in a deal that would create the world's fourth-largest car maker.


Peugeot's board was meeting on Thursday to discuss the proposal, amid growing speculation that a deal could be announced as early as next week.


Last week, Peugeot's chief executive, Carlos Tavares, said the company was open to a "friendly" merger with Mitsubishi Motors.


Mitsubishi was once part of the Renault-Nissan alliance, but sold a controlling stake to Nissan in 2016.


Mr Tavares said a merger with Mitsubishi would help his company expand its presence in Asia.


Mitsubishi Motors was hit hard by a scandal in 2016 over data cheating that affected some of its cars.

Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola has said that his side's Premier League title race with Liverpool will go down to the final game of the season.


City moved five points clear at the top of the table after beating Manchester United 2-0 on Sunday, with Liverpool not in action until their game at Southampton on Tuesday.


"We play against three monsters - Arsenal, Chelsea and Liverpool," said Guardiola.


"I think it will go to the last game.
You can guess, but you don't know."


City have five games left, with their final match of the campaign at home to Brighton on 11 May.


That is also the day Liverpool, who have six games left, are at home to Wolves.


"There are still a lot of games to play - 29 points," added Guardiola.


"We have done incredibly well so far but the important games are coming.
We have played in the Champions League midweek and the games are coming thick and fast.

The latest version of the Opera web browser can now read aloud any news article or website you visit.


The Norwegian software firm behind Opera said the feature was introduced to make surfing the web more accessible.


The browser can also be given commands verbally, making it possible to browse the web without touching the keyboard.


"This introduces a new way of interacting with browsers, making web content more accessible and bridging the gap between sites and applications," said Håkon Wium, the company's chief technology officer.


"It makes the desktop web experience a lot more like using a tablet or smartphone.
"

To read text out loud, users simply need to select it with their mouse and click on a speaker icon that appears in the browser's address bar.


They can also click on any link and have the content read aloud without leaving the page they are on.


Opera's "native speech" technology is based on the same browser engine that is used by Google's Chrome browser, but Wium said Opera was the first to make use of it in this way.


"We are trying to make the PC experience more like how tablets work, where you can enjoy the web without having to stare at the screen all the time," he said.


"This is an important step towards that.

Voters "reject EU by two to one"

The BBC has seen an exclusive poll it commissioned which suggests that a third of people in the UK would vote to leave the EU if there was a referendum tomorrow.


The poll puts support for the EU at 39%, with 51% opposed and 10% don't knows or wouldn't votes.


The findings will concern EU supporters who hope an in/out referendum will not be held tomorrow, or anytime soon.


The poll, carried out by ComRes, asked people how they would vote if a referendum on EU membership were held tomorrow.


Some 39% of respondents said they would vote to stay in the EU, with 51% saying they would vote to leave, and 10% saying they did not know or would not vote.


ComRes chairman Andrew Hawkins said the finding suggested that the country was still divided on the issue.


"There is no doubt that this is an extremely sensitive issue for the British public, with a clear divide in attitudes, and it is clear that there are very strong feelings on both sides of the debate," he said.


"As the government continues to weigh up its policy on this issue, it is clear that it faces a tricky decision with strong feelings on both sides.
"

The poll questioned 1,000 people aged 18 and over on 18 and 19 November.


It came as Prime Minister David Cameron prepared to meet European leaders in Brussels on Thursday to discuss his proposed EU reforms ahead of a summit in December.

text:
Queen have recruited a singer to front the band for their upcoming tour - their first since the death of Freddie Mercury in 1991.


The singer, Adam Lambert, 29, is best known for finishing as runner-up in the 2009 series of TV talent show American Idol.


He will join the band, comprising Brian May, Roger Taylor and John Deacon, at five concerts in Europe next summer with the possibility of more shows being announced.


Lambert will sing lead vocals on songs usually performed by Mercury, who died of Aids in 1991.


Queen's guitarist Brian May said he was "utterly delighted" at the "fantastic" addition of Lambert to the line-up.


"We first met Adam a few months ago and have had a number of subsequent meetings, we think he's brilliant," May wrote on the band's website.


"We were never going to find someone who resembles Freddie in his prime - that would be ludicrous - but Adam's a great singer and he can definitely fill those enormous shoes."


The band had considered using some of Mercury's recorded vocals on their upcoming tour but decided it would be "odd" for the audience.


"It's a pretty good approximation of what it might have been like - you're not going to get Freddie, but you've got a great singer," May told BBC Radio 4's Front Row.


The five concerts will take place at London's Hammersmith Apollo, the Netherlands' Amsterdam Arena and three shows in Poland next summer.

Ukraine has trimmed its target for privatisation revenues this year by more than half to $1.5bn (£1.2bn), according to the ministry of economy.


The aim had earlier been set at $3.7bn.
There are few investors keen on Ukraine's state-owned enterprises.


The ministry said it had revised its targets lower, because plans to sell large state assets had failed to materialise.
It is also looking to speed up the sale of smaller assets.


"We are not going to wait for the big privatisations.
Small and medium-sized privatisations will speed up Ukraine's economic growth," said Economy Minister Yulia Svyrydenko.


Privatisation proceeds aimed at helping Ukraine recover from war

The ministry said it was retaining its goal of raising $281m from the sale of state-owned stakes in agricultural firms.
That would include the sale of 100% plus one share in agricultural company Mriya.


The ministry said it was also aiming to raise $322m through the sale of other state assets, including aircraft engine maker Motor Sich and Ukraine's largest chemical plant, Azot.

The parties are launching their manifestos ahead of the election - with the Tories defending their record on taxation.


The Liberal Democrats have accused the Conservatives of putting the country's finances in jeopardy, while Labour says the Tories are not ambitious enough in their spending plans.


The BBC's political editor, Laura Kuenssberg, says it is an unusual move for opponents to agree on anything, but that the parties are "united" in their criticism.


The Conservative manifesto will be launched on Thursday, with the party defending its record on taxation, saying it has "cut taxes for 30 million people".


The party has come under pressure over the cost of living, with Labour, the Lib Dems and SNP all promising to scrap the rise in National Insurance payments that kicks in this year.


At Prime Minister's Questions, Labour leader Sir Keir Starmer accused the Tories of putting up taxes by £700 a year for anyone on an average wage - £1,500 for families - with the National Insurance rise, VAT going up on household energy bills and higher council tax bills.


He asked: "Isn't the truth that millions of working people are worried they are going to see an increase in their taxes under the Conservatives?"


But Boris Johnson insisted the government was "cutting taxes for everyone".


The prime minister said: "We are helping people on low incomes by reducing the basic rate of tax, we are helping people with the cost of fuel by reducing the surcharge on fuel and we are helping young people with the cost of living by increasing the National Living Wage, but Labour wants to put up taxes."


In his reply, Sir Keir again accused the prime minister of breaking his promise not to put up taxes, saying: "Taxes are going up next year by £700.

At Prime Minister's Questions, Labour leader Sir Keir Starmer accused the Tories of putting up taxes by £700 a year for anyone on an average wage - £1,500 for families - with the National Insurance rise, VAT going up on household energy bills and higher council tax bills.


He asked: "Isn't the truth that millions of working people are worried they are going to see an increase in their taxes under the Conservatives?"


But Boris Johnson insisted the government was "cutting taxes for everyone".


The prime minister said: "We are helping people on low incomes by reducing the basic rate of tax, we are helping people with the cost of fuel by reducing the surcharge on fuel and we are helping young people with the cost of living by increasing the National Living Wage, but Labour wants to put up taxes."


In his reply, Sir Keir again accused the prime minister of breaking his promise not to put up taxes, saying: "Taxes are going up next year by £700.

Labour battle plan 'hides Blair'

The BBC's political editor says the Labour leadership is concerned that the focus of their battle plan for the local elections in May is hiding the former prime minister.


David Dimbleby says the party is in "panic mode" after a string of opinion poll leads by the Conservative Party.


And he says the focus on local issues in the battle plan, drawn up by Labour's national executive, is a way of keeping the controversial ex-premier out of the spotlight.


The BBC's Nick Robinson, who also reports a swing away from Labour to the Tories, says the battle plan - released on the same day as the Tory local election launch - simply "will not work".


The plan includes using the first past the post electoral system - already used for local elections - to elect MPs, as well as using the existing system for elections to the Lords.


And it says Labour should "not be afraid" to speak up for the public services it has created, despite the "current mood of anti-government".


Our political editor, David Dimbleby, says he has been told by Labour sources that the battle plan has been drawn up because the party's national executive recognised that local elections were being overlooked.


And he says the focus on local issues is a way of keeping Mr Blair - who is still a focus of controversy - out of the spotlight.


"Panic mode"

The BBC's political editor says that after a string of opinion poll leads for the Conservative Party, Labour is in "panic mode".


The panic mode was illustrated, he says, by the way Labour has issued a series of "clarifications" of what its local election campaign battle plan really means.

The supersonic jet that shattered records and inspired a new era of commercial aviation has won the top Globes award.


The Concorde, a British-French supersonic passenger aircraft that flew at more than twice the speed of sound and pioneered a new era of commercial aviation, has won the prestigious Grand Prix award at the Globes de Cristal ceremony in Paris.
The Globes de Cristal awards honour the best in French culture and heritage and are voted on by members of the foreign press based in Paris.


The Concorde's victory in the aviation category at the Globes came on the 50th anniversary of its first flight, and marks the return of commercial aviation to the awards ceremony.
The supersonic jet was recognised for its groundbreaking design and engineering, as well as its contribution to the development of commercial aviation.


The Concorde entered service in 1976 and operated until 2003, when a crash that killed all passengers and crew members led to its retirement.
During its service, the Concorde broke numerous speed and distance records and became a symbol of luxury and speed.
It could fly from New York to London in less than three hours, and was a favourite of celebrities and business leaders.


The Globes de Cristal ceremony was held at the Hotel Potocki in Paris and was hosted by actress Isabelle Adjani.
In addition to the Concorde, other winners at the ceremony included actor Jean Dujardin, who won the best actor award for his role in the film The Wolf of Wall Street, and singer Vanessa Paradis, who won the best singer award for her album Love Songs.

text:
Two more senior executives have resigned from Fannie Mae, the US mortgage finance giant, as it continues to suffer heavy losses.


The latest departures came as Fannie Mae said it lost $2.2bn (£1.4bn) in the first three months of this year.


The firm has now lost more than $14bn over the past year.


The US government took over the firm in September 2008 after it suffered heavy losses on its mortgage loans.


Fannie Mae's chief executive, Michael Williams, resigned in March.


On Thursday, the firm's chief business officer, Stephen Swad, and its chief risk officer, Rob Van der Straeten, said they would leave Fannie Mae.


In a statement, the company said that Mr Swad, who had been with Fannie Mae for more than 16 years, was leaving to "pursue other opportunities".


Mr Van der Straeten said he wanted to "pursue opportunities in the risk management field".


Fannie Mae said its first-quarter losses included a $1.7bn pretax charge to reflect "deteriorating economic conditions" that have led to increasing levels of mortgage delinquencies and foreclosures.


The firm also said it would need about $6bn in additional federal funding this year on top of the $100bn it has already received from the US Treasury.

Two more senior executives have resigned from Fannie Mae, the US mortgage finance giant, as it continues to suffer heavy losses.


The latest departures came as Fannie Mae said it lost $2.2bn (£1.4bn) in the first three months of this year.


The firm has now lost more than $14bn over the past year.


The US government took over the firm in September 2008 after it suffered heavy losses on its mortgage loans.

Mr Van der Straeten said he wanted to "pursue opportunities in the risk management field".

Stock market turmoil fails to knock Johnson off the top

The FTSE 100 index plunged almost 200 points in morning trade, before recovering most of its losses later in the day.


The index dropped 1.5% in early trading, before finishing the day down 0.5% at 7,431.31 points.


That left the FTSE 100 up 4.7% on the year, but it follows a 13% surge in the first six months of 2021.


"As the old stock market saying goes; 'so goes January, so goes the year', said Jeffrey Halley, senior market analyst at Oanda.


"After a stellar 2021, stocks are off to a rocky start as 2022 gets underway, with investors weighing rising bond yields against prospects for higher earnings.


"It does, however, leave the door open for a pullback in the UK FTSE 100 index, which prior to today's drop, was trading around its highest levels since the spring of 2018.
"

In company news, cruise operator Carnival slipped 5.2% to £15.20 after hitting an eight-month low on Wednesday.


Drugmaker AstraZeneca rose 1% to £82.70 after saying its lung cancer drug had been approved in the US.


In the FTSE 250, builder Persimmon fell 2.8% to £28.64 as it warned that the surge in Covid cases in recent weeks had started to hurt staffing levels and supply chains.


But packaging firm DS Smith jumped 16% to 329p on news that it was acquiring US firm Interstate Resources for $1.5bn.

The bank held the rate at 4.75% today.
But it hinted that a cut was likely in the coming months, if the economic outlook deteriorates.


At midday, the bank's monetary policy committee announced its decision.


It said the outlook for UK inflation was "broadly in line" with its projection in May.


Since May, the pound has fallen by more than 5% against the dollar, partly due to the uncertainty over the Brexit deal.


That would usually suggest that the Bank of England might raise interest rates to keep a lid on inflation.


But the Bank said the drop in the value of the pound had helped keep inflation lower than expected.
It said it was "reasonable" to expect that softer growth would mean softer inflation.


It also said that global trade tensions had intensified since May, which was likely to affect UK financial conditions.


"The Committee therefore judges that the current stance of monetary policy is appropriate," it said.

UK regulators are planning to ban "trick" casino games that encourage players to keep betting even when they know they are going to lose.


The Gambling Commission says it will take action on games that "prey on the vulnerability" of players.


Games known as "loss-chasing" will be banned, such as those where it feels like players are close to winning.


The commission examined games featuring a "near-miss" - where a prize appears to be within reach, or where there is a sudden change making it look like the player has won.


Research has shown such games can encourage risky playing behaviour, inducing a "loss-chasing" effect where players think they are close to a win and so bet harder.


Game developers have also been accused of using "skewed" odds - making wins appear more likely than they actually are.


The Gambling Commission's chief executive, Andrew Rhodes, said: "We're determined to do all we can to protect players, especially on the eve of the new football season when viewership and in-play betting are due to peak."


He said fixed-odds betting terminals (FOBTs), which have been dubbed the "crack cocaine" of gambling, will also be looked at as part of a wide-ranging review.


The Association of British Bookmakers (ABB) has said it will work with the commission to "improve customer experience".


ABB chief executive Malcolm George said: "The ABB and its members have always sought to ensure that customers are treated fairly and that any gameplay is transparent and understandable.

Research has shown such games can encourage risky playing behaviour, inducing a "loss-chasing" effect where players think they are close to a win and so bet harder.


Game developers have also been accused of using "skewed" odds - making wins appear more likely than they actually are.


The Gambling Commission's chief executive, Andrew Rhodes, said: "We're determined to do all we can to protect players, especially on the eve of the new football season when viewership and in-play betting are due to peak."


He said fixed-odds betting terminals (FOBTs), which have been dubbed the "crack cocaine" of gambling, will also be looked at as part of a wide-ranging review.


The Association of British Bookmakers (ABB) has said it will work with the commission to "improve customer experience".


ABB chief executive Malcolm George said: "The ABB and its members have always sought to ensure that customers are treated fairly and that any gameplay is transparent and understandable.

Failing to plan for staff being infected with HIV is costing British businesses millions of pounds, according to a leading charity.


Terrence Higgins Trust said employers were not providing adequate training on HIV and were paying out for unnecessary testing.


It said this was leading to inefficient use of NHS resources and infringement of HIV patients' rights.


The trust launched its HIV and Employment Guide for employers on World AIDS Day, 1 December.


The charity is concerned that because of a lack of knowledge, some employers demand that all applicants who are HIV-positive take a HIV test - something that is voluntary.


Those who are HIV-positive and who do disclose their status may face discrimination in the workplace, the charity said.


This includes being passed over for promotion or being unable to do their job properly because of a lack of understanding among colleagues and managers.


The trust is also concerned that some employers are not providing adequate training on how to avoid unnecessary risk of HIV transmission in the workplace.


This means employees are not always able to do their jobs safely, it said.


The guide advises employers on how to avoid unnecessary costs caused by HIV, including the cost of replacing staff who have contracted the virus and who need to take long-term sick leave.

The streets have an album of the year.


The UK hip hop pioneer - real name Stephen Manderson - released his debut album, Original Pirate Material, in 2002.


It will be reissued on vinyl on 8 July with a bonus disc of previously unreleased material.


The release comes ahead of a comprehensive remastering of all of The Streets' back catalogue, which will begin later this year.


"There were no rules and no preconceptions, I was just making music with my mates in the hope that a few other people might like it too," he said.


"The fact that so many people have stuck with us for so long, still talks to me about it and connects with it, is amazing.
I'm thrilled that they get to hear these extra tracks - and I'm sure they'll go on to cherish and bump them like the rest of the album.
"

The Streets - then a one-man band consisting of Manchester-born rapper and producer Mike Skinner - released Original Pirate Material after a series of well-received EPs and singles, including Has It Come To This?
and Let's Push Things Forward.


The record, noted for its eclectic sampling and social commentary, was a critical and commercial success, being certified triple platinum and entering the charts at number two.

Developers Summit (DS) aims to create a collaborative platform for gamers and developers to help improve the overall gaming experience.
The event brings together developers, publishers, and industry leaders to share knowledge, exchange ideas, and explore new opportunities in the gaming industry.


DS offers a variety of sessions and activities designed to foster collaboration and innovation.
These include keynote speeches, panel discussions, and hands-on workshops covering a wide range of topics such as game design, development, and business strategies.


One of the key highlights of DS is the opportunity for developers to showcase their work and connect with potential partners and investors.
The event features a game showcase where developers can demo their games and engage with attendees to gain valuable feedback and exposure.


DS also focuses on exploring emerging technologies and trends in the gaming industry.
This includes sessions dedicated to virtual reality, augmented reality, and other cutting-edge technologies that are shaping the future of gaming.


Overall, DS is a unique event that brings together a diverse range of stakeholders in the gaming industry to collaborate, share knowledge, and drive innovation.
By providing a platform for developers and gamers to connect and work together, DS aims to help create a more vibrant and dynamic gaming ecosystem.

Canadian tennis player Bianca Andreescu has pulled out of the Australian Open, with a leg injury that she says was caused by "complications" from a blood clot in her arm.


The men's champion at the 2019 US Open - who had been scheduled to play in Melbourne on Monday - said the clot had been "triggered by a recent medication for a liver condition that I have been treating".


Canadian tennis player Bianca Andreescu has withdrawn from the Australian Open with a leg injury
The Toronto native, 24, said she was "devastated" not to be able to play in the Grand Slam event.


"I'm incredibly disappointed to not be able to play today," she wrote on Instagram.


"I was really excited to make my comeback today, but unfortunately, I will not be able to play.


"On the advice of my medical team, I have been advised that I cannot risk the possibility of an adverse event occurring during play that could cause me to miss out on the rest of the season.
"

Andreescu - who has not played a competitive match since September - said she began feeling "sharp pain" in her leg during training and a MRI scan on Saturday evening local time revealed a "small lesion" on her lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.


She wrote: "To manage this condition, I will be taking some time off to recover once I return to Canada.


"This unfortunately means that I will not be able to play in this year's Australian Open.


"I'm devastated by this news as I was really excited to make my comeback especially at one of my favourite tournaments, but I promise I will be back stronger and better than ever.

The number of text messages sent in the UK has broken records again with Brits sending an average of 63 messages a month, averaging out at 20 texts a day.


The figure has doubled in just two years, with marks the highest number of messages ever sent in the UK.


The findings come from Ofcom's annual Communications Market Report.
The report covers the four major mobile phone operators - EE, O2, Three and Vodafone.


Text messaging, or SMS, has been around for nearly 25 years and the format is showing no signs of waning.


When Ofcom first started recording text message figures in 2003, users sent an average of just 40 a month.


That figure peaked in 2008 when it reached a monthly average of 100.


The decline of messaging apps such as Blackberry's BBM, Nokia's Symbian Messenger, and Windows' Messenger, combined with the boom in smartphone use has led to an increase in SMS use.


Smartphones such as Apple's iPhone and Android devices generally come with pre-installed messaging apps that use SMS.


And the growth is showing no sign of slowing.

Middle distance runner Hassane El Guerrouj has announced he will compete in the cross country discipline at the IAAF World Cross Country Championships in March.

The 36-year-old, who won gold in the 1500m and 5000m at the 2004 Olympics, has not competed in the event since he was 16.

He will be one of seven Moroccan runners taking part in the championships in Bydgoszcz, Poland on 30 March.

"I am not coming to Bydgoszcz to win but to gain experience," said El Guerrouj.

"I have been speaking a lot with [coach]
Jama Aden and he is confident I can do well."

El Guerrouj has competed at the Olympics five times and also won four world titles indoors and outdoors over 1,500m as well as the 2003 world title over 5,000m.
He retired from the track in August 2012 after suffering from a series of injuries but returned to competition in March last year and has set a series of world best times in the 3,000m this winter.

"I never thought I would return to competition, never mind cross country," added El Guerrouj, who spent nearly three months last year receiving treatment in Spain for a chronic back problem.

"I am not afraid of the mud and I have always enjoyed cross country.
It is something new and I wanted to have a go."

Stormy year for property insurers 

Insurers are struggling after a spate of extreme weather events in 2022, leading to a surge in claims and a crunch on companies' profits.


The cost of claims linked to UK storms alone hit £1.25bn in the first nine months of the year, according to the Association of British Insurers (ABI).


It said the average cost of claims from storms over the past decade was £575m per year.


The industry body said the average insurance pay-out for domestic flood damage was £50,500, while the average claim for damage caused by wind was £22,500.


The worst storms to hit the UK in 2022 were on 12 and 13 February, when the country was buffeted by Storm Darcy - also known as Storm Eunice.


The Met Office said it was the strongest storm to hit the UK since the "Great Storm" of 1987 and the highest gust of wind ever recorded in England was recorded during the storm - 94mph (151km/hr) at Wight High Lighthouse.


The insurance industry said the cost of paying claims for the storm was likely to be well over £1bn.


The year also saw Storm Malik, which hit Scotland and northern England in November, and Storms Dudley and Eunice which both hit the UK in February.


In addition, Britain basked in record-breaking temperatures in the summer of 2022.


The Met Office said that across the UK temperatures averaged 15.9C (60.6F) - beating the previous record of 15.6C (60.1F) in 2019.

Triple jumper Jonathan Edwards has tipped fellow Briton Phillips Idowu for European gold in Munich.


Idowu, who won the 2006 world title and 2008 Olympic crown, is returning to the sport after a four-year retirement.


The 38-year-old won his sole major medal for Britain - silver - at the 2014 Europeans in Zurich behind Germany's Charles Friedek.


"He's going to be competitive," Edwards said on the BBC's coverage of the event.
"He's going to be right in the mix.
If he wins, it won't be a surprise to me.
"

Idowu, who also won world indoor gold in 2010, finished fourth at the British Championships in July - his first competition for four years.


Only this week, he tweeted he was "keeping the faith" ahead of his return to the continental stage in Germany.


Edwards, who won Olympic, world, and European gold in the triple jump during his career, added: "He's definitely got the X-factor.


"When Phillips Idowu is at his best, he's fearless.

Sales of gadgets such as smartphones, tablets and laptops are expected to rise to record levels this year.


The figure for overall sales of electronic gadgets is put at more than $830bn (£489bn) for 2013.


One expert said the growth in demand for gadgets was "absolutely insane".


Environmental group Greenpeace said the rise in sales demonstrated the need for recycling.


"There's an explosion of gadgets coming onto the market, the pace of change is rapidly increasing, and that's causing a lot of stress on behalf of consumers," said Gary Cook, a senior IT analyst at Greenpeace.


"Many of us are struggling to keep up with the latest trends and device, and that means that we're discarding our electronics quicker than ever before," he said.


The figures, from the US-based analyst firm Gartner, show that mobile phones will account for almost half of all gadget sales this year.


Smartphones are expected to sell particularly well, with sales up by nearly a third compared with last year.


Tablets are also selling fast, with more than 200 million expected to be sold this year, double the number in 2012.
And sales of traditional PCs, including laptops, are also expected to grow this year.

Pornographers, hackers and virus writers have emerged as the top cyber criminals in 2004, according to a report by security software firm Symantec.


The report reveals a growing trend in the criminal use of the internet, with one US server alone being used to distribute 33 million spam emails.


Symantec's annual Internet Security Threat Report details a year of "rapid change and massive growth" in cyber crime.


The report shows a significant rise in the exploitation of web services and vulnerabilities in mobile devices and other consumer electronics.


During 2004, Symantec processed more than 370,000 malicious code samples, almost triple the number from the previous year.


Malicious code is any program or code designed to gain unauthorized access to computer systems.


The report reveals that although the US is still the primary source of originating e-mail spam, other countries are fast catching up.


Symantec discovered that during 2004, spam emissions from the US dropped from 61% to 54%, whilst spam emissions from China rose from 9% to 13%.


"The sheer volume of spam being produced by these groups is phenomenal," said Vincent Weafer, senior director of Symantec's Security Response group.


"We are seeing a change in the way that spam is being used, with a large number of spammers now using it to promote their own commercial services and products," he added.

text:
Police in China have detained the chairmen of two dairy companies at the centre of a scandal over milk powder contaminated with industrial chemicals.


The general manager of Sanlu Group - the firm at the centre of the crisis - has also been taken into custody, police said.


It follows revelations that milk powder producers have been adding the chemical melamine to give false high protein readings.


Six children have died and more than 300,000 fallen ill from drinking milk and milk products laced with the chemical.


Police in the northern city of Shijiazhuang, where the Sanlu Group is based, made the arrests after the men volunteered to hand themselves in, state news agency Xinhua reported.


They have been charged with "endangering public security", which can carry the death penalty.


It is not clear how long the three men have been in custody.


The scandal, which first emerged last week, has already seen 22 people arrested, including those working for three dairy companies implicated in the scam.


On Thursday, police in the capital, Beijing, said they had arrested the general manager of a dairy firm whose milk products were found to contain melamine.


Wei Kuijuan, general manager of the Yili Industrial Group, was arrested in Beijing, a police statement said.

The group received the award in Edinburgh on Sunday for their show at London's Hyde Park last summer.

They beat U2, Red Hot Chili Peppers, The Darkness and The White Stripes to win the prize.

The awards ceremony was held at Edinburgh's Ingliston Exhibition Centre and hosted by US comedy duoMADtv.


Madonna opened the show with a performance of her new single, Music.


Did you know?

Scissor Sisters front man Jake Shears once worked as a back-up dancer for Madonna.

The Best New Act award went to The Stands, while Feeder won the Best Rock award.

US R&B star Alicia Keys took the Best R&B award, and pop group Blue received the Best Pop award.


The ceremony was streamed live on the internet for the first time, and the Best Web award went to Dido.

Tim Henman has warned Nick Kyrgios he still has some way to go if he is to be regarded as one of Australia's sporting icons.


The 24-year-old world number 36 has been voted the nation's most marketable athlete, ahead of cricket captain Steve Smith and tennis pair Ashleigh Barty and Casey Dellacqua.


But Henman, who reached the semi-finals of Wimbledon in 2004, said Kyrgios still had to prove himself.


"He's got a lot of the attributes but whether he wants to fulfil his potential is another question," Henman told BBC Sport.


"Only when he walks away from the game satisfied that he's given it everything he's got, then he can be regarded as a true great.
"

Kyrgios has been in fine form in 2018, winning his first title on home soil in Brisbane and reaching his first Grand Slam quarter-final at the Australian Open.


The former world number 13 also reached the final of the Acapulco Open and claimed three ATP Tour titles last year.


But he courted controversy at Wimbledon last year when he was fined for unsportsmanlike behaviour, swearing and throwing his racquet in a match, and appeared to concede a match due to discomfort from a knee injury despite appearing to feel fine moments earlier.


Kyrgios has also had an ongoing feud with fellow Australian Pat Cash, who said in December that "tennis deserves better" from the Canberra-born player.


Henman said Cash's comments were "quite understandable" but that Kyrgios needed to show more respect to his opponents.

England's white-ball captain Eoin Morgan and his predecessor, Joe Root, have both made themselves available for the tour of Pakistan planned for early next year but Ben Stokes and Jos Buttler are unlikely to be included in the squad, and Sam Curran is currently recovering from knee surgery.
It has also been reported that Yorkshire's Harry Brook is a possibility to be considered for the tour as a backup wicketkeeper batsman.


The PCB has invited England to play three ODIs and as many T20s in Pakistan from 13-22 October 2023 and the ECB has said it is "committed" to playing in the country.
The last time England played a limited-overs series in Pakistan was in 2015, when they played four matches including a T20 and won the series 3-0.


England players have not been averse to visiting Pakistan in the past with some of them playing in the Pakistan Super League but since an attack on the Sri Lankan team's bus in March 2009, England have been reluctant to play there with the ECB taking into account the players' and staff's welfare and security.


But with Pakistan successfully hosting the ICC World Cup 2023 matches - including the final at the Gaddafi Stadium in Lahore on 13 November - in a safe and secure environment and the PCB making every effort to make sure that all the visiting teams are comfortable and get top-class security, the ECB's concerns have been allayed to some extent.


The PCB has also informed the ECB that it will hire a charter flight to take the England team to Pakistan and avoid any exposure of the players to commercial travel.


"The safety and welfare of our players and staff is our first priority and we will not hesitate to postpone the tour if we do not feel it is safe to proceed," said an ECB spokesperson.
"We are in ongoing discussions with the PCB around conditions for the tour, working together to deliver a safe environment for the players and staff.
We will continue to take guidance from the UK government and relevant security teams.

But with Pakistan successfully hosting the ICC World Cup 2023 matches - including the final at the Gaddafi Stadium in Lahore on 13 November - in a safe and secure environment and the PCB making every effort to make sure that all the visiting teams are comfortable and get top-class security, the ECB's concerns have been allayed to some extent.


The PCB has also informed the ECB that it will hire a charter flight to take the England team to Pakistan and avoid any exposure of the players to commercial travel.


"The safety and welfare of our players and staff is our first priority and we will not hesitate to postpone the tour if we do not feel it is safe to proceed," said an ECB spokesperson.
"We are in ongoing discussions with the PCB around conditions for the tour, working together to deliver a safe environment for the players and staff.
We will continue to take guidance from the UK government and relevant security teams.

England centre Emily Scarratt will become the women's game's highest ever Test scorer as she sets her sights on breaking the 5000-point mark in the Six Nations.


Scarratt, 34, currently has 3,527 points and needs just 23 points in this year's Six Nations to pass Katy Daley-Mclean's mark.


She will reach the milestone if she scores two tries and kicks seven conversions in England's first two matches.


"It's a honour," said Scarratt.
"When you look at the calibre of players that have come before, it's a proud moment.


"It's something I if hadn't have thought about, never mind something I probably wouldn't have imagined would happen when I started playing rugby.


"I feel incredibly lucky.
"

Before this year's Six Nations Scarratt needed 35 points to overtake Daley-Mclean's mark, but having been involved in England's recent Quilter Internationals against the USA and Canada, the centre has scored 60 points so far this season.


The England men's record is held by Jonny Wilkinson, who scored 1,246 points in his 95 Tests between 1998 and 2011.


If Scarratt reaches the 5000-point mark it will be thanks to her formidable penalty and conversion rates.

Nepal's Gurkha community has said it is proud that its soldiers serving in the British Army will help with relief efforts following the tsunami earthquake in Indonesia.


Sunday's magnitude 7.5 quake triggered a tsunami that killed more than 300 people.


The UK has deployed HMS Diamond and HMS Albion to help with the aftermath.


British Gurkhas have been serving the UK for more than 200 years.
There are currently about 400 Gurkhas in the UK military.


Community leader Ang Tshering said he was thrilled their "smarts and braves" would aid victims.


UK Minister for the Armed Forces, Mark Lancaster, said he was "proud" of the Gurkhas.


"We owe them a debt of gratitude for their commitment to our country and for the incredible work they do around the world," he said.


"I am sure the whole country shares my pride in the Gurkhas who are currently serving our country, demonstrating their trademark loyalty, professionalism and bravery.
"

Why the Gurkhas matter

Gurkhas have been fighting for the UK since the early 19th Century, when the British East India Company recruited them to fight in the first war against Nepal.

A candidate in the Northern Irish Assembly has resigned after videos emerged of him singing a pro-Catholic song in a pub more than a decade ago.


Sam Cole, who was standing for the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) in next month's poll, was filmed singing the ballad "The Sash" in a Belfast pub in 2011.


The DUP had called on him to stand down and he resigned shortly before a press conference at which party leader Sir Jeffrey Donaldson was due to announce the decision.


"The Sash" is a 19th-century Irish folk song, which has become a anthem for Irish nationalists and Catholics.
It is widely considered to be a provocative song in Northern Ireland, where the DUP has tried to court pro-unionist voters ahead of the election.


"Sam Cole has decided to resign as a candidate for the Democratic Unionist Party in the forthcoming assembly election," a statement from the party said.


"This decision was taken after Sam acknowledged that a number of social media posts, which have emerged, are unacceptable and embarrassing and do not reflect the values or ethos of the Democratic Unionist Party.
"

The 30-year-old had been due to contest the seat previously held by Sir Jeffrey, who is standing in the same constituency - Lagan Valley.


The DUP's decision comes as the party continues efforts to convince voters that it is not out of touch after its leader, Sir Jeffrey, was filmed last week speaking at an event where a caller mentioned the pro-unionist UVF paramilitary group.


Sir Jeffrey has said that the caller's views were "not democratic, legal or reasonable" and that he had challenged them.

British biotechnology firm Phytopharm has signed a deal with Arizona-based Cactus Botanics to develop a new diet supplement that aims to help people lose weight.
The supplement, called ProGrade, will combine a cactus extract with chromium, a mineral believed to help control blood sugar and appetite.
The companies expect to launch the product in the US by the end of the year, followed by a European launch in early 2023.


The deal comes as obesity rates are on the rise, with the World Health Organization describing the surge as an "epidemic".
Obesity increases the risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, and certain types of cancer, and is one of the main factors behind the increase in non-communicable diseases.


According to the WHO, the number of people classed as overweight or obese has nearly tripled since 1975, with the majority of the increase coming from lower-income countries.
The pandemic has also led to an increase in unhealthy habits, such as eating too much and not exercising enough, which has contributed to an increase in obesity.


Chromium is a mineral that helps the body process carbohydrates and fats, and is believed to help control blood sugar and appetite.
The cactus extract is believed to help with weight loss by slowing the breakdown of food into glucose, which helps the body burn fat more efficiently.


The companies plan to market ProGrade as a diet supplement that can help people lose weight and improve their health.

The EU will lift its embargo on Chinese arms sales next year, European officials have agreed.


The lifting of the 16-year-old ban, which was imposed after the Tiananmen Square massacre, will take place in early 2004, provided China signs up to an international arms trade treaty due to be discussed at the UN in July.


China has been seeking the lifting of the embargo ever since it was introduced.


The decision, taken at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Brussels on Monday, was welcomed by the Chinese government.


"It is a positive step in the development of EU-China relations," the official Chinese news agency, Xinhua, reported.


"We hope the EU will continue to view positively China's peaceful development and address properly China's concern over the lifting of the ban," it added.


But the decision has been criticised by human rights activists both in Europe and in China.


"This will send completely the wrong signal to Beijing at a time when it is becoming ever more repressive," said Amnesty International's Asia-Pacific director, Nicholas Bequelin.


"This will only embolden China's brutal crackdown on dissent and provide it with more means to repress its own people," he said, speaking from Beijing.


The EU introduced the embargo in 1989, two years after the Tiananmen Square incident, when the Chinese army killed hundreds of pro-democracy protesters.

"It's a much bigger movie than we first thought," he said.


"It's probably going to be a trilogy.
I thought it was a single movie, but now I really think it is three movies."


Mr Jackson said work on the visual effects, which will be crucial to the success of the films, would take a long time.


"I don't think we will be able to release them until 2013, but that's not a problem," he said.


"We're not in a race with anybody.
It's going to be so much work to do this, I think it will be four years of solid filming.

Ukrainian steel producers have been told to stop the illegal sale of steel products in Russia, by the country's prime minister.

Mykhailo Fridtyshyn said the metal was being sold "under the guise of humanitarian supplies".

He added that the steel was instead being used to rebuild infrastructure in Russian-occupied Crimea.

Crimea's Russian-backed government later said it would block the export of metal products from the region.

Since Russia's annexation of Crimea in March, Ukrainian steel producers have been selling their products at a discounted price.

Mr Fridtyshyn said the state budget had lost more than $500m (£300m) because of the "unlawful" trade across the Kerch strait between Crimea and Russia.

"We consider this illegal scheme of metal exports to Russia as a threat to Ukraine's security and budget," he said.

"Metal is sold under the guise of humanitarian supplies and then is used to rebuild the infrastructure in the temporarily occupied Crimea."

Mr Fridtyshyn also said that the Ukrainian government had asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) to investigate the illegal trade.

He said the court had confirmed that it would examine the case.

Apple has launched a faster, cheaper and greener version of its Mac mini computer, which hasn't seen an update in more than three years.


The Mac mini 2022 has faster M2 processor chips, better graphics and a new discounted price tag.


It is Apple's first computer to ship without a plug, partly to cut down on packaging and partly because most people buying it will already have a USB-C charger.


"It's green, it's smart, it's more affordable," said Apple's chief marketing officer, Greg Joswiak, at the launch event in California.


"And it's the biggest update to Mac mini ever.
"

The new computer kicks the old $699 (£569) entry-level price tag to the curb, replacing it with a $599 (£499) model.


That base model comes with Apple's M2 processor, an eight-core CPU, and a ten-core GPU.
You'll need to pay $899 (£769) to get the M2 Pro chip with a 12-core CPU and up to a 19-core GPU.


Both versions come with 256GB of solid state drive storage, twice as much as the previous generation.


There are also two USB-A ports, an HDMI port for connecting a monitor, a headphone jack and a Gigabit Ethernet port for connecting to broadband.

Format wars between Blu-ray and HD DVD have "already damaged" the high definition DVD market in the UK, according to a retail study.


A survey by Retail Eyes found that the confusion among consumers over which format to buy caused sales of HD DVDs in the run up to Christmas to be "well below" expectations.


The study said that shoppers were put off buying machines capable of playing either Blu-ray or HD DVD, in case the format war ended up favouring the rival format.


"The format war has damaged consumer confidence in the whole category," the study said.


"Many consumers are reluctant to invest in a format that may become obsolete in the future.
"

The study found that just one in 200 UK shoppers purchased a high definition DVD player or recorder in the six weeks before Christmas.


Retail Eyes said that stock levels of the format were "generally good" but added that retailers should consider the impact of the format war when planning ahead for this year's Christmas season.


The study found that one in three shoppers would not buy any HD products because of the uncertainty surrounding the format war.


Last week, Japanese electronics giant Sony announced that it would buy out its rival Toshiba's share in a joint venture to produce HD DVDs.


The move all-but-ends the battle between Blu-ray and HD DVD to provide the next-generation optical disc for high definition movies and games.

A gardener has won not one but two coveted medals at a gardening show in Glasgow.


It is the first time in the 158-year history of the Glasgow Gardening Club that anyone has achieved the double.


Jim McColl won the club's annual show's top prize - the John Brown Memorial Trophy for best in show.


And he also picked up the Scottish Horticulture Club's medal for the best display of vegetables.


The 77-year-old retired teacher said: "I don't know how I have done it.
I am over the moon.
"

His success comes just two years after he started entering his vegetables and flowers into shows.


Mr McColl, who lives in the Glasgow suburb of Newton Mearns, grows 16 varieties of vegetable and 10 types of flower.


He said: "I have won many prizes but never anything like this.


"I entered the Glasgow Gardening Club's annual show for the first time last year and won the trophy for best newcomer.

"Choose hope over fear - Kennedy"

Like many others, I remember exactly where I was and what I was doing when I first heard about HIV and AIDS.
I was in high school, and for myself and my peers, it was a crisis occurring among adults that felt very distant.


In the decades since, I've worked with a series of HIV/AIDS organisations, most recently the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria.
From that vantage point, I have seen the crisis unfold and watched the remarkable progress that has been made to overcome it.


I remember speaking to a colleague working in Swaziland, one of the most HIV-affected countries in the world, about the fear that HIV causes, and how that thwarts efforts to fight it.


And yet, despite the terrible toll HIV has taken, the tide has turned.
The number of new HIV infections has dropped by one-third since 2000; the number of AIDS-related deaths has fallen by one-half.


These achievements did not happen spontaneously.
They are the result of long-term, well-funded, committed responses, both in terms of policy and funding.


But today, against the backdrop of the Covid-19 pandemic, that progress is at risk.

Video footage has emerged of a Conservative parliamentary candidate in the UK making a racially charged comment about Asian people.


Sam Gyimah, who was standing in the London borough of Chingford and Woodford Green, was recorded making the remark at a Conservative party fundraiser in November.


The former minister has apologised and said he is stepping down as candidate.


In the video, recorded at a private members' club in London, Mr Gyimah questions why Tory leaflets were not being translated into Punjabi.


"There are too many Asians, do you know what I mean?," he says.
"They're just everywhere, ain't they?"

The clip was shared with the BBC by James Baker, the chairman of the local Conservative association, who said he was "appalled" by it.


Mr Baker said the candidate had "failed to understand the very real impact his words can have".


"It is clear to me that Sam's comments were insensitive, and for that reason he has decided to step down as our candidate for Chingford and Woodford Green," he added.


Mr Gyimah, the former universities minister, issued an apology on Saturday, saying his comments were "clumsy" and "completely inappropriate".

Can Yahoo dominate next decade? 


Yahoo has unveiled plans to create a blockchain-based platform for encrypted email and cryptocurrency-based rewards.


The firm has filed a patent application in the US for a system that could encode emails to help prevent prying eyes from reading them.


The application also suggests users might be rewarded with cryptocurrency for using the service.


Yahoo already offers 1,000 Yahoo Coins for signing up for a Yahoo account, and filing the application shows the company continues to explore blockchain technology. 


The patent application outlines a system in which a blockchain would be used to encrypt and store email messages, with a cryptographic key held by the sender and recipient.


This would prevent the contents of emails from being revealed to anyone other than the intended recipients.


"Some embodiments may incentivise the use of the email platform," the application reads.


"For example, the email platform may reward users with a cryptocurrency for using the platform.
"

It goes on to explain that users might be rewarded for actions including "transmitting an email", "receiving an email", or "reading an email".

Zambia's president has said he is "confident and cautious" as the country becomes the first on the African continent to receive COVID-19 vaccines through the UN-backed COVAX scheme.


Ruling party leader Edgar Lungu received his shot live on TV on Friday, urging others to follow suit.


But the event itself was not without controversy.
Main opposition leader Hakainde Hichilema criticised the handling of the process, and questioned the timing of the president's vaccination.


Mr Hichilema, who disputed last year's presidential election results, said the vaccine should have been administered at a hospital, rather than at State House.


He added that as the leader of an opposition party, he did not believe Mr Lungu should have been given "preferential treatment" in receiving the vaccine ahead of healthcare workers.


Hasn't Zambia had its share of tragedy?


Yes.
Zambia is among the African countries that have suffered countless tragedies as a result of the pandemic.


It has recorded more than 27,000 cases and over 220 deaths - but the actual numbers are thought to be higher as testing is limited.

text:
Report attacks defence spending

Spending on defence in Nato member states will fail to meet agreed targets for another 12 years, a report by the organisation has said.


The report attacked the "defence spending trend" and said that even though members had agreed to increase defence spending by 4% a year, they would still fall $110bn short by 2024.


Only the US, Britain, Greece, Romania and Estonia are expected to meet the target of spending 2% of GDP on defence this year, it said.


The shortfall will grow to $170bn by 2024, according to the report.


The UK is set to spend £39.4bn on defence by the end of 2022/23, the report said.


That is in line with the government's ambition to increase spending to exceed the 2% target, it added.


UK defence spending as a percentage of GDP is due to increase from 1.5% in 2021 to 1.9% in 2022, before reaching 2.1% in 2024.


The report said that only nine of the 31 Nato members met the defence spending target in 2021 and that trend was continuing.


It also warned that Europe was facing its "most dangerous security situation in decades", with Russia's invasion of Ukraine posing the most serious threat.


The report's publication comes as defence ministers from across the alliance meet in Brussels to discuss how to respond to Russia's invasion.

Report attacks defence spending

Spending on defence in Nato member states will fail to meet agreed targets for another 12 years, a report by the organisation has said.


The report attacked the "defence spending trend" and said that even though members had agreed to increase defence spending by 4% a year, they would still fall $110bn short by 2024.


Only the US, Britain, Greece, Romania and Estonia are expected to meet the target of spending 2% of GDP on defence this year, it said.


The shortfall will grow to $170bn by 2024, according to the report.


The UK is set to spend £39.4bn on defence by the end of 2022/23, the report said.


That is in line with the government's ambition to increase spending to exceed the 2% target, it added.


UK defence spending as a percentage of GDP is due to increase from 1.5% in 2021 to 1.9% in 2022, before reaching 2.1% in 2024.


The report said that only nine of the 31 Nato members met the defence spending target in 2021 and that trend was continuing.


It also warned that Europe was facing its "most dangerous security situation in decades", with Russia's invasion of Ukraine posing the most serious threat.


The report's publication comes as defence ministers from across the alliance meet in Brussels to discuss how to respond to Russia's invasion.

We had chances to score and didn't take them.

The Liverpool manager said Dudek had been the victim of a miscarriage of justice following his costly mistake.


"People seem to want to hunt him down but he made some fantastic saves and I am happy with him," added the Spaniard.


Benitez believes the goal, which gave United a half-time lead they never surrendered, was avoidable.


"It was a set piece we had analysed and we knew what they would do," he said.


"We had talked about that and we made mistakes.

Bill Gates officially opened the CeBIT computer fair in Hannover, Germany.


The Microsoft chairman used his keynote speech at the event to launch a attacks on rivals and critics.


In his first appearance at the fair, Mr Gates said Microsoft was "definitely ahead" of its competitors.


And he took the opportunity to take a swipe at Sun Microsystems, which is feuding with Microsoft over Java.


The fair opens to the public on Thursday.


Mr Gates was joined on the stage by German Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder, who admitted he was a "PC man" and not a Mac user.


About 4,000 companies are exhibiting at CeBIT, which is the largest hi-tech fair in the world.


And it appears to be growing, with about 800,000 people expected to attend this year's event, which has the theme of "e-business and lifestyle".


Mr Gates, who took the wraps off a new Microsoft operating system earlier this month, said technology was becoming more and more important in people's lives.


"In the next two or three years, the advances will be more dramatic than ever before," he said.

The bodies, known as quangos, are accused of lacking transparency and accountability.


The government's quango watchdog, the Quango Commission, is to launch an attack on the "culture of secrecy" in some of the 1,000 public bodies.


Cabinet Office minister Francis Maude will demand that all quangos justify their existence.


The Tory MP said: "The age of the quango is over.
"

The coalition is examining all arms-length bodies, which cost £80bn to run every year.


The review could result in major reforms, with some institutions abolished and others have their powers transferred to ministers.


The Daily Telegraph has found that more than 200 quangos do not even have a website, making it impossible to find out who sits on their boards or how much they spend.


In addition, more than 150 do not publish their board members' attendance records - with some having not met for years.


More than 130 do not publish the salaries of their senior staff - with one boss reportedly earning £170,000 a year.


And more than 50 do not even publish their phone number or email address - including the Heritage Lottery Fund, which gives out £800m a year.

BBC One's flagship music show Top of the Pops is to end its run on the channel after more than 40 years.


The broadcaster has decided not to renew the programme's contract, which expires this month.


Presented by Reggie Yates, the final edition of the show will be broadcast on 30 July.


A BBC statement said: "Top of the Pops is a much-loved show and it's not surprising that BBC One wants to keep it."


The statement added: "We are in discussions about continuing the show in the future."


First broadcast in January 1964, Top of the Pops was shown every Thursday evening and at one point was the most-watched programme on British television.


However, audience numbers have declined in recent years and the programme's £150,000-a-week budget was described as "eye-watering" by a BBC source.


In May, BBC One controller Lorraine Heggessey defended the show, saying she was "very optimistic" about its future.


She said Top of the Pops would "continue to be part of BBC One's music offering".


A source close to the show said: "There have been cuts across the board at the BBC and music programmes have taken a particular pasting.

What does it mean to be a genius?


Someone intelligent, sure.
Someone who excels in a particular field - probably.
But there are an array of other popular interpretations.


A genius is someone who is eccentric; a madcap who thinks and behaves differently from the rest of us.
A genius is someone unconstrained by social norms, who lives on their own terms regardless of what anyone else thinks.


This is how Kanye West wants us to see him.
Since he burst onto the scene in the early 2000s, the rapper has deliberately cultivated this aura.


He didn't hide his ambition.
He released a debut album titled The College Dropout.

Andy Murray's former coach, Alex Davenport, has criticized the Wimbledon tournament for failing to "move with the times" after it declined to offer equal prize money to men and women players.
Davenport, who also coached two-time Grand Slam champion Victoria Azarenka, said Wimbledon had sent a message to young tennis players that women's tennis was not as important as men's.
She said: "It is a massive deal.
Wimbledon is such a prestigious event.
It is the pinnacle of the tennis year for a lot of players, particularly the Brits.
"So when you message young kids that are potentially picking up a tennis racket for the first time that that isn't important, that sends a harmful message.
"

Davenport praised the All England Club for awarding equal prize money in the junior and invitational events, but said that wider changes were needed to implement real change on the tour.
"There are many, many positives that Wimbledon do but this is certainly a legacy item that they need to sort out," she said.
"They need to move with the times.
These are the kinds of things that shouldn't happen in 2022.
