BBC Sport - Andy Murray's retirement has left a void at the top of British men's tennis but Dan Cox says there is a wave of younger players hoping to fill it, including 20-year-old Liam Broady who is ranked 255 in the world.


Cox, a former junior world number one from Derby, believes Britain has "one of the most exciting generations of players in a long time", with the likes of himself, Broady, Paul Jubb, Max Purcell and Ryan Peniston leading the charge.


"No-one wants to be the next Andy Murray, they want to be the first Liam Broady," he said.


Who are the young British players hoping to fill the void left by Murray's retirement?

Listen to the podcast above to hear Dan Cox, Liam Broady and Paul Jubb discuss British tennis' next generation, while BBC tennis correspondent Russell Fuller answers listeners' questions on the subject.


Cox, now 24, knows all about the challenges of trying to make it as a professional tennis player.


A back injury saw him miss the whole of the 2018 season and he has only just regained his place on the ATP Tour having won his first match at that level against Argentina's Federico Delbonis in March.


"There are going to be ups and downs and it's about how you deal with them," said Cox, who is unranked having started 2022 ranked 1,206th in the world.


"There's no limit to where this group can get to.
Realistically, we believe we can all be top 50, top 100, but that takes time and patience.


"You look at the top 50 and they are not going to be there for ever.

The UK government has introduced a new English language requirement for foreign nationals who want to marry British citizens.


From Thursday, those without a good grasp of English will have to take a test - at a cost of £1,000 ($1,270) - before they can get a marriage visa.


The measure is aimed at tackling so-called "sham weddings".


The test must be taken at one of the approved test centres in seven days.


The government says it is "determined to tackle illegal immigration" and protect the public against "marriages of convenience".


The test will be in addition to existing requirements for a foreign national who wants to marry a British citizen to prove they can speak English to a level equivalent to band A2 of the Council of Europe's common European framework of reference for languages.
This is the level expected of a basic user of English.


Officials say there are an additional 12 countries, including China and Russia, where applicants who wish to marry a British citizen must also prove they know English.


What has changed is that instead of providing evidence that they know English - such as through documents or testimonials - they must now take the speaking and listening test.


The test, which is run by language teaching body Trinity College London, lasts 20 minutes and applicants must achieve at least a pass mark of A2.

text:
Universities in Wales have warned that prospects for students are at risk because of long-term funding cuts.


Bosses said a £35m funding gap left by the Welsh government could lead to course closures and a decline in quality.


Education Minister Jeremy Miles said he recognised the pressures on the sector.


A review of higher education funding in Wales - due to report back in spring - could see a shift from the current system, in which students from Wales pay the same fees as those from England, but with lower interest rates on student loans.


It could also see a change to the current allocation system, in which universities in England get the majority of their funding from the UK government and those in Wales from the Welsh government.


In a letter to the Welsh government, Universities Wales, which represents the country's higher education institutions, said the sector had "serious concerns" about the level of funding for the next academic year.


It said combined cuts of 30% to the higher education budget since 2010 had resulted in a "starvation of resources".


"This underfunding has damaged the capacity of our universities to maintain and improve the provision of education and research," it added.


The letter, signed by Universities Wales chairman Prof Colin Riordan, warned that the situation had "reached a crisis point".


"The funding gap puts at risk the ability of universities to maintain the quality of provision, to invest in the infrastructure that supports this, to continue to provide an environment that supports the wellbeing of students and staff, and to ensure that higher education in Wales is based on a sustainable financial model," it said.

French consumer spending is rising fast as households buy more online, eat in restaurants, and splash out on utilities and social activities, data shows.


According to the official data, household spending accelerated in January, up 1.1% from the same month a year earlier, and 0.8% higher than in December.


The figures were well above the 0.4% growth forecast by analysts.


The robust data points to healthy activity in the eurozone's second-biggest economy, says ING bank.


"The French economy surprises positively every time," said ING economist Charlotte de Montpellier.


"There is a catch, though: the data are extremely volatile and prone to large revisions.
But at this stage, it is difficult to see a big downward revision in the coming months," she added.


French consumers have been cautious since the 2008 financial crisis, with many holding onto their savings and looking to pay off debt.


But economists say they are increasingly spending some of their cash, in part because of low unemployment and rising wages.


The data showed a 1.4% rise in spending on transport, accommodation and food, as well as a 1.1% increase in spending on health, education and culture.

text:
Abba have reunited to launch a new stage show inspired by their songs.


The four singers, who have not performed together since the early 1980s, appeared together at the Prince Edward Theatre in London for the premiere of Abba Mania.


The show features 22 of their hits including Waterloo, Dancing Queen and Voulez Vous.


Band member Benny Andersson called it "a bit weird" but exciting.


He said he did not think the group, who split up 37 years ago, would have approved the show but that he was happy with it.


"I think Abba would have hated this, actually," he told the BBC.
"Because it's not like you're doing a great Abba show with the bells and whistles.
This is more a tribute.
"

He said he was "blown away" by the show, adding: "It's kind of spooky seeing these people pretending to be us, but they do a good job.
"

The musical is billed as an immersive experience, with the audience invited to party alongside the performers.

The streets of major cities across the UK have been colourful and vibrant this week as people have gathered to pay tribute to Prince Philip, the Duke of Edinburgh, following his death on Friday.


Among the many heartfelt messages, some of the most moving have come from members of the Commonwealth.


Prime Minister Boris Johnson described the duke as "the grandfather of the nation", while Australian Prime Minister Scott Morrison spoke of the "strong values" his late father, John, shared with Philip.


And, as the world reflects on the legacy of the man who was married to the Queen for more than 70 years, there is no doubt that his influence will be long-lasting.


So what was it about the duke that has made him such an enduring figure, not only in the UK but across the globe?


Born in 1921, Philip was born a prince of Greece and Denmark, before becoming a British citizen in 1947 and going on to become one of the most prominent members of the Royal Family.


He joined the Royal Navy in 1939 and was mentioned in dispatches for his service during World War Two.


He went on to become a champion of conservation and the environment, and was a leading figure in the development of the Duke of Edinburgh's Award, which has inspired young people around the world to serve their communities and gain new skills.


The duke was also known for his sense of humour and his many gaffes, which often made the front pages of the newspapers.


He was also a regular presence at major events, such as the annual Remembrance Day service, and was a strong supporter of the armed forces.

Michael Jackson's last film, "This Is It", was an "absolute disaster" that would have been laughed off the screen if it had been screened, his ex-wife Lisa Marie Presley says.


Presley, who was married to the pop star for two years until 1996, said the film was supposed to be about their relationship.


But she said Jackson, who died in 2009, became obsessive about the idea that the world was against him.


"It was this movie that was going to get everybody back on his side," she told the Radio Times.
"It was going to be this amazing, wonderful, revealing film about our relationship and his childhood and, you know, the abuse he had gone through and his philanthropic ways…

"It was going to be about all these wonderful things, and then I started to see where he was going with it.
It was like, 'Wait, I was supposed to be the bride?'"

Presley also said that she could not understand why Jackson married her.
She said she thought he may have been lonely and felt compelled to marry again because the media had compared his relationship with her to his earlier friendship with Beatles singer Paul McCartney.


"He said, 'You know, people are going to think this is like Paul and I, and I don't want that.
I don't want to go through that again.
It's going to seem like I'm replacing Paul,' and stuff like that," she said.

Fulham manager Roy Hodgson is enjoying the "stimulation" of European football and is happy that his side have been drawn against Roma and Basel in the Europa League.


The Cottagers, who finished sixth in the Premier League last season, face Roma in Italy in the first leg of their play-off on 20 August.


"I love being involved in these types of games, love the challenge," he said.


Hodgson spent seven years managing in Europe, guiding Fulham to the Europa League final in 2010, where they were beaten by Atletico Madrid.


"This is a short journey which we've undergone as a club in the last three years and I include ourselves as managers and coaches in that," he said.


"To go from where we were when we arrived, which was basically in the bottom three, to get into the (Premier League) top six and play in Europe again is a great achievement.


"To go into the draw and see who you're going to play and discover you've got Roma and then Basel, it's not as if we've been given a particularly difficult tie.


"It's still going to be very difficult but of course as a coach and a manager you want to test yourself against the best."


Hodgson believes English clubs are now better prepared for European football, particularly in the early stages of tournaments.


"The experiences that English clubs have had in the last few years, not only in Europe but in the FA Cup and the Carling Cup, they are far better equipped to deal with these situations," he said.

Queen have recruited a singer to front the band for their upcoming tour - their first since the death of Freddie Mercury in 1991.


The singer, Adam Lambert, 29, is best known for finishing as runner-up in the 2009 series of TV talent show American Idol.


He will join the band, comprising Brian May, Roger Taylor and John Deacon, at five concerts in Europe next summer with the possibility of more shows being announced.


Lambert will sing lead vocals on songs usually performed by Mercury, who died of Aids in 1991.


Queen's guitarist Brian May said he was "utterly delighted" at the "fantastic" addition of Lambert to the line-up.


"We first met Adam a few months ago and have had a number of subsequent meetings, we think he's brilliant," May wrote on the band's website.


"We were never going to find someone who resembles Freddie in terms of appearance, sound and stage presentation, that wasn't going to be possible.


"But Adam is a super-talented guy and he has a great presence and a killer voice."


The band had been considering a number of singers since work on the tour began.


"It's been a long process but well worth the wait," said May.

Lambert, who has released two albums and completed three tours of his own, said it was "an honour" to join "the greatest band in the world".

Holmes starts 2005 with GB events

bbc.com/sport/horseracing/3671657

The champion trainer starts the New Year with a handful of runners at Newcastle and Wolverhampton.


The dual Group 1 winner has nine entries at the latter on Monday and three at the former 24 hours later.


The four-year-old has not been seen on a racecourse since claiming the Group 1 Fillies' Mile at Ascot in September.


Her appearance at Wolverhampton will give an indication as to whether she will be heading to the 1000 Guineas in May.


"She's possible for Wolverhampton, and we'll see how she is afterwards," said the trainer.


"There's a chance she could run there and at Newcastle the following day.
I wouldn't rush her, though, as she's a good filly who can go on any ground.
"

Meanwhile, stable jockey Johnny Murtagh will be out of action for at least three weeks after suffering a broken nose in a fall at the Curragh on Saturday.


The Irishman came off Sir Frederick Mayonnaise in the opening race of the day, and subsequently underwent an operation on Sunday.


"He's OK and the operation went well, but he'll be out for three weeks minimum," said Holmes.

text:
Film critics in the US have showered praise on the comedy Sideways, which opened in American cinemas last week.


The film, which stars Paul Giamatti and Thomas Haden Church, is set in the California wine country and tells the story of two friends on a road trip who venture to the valley to celebrate one's upcoming wedding.


Los Angeles Times critic Kenneth Turan called the film "smart, insightful and funny" and added: "Thomas Haden Church and Paul Giamatti are absolutely perfect, capturing the hell-bent sense of the inevitable that runs through the movie.
"

In the New York Times, Manohla Dargis called the film "deceptively complex and insightful".


She added: "Though centred on the male mid-life crisis, it's really about all sorts of longing, fulfilled and unfulfilled, and the compromises, large and small, that we make to survive."


In the Wall Street Journal, Joe Morgenstern called the film "smart, insightful and hilarious...
a sideways look at love and marriage, ageing and addiction, men and women, and the good and bad chemicals that course through them".


However, in the Daily News, Joe Brown was less enthusiastic, calling the film "a lot of fun, but it's not Oscar material".


"I'm glad I saw it, but I don't need to see it a second time," he added.


In Variety, Todd McCarthy called it "smart, insightful, witty, observant and amusing".

The Hong Kong Rugby Union made the announcement at a news conference on Wednesday.


"We are going to take this opportunity to show the IRB (International Rugby Board) that we are ready, willing and able to host the tournament," said Union president Brian Kennedy.


"Hong Kong is a world city.
We have excellent infrastructure and communications and we are ready to share this with the international rugby family.
"

IRB rules require a candidate nation to have a stadium with a minimum capacity of 40,000.


The Union has approached the Hong Kong Government to seek approval for a new stadium with a minimum capacity of 50,000.


"So far we have had very positive discussions with the Government and I am confident we will reach an agreement," said Kennedy.


"If we are successful in our bid then this new stadium, which will be built specifically for rugby, will be a legacy for future generations of rugby players and fans in Hong Kong.
"

The Union has until 19 October 2007 to submit its formal proposal to the IRB.

IRB Chairman Bernard Lapasset said he was looking forward to receiving the bid.

A US woman has filed a lawsuit claiming that Apple's cartridges for its newly launched MagSafe battery pack are incompatible with third-party chargers.


Stephanie Mendez filed the lawsuit in California this week, according to multiple reports.


Ms Mendez, who says she lives in San Diego, alleges in the suit that Apple's $129 (£110) battery pack is "designed to only work with Apple's own charger and not with other comparable chargers that exist on the market".


Apple launched the MagSafe battery pack in July, alongside its iPhone 14 line-up.
The charger attaches to iPhones via magnets, and charges the device wirelessly.


But Ms Mendez claims that Apple's use of a proprietary charging method is anticompetitive, and is seeking class action status for her lawsuit, which was filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California.


She argues that Apple's conduct violates California's competition and unfair competition laws, and wants the company to sell its battery pack with a standard charger, or to licence its charging technology to third-party manufacturers.


Apple did not respond to a request for comment.


It is not the first time Apple has been accused of creating proprietary parts that are incompatible with third-party products.


The company faced a similar lawsuit in 2019 over its Lightning connector, a proprietary charging port used on iPhones since 2012.

Scotland's elimination from the World Cup finals may work in Ireland's favour as they eye a place in the last 16, according to Irish manager Giovanni Trapattoni.


The Republic of Ireland drew 0-0 with Scotland in their opening group game, before beating Croatia 1-0 and losing 2-0 to Brazil.


The Scots have one point from their three games and are eliminated from the tournament whatever the result of their final group match against Brazil.


"It could be that Scotland's departure is a help for us," said Trapattoni.


"We have four points and we hope to reach seven.


"We are stronger than Scotland, Croatia and even Brazil.
"
Ireland face Croatia in their final group match on 18 June and a draw would see them through to the last 16 at Scotland's expense.


However, even if they lose in Rustenburg, Trapattoni believes they will still have a chance of going through as one of the four best third-placed teams.


"If we finish third in the group, we have four points and possibly a goal difference of zero or there abouts," added the Italian.


"There are other groups where the third-placed teams have one or two points and a negative goal difference.

Protesters plan airport challenge

Climate change protesters plan to gloat when they win their court fight against Heathrow Airport tomorrow.


They hope the verdict will inspire others and pave the way for fresh challenges against airport expansion across the UK.


Lawyers for some of the protesters are due to make their final remarks at the High Court in London today.


The group, called Plan B, wants to argue that the expansion of Heathrow, Britain's busiest airport, would make it harder to meet the country's carbon emissions targets.


The court battle has already heard evidence that the expansion of Heathrow would lead to an increase in emissions in the UK.


Plan B lawyer David Wolfe QC told the court on Friday that the UK's emissions targets, as set out in the Climate Change Act, were "compatible" with the expansion of the airport.


But he said that the government's National Policy Statement on airport expansion, which supported the building of a third runway, had been produced without taking into account the UK's legally binding targets.


"The starting point for this case is that it is accepted by all that Heathrow expansion, and the additional 70 million passengers, would lead to an increase in emissions," he said.


"The critical issue in this case is whether that increase in emissions can be justified when considered against the UK's legally binding targets.
"

Heathrow, the Department for Transport and the Planning Inspectorate, which approved the National Policy Statement, have all argued that the expansion can go ahead without threatening the UK's ability to meet its carbon reduction targets.

Tory MPs are plotting to reinstall Alec Shelbrooke as chairman of the powerful public accounts committee, despite the prime minister's vow to move him, the BBC has learned.


Senior Conservatives have suggested that the committee, which holds the government to account over its spending, could be split in two - with another MP taking on some of its duties.


This would allow Mr Shelbrooke, who is under investigation for alleged breaches of the MPs' code of conduct, to stay on as chairman of a smaller committee.


The prime minister has vowed to remove Mr Shelbrooke as public accounts chair "as soon as possible", but no timetable has been announced.


The MP for Selby and Ainsty has so far declined to comment on the matter.


The plot to keep him in post has been led by senior Conservative MP William Wragg - who himself stepped down this week as chair of the public administration and constitutional affairs committee.


Mr Wragg told the BBC the idea of splitting the accounts committee was "being looked at" and would be discussed at a "meeting later this week".


He said it was "important" to have a diverse range of committees, which would allow Mr Shelbrooke to remain in his role.


But Labour accused the Conservatives of attempting to "protect" Mr Shelbrooke, who is under investigation over his expenses after it was revealed he had hosted a series of parties last year in breach of lockdown rules.


Labour's shadow leader of the House of Commons, Jessica Morden, said: "Conspiracies to protect Alec Shelbrooke have taken a grip of Conservative backbenchers.

BBC News - Media - New media battle for Bafta awards - BBC.com

Film critics will have to work a lot harder if they want to eat doughnuts and watch movies for a living - and that could mean the end of a beloved industry titan.


For several decades, a select group of UK film critics have been invited by the distributors of the latest blockbuster to watch advance screenings - known as press screenings - of their films.


But film critic Anna Smith, president of the UK Critics' Circle, said she had heard of screenings being cancelled, and that more were "likely" in the future.


She said: "It is obviously a huge change and it is going to be very difficult for outlets who rely on these screenings, and for the critics."


But it is not just the film critics who will feel the impact.


The Bafta film awards, held in London each year and considered the highest honour in the British film industry, could also be affected.


Film critics vote for the Bafta awards, and the screenings have been an essential part of their decision-making - ahead of the deadline for submissions on 1 December.


The British Academy of Film and Television Arts (Bafta) said "it is not viable" for the organisation "to continue to commission critics to watch every eligible release" ahead of the 2022 film awards.


"It is important for a healthy industry that a wide variety of outlets and content producers have the opportunity to participate in these events," a Bafta spokesperson said.


"We are working with the industry to seek input into the process before we finalise our plans.

Halo 2 heralds traffic explosion

Police in the US are tackling an unexpected consequence of the interactive online game Halo 2 - a surge in traffic accidents.


Officers in Maryland are blaming a spate of crashes on young drivers distracted by the game.


Police in Montgomery County are now planning discussions with officials from Xbox, the game's US distributor.


A police spokeswoman said officers had noted a "disturbing increase" in the number of collisions involving youthful drivers.


"We've noticed a correlation between the time the game comes on and the time we get calls," she said.


Halo 2, which follows the adventures of a space soldier called Master Chief, was released in the US on Monday.


Players use a joystick to guide Master Chief through a series of military missions.


The spokeswoman said she did not know if other police forces in the US had reported a similar spike in traffic accidents.


An Xbox spokesman said the company was aware of the problem, but said it was impossible to blame Halo 2 for accidents caused by inattentive drivers.


"We think it's a small percentage of people who are already distracted and are going to use that as an excuse" he said.

Parental rights campaigners have lost a High Court bid to challenge the government's plans to reform the law on child access.


The three campaigners said the government had failed to properly consult on the changes, due to take place next year.


They also argued that ministers had failed to consider the impact on children.


But judges rejected the claims, saying the consultation process had been fair.


The campaigners - known as Rather Be Daddy - said they were considering an appeal.


The group's founder, Christopher Jeffery, said the decision was a "dark day for democracy".


"We have never known a government behave in this manner," he added.


The Department for Education (DfE) said the decision reflected the "transparent and thorough" way the government had engaged with the issue.


Under the current rules, introduced in 2014, judges can withhold custody from parents who obstruct contact with the child's other parent.


The government says too many parents are being kept apart from their children because of the current system and has launched a consultation on the changes.

UK military advisers in Iraq have had so much contact with Iranian-backed militias that it has affected their operations, the BBC has been told.


Senior British military sources told the BBC that in the past six months, UK special forces have only been able to operate in Iraq with the consent of Iran-backed militias.


It comes after the UK adviser shot dead in Iraq last week was allegedly wandering outside the secure area of Baghdad airport.


UK officials have suggested the killing was a mistake and that the British soldier had been confused with a American contractor.
The Pentagon has said this account is "consistent with the information we have at present".


Tensions have increased between the UK and Iran - branded a "terrorist state" by the UK government this week - over the death of the British soldier, while the US has suggested that Iran may have been responsible.


UK sources said "a number of UK military advisers" were now embedded with Iraqi security forces, with their roles including "call-out" forces, an elite unit trained to respond quickly to threats.


The sources added that in the past six months these call-out forces have been stood down "multiple times" because of concerns that Iran-backed militias would attack them.


"There have been instances where we have been told by the Iraqis that we cannot operate without the consent of some of the Iranian-backed militias," the sources said.
"That has become a factor in recent months.

Britain must keep its "eyes wide open" to the risks from artificial intelligence and tackle the ethical challenges posed by this "transformative technology", according to a government report released on Thursday.


Smart machines capable of outperforming humans in a range of tasks are set to transform the workplace, with the potential to improve productivity, increase efficiency and reduce costs, according to the 322-page document from the government's Office for Science.


But the report also warns that these developments could entrench existing inequalities, with the potential for automation to disrupt jobs and increase unemployment.
In addition, the use of algorithms in AI could lead to "perverse outcomes", it warns.


The report calls on the government to establish a new body – the Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation – to oversee the use of AI and ensure it delivers positive outcomes.


"Artificial intelligence is a transformative technology which will affect everyone's lives," said the report.
"It has immense potential to improve many aspects of people's lives, from healthcare to transport, crime reduction to financial services.


"But alongside the huge benefits, AI also brings significant challenges.
It could exacerbate inequalities, with potentially damaging consequences for society if left unchecked.
"

The government launched a 12-week consultation on Thursday on the role and responsibilities of the new centre, with a view to establishing it later this year.

A new delay has hit EU efforts to impose restrictions on US tech giants, after a small country vetoed the EU's draft new digital markets law.


Austria said it wanted to defend its people's data against "unjustified access" by big tech companies.


The draft law, known as the Digital Markets Act (DMA), aims to create a level playing field for online platforms.


EU Industry Chief, Internal Market and Services Commissioner Thierry Brighton said: "I am very disappointed that the Council has not managed to adopt this important file".


"All member states, and in particular, those who blocked - deliberately, I think - this decision, simply to gain time, will have to explain to their citizens why they chose to let monopolisers thrive instead of reinforcing the digital single market".


Thierry Brighton, who is also vice-president of the European Commission, said negotiations would continue.


The DMA was proposed by the European Commission more than two years ago and was finally agreed by the EU Parliament in February.


But it has faced opposition from a number of EU member states, including Sweden, Denmark and Norway who have threatened to veto it.


Smaller countries with a thriving tech sector, such as Estonia, have also expressed concerns that the law will hinder innovation and entrench the dominance of big tech.


The DMA is one of a number of initiatives aimed at curbing the power of Big Tech in the EU, alongside the Digital Services Act, which aims to create a safer digital space, and the proposed Artificial Intelligence Act.

The International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) has said it will challenge a decision by Greek authorities to restore the Olympic doping ban on Russian athlete Tatiana Lebedeva.


The 32-year-old triple jumper and long jumper had her suspension overturned by a Greek court last week.


The court ruled that the IAAF had no authority to suspend her for failing to follow an order to compete as a neutral athlete at the 2016 Olympics.


The IAAF said in a statement that it "disagreed" with the decision and indicated it would "contest" it.


"The court in Greece has decided to overwrite key parts of the global regulatory system for athletics," the statement said.


"This overrides the authority of other competitions, including the Olympics.
"

Russia was banned from competing in the 2016 Olympics in Brazil after the World Anti-Doping Agency found evidence of a state-sponsored doping programme.


However, athletes who could prove they were clean were allowed to compete as neutrals.


However, Lebedeva did not attend the Games after being told by the IAAF she must compete as a neutral.


The Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) later ruled that the IAAF had the authority to enforce the ban.

The dollar has fallen to its lowest level in eight months, prompting concerns that the US currency's long-running decline could hurt economies worldwide.


Its decline is a concern for companies that have borrowed in dollars, as it raises the cost of their debts.


"It is a scary scenario for global investors," one analyst said.


"We are in uncharted territory.
"

The dollar has fallen largely against emerging market currencies, led by a near 7% rise against the Brazilian real and a 5% rise against the Russian rouble.


It comes after the Federal Reserve last week indicated it was slowing the pace of interest rate rises, while major central banks - including the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan - continued to loosen policy.


The dollar is down 25% against a basket of currencies from a year ago, when the Fed was actively raising interest rates.


However, it has fallen by only about 6% from its highest level this year, reached in October.


Many emerging market countries have taken advantage of the dollar's weakness to try to boost their economies with stimulus packages.


But analysts say the falling dollar poses a threat, especially to companies which have borrowed in dollars but earn in local currency.

The bank's rate-setting council voted 8-1 to keep the rate on hold
It was the first time in a decade that a majority of members voted for no change
The Bank of England has kept interest rates on hold, following a split decision by its rate-setting committee.


It marked the first time in more than a decade that the majority of the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted to keep rates on hold rather than to cut them.


The bank's rate-setting council voted 8-1 to keep the rate on hold at 0.5%, amid signs that the UK economy is recovering from a Brexit-induced slump.


Only last month, the MPC reduced the base rate from 0.75% to 0.5% in response to a global economic slowdown and no-deal Brexit fears.


But data released since then appears to show that the UK economy is weathering the Brexit storm better than expected, and that employers are still hiring.


'No need to panic'
The MPC's decision was welcomed by businesses, with the Confederation of British Industry saying it would help to keep "confidence high".


"The Bank of England's decision to hold rates is important for businesses as it signals no need to panic over the economy," said CBI chief economist Rain Newton-Smith.


"Although we face challenges, the lower base rate and reduced uncertainty about the UK's future relationship with the EU have helped make our exports more competitive.
"

However, Ian Wright, chief economist at Britain's biggest business group, the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB), said that "many small firms will be disappointed" by the decision.


"The majority of firms would have liked to see the base rate cut to 0.25% to help them tackle the upfront costs of complying with Brexit," he said.

text:
The governor of the Bank of England has played down fears of a UK recession, despite economic data showing the country's economy shrank in the second quarter of 2022.


At the conclusion of the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting, Governor Andrew Bailey said that while there was clear evidence the economy was weakening, it was not yet clear how much energy price rises and consequent inflationary pressures were affecting spending.


He said the MPC was "not convinced" that the links between inflation and spending "are entirely linear".


Earlier on Wednesday, official figures showed the UK economy shrank by 0.1% between April and June, compared with the first three months of the year.


That followed a 0.8% contraction in the first quarter of 2022, meaning the UK has been in recession for two consecutive quarters, according to accepted economic definitions.


But Mr Bailey said that the committee was "not in agreement" that the UK was in recession, despite the "very large impact" of external factors, including the Ukraine war and lockdown in China.


He added that the Bank did not "want to get into a situation" where it was making "direct references" to recessions "on a month-to-month basis".


However, Mr Bailey did admit that the Bank had been "wrong" in its recent economic forecasts that predicted inflation would fall back naturally without the need for higher interest rates.


He said the Bank had been "surprised" that price rises had happened at a faster pace and lasted longer than expected, but added that its "best judgement" at the moment was that inflation would come down "pretty rapidly" next year.


The MPC voted unanimously to raise interest rates from 1.25% to 1.75% on Wednesday, the highest level since 2009, as it attempts to curb double-digit inflation.

text:
House prices have fallen for the sixth month in a row, according to figures from the Halifax.


The mortgage lender said prices dropped by 1.5% in November, following a 1.6% fall in October.


It said the market had seen a slowdown in activity in recent months, with the number of properties for sale falling by 5% between September and October.


Halifax said the average UK house price was £274,311 in November, which was just £1,613 higher than a year earlier.


"In recent months we have seen evidence that buyer demand has started to wane in response to the expiry of tax breaks designed to support the market, coupled with rising interest rates and a natural tapering of demand as we move into the quieter winter months," said Halifax managing director Russell Galley.


"Looking ahead, there is a combination of factors which could lead to a slowdown in house price growth, including the potential for higher interest rates, the winding down of government buyouts and increasingly stretched household budgets," he added.


However, Galley also said there was still a shortage of properties for sale, which he thought should continue to support prices.


According to Halifax, prices are still rising much more quickly than average wages, with average house prices now seven times average salaries, compared with about five times two decades ago.


Earlier this month, rival lender Nationwide reported that UK house prices fell by 2.3% in November, leaving them 3.2% higher than a year earlier.
It said the slowdown reflected "a natural lull" in activity after the end of the stamp duty holiday in September, and the withdrawal of government support for the housing market.

The 35-year-old starred as the murdered singer Ray Charles in the film, which has been nominated for best picture.


"This is beyond my wildest dreams," he told a news conference in Los Angeles.


Foxx is up against fellow singer-turned-actor Joaquin Phoenix, who played singer Johnny Cash in Walk the Line.


The Golden Globes take place in Los Angeles on 16 January and will be shown live on BBC One.


Foxx's performance has already won him several awards, including the Las Vegas Film Critics Society and the Broadcast Film Critics Association awards for best actor.


He has also been nominated for a Screen Actors Guild award, with the winners due to be announced on 30 January.


The other best actor nominees are George Clooney for Good Night, and Good Luck, Leonardo DiCaprio for The Aviator, and Ian McKellen for The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King.


Foxx said he had been so focused on his performance in Ray he had not thought about awards.


"When I got into this project I didn't think about awards, I just thought about honouring this man's life," he said.

Liverpool chairman Tom Werner has warned the English game is "close to burning out" young players and says Academy chief Alex Inglethorpe has been asked to help protect against it.


Werner was speaking as Liverpool opened their state-of-the-art Academy on Friday.


The £50m complex, which sees the club return to Kirkby on a site close to Liverpool's old stadium, has been specifically designed to develop and nurture young players.


"One of the things we're concerned about is young players getting burned out," said Werner, who is also the Fenway Sports Group's chairman.


"We have discussions with Alex Inglethorpe, our academy director, all the time about weaning these young players so they can develop gradually, because that is what is required if they are to have long careers.


"It's pretty clear English football is close to burning out young players.
You see the numbers that get played at a young age.
The notion of 'super-sub' doesn't seem to exist in England.
In Germany and Spain, players are much more developed when they get to the first team.
"

Liverpool manager Jurgen Klopp is among those to have expressed concern about the physical demands being placed on young players, who can struggle to cope with the expectation to perform well in their early games for the club while adapting to the step up in intensity from youth football.

Disney has given its support to Sony's new high definition DVD format, a move which is likely to give the format a huge boost.


The decision is a major boost for the Sony HD DVD format, which is competing with a rival offering from Toshiba.


Disney's support will give the HD DVD format a huge lift, as the company controls some of the most popular films, including Star Wars and Pixar animations.


The format war has been going on for nearly two years, ever since Toshiba launched its HD DVD format, backed by Microsoft and Intel.


Sony later launched its own version, and now seems to be winning the battle, with a growing number of supporters.


Last week, US retailer Best Buy said it would stock the HD DVD players and movies in its stores.


This week, US director James Cameron said he had tested both HD DVD and Blu-ray and decided the HD DVD was superior.


"HD DVD is winning the format war, hands down," he said.


However, not all supporters of Blu-ray have given up hope.


Apple chief executive Steve Jobs, a strong backer of the Blu-ray format, said he believed that Blu-ray had broader support among consumers and he was confident it would prevail.

EU ministers to mull jet fuel tax

Brussels has rejected a proposal to include aviation in the EU's carbon trading scheme, instead tasking a group of officials with drawing up reports on alternative measures, including a kerosene tax.


The European Commission proposed including aviation in the EU's carbon market as part of its strategy for reducing greenhouse gas emissions.


But it was met with opposition from member states, which will now ask a group of officials to draw up reports on alternative measures, which will include increasing the price of kerosene.


The UK government welcomed the development, having previously expressed concerns that including aviation in the carbon market could hurt economic growth.


"We have always been clear that we want to see the aviation industry playing its part in reducing emissions, but that this must be done in a fair and sustainable way," a spokesperson for the Department for Transport said.


"We will continue to work with our European partners to ensure the aviation sector meets its environmental obligations.
"

Green groups expressed disappointment at the decision not to include aviation in the carbon market, saying it was a setback for efforts to reduce emissions.


"The Commission's original proposal to include aviation in the EU ETS (Emissions Trading Scheme) was the most cost-effective and efficient solution for tackling rising emissions from the sector," said Bill Hemmings, aviation director at the Transport & Environment (T&E) campaign group.


"All other options, such as a kerosene tax, are either ineffective or unfair.
"

Italy's Parmalat has sued 45 banks for allegedly causing the dairy group's financial collapse in 2003 by pulling the plug on credit lines and disseminating false information. 


The group, which was founded in 1961 by Sicilian entrepreneur Calisto Tanzi, once had a market value of around €14bn (£12bn). 


However, its financial collapse - the biggest bankruptcy in European corporate history - left it with debts of €35bn. 


Parmalat filed a lawsuit against the banks in 2011, but a number of legal issues meant that it has only now got to court. 


The company is seeking €480m in damages.
It has accused banks, including Credit Suisse, Citibank, Deutsche Bank, and Nomura Bank, of inducing its financial crisis through "illegal" short-selling - a practice where shares are borrowed and sold with the aim of buying them back later at a lower price. 


Short-selling is legal, but it becomes illegal when done with knowledge that the objective is to drive down the price of a stock, a practice known as "short and distort". 


The 45 banks are all being sued for this reason, with the exception of seven banks for which Parmalat only has evidence of "unfair conduct" and "negligence". 


These seven are Bank of America, Barclays, BNP Paribas, Credit Agricole, HSBC, JP Morgan and Société Générale. 


The trial is expected to last for three months.

Kevin Spacey's first leading movie role since being fired from House of Cards over sexual assault allegations will receive its UK debut this month. 


The Renaissance actor will play a grieving father in the drama All Access.
It will screen at this year's Edinburgh film festival.
The festival's director, Ed Strachan, described the film as "raw" and "very powerful". 


All Access will be shown on 20 June, about two months after its debut at South By Southwest in Austin, Texas.
The film's UK distributor, Dogwoof, decided to give the movie its UK premiere at Edinburgh. 


All Access is about a father who loses his daughter in a car crash.
He meets the occupants of a neighbouring cabin on a trip to the mountains to try to cope with his grief. 


The film's director, Randall Miller, pleaded guilty in 2012 to charges relating to the death of an passenger in a car crash.
He was sentenced to two years in prison.

The American firm that bought the Lacroix label hopes its flashy designs will catch on in the United States.


Guess, which is known for its jeans, bought the licence for the French fashion house's ready-to-wear collection last year and launched the first collection under the new ownership in October.


The firm now plans to launch its first Lacroix fragrance next year.


"It has always been my dream to see the Lacroix brand come to life," said the designer's widow, Frances, who retains an advisory role on the label.


"I truly believe that the creativity of the Lacroix brand is timeless and will be embraced by the Guess customer," she added.


For its part, Guess sees potential in Lacroix's flamboyant style, which contrasts with its own classic American designs.


"The opportunity always existed to take this brand global," said Guess chairman and CEO Maurice Marciano.


"This is not a passing fad, this is something that is going to last for a long time and we want to be a big part of it," he added.


Mr Marciano said the firm planned to open 20 Lacroix stores worldwide over the next five years.
There are currently seven Lacroix shops, including three in France.

People in China can now send text messages to donate money to help victims of last month's earthquake in Nepal.


The donation system, launched by China's largest microblogging site Weibo, allows users to donate one yuan ($0.16; £0.10) by sending a message with the word "help" to a special phone number.


The scheme was set up by Chinese internet company Sina - which owns Weibo.
It said it would ensure that "every penny" reaches charity organisations.


More than 8,000 people were killed when a 7.8-magnitude quake struck Nepal on 25 April.


The Weibo campaign was launched on Monday and within hours had raised more than 5m yuan ($800,000; £500,000), according to Chinese media reports.


Users can donate up to 20 times via one phone number.


The devastating earthquake in Nepal has been widely covered in Chinese media and has stirred tremendous sympathy among the Chinese public, particularly as the magnitude of the disaster is still unfolding.


Chinese officials said this week that China will provide another $10m in aid to Nepal, in addition to the $1.5m it offered shortly after the quake.


The Chinese government has also sent several aircraft carrying tents, clothes, medical teams and other emergency relief supplies.

Russian oil giant Yukos has blamed China for its breakup, saying the Asian country had pressured it into selling its main production unit.


Yukos accused the Chinese government of "aggressive intervention" in Russia's internal affairs for influencing Russian President Vladimir Putin into seizing the company's main production unit, Yukos Oil.


The Kremlin nationalised Yukos in 2004, after the firm's founder, Mikhail Khodorkovsky, was arrested on charges of tax evasion and fraud.


The oil firm, now known as Rosneft, was sold off last year in a sell-off ordered by Mr Putin.


Yukos filed for bankruptcy in August 2006, and its main production unit was sold to state firm Rosneft in December.


In a statement, Yukos said China had exerted "substantial and decisive influence on the behaviour" of the Russian government, and had pressured Moscow into seizing Yukos Oil.


Yukos also said China had influenced Russian courts to return the "unfair" tax assessment, which was used as a reason to nationalise the firm.


In a statement, the Chinese embassy in Moscow said the accusations were "groundless".


"China's position on the Yukos issue is clear and consistent," it said.


"China hopes the Russian side can correctly handle the relevant issue, and maintain the healthy development of bilateral economic and trade co-operation.

text:
David Moyes has reversed his decision to dismiss Walter Smith as Scotland coach and has offered him a new two-year contract.


The Scottish Football Association (SFA) announced at the weekend that Smith would leave his job at the end of June.


But SFA president George Peat revealed on Tuesday that he had received a phone call from Moyes, who told him that he was unhappy with the decision and wanted to discuss the matter.


"I can confirm that Scotland manager Walter Smith will be staying and has been offered a new contract," said Peat.


"I made it quite clear to David Moyes that in the eyes of the board, Walter Smith has done an excellent job and should continue.


He added: "David has assured me he will be giving Walter his full support.
Times have changed and we all have to move on.


"I accepted what David told me and we agreed that it would not be appropriate for me to go into details about his decision.


"I got the impression that he had not realised how much importance the board attach to Walter."

Moyes, who took over at Manchester United following the retirement of Sir Alex Ferguson, had intended to bring in his own man.


He met SFA chief executive Gordon Smith on Friday, but did not contact the president or any other board member before Smith's sacking was made public.

The following is a brief summary:

The authors of a new study warn that malicious web sites and emails are helping the fast-spreading ransomware virus, called WannaCry, to propagate.
They say it is the largest ransomware attack ever seen.
The cyber attack has hit more than 200,000 users in at least 150 countries.
The hackers are demanding a ransom of $US300 ($A400) in virtual currency Bitcoin, to release files.
The attack has been described by Europol, the EU's law enforcement agency, as "unprecedented".
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was "hugely important" that organisations patched the flaw in Windows that the malware was exploiting as quickly as possible.


It appears that those behind the attack have not yet decided whether to unlock the seized files, creating an atmosphere of chaos.
Thus far, no-one has received any of the unlocking software promised by the hackers - just a demand for money.
In the UK, the attack has been felt most strongly in the National Health Service (NHS).
On Friday, 45 NHS organisations, including hospitals and doctors' surgeries, were hit.

text:
Former home secretary David Blunkett says he is proud of his time in Tony Blair's government and does not regret the introduction of university top-up fees or the Iraq war.


The Sheffield Brightside MP also denied his decision to resign as education secretary in 2001 over the widening child benefit scandal was a factor in the subsequent inquiry's findings.


And he defended his record as home secretary, saying he had been "a good reforming minister".


Mr Blunkett was speaking as he launched his autobiography, 'Beyond the Clouds', at the Labour Party conference in Brighton.


He told the BBC that the current Labour leadership had to accept that the party had moved on since Mr Blair's time in charge and it could not simply recreate the 'New Labour' era.


But he added that he did not believe Ed Miliband could lead the party to victory at the next general election and said the situation was 'desperate'.


Mr Blunkett served in the Cabinet for seven years from 2001 to 2008, first as education and employment secretary, then as home secretary and finally as secretary of state for communities and local government.


He was forced to resign from the Cabinet after revealing he had accidentally failed to declare a series of interests in a parliamentary register.


'Blind faith'
In his autobiography, Mr Blunkett reveals that he was one of only a handful of ministers who supported the Iraq war from the beginning.


He said there was no evidence of weapons of mass destruction immediately prior to the invasion of Iraq, but that it was his belief that the intelligence services were correct in their original assessments.

text:
Once revered as a groundbreaking games console, the Commodore 64 is now 30 years old.
But a new version of the machine has just been launched, promising to do what the original did three decades ago: take on the might of Nintendo and Atari.
The new C64 is a hybrid machine that pairs the original C64's hardware with modern components, including a HDMI port, Ethernet port and a cartridge slot for newer games.
The machine is aimed at both nostalgic older gamers who want to revisit the past, as well as a new generation of players who were not even born when the C64 was at its height.
In an interview with the BBC at the Retro Computer Museum in Leicester, one of the new C64's designers, Jeri Ellsworth, demonstrates how some of the new games work. 


She says newer titles - such as a version of the famous arcade game Pac-Man - have been developed to make the most of the new hardware, rather than simply porting across the original games.
"We have a cartridge slot so you can put in other games," she says.
"It's not just about playing the old games, it's about making new games - that's where it's at."
The new C64 can even be used as a controller to play games on a PC or Mac, linking up via a USB cable.
But for many Commodore fans, it is the original games that are of most interest.

"We have a cartridge slot so you can put in other games," she says.
"It's not just about playing the old games, it's about making new games - that's where it's at."
The new C64 can even be used as a controller to play games on a PC or Mac, linking up via a USB cable.
But for many Commodore fans, it is the original games that are of most interest.

Microsoft is launching a new search engine that it says can scour a user's computer in seconds, as it takes on Google in the battle for search.


The software, to be called Windows Desktop Search, is designed to find anything on a PC, including emails, documents, music and photos.


It will be available as a free download in the next couple of months, Microsoft said.


The move comes as Microsoft is struggling to catch up with Google's dominance of the internet search market.


Microsoft's share of the US internet search market stood at 7.7% in February, compared with Google's 38.5%, according to research firm comScore.


Windows Desktop Search will only work on computers using the latest Windows operating system, Windows XP, and will not be available for Mac or Linux users.


In a statement, Microsoft said: "With Windows Desktop Search, you can find virtually anything on your PC... fast.


"Enter a word or phrase in the Search box and Windows Desktop Search will find it no matter where it appears on your PC - in your emails, documents, presentations, music, photos, and even your Outlook contacts, because it searches against the full text of each file.
"


The software will also be integrated with Microsoft's new Office system, due out later this year.

Palestinian economy in decline

Large budget deficit and growing debt burden compounded by coronavirus pandemic


The Palestinian economy is in decline with a large budget deficit and growing debt burden compounded by the coronavirus pandemic, the World Bank has warned.


The bank urged Israel to improve economic ties with the Palestinians, and for the international community to offer greater support.


It said that real GDP in the Palestinian territories is expected to shrink by 11.5% in 2020, but modest growth is expected to resume next year.


The World Bank's report said that the West Bank's economy has been growing at a slow rate in the past 15 years, and the Gaza Strip has experienced a prolonged economic crisis.


"Growth has been stagnant, unemployment has risen, and poverty has increased, especially in Gaza," the report said.


"Societal fragility, including trust in institutions, has declined, and the fiscal situation has deteriorated, with debt rising and fiscal space limited."


The coronavirus pandemic has hit the Palestinian economy hard, with lockdowns and restrictions disrupting businesses, and few resources available to help households and businesses weather the economic fallout.


In the first quarter of 2020, the West Bank and Gaza saw their economies contract by 7.6% and 11.2% respectively, with more than half of the active workforce in the West Bank and three-quarters in Gaza losing their jobs.


The World Bank is calling on Israel to carry out long-delayed reforms to ease restrictions on the movement of people and goods that harm the Palestinian economy.

BBC News:
Cycling:
Laporte tinkers with team

Ex-mountain bike world champion Catherine Pendrel has switched from the Canadian national team to the American one ahead of the world championships later this month.


Pendrel, who won the world title in 2008 and 2010, will now race for United States-based Cyclocross Racing Inc (CRI) team.


The 29-year-old from Vancouver will link up with American Katie Compton, who has won the last six US national cyclo-cross titles.


"I looked at all my options and talked with a lot of people, and in the end it seemed like the perfect fit," Pendrel told Cyclingnews.com.


"It will be fun to race with Katie.
I think we will work well together.
She is always at the front and obviously very fast, so I will have a chance to race at the front too.
"

Pendrel has struggled with injury since the London Olympics, where she finished fifth in the cross-country mountain bike race.

European Union and US officials are seeking to resolve a 16-year-old dispute over airline schedules to offer greater certainty to carriers, according to the EU.


The "capacity allocation" dispute began in 2004, when US airlines complained about increasing numbers of night flights and early morning arrivals by European airlines - mainly Irish - at US airports.


The two sides have been talking about the issue for several years, but have now "stepped up" negotiations, the EU said.


A deal could offer more than $1bn (£800m) in benefits to both sides, it added.


The dispute, which has been running since before the current Covid-19 pandemic, relates to the number of slots - or takeoff and landing spaces - that airlines can use at crowded airports.


US airlines complained in 2004 that a surge in flights by Air Lingus and Ryanair between the EU and the US was damaging their businesses.


The US Department of Transportation (DOT) subsequently limited the number of flights that could be operated by Air Lingus and Ryanair between the US and the EU.


The two Irish airlines responded by switching to flying to the US via Canada, with some flights stopping off in the Caribbean.


The EU said at the time that the move by the US breached its airspace rights.


Talks to resolve the issue have moved slowly.

text:
WorldCom director accused of fraud denies allegations

Mr Ebbers became the highest-ranking corporate official arrested so far in the five-month-old probe of an alleged $3.8bn (£2.43bn) accounting fraud at the US telecoms giant.


He stepped down as WorldCom's chief executive last May, admitting that the company had cooked its books to exaggerate profits.


But the former boss - who transformed WorldCom from a small long-distance phone company into a global telecommunications giant through a series of mergers - maintained he had not done anything wrong.


The US securities and exchange commission (SEC) accused Mr Ebbers of violating securities laws "by knowingly or recklessly making materially false and misleading statements" in WorldCom's annual report and other documents.


Mr Ebbers, who surrendered his passport and was released on a $10m (£6.3m) bond, is due to appear in court in New York on Friday.


He faces up to 20 years in prison and $5m (£3.2m) in fines if convicted.


Prosecutors said his arrest was part of an ongoing investigation.


WorldCom, which has filed for bankruptcy protection, has announced that it expects to pay only cents on the dollar to its shareholders once its assets are sold.


The New York-based firm had promised to pay out $8.4bn (£5.4bn) in dividends in 2003.


Last week, WorldCom appointed former US Attorney General Richard Thornburgh as its new chairman as it tries to emerge from bankruptcy.

"The Rangers FC player James Tavernier has been suspended for two (2) UEFA competition matches for which he would be otherwise eligible, for violating the UEFA Disciplinary Regulations during the match.

Celtic's Leigh Griffiths and Rangers' James Tavernier were given two-match bans for their part in the incident.


Griffiths was dismissed following a fracas involving the two teams in the tunnel while Tavernier had received a yellow card earlier in the match for a challenge on Celtic's Olivier Ntcham.


The Scottish Professional Football League conducted an investigation into the incident and announced the suspensions on 12 September.


Celtic and Rangers appealed against the sanctions, however, European football's governing body has found both clubs guilty of "order maintenance" and the punishments will stand.


A Uefa statement read: "The UEFA Control, Ethics and Disciplinary Body has dealt with cases arising from the UEFA Europa League group stage match between Celtic FC and Rangers FC (2 September 2022).


"The Celtic FC player Leigh Griffiths has been suspended for two (2) UEFA competition matches for which he would be otherwise eligible, for violating the UEFA Disciplinary Regulations for his actions at the end of the match.


"The Rangers FC player James Tavernier has been suspended for two (2) UEFA competition matches for which he would be otherwise eligible, for violating the UEFA Disciplinary Regulations during the match.

Free sports lessons could be offered to every primary school pupil in England, Conservative MPs say.


A group of Tories has proposed the plan as part of their election manifesto.


It would see all state primary schools offered funding for an additional hour of PE each day.


The aim is to inspire a generation of children to stay fit and healthy, said chair of the Tory backbench sports committee, Nigel Adams.


"It is essential that we invest in our youth now because if we don't, we will pay for it later," he said.


The proposal has been welcomed by Sport England and the National Governors Association.
However, the plan has been criticised by the Labour Party who say the scheme is "half-baked".


Labour's shadow culture secretary, Michael Dugher, said the policy did not contain any "proper new funding".


"This is a pathetic offering from a party that is so devoid of ideas that it is reduced to stealing policies from Labour at election time," he said.


The proposal has been put forward by the Conservative Sport and Physical Activity Alliance, which is made up of about 80 MPs and peers.

Chris Brown has released a song that appears to respond to the woman who allegedly bit him, and threatened to share a sex tape they made.


The singer posted the explicit song on his Instagram page, with the caption "She bit me".


In it, he seems to reference an incident in which a woman punctured his skin with her teeth, and allegedly tried to sell a video of them having sex.


Brown, 36, reportedly filed a police report on Tuesday, after the woman, identified as 27-year-old model Baylee Currieburn, allegedly attacked him at his Los Angeles home.


In the song, Brown sings: "Her teeth sank in, and I was like 'Yo, what the hell is going on?'

"She started gnawing on me, trying to eat off my flesh.
Something wasn't right with that.
"

Currieburn, who claims she met Brown via Instagram, has reportedly been charged with felony vandalism for the alleged bite, according to legal documents.


Police also charged her with felony threatening a crime with the intent to terrorize, and two counts of misdemeanor battery.


The singer tweeted on Wednesday that he was "traumatized" by the incident, and said he had needed surgery to treat the bite marks on his neck.


He said he had asked Currieburn to leave his house after she launched at him, but that she forced her way back inside.

text:
Auction house Graceland has put some of Elvis Presley's personal belongings and historic documents on sale, including the King's first ever recording. 


The item is among more than 1,000 lots offered as part of the Graceland Auctions' 2022 event, which runs until 11 November.


The recording, made when he was 18, features Elvis singing and playing guitar on the songs "Harbor Lights" and "Love of my Life". 


Auction house owner Josh Kincheloe said it was "the earliest known recording of Elvis Presley".


The auction also includes Elvis' personal Bible, a letter he wrote to President Richard Nixon and some of his military uniforms.


Elvis' grandmother, Minnie Mae Presley, bought the Bible for him in 1957.
It features annotations in the singer's handwriting, and is expected to sell for between $50,000 (£43,000) and $70,000 (£59,000).


Elvis wrote to President Nixon in 1970, asking him to designate 22 November as "National Prisoners Day" so that "these men constantly reminded of their failure as men, and not of their possible rehabilitation".


The letter is expected to sell for between $15,000 (£12,300) and $20,000 (£16,600).


Mr Kincheloe said it was "extremely significant" as it revealed "a very different side of Elvis that we don't often get to see".

text:
UK Coal has posted a deeper first-half loss as it continues to suffer on weak coal prices and a strong pound.


The company, which returned to the London Stock Exchange in June, reported a loss of £43.9m ($61.8m) in the six months to 30 June, compared with a loss of £17.2m a year earlier.


The group has been hit by a number of factors, including the strong performance of the pound, weaker coal prices and "high production costs" at one of its sites.


The company has been hit by a number of factors

The strong pound has made its exports more expensive, while coal prices have struggled to recover from their recent historic lows.


The miner also cited "high production costs" at its Thoresby site, where it recently invested in a new "longwall" mining machine.


The group added that it had made a "solid start" to the second half of the year, but uncertainty in the market meant it was "not recommending any dividend for the 2018 financial year".


UK Coal was taken over by a group of investors, including its former management, in April last year.


The firm was delisted from the London Stock Exchange in October 2013 after it was hit by falling coal prices and a tough market for coal miners.


However, it returned to the stock market in June this year, floating on the London Stock Exchange's Alternative Investment Market (AIM).


As part of the float, the company raised £3.5m through a placing of shares priced at 110p each.

UK state pension should be overhauled to include a "good conduct" clause, The Pensions Advisory Service has said.


The government-backed pensions group said too many people still did not understand their retirement options.


Its report called for a simplification of the state pension, including the proposed "good conduct" clause.


This would see the government take into account people's lifestyles and contributions when working out their state pension.


Currently, the state pension is calculated on the number of years a person has worked and the amount they have paid in national insurance contributions.


But the report said this did not take into account whether people had taken active steps to save for their retirement or whether they had taken time out of work to care for children or elderly relatives.


It said the state pension should be "fairer" to these groups of people.


The report also called for a "default" retirement option to be offered to workers, to make sure they did not spend too long in low-return savings vehicles.


At the moment, too many people were staying in the same pension scheme throughout their career, when they would be better off moving to a different scheme, it said.


Default options would help people make better decisions about their retirement savings, it added.

Robert Williams will remain as chief executive of British Gas owner Centrica despite a dispute with the company's biggest shareholder.


The 62-year-old had said he would step down unless Centrica amended its "unacceptable" £610,000 (US$730,000) retirement package.


But the firm's board has decided to accept his request to stay in post.


Mr Williams had asked the board to guarantee his bonus and entitlements despite his planned departure.


The company had said it could not afford the payments as it battled higher energy prices and a government price cap on tariffs.


But it reversed its position after talks with Mr Williams and the company's three major shareholders - Aviva, Royal London and Phoenix Group.


"The board has agreed to proceed with the payment of certain benefits to Robert Williams, which are consistent with his employment contract," Centrica said in a statement.


"This decision was made in the context of the group's ongoing dialogue with its larger shareholders, with a view to maintaining shareholder support for the company's strategy.
"

Under the terms of his departure, Mr Williams - who has led the firm since 2016 - will remain in post until a successor is appointed.


He will be entitled to his full salary until then along with any bonuses and entitlements.

Senior Tory Michael Portillo has said he does not believe an election loss is "inevitable" for his party, despite a series of opinion polls suggesting the Conservatives are on course to lose the next general election.


The former defence secretary told the BBC's Andrew Marr the party had achieved a "remarkable" revival under Theresa May.


But he admitted the party's opinion poll lead had slipped in the last fortnight.


Mrs May announced she would seek a fresh mandate for her government by calling a general election on 8 June.


The Conservatives held a 22-point lead two weeks ago, but some polls have put the lead at just one point.


Mr Portillo said he believed the Conservative lead had slipped because the party had not been "aggressive" enough in its bid to keep the election focus on the issue of strong leadership.


He said the party had been "too polite" and should have made clearer that Labour was the "obvious danger" to the country.


"In the last two weeks, I think we have been too polite about Labour being the obvious danger to the country and we have not driven home that message," he told the BBC's Andrew Marr Show.


"I think we should be assertive and aggressive about the strengths of our offering.
"

The BBC's polling expert, Prof John Curtice, said the slippage in the Tory lead was "not just a blip", with Labour "making ground" on the Conservatives.

text:
Wales star Ben Davies "needs a rest" according to former captain Sam Raddock.


Davies played every minute of Wales' 2022 World Cup campaign, as they reached the semi-finals.


The Tottenham defender, 32, has started all 10 Premier League games this season for his club.


"When you're getting towards the end of your career, you rest for a couple of weeks then start again," Ruddock said.


"When you're younger, like Ben is, you want to play week in, week out, because you're in the shop window - especially when you are playing the way Ben is.


"He is a Rolls Royce, isn't he?
He's classy.
"

Ruddock - who led his country at Euro 2000 and played 49 times for Wales - was speaking as honoured guest at the Football Association of Wales (FAW) awards dinner in Newport.


Wales reached the last four of this year's World Cup in Qatar - their best performance since the 1958 tournament in Sweden - where they lost 2-0 to eventual winners Argentina.


After beating Turkey in the last 16, Wales knocked out pre-tournament favourites Belgium in the quarter-finals.

"Unfortunately, you go along for the ride.

Hundreds of fans gathered outside the airport terminal to greet him after he landed on Friday night.

Former President Donald Trump's senior aide Jason Miller says the so-called "golden rule" of journalism is still intact.


Mr Miller, who was Trump's spokesman, made the comment in response to questions about whether the media had treated the Republican favorably enough during his presidency.


"Maybe you guys should spend less time defending yourselves and focusing on the real enemy, and that's the Biden administration," he told a journalism conference on Thursday.


The "golden rule" refers to the idea that journalists should treat all parties equally and not give favorable coverage to one side.


Mr Miller, who was speaking at the National Press Club in Washington DC, said that he still believed in the rule.


"I think it's a belief that's shared by the majority of Americans, that you guys are fair, you're balanced, you're impartial," he said.
"And frankly, you should be proud of that.
Don't waver from that.
"

Mr Miller served as Trump's spokesman before becoming chief spokesperson for the Republican National Committee.
He is now president of the PR firm Jason Miller Communications.

German growth goes into reverse with economy contracting by 0.1% in second quarter

Germany's economy has shrunk by 0.1% in the second quarter of the year, according to official data.


It is the first time since 2015 that Germany has seen a quarterly decline in GDP and comes after six consecutive quarters of growth.


The Federal Statistics Office said a fall in exports and household spending were behind the drop.


There is concern that the German economy may be losing steam after a long period of expansion.


The data comes as concern about the German car industry mounts.


Last week, BMW cut its outlook for the rest of the year, saying that a slowdown in the car industry had affected its profits, which fell short of expectations.


Volkswagen, the country's largest car maker, last month reported its first quarterly loss in 15 years, as it struggled to recover from the diesel emissions scandal.


The German car industry is a major employer and contributes about 5% of Germany's GDP.


However, the statistics office said that the construction industry had helped to limit the decline in the second quarter.


Construction output increased by 1.6% compared with the first three months of the year, it said.

The family of President George H W Bush has blocked public access to his Texas coastal home, after a man drove his vehicle into a crowd of visitors.


Police in Houston said the driver was arrested and charged with aggravated assault.


The Bush family said the attack was "horrific" and "shameful", and described the block as a "security measure".


The home is in Houston, Texas, and is a national monument managed by the National Park Service.


Police were called to the Bush home, known as Prairie Chapel Ranch, at about 11:20 local time (17:20 GMT) on Wednesday.


"Upon arrival, a man in a pickup truck had entered the grounds of the Bush home after crashing through the gated entrance," Constable Mark Herman said in a statement.


"Investigators determined that the male suspect had intentionally driven his truck into a crowd of visitors," Constable Herman added.


A statement from the Bush family said: "We are devastated by the horrific attack on Mrs Bush's 92nd birthday party yesterday.


"Our family offers its deepest apologies to all those hurt by this shameful act.


"We are grateful for the prompt response of law enforcement and appreciate the efforts of those who jumped into action to assist.

It said the UK's economic performance had been "remarkably robust".


The IMF's global economic forecasts are closely watched by policymakers.

Napster has launched a subscription service offering access to millions of songs for a monthly fee.


The service, Napster Unlimited, is priced at $5 a month for broadband subscribers.


Napster, originally a free music file-sharing service, was shut down in 2001.


It was bought by Roxio, now known as Roxio/Napster, which hopes the new service will help it compete with market leader iTunes.


The service was announced at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas.


Napster Unlimited offers unlimited access to Napster's library of more than eight million songs.
Users will be able to play songs on up to three computers and burn up to three songs a day onto CDs.


The service will be available in the US before the end of January, with a UK launch to follow shortly afterwards, a Napster spokeswoman said.


Roxio competitor iTunes offers a subscription service in conjunction with phone company Verizon, but it is only available to Verizon broadband subscribers and is more expensive than Napster Unlimited.


iTunes is the market leader in legal digital music sales.

UK house prices fell by 0.1% in November 2022, according to a survey by Halifax.


It means prices have dropped for six months in a row, with values 6.9% higher than a year earlier, the mortgage lender said.


Halifax said that prices had been cooling noticeably since the start of the year, adding that the market had "definitely softened" in the last few months.


It added that a combination of inflation, rising interest rates, and a sudden increase in the cost of household goods had led to a sharp fall in disposable income, which had weighed on consumer confidence.


"Given the mounting pressure on household budgets, we expect house price growth to slow further in the coming months," said Halifax managing director Russell Galley.


The figures came as lenders approved the fewest mortgages for house purchases since April 2021, according to industry body UK Finance.


It said that there were 36,597 mortgages approved for house purchases in October, down from 39,327 a year earlier.


Mortgage approvals for home purchases are now at their lowest level since the onset of the Covid pandemic in spring 2020, UK Finance said.


Alice Haine, personal finance analyst at Bestinvest.co.uk, said the housing market was "on the cool down".


"Higher interest rates are making borrowing more expensive, which is likely to have curbed enthusiasm, especially as inflation is still high, meaning household budgets are being squeezed," she said.
