Bayern Munich president Uli Hoeness has warned against the appointment of Laurent Blanc as the new France coach.


The former France captain has emerged as a leading candidate to replace Raymond Domenech after the national team's disastrous showing at the World Cup.


But Hoeness, a former Germany captain, believes Blanc's lack of top-level coaching experience would be a hindrance.


"It's a great shame that French football didn't look for a manager with real top-level experience," he told L'Equipe.


"Appointing Blanc would be a mistake in my view.


"He's done very well with Bordeaux, there's no doubt about that, but that doesn't necessarily mean he is ready to coach France."


Hoeness believes former England manager Sven-Goran Eriksson - who has also been linked with the job - would be a better appointment.


"Eriksson has experience of coaching a national team and that could be important for France," he said.


"He has achieved good results with England and Ivory Coast and he is someone who could be interesting for the French federation.
"

Blanc has been linked with the France job since Domenech was dismissed following the team's early exit from the World Cup.

Sir Ian Corbett, the former director-general of the BBC, has attacked the "dumbing down" of television, arguing that the public service channels are in danger of "losing their way".


Corbett, who was director-general of the BBC from 1982 to 1987, was speaking at the launch of a new book about his predecessor, Hugh Greene.


"There are signs that some broadcasters are already moving in that direction
[of dumbing down]," he said.


"I think they are misunderstanding their publics.
I think they are doing themselves a disservice and, in the end, they will do the public a disservice."


He argued that the public service channels - BBC1, BBC2, Channel 4 and Channel 5 - were "in danger of losing their way".


"They should be providing alternative views," he said.
"They should be providing stuff that isn't immediately accessible but which is worthwhile because it stretches your mind.


"I think they are in danger of forgetting that.

Broadband takes on TV viewing

TV viewing figures on all formats have fallen year on year for the first time since records began, official data shows.


The audience research body Barb said analogue and digital TV viewers watched an average of 3.4 hours of television a day in April, down from 3.6 hours in 2007.


But broadband usage - including web and video - soared, with uploads and downloads increasing by more than 40%.


The figures reflect the growing popularity of the internet as a source of news, entertainment and communication.


They also show the average UK adult now spends almost four hours a day using the internet, compared with less than three hours watching TV.


Of those, more than 80% use the internet daily compared with 60% who watch TV every day.


The data also reveals the average time spent online has increased by at least a quarter in the last year, with the average user spending 14.7 hours a week online, up from 11.8 hours in 2007.


"These figures confirm the directional shift of media consumption in the UK, away from linear broadcast TV towards on-demand TV and broadband," said Jane Ostler, lead analyst at media buyer Carat.


"However, it's too early to state that the age of TV is over, or that the future is solely online," she added.


TV still attracts the largest audiences, but the data does suggest that people are watching less television as they spend more time using the internet.

text:
Brits return Keane to number one

Keane have made it a hat-trick of UK number ones with their latest offering, "Perfect Symmetry".


The band scored their first number one in 2004 with "Somewhere Only We Know", followed by "Is It Any Wonder?" in 2006.


"Perfect Symmetry" has now held on to the top spot for a second week, becoming the fastest-selling release of 2008, the BBC has reported.


The album saw off competition from Leona Lewis, who slipped to number two with her debut, "Spirit", and Muse, who entered at three with "The Resistance".


Keane's achievement marks the first time in a year that the same artist has held the top spot for two consecutive weeks.


The last artist to do so was Cascada with "Everytime We Touch" and "What Hurts the Most".


Keane, who released their debut, "Hopes and Fears", in 2004, said they are "delighted" with the news.


The group released "Perfect Symmetry" in October after a five-year break.


Frontman Tom Chaplin recently told the BBC that the album's title summed up the album's content.


"It's about finding perfect symmetry within your own life, and that can apply to love, to friendship, to family - any kind of relationship you have," he said.

BMW is to spend £100m on a new UK engine plant to produce petrol and diesel engines for the Mini.


The German carmaker said the factory in Hams Hall, Warwickshire, would create about 150 jobs and open in 2020.


It will produce three and four-cylinder engines for Mini models made in Oxford.


BMW said the investment was part of its plans to ensure "long-term production competitiveness".


The company already has an engine plant at Hams Hall where it employs 550 people.


That site will close when the new one opens.


Mini production has been growing steadily, with more than 200,000 cars made in the UK last year.


The bulk are produced in BMW's main UK factory in Cowley, Oxford, which has undergone a series of expansions in recent years.


But around 15,000 Minis are made at a plant in Graz, Austria, which will be closed as part of a restructuring of BMW's European operations.


Production of the Mini Countryman model will be shifted from the Netherlands to Cowley in early 2017.

Soaring oil 'hits world economy'

The soaring price of oil has pushed up the rate of inflation in the world's biggest economies, forcing households to cut back on spending, according to a leading economic think-tank.


The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) said that high oil prices, partly due to the war in Ukraine, were the main reason for the jump in inflation.


It said the price of Brent crude oil would have to fall to around $88 a barrel to bring inflation back to the average level seen over the past decade.


The think-tank said that inflation was likely to be higher than predicted, and that central banks may have to raise interest rates even higher than expected.


The OECD's outlook for the world economy is gloomier than three months ago, with inflation expected to be higher and growth slower.


The organisation expects the global economy to grow by 3.1% this year, down from its forecast of 3.8% made in November.


It also expects inflation to be higher, at 6.3%, up from its previous forecast of 5.6%.


The OECD warned that the war in Ukraine was creating "additional uncertainty" for the world economy.


It said that the war, along with other factors such as the price of oil and the spread of Covid-19, were the key reasons for the downward revision of its growth forecast.


The organisation said it expected the US economy to grow by 2.4% this year, down from its previous forecast of 3.0%.

"He's a world-class player and it's important he's recognised as such," Rodgers said.


"He's been brilliant for me in my time here and he'll continue to be so.
I see this as an important period for him moving forward.
"

Gerrard made his Liverpool debut in 1998 and is the club's third highest all-time appearance maker.


He has won the Champions League, Uefa Cup, FA Cup and League Cup with his boyhood club, as well as the Uefa Super Cup and Fifa Club World Cup.


Gerrard has been tempted to leave Liverpool previously, with Chelsea interest last year, but this time he has not ruled out staying at Anfield.


He said: "I'm not sure how the club views things.

The government has been accused of "playing politics with people's lives" over its changes to asylum seeking.


The Archbishop of Canterbury, Rowan Williams, said the government was setting out to create a "climate of fear" with its new immigration bill.


Speaking in the House of Lords, he said the bill contained "dangerous" provisions.


The government said the bill would make the asylum system "fairer and more efficient".

Spaniard world number two Nadal won the final 11 games of the match to beat Russian fifth seed Rublev in a one-sided encounter.


The 35-year-old Spaniard took the opening set against Rublev, 25, after being a break down before taking control.


Nadal's victory meant he matched Novak Djokovic's record of six titles at the season-ending event.


The match between Nadal and Rublev was the first singles match of the tournament after rain disrupted the schedule on Sunday.


The pair had not met since 2019, when Nadal won all three of their matches, including a final in Rome.


Rublev, who is part of a new generation of players looking to challenge the likes of Nadal, Djokovic and Roger Federer, played well in the early stages but could not maintain his level.


The Russian had break points in the opening game of the match but could not take them and Nadal broke serve in the next game and again in the final game of the first set.


That proved the catalyst for Nadal to take control, dropping just five more games as he improved his head-to-head record against Rublev to 7-1.


Nadal will be hoping to continue his good form in the Red Group, which also features Djokovic and Daniil Medvedev, when he faces the world number one on Tuesday.


"I played a great match against a tough opponent and in general terms I am super happy," Nadal said.

The Conservative Party has rejected calls to readmit a MP it expelled from the parliamentary party last year.


Christian Wakeford was ejected from the Tory group after defecting to the Labour Party.


On Tuesday, former Conservative leader Sir Iain Duncan Smith said the MP should be readmitted.


But Tory chairman Oliver Dowden said the party had "moved on" from Mr Wakeford, who he said had "chose to leave".


Mr Wakeford, who represented Bury South, switched allegiance in November 2022, claiming then - as now - that the Tories had become a "toxic brand" and were not fit to lead.


In a dramatic day in the Commons, the MP told Prime Minister Boris Johnson he no longer represented the people of Bury South - before announcing he was joining Labour.


That led to Tory MPs swiftly ejecting him from the Conservative Party group in the House of Commons.


Sir Iain Duncan Smith had called for the Conservative Party to "forget the past" and readmit Mr Wakeford, saying the MP had not been motivated by money when he switched sides.


Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking podcast, the MP for Chingford and Woodford Green said: "I think if somebody crosses the floor, if they decide they want to come back and give it a second thought and say, 'Look, I've decided I made a mistake, I want to come back,' I think it's time for us to say, 'Yes, OK, you can come back in.'
"

But Mr Dowden told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the party had "moved on" from Mr Wakeford, adding he had "chosen to leave".

Striking teachers, firefighters, and railway workers were joined by nurses and other health workers on the second day of a national strike in Wales.


Nurses and other health workers who are members of the Unite union will join the strike on Wednesday.
They will be followed by teachers, who are members of the National Association of Head Teachers and the National Union of Teachers.


Public sector workers across Wales have been striking over pay.
The Welsh government says it cannot afford to meet the wage demands of workers.


Negotiations have been held between the government and the public sector trade unions.
But talks broke down at the weekend, with no new dates for further discussions agreed.


Wednesday's strike is the first time nurses have gone on strike in Wales.


Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said: "Our nurses have been left with no choice but to take strike action in an attempt to improve pay and staffing levels.
"

Pension schemes managed by the UK's biggest employers have seen their funding positions improve in the past year thanks to healthy investment returns and higher contributions from scheme sponsors.
According to consulting firm Mercer, the 100 largest pension schemes had combined assets of £97.2bn at the end of last year.
This compares with £86.8bn in 2020.
Over the same period, the schemes' combined deficit fell to £56.4bn from £64.5bn.
David Ellis, senior partner at Mercer, said: "Sponsors have continued to focus on improving scheme funding and securing benefits for members.
"

The news comes as schemes prepare for changes to the way they measure pension fund solvency that come into force in 2023.
The pensions industry is hoping the Government will clarify how they will implement new regulations affecting pension transfers.
Five million people saved in defined benefit pension schemes face changes to how their retirement savings are calculated.
Changes to pension transfer values could mean scheme members get less money if they choose to leave their pension schemes.
The industry body for pension schemes, the Pensions and Lifetime Savings Association, has urged ministers to make changes so that schemes can implement the new rules from April as planned.

UKIP has been talking up the prospects of electing its first MP at next month's by-election in Rochester and Strood.


Its candidate, Mark Reckless, is favourite to win the seat, which was held by the Conservative Party before he defected to UKIP.


And the party is also boasting about the impact its candidate in Yorkshire, Nikki Sinclaire, could have at the 2015 general election.


But it is the candidate in third place, at Bethnal Green and Bow in London, who could prove to be UKIP's secret weapon, boosting the chances of both Mr Reckless and Ms Sinclaire.


It is a safe Labour seat, whose MP is Rushanara Ali - so the chances of UKIP winning it are tiny.


But the party is using the by-election as a testbed for its campaign machinery ahead of next year's general election.


And the candidate they have chosen, Lawrence Webb, could end up having a significant impact on the two seats UKIP thinks it can win.


In 2010, he came third in Essex Police's campaign to recruit police community support officers, with more than 1,000 people voting for him.


He then applied to be a UKIP candidate and came third in the London mayoral election in 2012.


He has managed to get himself selected as UKIP's candidate for Bethnal Green and Bow twice - the first time he stood down so the party could field someone else who was subsequently elected as an MEP.

Chelsea's winning start to the season came to a halt as Chris Wood's strike and a Ben Mee own goal handed Burnley a 2-2 draw at Stamford Bridge.


The Blues looked to be heading for a win that would have seen them join Liverpool and Manchester City as the only sides with maximum points after two games.


Alvaro Morata's first goal since his move from Real Madrid put Chelsea ahead in the first half but Wood capitalised on a poor clearance from Cesar Azpilicueta to level before half-time.


Mee then turned in a Wood cross early in the second half to put the visitors in front, but Burnley's cheers were silenced by a wonder strike from Marcos Alonso and Chelsea captain Gary Cahill's late red card.


The defender was given a second yellow card following a challenge on Wood, leaving his side to see out the final minutes with 10 men.


The draw means Chelsea have four points from their first two games, while Burnley have two.


Here are the key points from the game:

1.
Chelsea struck the woodwork twice with Pedro and Cahill going close, while Burnley's Stephen Ward was sent off late on following two bookings.


2.
The Blues had 71% of possession and registered 12 shots to the visitors' five, but Sean Dyche's side managed to hold on for a draw.

The UK should give developing countries £5.5bn ($6.6bn) to fight AIDS, Gordon Brown has said.


The former prime minister made the call ahead of the G8 summit in Canada next week.


He said the "penny-pinching" of recent years had to stop if the world was to make a real impact on the disease.


And he said a comprehensive strategy was needed to tackle the virus, including affordable drugs, more prevention and a rollout of testing.


The UK has already spent £15bn on fighting the disease in the developing world.
But Mr Brown said this was still not enough.


He said: "Diseases know no borders and in a world as interconnected as ours, neither can our efforts to combat them.
"

Mr Brown said he was encouraged by the progress that had been made in the last decade, with more than two million lives saved in Africa.


But he added: "We are now at a pivotal moment.
Without greater action, AIDS could explode in the developing world.

Plans to create a "super union" for journalists in the UK have been touted as a way to tackle the growing power of tech giants like Google and Facebook, following the collapse of the industry's regulator.


The News Media Association (NMA), which represents UK news media outlets, made the proposal to merge the National Union of Journalists (NUJ) and the Broadcasting, Entertainment, Communications and Theatre Union (BECTU) at the weekend.


The plan would create a union of more than 40,000 journalists, making it the largest journalists' union in the world and one of the biggest in the UK.


It comes after the collapse of the News Media Association's regulatory body, the Independent Press Standards Organisation (IPSO), following the departure of a number of major publishers including the Guardian, the Financial Times and the Daily Mail.


IPSO's demise has led to calls for a new system of independent press regulation, with some arguing that the UK needs a "super regulator" to tackle the dominance of tech giants like Google and Facebook, which have been accused of using their dominance to exploit news publishers.


The NMA's proposal for a "super union" would give journalists more power in negotiations with publishers and help them fight for better wages and conditions.


It could also give journalists a stronger voice in the debate over press regulation and help them campaign for a new system that is independent of both the government and the industry.


The idea of a "super union" has been welcomed by some journalists, with one NUJ member saying it was a "great idea" that would give journalists "more clout".


However, others have expressed concern that it could lead to a dilution of the NUJ's core values and a loss of its unique identity.


The NUJ's general secretary, Michelle Stanistreet, said the union would "consider any proposal that enhances our ability to better defend journalists and our industry".

The IMF has agreed to give Turkey a fresh loan of more than $3bn to support the country's economy.


The announcement came at the end of a visit to Ankara by the IMF's managing director, Kristalina Georgieva.


She said the $3.6bn (£2.8bn) loan would be subject to regular reviews "to ensure it remains tailored to Turkey's needs".


The lira has lost more than 40% of its value since the start of the year.


Ms Georgieva said the IMF was "pleased to support Turkey's ambitious and decisive policy agenda".


The loan agreement comes after Turkey's finance minister announced a new economic programme to revive the struggling economy.


The reforms include reducing the government's expenditure and current account deficit, boosting exports and increasing the country's revenue.


However, the Turkish lira fell 5% against the dollar after the loan was announced, before recovering its losses.


The currency has been hit by the Turkish government's attempts to reduce inflation, which stands at around 20%, by raising interest rates.


But analysts say the rate hikes are not enough to tackle the country's inflation problem.

Chelsea looked set to secure their place in the last 16 of the Champions League despite a 3-3 draw with Zenit Saint Petersburg as Ben Chilwell's strike appeared to have won the game, but a 92nd minute equaliser from Magomed Ozdoyev took the game to penalties, in which the Blues would ultimately lose following a save from Zenit's goalkeeper from Chelsea's fifth penalty. 


Chelsea had taken the lead early on when Christian Pulisic capitalized on a mistake in the Zenit defence before tapping the ball beyond Stanislav Casteels in the sixth minute.
The American forward almost doubled Chelsea's lead shortly after when his close-range shot was palmed away by Casteels.


The visitors responded shortly after when Wendel's header from a corner was pushed onto the post by Kepa Arrizabalaga.
But the hosts remained on top and took a 2-0 lead when Hakim Ziyech's cross was controlled and finished by Timo Werner.


The Blues had chances to put the game to bed before half-time, as Ben Chilwell hit the post and Werner saw an effort cleared off the line.
But they were made to pay for their misses as the half-time substitute Artyom Dzyuba pulled one back for Zenit just after the hour mark when he headed home from a free-kick. 


The game was turned on its head when Wendel scored with a powerful strike following a quick counterattack to make it 2-2 with 20 minutes to go.
There were just nine minutes remaining when Chilwell scored from a tight angle to seemingly win the game for Chelsea. 


But there was to be one last twist as Magomed Ozdoyev scored in the 92nd minute to take the game to penalties, and Zenit ultimately won the shootout 4-1.

The former boss of failed US telecoms firm WorldCom has pleaded not guilty to fraud charges.


Bernard Ebbers appeared in a New York court on Tuesday to face charges he concealed more than $3.8bn in losses from shareholders.


The 65-year-old former WorldCom chief executive officer (CEO) entered his plea before US District Judge Barbara Jones.


He was freed on bail pending his trial, scheduled to begin on 1 November 2004.


Prosecutors had argued that Ebbers should be denied bail, claiming he posed a flight risk.


They said he had access to large sums of cash and property in Canada, and that mental health tests had indicated he was likely to flee the US.


But Judge Jones ruled that Ebbers could be released on a $10m (£5.6m) bond, and ordered him to remain in the US, surrender his passport and restrict his travel to the New York area.


She also barred him from contacting WorldCom's three other former chief executives and a number of the firm's accountants and lawyers.


Ebbers was arrested on Friday at his home in Houston, Texas.


At the time of his arrest, US Attorney General John Ashcroft said: "Mr Ebbers operated WorldCom like a Ponzi scheme, relying on the constant infusion of new shareholders' money to cover up the fraud.

The price of petrol has been frozen for the twelfth month in a row, the chancellor has said.


Rishi Sunak said he would exercise his power to delay the inevitable increase in line with inflation until March next year.
The move will save motorists an average of £1.30 per litre, or £19 per tank.


The chancellor said the measure, which will apply to diesel and petrol, was part of the government's plan to help people with the cost of living.


Mr Sunak said: "We know that people are worried about the cost of living, so to help with that we're freezing duty on petrol," he said.


The decision mirrors last year's freeze, which was also announced in November and lasted until March.


The announcement was met with a mixed reaction from motoring groups.


The RAC said the move would provide some relief from record prices, but added it was "only a temporary solution".


"We need to encourage drivers to swap to electric cars, by improving charging infrastructure and offering financial incentives," said RAC fuel spokesman Simon Williams.


"But upfront costs need to be reduced too, especially as inflation is now starting to bite into household income.

Former England boss Robson warns current coach Mourinho about the dangers of burning out his career.
Mourinho has won trophies at every club he has managed, but Robson says he should not be judged solely on his success.
Mourinho was appointed Tottenham manager in November 2019 and although he led the club to a Carabao Cup final and a Europa League final last season, they finished in sixth place in the Premier League.


Robson said he did not believe the "maverick" Portuguese manager would end his career at Spurs.
"They [Spurs] are a top, top club, but it's difficult to break that top four at the moment," he added.
"That's where Jose wants to be - he wants to be winning league titles.
"I think he would like to get back into the Premier League and have another crack at trying to win the title."


Mourinho succeeded Robson as manager of Porto in 2002 after he had guided the Portuguese side to a Champions League triumph a year earlier.
He went on to win the competition again with Barcelona in 2006, Inter Milan in 2010 and Real Madrid in 2013.


Robson said it was important his old friend did not "rush into things" after leaving Spurs.

Irish rugby legend Brian O'Driscoll and former Australia captain George Gregan have been leading a group of former footballers and rugby players delivering aid in Ukraine.


The group, known as the "Class of 2001", was delivering medical kits to the town of Irpin, just outside Kyiv.


It also included former Wales captain Gareth Thomas, Australian rugby great Peter FitzSimons and Scotland's Andy Nicol.


The group was put together by the charity Unicef, and the players were joined by ex-England goalkeeper David James and former England women's captain Casey Stoney.


"It is so upsetting to see the destruction here," said O'Driscoll.
"But the spirit of the people is something else.
They are so proud and grateful for any help we can give them."

O'Driscoll, 44, is an Irish rugby union icon, having earned 128 caps for his nation and led them to victory in the Grand Slam in 2009.


Gregan, 50, is considered one of the greatest scrum-halves in rugby history, earning 139 Australia caps and winning the World Cup in 1999.


Both were named in a list of the 20 greatest players of the professional era in 2003.

text:
Paris promise raises Welsh hopes of reaching World Cup knockout stages for first time ever

Having already secured a spot in the World Cup knockout stages for the very first time, Wales now have their sights set on a historic quarter-final appearance.


Defeats for Croatia and Belgium on Wednesday means Wales' 1-1 draw with Switzerland was enough to see them through to the last 16 as group winners.


With the so-called 'Group of Death' behind them, Wales' reward is a last-16 tie against Group D runners-up Morocco on Saturday.


But to make history by reaching the quarter-finals, Rob Page's side will have to do it the hard way by beating the African nation in Al Rayyan.

The demise of Dirty Den at the hands of his onscreen wife, Angie, is one of the most memorable moments in soap history.
It was watched by almost 14 million viewers, making it one of the most watched episodes of EastEnders ever.

In retaliation, Den served Angie with divorce papers and slept with her sister, Sue (played by Sadie Frost). 


However, their marriage was far from over.
Angie managed to convince Den to give their relationship another chance, and the couple reunited.
But their happiness was short-lived. 


A year later, in April 1999, Den discovered that Angie had been lying to him about her affair with Ian.
Enraged, he flew into a rage and violently attacked her. 


As he tried to strangle her with his bare hands, Angie's son, Ricky (played by Sid Owen), entered the room and tried to stop Den.

The Indian government has called for reforms to the international trade rules to alleviate the impact of economic sanctions imposed by other countries.
Speaking at the World Trade Organization's (WTO) ministerial conference in Geneva, Switzerland, India's Commerce Minister, Ms. Gina Gopinath, said that the current trade rules allow some countries to strong-arm others through the use of sanctions and tariffs.


"They (sanctions) strangle economies, they disrupt jobs and they deprive people of much-needed services and supplies," Ms. Gopinath said.
"Economic sanctions are imposed selectively on one country or subgroup of countries, with no option for appeal or redress.
"

Ms. Gopinath said that there was a need for fairer rules on trade to prevent the powerful from "bullying" the vulnerable.
She said that the WTO's role should be to ensure that all members are treated fairly and equitably.
The minister also called for the WTO to be given the power to adjudicate on trade disputes and to impose penalties on countries that violate trade rules.


This is not the first time that India has called for reforms to the international trade rules.
In the past, India has also called for the WTO to be more transparent and to provide more opportunities for developing countries to have their voices heard.
With a view to making decisions faster, the WTO's director-general Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, has also been trying to reinvigorate the organization's top-down approach to decision-making.

The first five spots were taken by different Harry Potter titles between May and September 2007.

John McEnroe, Mark Philippoussis and Tim Henman have all suffered with slumping testosterone levels, according to a newspaper report.


The Mail on Sunday said the trio's careers were ultimately hampered by the condition, which reduces strength and stamina.


In response, Henman described the story as "utter nonsense" and McEnroe said he "did not recall" the incidents.


But Mario Bartolini, a former Olympic weightlifter who has advised Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic, said low testosterone should be treated as any other injury.


Bartolini said it was "not normal" to see top-20 players suffering from the condition, adding testosterone supplements should be "regulated by the ATP and not by shady doctors or hackers".


Former British number one Henman said: "I'm happy with my career and what I achieved, and I haven't got any regrets.


"I'm comfortable with my decisions and how I played.
I didn't do anything wrong.
"

Henman, 46, said he would be "happy to take a test" to prove he had not taken supplements.


The newspaper reported that Bartolini claimed to have given testosterone supplements to McEnroe, Henman and Philippoussis while they were on the ATP tour.

The Korean government has announced a spending package worth $430bn as officials warned that without urgent measures, the economy would shrink by more than 1% next year and fall into a technical recession.


The announcement followed data showing that in the third quarter of 2022, the economy contracted by 0.4%.
It added to concerns that the economy is slowing after growth slowed to 0.7% in the second quarter.


"The economy is facing serious challenges," said finance minister Choo Kyung-ho.
"This package is a pre-emptive, transformational investment for the future.
"

The plan includes money for public sector pay rises, subsidies for heating costs, and a one-off payment for families with children.


There will also be funds available for small businesses struggling with the rise in interest rates, and extra government borrowing has been ruled out.


South Korea is a major player in the global economy as an exporter of semiconductors which are used in products ranging from smartphones to cars.


But its economy has been hit by the Covid-19 pandemic, the war in Ukraine, and a slowdown in China, one of its major trading partners.


The government has been reluctant to restore its pandemic stimulus measures for fear of adding to rising inflation.

Dame Alicia Markova, who has died aged 98, was one of the greatest ballerinas of the 20th century, celebrated for her beauty, elegance and impeccable classical technique.


Her greatest triumphs were as a member of the Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo, where she performed as a principal dancer between 1938 and 1947.
A muse to the company's founder, the choreographer George Balanchine, she appeared in some of his most famous works, including Apollo (1928), Serenade (1934) and Concerto Barocco (1941).


Markova was born in London in 1910 to Russian émigré parents who had escaped from the Imperial Russian Army after the revolution four years earlier.
They returned to Russia in 1914 but, with the country again in turmoil following the revolution of 1917, eventually settled in London in 1921.


Markova received her initial dance training in London, studying first with Serafina Astafieva, a former Imperial Russian Ballet dancer who had once partnered Vaslav Nijinksy, and then with Léonide Massine, a leading dancer with the Ballets Russes.


She made her debut as a soloist with the Markova-Dolin Ballet in 1931, and her success in the role of Giselle the following year led to her engagement by the Ballets Russes de Monte Carlo.


Markova became the company's prima ballerina in 1938 and was celebrated for her dramatic intensity and emotional depth.
She had a particular gift for expressing joy, and one of her most celebrated roles was as Spring in Balanchine's Coppélia (1939).


Among her other most celebrated roles were Aurora in Sleeping Beauty (1938), the sylph in La Sylphide (1940) and the second violin in Concerto Barocco (1941), a role created for her by Balanchine.

Despite competition from streaming, the US box office is heading for a record $6.8 billion gross in 2022, with admissions at their highest level since 2019.


The box office total for the year is 18% higher than in 2021 and just 2% below the pre-pandemic record set in 2019.


The figures from industry body Comscore are compiled from box office data collected from cinema ticketing websites.


Four films have made more than $500m this year led by Marvel's Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness with $955m.

The other three are Disney's Avatar: The Way of Water, which has made $855m, Marvel's Black Panther: Wakanda Forever ($802m) and Jurassic World Dominion ($716m). 


But it has also been a good year for smaller films.
The Marvel blockbuster Avengers: Endgame held the previous record for highest-grossing film released in a year, with $2.8bn in 2019. 


This year, four films have made more than $100m, led by James Cameron's Avatar: The Way of Water. 


But Disney's live-action remake of Pinocchio has also done well, as have Sony's Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse (Part One) and Paramount's Top Gun: Maverick. 


"Streamers are competing with theatres for content and that's benefiting theatre owners," said Comscore's media analyst Paul Dergarabedian.


"Streamers have realised that it is a mutually beneficial relationship.

The hunt for Harry Potter's arch-enemy, Lord Voldemort, has begun in the third installment of the Harry Potter film series, "Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban."
This chapter in the young wizard's life takes him to the perilous and mysterious Azkaban prison - a journey that could shed light on the grown-up world he is beginning to perceive.


In this film, Harry (Daniel Radcliffe) learns that his nemesis, Sirius Black (Gary Oldman), has escaped from Azkaban and is coming for him.
The Ministry of Magic refuses to believe that Sirius is a threat, but Harry is certain that he is coming to kill him.
With the help of his friends Ron (Rupert Grint) and Hermione (Emma Watson), Harry sets out to find Sirius and protect himself and his loved ones.


"Prisoner of Azkaban" is the best film in the Harry Potter series.
Dark, eerie, and packed with thrilling action and intricate plots, it is a must-watch for fans of the wizarding world.
The film's plot is more mature and complex than previous installments, and it explores darker themes such as betrayal, deception, and the consequences of unchecked power.


Oldman's performance as Sirius is a standout.
He brings depth and complexity to a character that could have been a one-dimensional villain.

The UK and Spain have begun a week of talks on the future of Gibraltar, the British territory on Spain's south coast.


The Rock has been a British fortress since 1713, but Spain has long argued that it should be returned.


The UK says it is committed to defending Gibraltar's 300-year-old Britishness, and does not want to share its sovereignty.


Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Garcia-Margallo said before the talks began that they should result in Britain ceding sovereignty over Gibraltar. 


"We aspire to regain the complete sovereignty of Gibraltar and hope to reach an agreement on that," he said. 


But Gibraltar's Chief Minister Fabian Picardo said: "We are not a bargaining chip between Spain and the United Kingdom.
"

Mr Picardo said Gibraltar had been cleared of all debt and was in a position to declare financial autonomy from the UK, making it "the first colony to evolve into a democracy in 160 years". 


"We are a proud people that aspire to be masters of our own destiny," he said. 


The talks were to be led by UK Minister for Europe David Lidington and Spanish State Secretary for European Union Affairs, Marco Aguiriano, on Monday and Tuesday.


On Wednesday and Thursday, they will be joined by Gibraltar's deputy chief minister, Dr Joseph Garcia and the territory's attorney general, Michael Llamas.

The release of the documentary "Michael" signals the "end of an era", according to fans of the King of Pop, Michael Jackson.


The documentary, which premiered at the Sundance film festival, is billed as the final film in a trilogy, concluding over a decade's work by director Andrew Eastick.


But fans who have followed the singer's career believe the documentary could signal other things.


"It is the end of an era - the era of Michael Jackson, the greatest musician of a generation," one fan told the BBC.


"He survived the Beatles - yes the Beatles were huge but they hadn't anything like the global appeal of Michael Jackson," they added.


Another fan said: "He elevated pop as an art form and remained relevant even after his death.


"He's the greatest performer of all time and this documentary underlines that.
He is the epitome of cool."


But the fan, like many others who have been raving about the documentary on social media, believes the film signals more than just the end of Jackson's era.


"For me it signals the end of an era for documentaries," they said.

Britain will no longer tolerate the "chronic and systemic" failure of other countries to criminalize hijacking planes, the foreign secretary has said.


Dominic Raab said such action was needed to tackle a "startling" rise in hostage-taking and suicide bombings.


Writing in the Sunday Telegraph, he said the UK would "take the lead" in imposing sanctions on any state that failed to act.


Mr Raab said another seven countries had joined the UK and US in taking action since the start of the year.


The foreign secretary's comments come after the Manchester bombing trial heard that Islamic State (IS) had planned to target aircraft.


John Thompson, a member of the UK's Joint Terrorism Analysis Centre (JTAC), told the trial of eight people accused of plotting the Manchester Arena bombing in 2017 that IS had aimed to "gain leverage" by seizing aircraft.


The defendant Elshafee Elghnawni, who denies being involved in the plot, told the court he had been instructed to carry out a hijacking as part of his terrorist training in Syria.


Mr Raab said the "absurd" criminalization of aircraft hijacking in some countries had allowed IS to "exploit" Britain and other countries as a "safe haven" for hostage-taking and suicide bombings.


"Second, we will impose sanctions on any state that fails to criminalize this practice - going further than the UK has done before," he added.


"And third, we will take the lead in introducing a legal obligation on airlines and insurers to give advance notice of any impending hijack - so we can intervene to prevent it.

John Thompson, a member of the UK's Joint Terrorism Analysis Centre (JTAC), told the trial of eight people accused of plotting the Manchester Arena bombing in 2017 that IS had aimed to "gain leverage" by seizing aircraft.


The defendant Elshafee Elghnawni, who denies being involved in the plot, told the court he had been instructed to carry out a hijacking as part of his terrorist training in Syria.


Mr Raab said the "absurd" criminalization of aircraft hijacking in some countries had allowed IS to "exploit" Britain and other countries as a "safe haven" for hostage-taking and suicide bombings.


"Second, we will impose sanctions on any state that fails to criminalize this practice - going further than the UK has done before," he added.


"And third, we will take the lead in introducing a legal obligation on airlines and insurers to give advance notice of any impending hijack - so we can intervene to prevent it.

The media regulator has fined Viacom £1.8m for airing a documentary that it ruled was indecent.


Ofcom ruled that the Channel 5 show, Murder at the Cottage, did not need a warning despite "graphic" scenes.


The watchdog launched an investigation last year into the show, which included footage of a dead body.


Channel 5 said it did not agree with Ofcom's ruling and planned to appeal.


The fine is the latest in a series of high-profile decisions on TV standards.


Ofcom said Murder at the Cottage, which was aired in September 2021, broke rules on offensive content.


The documentary showed the bodies of two murder victims being removed from a house, Ofcom said, adding that it "judged the footage to be graphic and explicit".


But the regulator ruled that a warning at the start of the programme would have "undermined the editorial value of the footage".


Instead, it said a "precise and factual" introduction to the programme - which was broadcast at 10pm - was sufficient.


Under the rules, broadcasters must include a warning at the start of a programme if there is "material that is likely to offend generally accepted standards".

The story details emerging societal changes in Saudi Arabia and the slow shift in public perception regarding the role of women in society.
Specifically, the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development has announced that it will employ more women in the government sector to boost female participation in the workforce.
Currently, the unemployment rate for women is roughly 33 percent, in comparison to 13 percent for men.
The ministry hopes that employing more women in government offices will help even out the playing field across all sectors. 


This announcement comes on the heels of the Saudi government's recent decision to lift the ban on women driving.
While the ministry's initiative is a positive step towards gender equality, it is not without its share of challenges.
The country's conservative society has long been opposed to women working outside the home, and there are concerns that women may face discrimination and harassment in the workplace. 


Despite these challenges, the ministry remains committed to its goal of increasing female employment.
It has launched a number of initiatives to encourage businesses to hire more women, including offering tax breaks and other incentives. 


The story ends by exploring the broader implications of these changes for Saudi society as a whole, and whether they signal a new era of gender equality in the kingdom.

text:
Hitachi has built what it claims is the world's fastest robot.
Together with the University of Tokyo and other partners, the Japanese electronics maker developed a robot that maneuvers by bouncing off walls and can clean a room in under 10 minutes.
Unlike other speedy robots, which are typically wheeled, Hitachi's new robot—called Rapid Explored Rectified Orientation Tracking (REROT) Robot—has legs like a insect, enabling it to traverse uneven surfaces at speeds of up to 5.6 meters per second.
According to Hitachi, that is the fastest speed achieved by a robot on legs. 


The robot measures approximately 5.1 inches long, 3.5 inches wide, and 2.7 inches tall.
It navigates by keeping a wall about 1 to 2 feet to its left throughout its movement.
Its two legs are modeled after those of an insect, and they enable the robot to traverse uneven surfaces at high speeds.
Its unique leg movement is inspired by how a person would run on a slippery road, and the robot uses its legs to maintain balance as it moves. 


The REROT Robot can clean a room in under 10 minutes, which is significantly faster than the average household robot.
It can also be used for various other applications, including transportation and inspection.

text:
Sony revealed the PlayStation 5 in June 2020 ahead of its November launch.
That was nearly three years ago, and since then, the $499 console has remained stubbornly out of stock.
All the while, its list of games has grown at a glacial place, with each new title immediately becoming another highly sought-after commodity.
Today, there are still only two PS5 exclusives: Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart and Demon’s Souls (which is also available on PC).
Meanwhile, the cheaper, less powerful Xbox Series S has enjoyed relative abundance, and Microsoft continues to rack up exclusive day-and-date releases, including several on Game Pass.
It’s clear at this point that the PS5 arrived before it was ready — but why? 


Sony’s part of the blame is that it focused too much on hardware, but Microsoft also deserves credit for being more aggressive with Game Pass, and for giving its first-party studios more time to cook up AAA exclusives.
Despite the PS5’s lack of must-have games, Sony has sold 7.8 million units as of September 30th, according to its recent earnings report.
That’s not an embarrassing number, given the stock issues the company has faced, but it’s also not a particularly impressive one either.
By comparison, the Xbox Series X and Series S have sold a combined 30.2 million units.

The departure of a senior figure from UKIP has sparked a new row over the future of the party as it continues to be riven by in-fighting.


Harry Foster, who was deputy chairman of UKIP, announced on Saturday that he was joining a new party - Veritas - in order to oppose the Conservative Party and what he described as "the woke cult".


The move increases the likelihood of a split in UKIP - which was founded to fight Brexit but has been through months of in-fighting, including the suspension of its former leader, Nigel Farage.


It comes after the party's only MP, Robert Jenrick, announced he was stepping down from his role as spokesman for the party.


In a statement, Mr Foster said he was "delighted" to be joining Veritas.


He claimed the Conservative Party was "no longer fit for purpose" and that Veritas offered an opportunity for "common sense Conservatives" to fight for their beliefs.


The launch of Veritas, which was announced earlier this month, has been criticised by some as a vehicle for former Conservative MPs to keep themselves in the public eye or to pursue other political careers.


Mr Foster was elected as a UKIP local councillor in 2017 and became the party's deputy chairman in 2020.


He is the second senior figure to leave UKIP recently, following the resignation of chair Richard Braine who left to become an independent in October.


At the time of his departure, Mr Braine said he did not believe UKIP's leadership was doing enough to tackle "racism, sexism and homophobia" in the party.

The cost of natural gas insurance is set to rise, the Association of British Insurers has said.

The industry body said it would be unfair to expect insurers to foot the bill for the rising cost of claims caused by global warming.

The ABI said insurers would have to increase prices to cover the estimated £200 extra cost of claims for burst pipes this winter.

The association's director, Stephen Haddrill, said: "To expect insurers to absorb these costs would be completely unfair and will simply result in higher prices for consumers.
"
The warning came as the government launched a consultation exercise on helping households facing high energy costs.

The association said claims for burst pipes had doubled to £200m in the past two years as temperatures fell.

An ABI spokesman said: "Claims for burst pipes have doubled in the past two years and insurers have seen first-hand the financial and human impact of extreme weather events.
"
In addition to higher prices, the association said the lack of insurance capacity in the market could also affect the ability of firms to offer insurance cover for burst pipes.

"This year, more insurers have restricted their capacity to offer this insurance, meaning consumers may find it harder to find affordable cover," the ABI said.

The association said it was unclear whether the increase in insurance costs would be passed on to consumers in the form of higher prices or reduced cover.

The deal values Domecq at $1.36bn (£900m).
Shares in the Spanish firm surged by more than a third on the Madrid stock exchange.
Domecq's main brand is Jose Cuervo tequila, the world's biggest selling tequila.
It also makes Kahlua and Sauza tequila.
If the deal goes through, Paris-based Pernod Ricard's portfolio would swell to around 40 brands.


Pernod is best known for its aniseed-flavoured pastis and its best-selling vodka, Absolut.
The group has been keen to expand its range of spirits and boost its presence in the important US market.
"This is a good deal for us.
It's a very good fit," said Pernod's chairman, Patrick Ricard.

The feature is designed to work with the Windows 10 and Windows 11 operating systems, and it can be accessed from the taskbar or the start menu.


With "Windows Search," users can search for information on their computers by entering keywords or phrases into the search bar.
The search feature will then return results that match the user's query, including documents, files, web pages, and other information.


In addition to searching for information, "Windows Search" can also be used to launch applications, access settings, and perform other tasks on a computer.
This makes it a useful tool for users who want to quickly find information or perform common tasks on their computers.


Microsoft has announced that "Windows Search" will be available as a free update for users of Windows 10 and Windows 11.
The feature will be available for download from the Microsoft website, and it will also be available as a pre-installed feature on new computers that run the Windows operating system.

Britain's youth are leading the way in Europe's gig economy, according to a study of people who share their earnings on the Bolt ride-hailing app.


Those in the UK median age bracket of 26 to 35 made the most on the Estonian-founded platform per hour on average - ahead of their Dutch and French counterparts, the study found.


The app has seen a surge in usage since the pandemic, particularly among younger people seeking flexible work.


The study covered March 2021 to February 2022.


In the UK, the median hourly earnings for a driver on Bolt was £17 ($21.60) compared with £14 in France and £12 in the Netherlands.


The average British driver on the platform was 30 years old, while the average Dutch driver was 41 and the average French driver was 36.


The study said British drivers were more likely to work longer hours, with their weekly average of 30 hours higher than the 25 hours worked by Dutch drivers.


It also found UK drivers were more likely to live in urban areas than their European counterparts.


Bolt carried out the study to mark the expansion of its services in the UK, which began with London in 2019 and has now rolled out to 30 British cities.


The company said it had seen a surge in drivers in the UK, with the number of active drivers growing by more than 530% in 2021.

"That's not fair play."
In the British version of Wife Swap, couples trade wives for two weeks.
The show is aired on BBC One and is a ratings success.
The American version, which debuted on ABC last month, is hosted by Mark Consuelos and has been a hit for the network.


RDF USA described the lawsuit as "without merit".
"This is a straightforward case of the 'rip off' and 'knock off' of an original format," said RDF's lawyer, Robert Schwartz.
"We will defend this case vigorously."

Oil prices fell on Monday after a three-day rally, as concerns about the outlook for demand in China and the possibility of higher interest rates weighed on the market.


Brent crude futures were down $1.16, or 1.5%, at $73.40 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures fell $1.25, or 1.7%, to $70.55 a barrel.


China, the world's biggest oil consumer, has seen a surge in COVID-19 cases, with the largest wave of infections in six months.


The country's health authorities have stuck to a policy of zero-COVID, involving lockdowns and mass testing, slamming the brakes on economic activity.


"The sell-off in oil markets is primarily due to demand concerns out of China," said Nishant Bhushan, chief business officer at oil analytics firm Vortexa.


"With China's zero-COVID strategy prompting fresh lockdowns, the concern is that this could impact demand by as much as nearly half a million barrels per day," he added.


Another factor weighing on oil prices was the stronger US dollar, which tends to weigh on commodities priced in the currency.
A higher US dollar makes oil more expensive for buyers using other currencies.


The US dollar was boosted by a hawkish shift in tone from the US Federal Reserve, with the central bank likely to raise interest rates by 50 basis points next week after data showed wholesale prices rose 11% in November from a year earlier.


Investors were also awaiting fresh oil supply data from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and its allies, together known as OPEC+, on Tuesday.

The curtain has fallen on one of the most famous families to appear on TV, as MTV axes The Osbournes.


The show, which debuted in 2002 and turned the Osbourne family into reality TV stars, will not be coming back for a sixth season, a network spokesperson confirmed on Friday.


The announcement comes several months after Ozzy Osbourne, 67, revealed he had been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease.


The series, one of the first in the reality TV boom of the early 2000s, followed the household's day-to-day life as they lived in Beverly Hills, California.


Apart from Ozzy – known for his decades-long career as the lead vocalist of heavy metal band Black Sabbath – the show also featured his wife, Sharon, and their two children, Kelly and Jack.


Sharon Osbourne, 68, told TalkTV in May she planned to step back from her television career to focus on her family, citing her husband's illness as the reason.


"I've worked my whole life and I really want to be with my husband and see to him and see to things at home," she said.


"I have absolutely no doubt that Sharon will be returning to work in the future, but for now she's going to be spending time with her family," her spokesperson told Variety at the time.


Last week, Ozzy – who disclosed his Parkinson's diagnosis in January – announced he was cancelling his upcoming tour dates citing his illness.


"It's the only tour I've ever cancelled," the singer said in a statement.

Here is a sample of a BBC news article about the rock band Foo Fighters topping a British talent poll:

The New York rock band Foo Fighters top the annual BBC Radio 2 listener poll, the Sound of the 90s.
The vote, which launched in 2008, asks listeners to pick their favorite artists from across the decades.


The group – fronted by former Nirvana drummer Dave Grohl – received more than 500,000 of the 2.6 million votes cast.


They beat The Beatles, who came second, and Adele, who came third.


“We’ve always been humbled at the love we receive from the UK,” said Grohl.
“But to be recognized in this way, alongside so many other great artists, is a genuine honor.”


The prize comes 25 years after the band formed, and a decade after they last topped the charts with the 2011 album Wasting Light.
Their most recent album, Medicine at Midnight, was released in February 2021.


This year marks the first time the poll has been opened to voters outside the UK, with people from more than 100 countries taking part.


The Beatles, who came second, are still regarded as one of the most successful acts of all time – but this is the first time they have featured in the top five of the Sound of the 90s poll.

The UK government has been criticised for its plans to send some migrants to a processing centre in Ascension Island thousands of miles away in the Atlantic.


The scheme - part of tougher immigration measures announced by Home Secretary Theresa May - is designed to discourage migrants from making dangerous journeys across the English Channel.


Ministers say the centre on the island, which is a British overseas territory, will be used to process migrants' claims "fairly and efficiently".


But Labour called the plan "inhumane".


Ascension Island is a volcanic island halfway between Africa and South America, with a population of fewer than 1,000 people and temperatures reaching up to 40C (104F).


It is part of the British overseas territory of Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha - best known as the location of the former prison camp where Boer prisoners of war were held during the Boer War in the early 20th Century.


The island has a naval base - long attached to the UK's interests in the South Atlantic - and is a stopping-off point for Royal Navy ships, as well as an important satellite ground station.


Building work is already under way to transform an abandoned US airbase on Ascension - which is twinned with Saint Helena - into a migrant processing centre.


The exact location has not been disclosed, but it is understood to be on the island's sweltering coastline.


The plans, first reported by The Times, have been criticised by politicians and charities.

The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) issued a warning on the impact of subsidies offered by countries on fisheries.
The impacts are detrimental to the sustainability of fish stocks and the ecosystems and livelihoods connected to them.


The warning follows a study on fisheries subsidies, a key issue behind overfishing.
The study was led by the FAO and conducted with the assistance of the European Union.
It found that approximately $14 billion in annual fisheries subsidies encourage continued overfishing.
Of this total, $1.3 billion dollars are offered by countries whose fisheries are already sustainably managed. 


The study found that these subsidies contribute to declining fish stocks, with implications for the livelihoods of fishers and the food security and nutrition of billions of people.
The findings of the study were validated at a technical workshop attended by representatives from more than 30 countries.


The study concludes that the impacts of fisheries subsidies urgently need to be addressed through the rules of the World Trade Organization (WTO).
The WTO's Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures (ASCM) establishes rules on the use of subsidies.

Eminem has made chart history by becoming the first artist to score ten consecutive number-one albums in the UK. 


The musician's latest record, entitled "Curtain Call 2", a compilation of his hits, entered the charts at the top spot, pushing the Beatles' "Abbey Road" to second place. 


The "Curtain Call" album celebrated Eminem's 50th birthday and marked 25 years since the release of his debut major-label album, "The Slim Shady LP". 


The 47-year-old rapper boasts a total of 15 UK number-one albums.
Only three other musicians have achieved more: the Beatles (with a total of 17), Elvis Presley (16) and Robbie Williams (14). 


Eminem, born Marshall Bruce Mathers III, burst onto the scene in 1999 with the release of "My Name Is". 


His debut major-label album, "The Slim Shady LP" (released in early 1999 in the US and the following year in the UK), became the fastest-selling solo rap album in history. 


Despite Eminem's chart success, his albums have not always been well received by music critics. 


His best-selling album, "The Eminem Show" (2002), was praised by the New York Times as "bold and cunning".
However, other records were described as "mediocre" and "lazy" by Rolling Stone.

Music fans are warned they risk getting their computers infected with viruses if they continue to download songs from Apple's iTunes store, according to internet security company McAfee.
McAfee claims a quarter of the 50 most popular songs in the US at the moment have been targeted by hackers.
It says viruses are being hidden in the popular MP3 files, which could damage people's computers.
McAfee has contacted Apple to warn them about the problem.
"This is the first time we've seen this technology used in this way," said Gene Signorini, a McAfee spokesman.
"It's a very new and very concerning development.
"

McAfee discovered the viruses after a six-month investigation.
It found that the popular music files were being used to deliver malware through a process known as "steganography".
The viruses are hidden in the headers of the MP3 files and are only discovered once the song has been downloaded.
McAfee found viruses in 25% of the most popular songs downloaded in the past month.

The internet is relying on an ageing domain system that is being exploited by online scammers, security experts have said.


The system, known as ICANN, controls the database of web addresses - such as google.com - and the allocation of new internet domains.


It is currently running out of the addresses it has available - notably .com
and .org - which are seen as the most trustworthy.


ICANN has started selling hundreds of new generic top-level domains - such as .app, .bank, and .pharmacy - but these are seen as less secure.


It is not adding enough of the new secure domains to meet demand, and is being urged to speed up the introduction of more.


Writing in the MIT Technology Review, security experts said that the internet was facing a "crisis" because of the shortage of trustworthy domain names.


"The first step in many online attacks is to get users to click on a link, and domains are crucial to that first step," the magazine quoted Dan Kaminsky, chief scientist at security firm White Ops, as saying.


"We are running out of names for people to trust.
"

Dr Emily Taylor from Oxford University's Internet Institute agreed, and said that the issue needed to be addressed.

The Academy Awards, also known as the Oscars, is one of the most prominent award ceremonies in the world.
The first award ceremony took place in 1929 and since then has been held annually.
The Oscars is an important event in the film industry, with many seeing it as the highest honour that can be awarded to a filmmaker or actor.


Throughout the years, the Academy Awards have undergone many changes and transformations.
Initially, only male actors were permitted to be nominated and win an award.
Despite women making significant contributions to the film industry since the early days, they were not recognised by the Academy.
It was not until the 1980s when the Academy began to recognise the achievements of female filmmakers and actors by introducing the Best Actress award. 


The Academy Awards have also been criticised for not representing enough diversity on the screen.
Over the years, the Academy has tried to address this issue by introducing new categories and making changes to the voting process.
These changes have led to an increase in the number of diverse nominees and winners.

Mitsubishi Motors and Peugeot S.A. are in talks to develop batteries and electric vehicles together, joining other Japanese and French automakers in a push to lower the cost of ahead of a widespread adoption of EVs in Europe.


The companies said in a statement Thursday that they are exploring a partnership in the supply of batteries for EVs and plug-in hybrids, as well as cooperation on research and development.
The announcement sent Mitsubishi Motors stock soaring 19 percent Thursday in Tokyo. 


The French and Japanese automakers are already collaborating in other areas.
In 2016, they joined forces with Toyota to develop compact cars for the European market.
Through that deal, Peugeot and Citroen have access to Toyota's hybrid technology, while Toyota gains entry to Peugeot's diesel engine know-how.


Toyota has also signed a memorandum of understanding with Mitsubishi Motors to study cooperation in the development and production of batteries for electric vehicles.


Peugeot parent company PSA Group, which also makes cars under the Citroen, Opel, and Vauxhall brands, has pinned its electrification strategy on a £100 million ($135 million) UK factory that will produce batteries for its electric vehicles.
The facility will open in 2024 with a production capacity of over 200,000 units, supplying the needs of its European brands.


For Mitsubishi, the talks with Peugeot come after it outlined its own plans to strengthen its lineup of EVs and PHEVs in an effort to cut carbon emissions and meet environmental regulations in its key markets.

MPs from several parties have demanded to know how a budget leak happened, as the government was forced into a U-turn over its plans to raise national insurance.


The Commons Treasury Select Committee said it wanted to hear from the Treasury and HMRC about the leak, which happened last weekend.


In Saturday's leak, a genuine-looking mock-up of the Budget document was posted online.
It showed that the government was planning to raise taxes to fund social care.


The Treasury has said it is investigating the leak, but MPs want to know the results of its probe by Friday.


The Conservative MP and committee chairman, Mel Stride, said it was "absolutely right" that the Treasury was investigating the leak but added that "it's important that the select committee follows this up as well".


He said the committee had written to the Treasury and HMRC "asking for further information on the extent of the leak, any evidence of where it may have originated from and the impact of this leak on the broader political debate".


"We would like to see a response to our inquiries by Friday of this week," he added.


The Liberal Democrats have called for an inquiry into the leak.


The party's Treasury spokesperson, Christine Jardine, said: "This was a disgraceful and dangerous leak, and the public deserve to know how it happened.

The BBC has been advised to adopt "more impartial" wording in its reporting on Iraq following criticism from government ministers and MPs.


The director of BBC News, Richard Sambrook, has written to the chairman of the Commons Foreign Affairs Committee, saying the corporation will adopt the changes.


The advice followed a complaint by Conservative MP Andrew Robathan.


And Foreign Office minister Mark Malloch Brown accused the BBC of "poor" and "biased" reporting on Iraq. 


In his letter, Mr Sambrook said the BBC recognised the "depth of feeling" and that Director-General Mark Thompson had asked him to look into the issue.


Mr Sambrook said the corporation had "no intention of acting as cheerleader for any particular course of action".


But he added that in the "heat of debate" the BBC had not always been as careful as it should have been over the choice of words.


The director of news said the BBC would "redouble our efforts" to be impartial.


"In particular we will review our output to ensure that we continue to use language which is impartial and does not favour one particular course of action over another," he wrote.


"I can confirm that we will adopt the changes of wording that you suggest.

The Da Vinci Code, a book and a film which sparked a rush of interest in symbology and ancient history, is lousy history, according to a historian.


Professor Andrew Roberts, of Royal Holloway, University of London, said the best-selling novel was "full of errors".


Author Dan Brown, who has sold more than 80 million copies of the book, admitted at its launch that he had taken "huge liberties" with the facts.


But Professor Roberts said even basic errors were made, such as the location of an ancient church.


"It is full of errors and I think that people think it is much more historically accurate than it is," he said.


"Even basic things like the location of the church of Saint-Sulpice in Paris - that's completely wrong.


"It's not across the road from the Louvre, it's a good mile away and there's no underground river connecting the two."

Does it matter?


Professor Roberts said it was "quite amusing" to see how people had been taken in by the novel, but added that the inaccuracies had potentially negative consequences.


"I think it is a problem because the readers of the Da Vinci Code think that they have learned something about Christianity, about the history of the Roman Empire and about art," he said.


"They go to museums and they see things and they think they know the story, and they don't."

England's ill-disciplined World Cup campaign ended with a whimper as they were out-played and out-muscled by a young, vibrant and skilful Australia side, who booked a semi-final meeting with Trans-Tasman rivals New Zealand.


A ninth defeat in a row - the team's worst run for 34 years - was assured before halftime as a 13-6 scoreline reflected the dominance of the Southern Hemisphere side, who scored four tries to England's two.


But it was the manner in which England surrendered meekly that will cause most concern for director of rugby Clive Woodward, whose side were out-thought and out-fought in every department.


For much of the first half, England were buoyed by a partisan crowd who cheered their every move but, once again, they were unable to deliver on the promise of their early play.


A well-taken try from Jason Robinson and a penalty from Jonny Wilkinson after just eight minutes gave England an early lead but that was as good as it got for the home side.


The introduction of Elton Flatley at fly-half for the Australians proved an inspired move as his precise kicking and calm authority helped turn the tide.


A well-taken try from centre Matt Giteau, who exploited acres of space in the English defence, and a Flatley penalty put the Wallabies ahead after 21 minutes.


Winger Chris Latham then scored Australia's second try in the corner, Flatley missed the conversion but added a penalty goal minutes later to give his side a 13-6 half-time lead.


England's lack of discipline was once again their downfall as Wilkinson, Robinson and captain Martin Johnson were all sin-binned as the pressure finally told.


The crowd's fervour was dampened by the sight of England's star centre Mike Tindall being helped from the field after injuring his shoulder in a tackle early in the second half.

Italy produced a spectacular second-half show to score seven tries in a 41-19 victory over Ireland in Rome on Saturday.


The hosts led 19-17 at half-time but were pulled apart in the second half as Italy scored four tries in a magnificent 12-minute spell.


Italy have now won three of their five matches in this year's Six Nations Championship.


They began brightly and took the lead when Edoardo Padovani scored in the left corner after a brilliant solo run in which he beat three Irish defenders.


Ireland struck back with a try from winger Keith Earls, who produced a superb finish in the right corner after a fine pass from Conor Murray.


Italy went back in front when Angelo Esposito scored a superb try, running across the pitch before diving under the posts.


The hosts continued to pressure Ireland and were rewarded with a penalty try as Murray was tackled without the ball after a quick tap penalty.


Ireland came close to scoring their third try when Jamie Heaslip was brought down just short of the line. 


Italy went in at the break trailing by two points after Tommaso Allan landed a late penalty.


The hosts came out firing after the restart and Luca Sperandio scored in the left corner to extend the lead.

text:
Microsoft is set to launch a blogging service on Tuesday, in an attempt to attract users who want to write longer-form content than the short text messages favoured by the Twitter microblogging service.


The software giant will unveil Windows Live Spaces, which will be integrated with its existing Windows Live services, at a launch event in New York.


The move comes as Microsoft continues to try to expand its social-networking offerings, a category of internet services that has grown enormously in the past year.


Windows Live Spaces is not a revolutionary new service.
Instead, it is based on the Moveable Type publishing system, developed by a company of the same name.
Microsoft struck a deal with Moveable Type to develop a custom version of its software for Windows Live users. 


Like most blogging services, Spaces will offer users the ability to publish text, photos and other media.
It will also have built-in support for RSS feeds, a technology that allows internet users to subscribe to a blog or other information outlet, and then read the content using software called a newsreader.


What is more, Spaces will be integrated with Microsoft's other Windows Live services, such as the Windows Live Messenger instant-messaging software and Windows Live Mail email service.
This means that Spaces users will be able to communicate with and read emails from their friends who are using other Live services, all from within the blogging interface.

Former Brookside creator Phil Redmond has made a surprise return to Channel 4 to make a new documentary about the Liverpool care crisis. 


Redmond's company, Phil Redmond Productions, was commissioned by the channel to make a film exploring the city's care crisis.
The 90-minute film, titled Liverpool Care Crisis, will be aired in 2024. 


Liverpool Care Crisis will highlight the increasing pressure on social care in Liverpool as the population ages.
The film will also explore how the city's care staff are coping with the challenges. 


Channel 4's head of documentaries, Nick Hornby, said: "Phil is a brilliant filmmaker.
He is also a Liverpudlian with a passion for telling the stories that need to be told about his city.
I'm really happy he's making this important film for Channel 4." 


Redmond said: "I am delighted to be working with Channel 4 on this very important film for Liverpool.
It is a critical issue that needs to be explored and I hope it will lead to a wider discussion of how we can all work together to solve the care crisis in the city."

The father of a young Iraqi woman, who died in 2019 while attempting to join ISIS, has won a landmark court case, in a probe described by prosecutors as "the first of its kind".
Rabia Kamil's father filed a criminal complaint in the French city of Rouen against the Islamic State group, as well as against his daughter's spouse and another man, who had helped prepare the couple's journey from Iraq to Syria. 


In a verdict delivered earlier this week, a judge ruled that the two men had facilitated Rabia Kamil's journey - an attempt to join ISIS - knowing that it risked her safety.
The judge described her death as "foreseeable". 


The only defendant present at the trial, Rabia Kamil's husband, was sentenced to four years in prison, while the other man received a three-year term, both with suspended sentences.
However, the judge did not find enough evidence to convict ISIS. 


The presiding judge said the group had "played on the couple's religious and ideological convictions" and that ISIS had deceived them.
The judge added that ISIS had left them "to their fate". 


The couple's daughter, aged three, has been placed in the care of the French authorities.
During the trial, Rabia Kamil's father asked for his grandchild to be placed in his care, but his request was denied.

The Telegraph, a 200-year-old newspaper, has announced that it will be cutting 90 jobs as part of a cost-saving restructure.
This move comes as the newspaper industry struggles to adapt to the changing media landscape, with many readers moving to digital platforms for their news.
The Telegraph, which has a daily circulation of just under 200,000, has seen a decline in print advertising revenue, leading to the cutbacks.
The newspaper's owner, Telegraph Media Group, has said that the redundancies are necessary to ensure the long-term future of the company. 


The redundancies will affect a range of departments, including news, sports, and features.
The Telegraph has said that it will be focusing on its digital offerings, with a new website and an enhanced subscription service. 


The news of the job cuts has been met with concern from the National Union of Journalists (NUJ).
A spokesperson for the NUJ said that "it is a terrible day for quality journalism and a dark day for the dedicated and skilled workers at the Telegraph". 


It is clear that the Telegraph is facing a difficult time as it transitions to a more digital-focused operation.
However, the newspaper has a rich history and a loyal following, and it is hoped that the cutbacks will allow it to continue to serve its readers for many years to come.

Friday saw crude oil prices jump above the $50 per barrel mark, increasing more than 2% in the last session alone.
This comes after data released showed that US crude stockpiles were falling, with concerns of a global economic slowdown seeming to fade.
This marks a 13% increase in the price of oil over the past month, with prices now having nearly doubled since hitting a 2-year low in October.
The rebound has come as a surprise to many, given the continued strength of the dollar and the harsh weather that has hit many parts of the world.


Amongst the factors contributing to the price increase are the ongoing Opec+ supply cuts, as well as the weakening of the dollar.
The Opec+ group, which is made up of major oil producers including Saudi Arabia and Russia, has been cutting its output in an effort to boost prices.
Meanwhile, a weakening dollar tends to make commodities priced in dollars more expensive for other countries to buy.


Consumers are likely to feel the impact of higher oil prices in the form of higher prices at the pump.
However, with the US Federal Reserve expected to raise interest rates again next week, the dollar is likely to retain its strength, providing some support for oil prices.


For now, it appears that oil prices are on the rise and it remains to be seen whether they will continue to climb.
