The students at the Kisaruni All Boys Secondary School in Kenya certainly stand out.
Unlike most other teenagers, these kids are eagerly cradling their handheld calculators, punching in numbers and working on math problems as they wait for class to start.


This unusual sight is the result of a new program implemented at the school called Calculation Nation.
It is designed to improve the students' math skills by encouraging them to use calculators for every equation, every day. 


Started as a pilot program in 2019, Calculation Nation was the brainchild of Bob McCormick, a former teacher and the founder of Calculator Classroom, a nonprofit organisation in Portland, Oregon, that provides free calculators to students in Africa.
To date, the organisation has donated more than 26,000 calculators to students in Kenya. 


"I realised that for American students, using calculators is a given, but in Africa, students don't have them at all," McCormick said.
He pointed to research from Harvard University that showed the benefits of using calculators in the classroom.
The study found that students who used calculators were able to solve problems more accurately and efficiently than those who didn't. 


McCormick reached out to Kisaruni All Boys Secondary School, an institution that serves students from the Maasai community, an indigenous group in Kenya with a long history of discrimination and poverty.

The UK is “heading in the wrong direction” in regards to its handling of COVID-19, Professor John Ashton, a former regional director of public health for north-west England, has said.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s World at One programme, he said that the UK had “lost its grip” on the epidemic and that the recent plan to scrap COVID-19 restrictions was “difficult to understand”.


He commented: “I think we are heading in the wrong direction
and I think we need to do something about it pretty quickly because this virus is not going to go away.”


Professor Ashton argued that a “middle way” was needed, whereby the government advises citizens on how to manage their risks.
This comes after Prime Minister Boris Johnson announced that mandatory masks, COVID-19 passports and social distancing would end in England on 27 January.


Speaking to MPs on Wednesday (04 January), the prime minister said the UK government “cannot keep the country indefinitely in a state of lockdown”.
He argued that the restrictions were having “damaging consequences” on people’s mental health and livelihoods.


However, Professor Ashton said that “locking down completely” was not under consideration and “nor should it be”.


Instead, he suggested that the government could be taking steps to slow the spread of the virus, such as advising people to work from home and introducing COVID-19 passports for large events.

text:
The BBC has lined up a stellar cast for its latest ambitious drama, which tells the story of the 2004 Asian tsunami.


The eight-part series, titled Tsunami: Survival Island, was announced by the BBC on Tuesday.


It will star Martin Clunes, Matthew Macfadyen, and Jill Halfpenny from BBC One's hit drama Showhide, and Bollywood star Shahzad Latif.


They will be joined by Peter Guinness, Amara Karan, and Joe Claflin.


The series will be produced by Ireland's Dancing Ledge Productions for BBC One and BBC iPlayer.


It tells the story of the massive wave that devastated parts of Asia and how it affected people from different countries and backgrounds.


The cast will play characters with different relationships and stories who are holidaying in Thailand when the tsunami hits.


They must fight for their lives as they are swept back to the hotel and taken to a nearby island.


The show will be executive produced by Dancing Ledge's CEO, Anne Brogan, and co-executive produced by Christian Smith.


Brogan said: "This is a powerful story of survival and human resilience in the face of unimaginable tragedy, told with sensitivity and respect for the events that took place 15 years ago."

Macfadyen said: "I'm really looking forward to working with this talented group of actors and I'm so excited to be part of this show."

Among the many European and US airlines scrambling to replace their ageing fleets with more fuel-efficient aircraft, Irish ultra-low-cost carrier Ryanair has emerged as one of the winners.
On 29 March, the carrier announced that it had agreed a deal with Boeing to purchase 75 new 737 MAX aircraft, with the option to buy a further 50.
The deal, including the options and excluding aircraft previously ordered, is for a total of 135 aircraft, and is thought to be worth around $4bn at the list price.


The first of the new planes are expected to be delivered at the end of next year, and will continue to be delivered until 2028.
They will replace the airline's existing fleet of Boeing 737-800 aircraft, which are being phased out as their airframes reach the end of their useful life.


Ryanair has taken a big bet on the 737 MAX, which has been plagued by safety concerns and a lengthy grounding since March 2019.
The aircraft's return to service in the US and Europe is still pending, but Ryanair is confident that Boeing will overcome its difficulties and that the plane will be back in the air by the summer.


Although the deal has boosted Boeing's order book, it has also given fresh hope to Airbus, which has been trying to sell its A320neo aircraft to Ryanair for some time.
The Irish carrier has previously said that it was in talks with both Boeing and Airbus about a possible order, and that it would select the supplier that could offer the best price and delivery dates.


However, with the Boeing deal now confirmed, it seems that Ryanair has decided to stick with the US manufacturer, at least for the time being.

The BBC has learned that Sony has sold more than 30m PlayStation 3 (PS3) games and entertainment devices since its launch in March. 


The news comes as Sony unveils a new, faster processor for the device in an attempt to keep up with the best selling Wii console from Nintendo.
The new 80GB version of the PS3 will go on sale in Europe on 20 October, priced at £425.
It will have a new, faster processor, and a bigger, higher capacity hard disk drive. 


The move comes after Nintendo announced a lower price for the Wii, and the imminent release of the Microsoft Xbox 360, due out next week.
All three devices are vying for position as the must-have games console this Christmas. 


The new PS3 will have a Cell processor running at 3.2GHz, up from the current 3.0GHz, and the RAM memory has been boosted from 256MB to 384MB.
The new, larger hard disk drive will be able to store more games, music, videos and other data. 


Sony said the new PS3 will have a quicker response time, enhanced high-definition graphics, and improved picture quality.
It will also be able to run the increasingly popular digital television service, BBC iPlayer.

Ukrainian authorities have accused a Russian businessman of stealing thousands of tonnes of steel and aluminium which were earmarked for export but were instead sold within Russia, causing billions of dollars in losses to Ukraine's state budget.
Authorities in Kyiv said the stolen goods were used to benefit Russia's military and were used as collateral for a $7.4bn loan to Russia by a subsidiary of Russian steel and aluminium producer United Company RUSAL.


The aluminium alloy was meant to be sold to China and the steel to Poland, but it was stolen "at different stages of the supply chain", according to a high-ranking official in Kyiv.
Internal documents seen by the BBC show how the metal was diverted and sold within Russia.
The aluminium alloy, which was ready for export from the Ukrainian port of Mariupol, was instead moved to RUSAL's factory in Krasnoyarsk in Siberia.


The theft came to light as a result of an investigation by anti-corruption police in Ukraine, who found internal emails and documents detailing the scheme.
Police have so far refused to comment on the case.
The metals were sold to a Russian company, according to the documents seen by the BBC.
The documents also show that the proceeds of the sales went to a bank account controlled by RUSAL.


RUSAL, which is one of the world's largest aluminium producers and is registered in Jersey, did not respond to requests for comment.

A study carried out by the University of Texas showed that people were unable to correctly identify the sponsored advertisements on search engine results pages (SERPs).
When shown screenshots of Google search results, participants pointed out advertisements as fewer than 25% of the time, despite the presence of cues like "Ad" or "Sponsored." 


One of the authors of the study, Amanda Broderick, commented on the low number of participants able to discern between ads and search results, noting that "just because something is labeled 'Ad' doesn't mean that people will notice that it's an advertisement."
This failure to identify advertisements relates to a concept from psychology known as inattentional blindness, which causes people to miss obvious facts when their attention is focused elsewhere. 


The authors of the study suggest that the low ability to recognize ads is due to the design of SERPs, which often place ads and search results in similar formats.
Additionally, people may be more focused on the search results themselves rather than the ads that appear on the page.
The authors suggest that search engine designers should make ads more distinct from search results to improve transparency and help users make more informed decisions. 


The study's findings highlight the need for search engine users to be more vigilant in identifying advertisements and interpreting information on SERPs.
It is important to be aware of the potential for ads to influence search results and to consider the motivations of the companies behind the advertisements. 


Overall, the study suggests that people are unable to reliably identify advertisements on SERPs, which has implications for the credibility of information and the influence of advertising on search engine users.

Bernie Ebbers, the former chief executive of collapsed telecoms firm Worldcom, has launched his defence against a $1.7bn fraud charge.


Mr Ebbers, who is on trial in New York, claims he was misled by subordinates and had no knowledge of false accounting.


His lawyer, David Bernick, told the court Mr Ebbers was an "innocent man", and had put "his heart and soul" into Worldcom.


But prosecutor David Anders said Mr Ebbers "knew what was going on" and had "participated in the fraud".


On Tuesday, the court was shown a memo which Mr Ebbers sent to Tony Rutkowski, a Worldcom finance director, with comments highlighting expenses accounted for in the firm's books.


"We are going to have to change our accounting practice," the memo said.
"We cannot keep doing this.
"

Mr Ebbers' lawyer suggested that his client had been complaining about how the company was keeping its books and not the existence of false entries themselves.


But Mr Anders said the memo showed Mr Ebbers' knowledge of Worldcom's "improper accounting" and his "awareness of the fraud".


Mr Ebbers, who resigned as chief executive in April 2002, is the most senior former executive at Worldcom to face trial.

Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas has urged the United Nations to hold Israel to account over "attacks" in the occupied West Bank, in his first speech to the UN security council in person since 2009.


Abbas accused Israel of violating international law with "unprecedented" measures in the West Bank, including "illegal settlement construction, land appropriation, and forced displacement".


"I will not tolerate violations of the national rights of the Palestinian people, and I will not tolerate the destruction of our capabilities," he said.


The speech came after a period of heightened tensions in the region, which saw a series of attacks in the West Bank, including a shooting in late August that killed an 18-year-old Palestinian.


Israel has accused Iran of being behind the attacks.
The Iranian government has denied the allegations.


In his speech, Abbas called on the international community to take action to stop "Israeli aggression and terrorism".


"The world must stand against the illegal and aggressive behaviour of Israel," he said.
"It must provide the necessary support to the Palestinian people to enable them to enjoy their rights, including their right to self-determination.
"

Cairn Energy shares have dropped following a setback for its Greenland oil exploration plans.

The oil and gas exploration company has failed to find commercial quantities of oil in Greenland after drilling into the structure of a high-risk prospect – the Horseshoe project.

It said it had found a “substantial” gas accumulation, but added there was no sign of commercial oil.

In an update to the London Stock Exchange, Cairn (updwntools.com://www.updwntools.com/share-price/cairn-energy-plc- Cairn) said that the Horseshoe-1 well had been successfully drilled to a depth of 5,000m in 1,424m of water.


But it added that while the well had encountered a “substantial gas accumulation”, there were no commercial hydrocarbon shows.

The well will be plugged and abandoned as planned, with the rig moving to the nearby Agar-3 prospect, the company said.


“While naturally disappointing, these results are valuable because they reduce the range of possibilities for this particular prospect,” said Cairn chief executive Simon Thomson.


“We continue to believe the remaining five licences in Greenland offer significant potential across a broad range of play types and we look forward to drilling the Agar-3 well, which will hopefully deliver a successful outcome.”


Greenland, the world’s largest island, is a part of Denmark, although it does have autonomous powers.


It has attracted increasing interest from fossil fuel firms because much of the country is thought to hold vast reserves of oil and gas.

The UK's advertising watchdog has censured a Channel 4 promotion for the US crime series CSI, saying it mislead viewers.


The Committee of Advertising Practice (CAP) said the trailer did not make clear that the programme was a drama and not a documentary.


Channel 4 has been forced to run a lengthy statement, screened after the programme, making clear its fictional status.

Music legend Courtney Love has avoided jail time for possessing crack cocaine and a revolver in her carry-on bag shortly after landing in Oregon to attend a music festival.
Love, 60, was instead placed on probation for three years and ordered to pay a fine of $370,000 following the sentencing hearing in Portland on Thursday.
In addition, the judge ordered her to attend addiction treatment and undergo mental health and substance abuse evaluation. 


Her attorney said Love, whose band Hole was once one of the world’s most influential rock groups, wanted to plead guilty to both charges and put the case behind her.
“Courtney is happy with the resolution,” attorney Robert Axler said.
“She accepts responsibility.
This is an important step for her to take.
It’s an important step toward getting her life back.”


Love was arrested in October 2020 at the airport in Portland, Oregon, after she was caught with nearly two ounces of crack cocaine and a revolver in her carry-on bag.
She had flown from New York City with a stopover in Texas.

Entertainment giant Electronic Arts (EA) has outlined plans to create television and film content based on its video game franchises, principally around its sports titles but also including its action games such as Battlefield. 


The company has appointed EA Sports general manager Sean Ramjolesingh to lead its new initiative as executive vice-president of global television, film and immersive content.
He will build a team to create “high-quality, narrative-driven content” based on the IP in EA’s portfolio.


The drive mirrors the strategy of gaming rival Microsoft, which has had success with its Xbox Game Pass subscription, and Netflix, in turning video games into television content.
It also reflects the growing convergence of the video games, film and TV industries as audiences become less interested in traditional distinctions between them.


EA itself is no stranger to in-house video game adaptations.
It previously created an unsuccessful TV series based on its popular FIFA football game. 


The company said it believed there was now “a golden opportunity” to reach a wider audience on streaming services and TV networks “by doing narrative-driven, character-focused stories with global appeal”.


“As the lines continue to blur between interactive and linear entertainment, there are more opportunities than ever to reach new audiences and tell stories in new ways,” said EA chief executive Andrew Wilson.


“Our goal is to build on our strengths to deliver new forms of entertainment and unlock new revenue streams, while preserving the integrity of our brands with stories that complement our existing franchises.”

And parents are worried about their children's safety in the online gaming community.
Fortnite, released in 2017, is a battle royale game.
It is free to play and popular with children and young people.
It is reckoned that there are millions of players across the world. 


One council offering the classes is Plymouth.
It provides a two-hour session called "Parent Camp".
It covers how to set up parental controls and how to talk to children about online bullying. 


Sarah Hunt is a digital leader at Plymouth City Council.

The Oscars race reaches its final furlong with a glut of awards shows barely keeping ahead of the pack. 


The Oscar nominations, announced on Tuesday, gave us a clearer picture of the films in the running for this year's top honours.
But with the BAFTA awards just a day away, the Oscars race is still wide open. 


Most analysts agree that the best picture race is shaping up to be a contest between "Everything Everywhere All At Once" and "The Banshees of Inisherin."
The former leads the pack with nine nominations, while the latter is close behind with eight.
Both films are nominated in each of the top categories, including best picture, best director, best actor, and best actress. 


But it would be a mistake to count out the other top nominees, including "All Quiet on the Western Front," "Avatar: The Way of Water," "The Fabelmans," "Tár," and "Top Gun: Maverick."
Each of these films has generated a significant amount of buzz and could easily take home the top prize. 


In the acting races, Brendan Fraser (for "The Whale") and Michelle Yeoh (for "Everything Everywhere All At Once") are the clear favorites in the best actor and best actress categories, respectively.
But both face stiff competition from their fellow nominees, including Brendan Fraser's "The Whale" co-star, Hugh Jackman, and Michelle Yeoh's "Everything Everywhere All At Once" co-star, Jamie Lee Curtis.

Wasps produced a heroic second-half comeback against Leicester Tigers in a thrilling Premiership Rugby clash at the Coventry Building Society Arena.


The visitors led 24-6 at half-time but Wasps scored five tries after the break to win 31-37.


Sam Aspland-Robinson, Joe Simpson, Michael Le Bourgeois, Tom Cruse and Alfie Barbeary all went over for Wasps.


Simpson converted three of the five tries for a 100% success rate and he also kicked a penalty.


Owen Williams, Tommy Reffell, and Hanro Liebenberg all scored for Leicester, with George Ford converting all three.


Ford also kicked a penalty in the first half but it was not enough for Tigers.


Wasps suffered an early blow when captain Joe Launchbury was forced off with an injury after six minutes.


The visitors opened the scoring through Williams after 11 minutes following good work from Matt Scott and Ford.


Wasps went close to scoring through Tom West but the television match official adjudged the ball was held up.


Ford extended Leicester's lead to 10 points with a penalty and the visitors scored their second try when Reffell crashed over following a lineout.

The BBC reports that a British court has ordered the freezing of £35 million ($46 million) in bank accounts owned by the family of former Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet. 


The ex-dictator, who is now gravely ill, is himself subject to an order freezing £5 million ($6.5 million) of his own assets. 


Lord Justice Thomas, announcing the latest order, said it was designed to ensure that neither Pinochet nor his family would be able to evade the judgment won by victims of human rights abuses during his regime. 


The victims' lawyers said the order meant the victims could now "at last be compensated for the egregious crimes committed by Pinochet and his regime". 


Seventeen accounts in the name of Pinochet and his wife were frozen earlier this year.
At the time the bank said it was acting on an order from the Home Office.


But lawyers for Pinochet argued that as a former head of state, he was entitled to immunity. 


They also claimed that freezing the accounts would cause "exceptional hardship" to his family.


However, at a later hearing, the Home Office said immunity did not apply in this case as Pinochet was accused of crimes against humanity. 


The judge said there was no evidence the ex-dictator had lived in the UK and therefore the Home Office had been correct to reject his claim for immunity.

Davis won an Emmy and a Golden Globe for the role in 1977. 


He also played the role of Star Trek's Admiral William Rolleston in the 1989 film Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country.

BMW is splashing out £100 million to future-proof the Mini plant in Oxford against the threat of Brexit.
The German car-maker said the investment will create about 1,000 new jobs by 2022 and secure the site's production outlook for the next decade.
The bulk of the money will be spent on upgrading and expanding the plant's facilities including body shops and paint shops.
About £50 million will be for a new "state of the art" paint shop that will be located at the southern side of the site.
The remaining £50 million will be used to upgrade the plant's infrastructure as well as "support an ongoing significant recruitment drive". 


The investment comes after BMW warned that a bad Brexit deal could result in the company shifting production to the Netherlands.
Last month, the car-maker announced that it would close its plant in Swindon, with the loss of about 2,500 jobs. 


The site in Oxford currently produces about 1,000 Minis a day.
The car plant was originally opened by the British Motor Corporation in the early 1960s.
It was later owned by British Aerospace and BMW took over in 1994.

The team from Zambia have plenty of reasons to feel confident as they head to the Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon), which starts on Sunday in Cameroon.


This time last year, they were preparing for the play-offs, knowing that failure to win would send them back to the drawing board, having missed out on qualifying for a second successive tournament after an impressive showing in 2020.


But they dispatched Botswana and then Tunisia to secure their place at the 24-team event and are now looking to improve on their quarter-final finish in Egypt three years ago.


While Zambia are not among the favourites this time, they are perhaps fortunate that the draw has been kind to them.


They are in Group B alongside Senegal, Guinea and Zimbabwe and will play all their games in the capital, Yaoundé.
Their first match is on Monday, when they take on Guinea.


"I think we have a very fair group, and I believe we have what it takes to progress," Zambia coach Beston Chambeshi told the media.


"There are no underdogs any more in football.
Any team that has qualified for the Nations Cup has the capacity to do well.
We are going to approach every game with a lot of respect."

Electronics retailer EMI saw its shares plunge 10% in early trading today, after the company issued a profit warning.
The warning came as EMI reported a 26% decline in pre-tax profits for the six months to October 31, 2023.
The company cited difficult trading conditions and a decline in customer numbers for the profit fall.
It also announced that it would be undertaking a strategic review of the business, which could lead to the closure of more than 100 stores.


EMI's problems come as no surprise to industry watchers, who have been expecting the company to issue a profit warning for some time.
The retailer has been struggling to compete with cheaper rivals, such as Amazon and eBay, as well as facing increased competition from traditional high street stores.


The company's chief executive, Alan Peterson, said that the trading environment had been "challenging" and that the company was "reviewing its strategic options".
He also said that EMI was "committed to improving its performance".


Shareholders will be hoping that the company can turn things around, as its stock has now fallen by over 50% in the past year.
With competition in the electronics retail space only set to increase, EMI will need to find a way to differentiate itself from its rivals if it is to survive in the long term.

Steve W. Bell, who suffered from diabetes and other related health problems, died unexpectedly at his home early on Saturday morning, according to a spokesman for the fast-food company.


Mr Bell, who was chief executive of McDonald's UK, was considered a rising star in the company's global hierarchy and seen as a possible successor to Ralph Alvarez, the outgoing chairman and chief executive.


McDonald's confirmed the death, saying Mr Bell was a valued member of the company's management team.


"He was a brilliant marketer and talented executive who played a major role in the development of McDonald's UK," it said in a statement.


"His contribution to the growth of the business over the last 10 years, during which time the company has doubled in size, been hugely significant.
"

Mr Bell joined McDonald's in the UK in 1996, taking over as chief executive three years later.


He transformed the way the company marketed itself, making greater use of television and other media and increasing its advertising budget from £19m to £58m.

Sales at McDonald's restaurants in the UK rose from £1.86bn to £2.8bn over the same period.


Mr Bell also forged partnerships with Disney, the BBC and the Premier League football clubs to reach a wider audience.


A strong advocate of healthy eating, he launched a range of salads and fruit bags, and improved the nutritional content of Happy Meals.


Last year he oversaw the opening of the chain's 1,000th British restaurant in Sheffield.

The veteran Nigerian author, Buchi Emecheta, has died at 74.


Her debut novel, Concubine, was published in 1966, and she went on to become one of the world's best-known female writers, with more than 20 novels and several short stories and essays.


She died in London on Monday, her family said, without giving details.


"Buchi was a great storyteller and her books will continue to be read and loved by readers all over the world," they said in a statement released by the United Kingdom's Guardian newspaper.


The novelist had been suffering from breast cancer.


Her most famous books include The Joys of Motherhood, published in 1979, and Double Yoke, published in 1973.
The latter was adapted for a film in 1982.


She was appointed officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in 2006 for services to literature.


Her novels, mostly set in Nigeria and featuring strong female characters, typically tackled issues such as polygamy and the role of women in society.


She once said of her writing: "If my books can help somebody, if they can make somebody understand somebody else's life better, then I have achieved something."

By using net fingerprints, organizations can gain a deeper understanding of their network's activity and detect potential threats more quickly.
This can help them to take action before a cyber attack can cause significant damage.
In addition, net fingerprints can be used to track and monitor the activity of cyber criminals, helping organizations to stay one step ahead of potential threats. 


The use of net fingerprints is a game-changer for organizations looking to protect their networks and data from cyber attacks.
With the growing demand for cybersecurity experts, this innovative approach can help organizations to bridge the gap and secure their networks from potential threats.

Profit at China's largest bank has jumped almost 30% in the first nine months of the year, the bank has announced. 


Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) said it earned 425.7bn yuan ($62bn; £46bn) in the period. 


The bank's chairman, Yi Huiman, described the performance as "satisfying" in a statement that accompanied the results. 


He added that the bank was "fulfilling our responsibility to promote stability in the financial sector".


The bank's earnings were up 28.7% on the same period last year, when it earned 324.5bn yuan.


ICBC, which is state-owned, is the world's largest bank by assets.
It is also one of the Big Four state-owned commercial banks in China. 


The bank's earnings were up 10% year-on-year in the third quarter of the year, when it earned 139.1bn yuan.


The bank said its net interest margin - a key measure of profitability - improved in the first nine months of the year, but this was offset by an increase in impairment losses on investments.


China's banks have been hit by a slowing economy and the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic, but they have been helped by interest rate increases which have improved their net interest margins.

Microsoft has released security patches for a record 137 vulnerabilities, including one that is being actively exploited by attackers.
The software giant issued nine security updates to address a wide range of vulnerabilities, including a remote code execution flaw in Windows Print Spooler that is already being exploited.
This is the largest number of patches that Microsoft has ever released in a single month.


The biggest concern for security experts is the remote code execution flaw in Windows Print Spooler.
This vulnerability allows attackers to execute code on vulnerable systems remotely.
This flaw is already being exploited in the wild.


"Microsoft is aware of attacks that attempt to exploit this vulnerability through the use of specially-crafted prints delivered to the Spooler service," the company said in its advisory.
"An attacker could then install programs; view, change, or delete data; or create new accounts with full user rights.

The legendary Godzilla has been given a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in recognition of his contribution to the film industry for the past 66 years.
The star was presented to Godzilla at a ceremony in Los Angeles hosted by the Hollywood Chamber of Commerce and is the 2,688 star on the walk.
"Godzilla is a symbol of Hollywood," said Rana Ghavami, chair of the Hollywood Chamber of Commerce.
"Throughout the decades, Godzilla has become a globe-spanning icon and we are thrilled to welcome him to our Walk of Fame."


The legendary monster, first seen in 1954 in Japan, has appeared in 36 films to date, providing excitement to fans all over the world.
His star is located in front of the Hollywood and Highland complex, not far from the Dolby Theatre, where the Oscars are held each year.
"We are excited to welcome Godzilla to our Walk of Fame," said Ellen K, a representative of the Hollywood Walk of Fame.
"As a legendary symbol of Hollywood, he is a perfect addition to our iconic attraction." 


This year marks the 66th anniversary of the release of the original Godzilla film, as well as the premiere of the latest film in the franchise, "Godzilla: King of the Monsters," which was released to theaters in May.
The film featured an all-star cast, including Kyle Chandler, Vera Farmiga, and Millie Bobby Brown.

Andy Murray's hopes of a fairytale finish at SW19 came to an end as he was knocked out of Wimbledon in the third round by big-serving American John Isner.


The former world number one, who had knee surgery in February, was unable to convert any of his eight break points as Isner won 6-4 7-6 6-7 7-6.


It was a typically tough encounter on Centre Court between two players who have never lost a match on the Grand Slam stage when taking the tie-break to a third set.


But it was the American who emerged victorious to set up a last-16 meeting with Canada's Felix Auger-Aliassime.


Isner, who served a record 113 aces in his first-round match, fired down 25 aces against Murray and made only nine unforced errors on his way to victory.


The 34-year-old's serve was the key difference in the match, with Murray unable to make any breakthrough on his return.


Isner has now reached the fourth round at Wimbledon for the sixth time in his career, with his best result a run to the semi-finals in 2018.


Murray, who has been struggling with his movement, was unable to pressurise Isner's serve and make the most of his own potent weapon - his forehand.


The Scot has worked tirelessly to get fit for Wimbledon after undergoing surgery on his troublesome right knee, but he has struggled to find his best form.


Despite that, he can take heart from his performance against Isner, who has been in fine form in the last year and will be a serious contender for the title.

Former Germany goalkeeper Jens Lehmann has criticised Mesut Ozil for his decision to retire from international football, saying he should have "taken responsibility".


Ozil, 29, announced in a tweet he was "retiring for good" from international football with immediate effect, adding he had "experienced mixed feelings" about Germany.


"It is with a heavy heart and after much consideration that because of recent events, I will no longer be playing for Germany at international level whilst I have this feeling of racism and disrespect," he said.


The Arsenal midfielder, who is of Turkish descent, was criticised by the German football association for his meeting with Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdogan in May.


Lehmann, who was in goal for Germany when they won the World Cup in 2014, said Ozil should have taken ownership of his decision rather than "putting the blame onto others".


"I think it would have been better if he had taken responsibility on his own behalf," Lehmann told BBC Radio 5 Live's Football Daily podcast.


"Don't blame others, don't blame the political situation, and don't blame your manager.
He is a big player, a big character, and I think he could have dealt with it in a different way.


"He could have said 'for tactical reasons, I am not selected anymore, I don't want to argue about it'.


"But he's not done that, he's kind of put the blame onto others and not taken ownership of his decision, and that is disappointing."

The boss of car maker Renault has described 2022 as a "great year" for the company, despite a fall in car sales because of the coronavirus pandemic.


Renault's domestic sales rose 9.8% to 551,880 vehicles, but that was more than offset by a decline in sales in Russia, where the company recorded a 25% fall to 47,792. 


Renault's alliance with Nissan, which owns 15% of the French carmaker, helped deliveries rise in South Korea, where the Nissan-Renault Automotive Korea joint venture saw sales jump nearly tenfold to 152,884.

Renault boss Carlos Ghosn said: "2022 was a great year for Renault, despite the difficulties caused by the pandemic and the war in Ukraine. 


"In particular, the growth in our electric vehicle sales, with more than five times more Zoes sold compared to 2021."

Zoe is a subcompact electric car manufactured by Renault.


Last year, Renault hit its target for electric vehicle sales, with more than 41,000 sold.
That figure rose to more than 91,000 including LCVs (light commercial vehicles). 


Overall, the company sold 517,695 electric vehicles, an increase of more than 41%. 


The group also recorded a record profit of €8.8bn (£7.5bn) for 2022, compared with €4.3bn (£3.7bn) the previous year.

An alliance of Scottish fishing groups will appear before MPs in Westminster tomorrow (Wednesday) to demand that fisheries remain “at the heart” of the UK’s future relationship with the EU.  


The Scottish Fisheries Coalition, which represents groups covering the whole of the Scottish fishing industry, will tell the Scottish Affairs Committee that fisheries must be negotiated “as a package” along with other issues, such as trade. 


They will urge MPs to press for annual negotiations on fishing access, rather than waiting for the full term of the wider trade negotiations to be completed. 


And they will call for the UK government to begin preparatory work now for a no-deal outcome, amid concerns that the industry could be hit by tariffs of up to 80%. 


Coalition member Bertie Armstrong, who is also chief executive of the Scottish Fishermen’s Federation, said: “The UK government’s stated ambition of seeking a [free trade agreement] with the EU is wholly welcome, but MPs need to understand that the consequences of failing to reach an agreement could be catastrophic for our industry. 


“Tariffs of between 60% and 80% could be levied on our exported seafood, prices will plummet, thousands of jobs will be lost and communities already suffering from decades of decline will be dealt a hammer blow.” 


The Scottish Affairs Committee is conducting an inquiry into the future of the Scottish fishing industry after the UK leaves the EU. 


Its latest evidence session will hear from the Scottish Fisheries Coalition, made up of eight member organisations covering all sectors of the industry, including the commercial, charter and shellfishing sectors, as well as representatives of fishermen in Scotland’s islands and remote rural communities. 


Armstrong added: “The UK government has a responsibility to provide urgent clarity on its plans for the future, and we welcome the opportunity to make our case to the Scottish Affairs Committee. 


“Fisheries must be at the heart of the UK’s future relationship with the EU.

The stars have arrived in Hollywood for the most glamorous night of the year - the Oscars.
It's the first time in three years that the ceremony has gone ahead face to face, after the Covid-19 pandemic forced the Academy to hold a virtual event in 2020 and postpone its plans for an in-person ceremony in 2021.
This year, the event is taking place at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles, with a star-studded guest list, including top nominees Brendan Fraser, Michelle Yeoh, and Austin Butler, as well as nominees Salma Hayek, Brendan Fraser, and Japan's "Demon Slayer" animation team. 


For decades, the Oscars have been the most prestigious award ceremony in the film industry, with winners often heralded as the best in their field.
The awards are voted on by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, a group of around 10,000 actors, directors, writers, technicians, and other film professionals.

The UK has seen a disproportionate number of severe weather events this year, from record-breaking temperatures in the summer to consecutive storms causing flooding and infrastructure damage.
This unprecedented run of extreme weather has resulted in a surge in insurance claims, with the industry paying out £1.2bn in the first nine months of 2022.
This figure is expected to rise further as the full extent of the damage caused by Storm Barra, which hit the UK in December, becomes clear.
These costly natural disasters are taking place in the context of an ongoing cost of living crisis, with household budgets already stretched thin. 


The storms have caused a variety of problems for homeowners, from collapsed roofs to flooding and power cuts.
Many of these issues are not covered by standard insurance policies, leaving homeowners to foot the bill for repairs.
In response to this, some insurers have launched special policies to cover the increased risk of extreme weather, but these policies come at a premium and are not available to everyone.


While insurers have increased their premiums to account for the higher risk of claims, this has not been enough to cover the rising costs of claims.
As a result, many insurers have withdrawn from the market, leaving homeowners with fewer options for coverage.
Those who remain in the market have had to raise their premiums significantly, making insurance unaffordable for many.

England captain Owen Farrell paid tribute to his "good friend" and former teammate Maro Itoje after Billy Vunipola's injury against Japan ruled him out of the rest of the November Tests.


Farrell will lead England against Australia on Saturday in the second of four Tests at Twickenham.


Both teams have a chance to win the Cook Cup, with England topping the table because of their superior points difference.


Australia make six changes to their side for the match as they bid to avenge their 2023 Rugby World Cup quarter-final loss to England.


One of those changes sees Itoje replace Vunipola, who suffered a calf injury early on in the 60-5 win against Japan.


"We have known each other for a long time and he is a good friend of mine.
It is sad to see him go, but these things happen," Farrell told BBC Radio 5 Live.


"It seemed to happen so quickly, but he seems to be in a good place and is happy with the decision that he has made.


"Sometimes things aren't meant to be and you have just got to accept that.
He will be a big loss but it does provide an opportunity for someone else."

Hundreds of thousands of civil servants in the UK are to be balloted on strike action in a dispute over pay, the Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union has said.


The ballot - the largest in a generation - will open on 11 January and close on 28 February.


It will open the same day as a strike by nurses, with the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) also in a pay dispute with the government.


PCS general secretary Mark Serwotka said the union was "going for broke" in its campaign for better pay.


He said the prime minister and chancellor could stop the strike by "opening their wallets".


The PCS, which represents workers in departments including HMRC, the Home Office and Ministry of Justice, as well as NHS admin staff, has asked for a 10% pay rise.


The union is also demanding a "cost-of-living adjustment" to all pay points, meaning all civil servants would receive a pay rise in line with the current rate of inflation - currently at 10.7%.


Mr Serwotka said the government was "forcing our hand" by "refusing to talk" to the union about pay.


He accused the government of "bare-faced cheek" in asking civil servants to accept a below-inflation pay increase at a time when ministers had given themselves a pay rise and a minister had been appointed to oversee a "pay rise for ministers".


"The prime minister and chancellor can stop this strike tomorrow by opening their wallets and putting some money on the table," he added.

Music is at a "zombie" state in Germany, dominated by US pop and chart-topping hits from the 1990s and early 2000s, according to a prominent classical music critic.

Daniel Barenboim warned that the country was no longer producing music which was " competitve on the international market" and risked becoming a "museum" of its own musical history.

The conductor and pianist, who is Spanish-Argentinian and has lived in Germany for 40 years, said he felt a "sense of panic" about the lack of infrastructure to support young musicians.


His comments came in a interview to be published on Sunday in the weekly Der Spiegel on the eve of his 80th birthday on 15 November.


Barenboim accused the country's arts establishment of ignoring the current generation of musicians in favour of celebrities and vintage stars who appealed to a mainstream audience.


"Pop and old stars are booked for the next 10 years.
There is no space for young musicians," he said.


"Nothing happens anymore, and that's why Germany has become a museum country.
Either you play Bach and Beethoven or you play pop music.
There is no in-between."

Britain's longest-serving Prime Minister in the 21st century announced his resignation yesterday, warning that the country's "darkest hour" lay ahead.


In a speech drawn up ahead of Sunday's fifth anniversary of the Brexit vote, Boris Johnson urged MPs to get behind the government's Plan B Covid restrictions, saying that the country owed it to the nurses who were "working flat out" to combat the Omicron variant.


And in an indication that he will not be leading the Tories into the next general election, due by 2024, he said it was time for the "party of low tax" to prove it could clear up the "congestion" of regulations introduced by Labour.


In a statement released after midnight, he said that it was "time for me to make an honest assessment" of the situation facing the government.


"I have concluded that we should not be asking people in this country to accept a higher level of taxation," he said.


"I passionately believe that this country should be a place where opportunity is equal for everyone, where everyone can go as far as their talents will take them, and where every child, whatever their background, can aspire to succeed and to be judged on their merits.


"But unless we take immediate action to get debt under control, we are going to go on creating problems for future generations.
That's not what I came into politics to do.
"

Mr Johnson said that he hoped a new leader would be in place by the party conference in October.


The pound rose slightly on the news, which came after a tumultuous week in Westminster that saw 100 Tory MPs defy Mr Johnson in a vote on Tuesday.

Portishead return with their first album in eight years.
It's been a long time coming for Portishead, the trip-hop pioneers who released their last album, 'Third', back in 2008.
Their return has been heralded by a new track, 'Where We Go', featuring vocals from Mercury Prize nominee Kakuta.
The release of 'Where We Go' marks the band's first new material in over a decade, and comes ahead of their long-awaited fifth studio album, 'Ultra Mono', which is set for release in June. 


'Where We Go' is a markedly different sound for the band, fusing their trademark trip-hop sound with elements of ambient and industrial music.
The result is a brooding, atmospheric track that is both haunting and beautiful.
The new album 'Ultra Mono' is said to be a return to Portishead's roots, with the band's trademark sound of trip-hop, jazz, and other influences.
It's a welcome return for one of the most innovative and influential bands of the past few decades. 


In other news, Portishead frontman Geoff Barrow has debuted a new solo album under the name of Sweet Billy.
'Fear Stories' features vocals from Ben Sedgemore of fellow trip-hop pioneers, Moloko.

The BBC has learned that thousands of acres of land in the UK have been fraudulently sold to secretive offshore companies, in a scam that has cost taxpayers millions of pounds.
The land, in some of the most desirable areas of the country, is sold for a fraction of its worth before being resold to innocent buyers for a huge profit. 


The scam works like this.
Fraudsters first target public sector workers, tricking them into signing up to seminars and buying overpriced goods.
They then use the information they have gathered to create fake identities, often of retired public sector workers, and use these to set up companies.
This can involve the use of false passports and other forged documents. 


The companies are then used to register the land in the victims' names.
They target land owned by local councils, the NHS, and the Ministry of Defence, as well as universities and other public bodies.
The land is often near valuable infrastructure, such as train stations and schools. 


Once the land has been registered, it is sold on to other companies, often based in offshore tax havens such as the British Virgin Islands, Gibraltar, and Guernsey.

The government has announced plans to improve the quality of care for elderly people by giving them more control over the services they receive.
The scheme, which will be tested in several areas of the country, will allow patients to choose their own care provider and decide how their needs are met.


The aim is to give patients more say in their own treatment and to improve the overall standard of care.
Under the plans, patients will be given a personal budget, which they can use to purchase the services they require.
This could include anything from home help to respite care.


Health and Social Care Secretary Sajid Javid said the scheme would give patients more control over their care and help to improve the overall standard of services.
He said it would also provide more support for carers, who often struggle to cope with the demands of looking after an elderly relative. 


"The best decisions about people's care are often made by the people themselves or their closest allies, not by bureaucrats or officials," he said.
"That is why we are putting people in control of their care and allowing them to make decisions about what matters most to them." 


The plans have been welcomed by many in the care sector, who have long called for more patient involvement in care decisions.

The number of people in the US who are employed or looking for work rose unexpectedly in September, official data shows.
The labour market was expected to weaken after a burst of hiring in August as coronavirus cases surged, but data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) showed further gains in the unemployment rate.
The rate rose to 4.8% in September from 4.5% in August, according to the BLS data released on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, the number of non-farm payrolls increased by 194,000 in September, beating estimates of about 155,000. 


In the report, BLS noted that there was a decline in government jobs last month, with state and local education seeing job losses.
But the worst of the layoffs appeared to be over, as most school districts have started the new academic year and hired staff.
The report also showed that the number of jobs in the food services and drinking industry declined, as well as in the arts, entertainment, and recreation industry. 


The report was released as Federal Reserve officials concluded their latest two-day policy meeting.
The central bank said it would soon start reducing its monthly bond purchases, but held off on raising interest rates, saying it was still assessing the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic on the labour market. 


The yield on the 10-year US Treasury note rose following the jobs data release, reaching 1.6% ahead of the Fed's decision.

Sea Inside, the winner of the 2007 Spanish Film Prize (Goya Award) for Best Documentary, has struck twice at the Cinema Eye Honors awards, considered the "Oscars" of documentary filmmaking.
The film, directed by Juan Antonio Bayona and produced by Guillermo del Toro, won the Audience Choice Award at the 4th Annual Cinema Eye Honors awards, held on January 13 in New York City.
In addition, the film's music composer, Fernando Velázquez, won the award for Outstanding Achievement in Music. 


"I'm pleasantly surprised.
I did not expect this.
I'm very happy that the people have chosen the film," Bayona said in a statement.
He dedicated the award to del Toro, who produced the film through his Tequila Gang production company. 


Sea Inside is based on the autobiography of Ramon Sampedro, a Spanish man with a terminal illness who fought for the right to end his life with dignity.
The film follows Sampedro's fight, through his relationship with Julia, a journalist who is also his girlfriend.
The film also explores the feelings of his family members, who support his decision but face internal struggles with their beliefs.

text:
Former Olympic champion Kelly Holmes has said "it's a bit weird" to be asked for her views on the doping scandal that has engulfed British Cycling and Team Sky.

Holmes, who won 800m and
1500m gold at the 2004 Athens Olympics, said "it was a different era" when she ran, adding that she was "not sure I believe" some of the allegations about cyclists using performance-enhancing drugs.


The 44-year-old was speaking after being appointed a member of the British Olympic Association's (BOA) athlete commission.


Her comments come in the wake of a series of investigations into doping in cycling, including UK Sport and Cycling Weekly's 'Catch Me If You Can' investigation earlier this year.


And the BOA has appointed a former head of UK Anti-Doping, Andy Parkinson, to conduct an independent review into British cycling to investigate "alleged failings" ahead of the Tokyo 2020 Olympics.


"It's a bit weird answering questions about cycling when I'm on the Olympic committee because I know nothing about cycling," Holmes told the PA news agency.


"It was a different era, I'm not sure I believe everything that is said.
I just know that I never got asked to take drugs, I was never offered drugs - I was never exposed to it.


"So for me to comment on the sport now, I don't think it's fair because I don't know enough about it.
"

Holmes' appointment to the BOA's athlete commission was announced by Dame Katherine Grainger, the chair of the body.

Anti-war campaigners have called on the British government to set a timetable for the withdrawal of troops from Iraq.


The call came at the end of a march in London attended by hundreds of people.


Carrying placards reading "Don't add to the slaughter", and "Brits - go home", the marchers gathered in Parliament Square for a rally.


Among the speakers was Robert Kennedy Jr, son of the late US senator Robert Kennedy, and the former MP Tony Benn.


Mr Kennedy said British soldiers were being used as "cannon fodder" in Iraq.


"We demand that our government bring our troops home," he told the crowd.


"Not tomorrow, not next week, but now."


The marchers included Iraqis, Britons and people of other nationalities.


Police said about 250 people took part.


The rally was organised by the Stop the War Coalition, which argues that the war in Iraq has not improved security in the region and that terrorism has increased as a result.

"In this case, the trailer was deemed to be biased and, as such, it was not shown on our networks."

Martin Freeman, the actor and comedian who is a supporter of the Conservative Party, criticized the decision on Twitter, saying: "Jesus Christ indeed, the BBC won't run the trailer for Passion because they think it's too political.
"So essentially any reference to Jesus is political but the many references to Stalin in Wolf Hall are just part of the general historical context.

The very poorest people in Colombia are having their savings eaten away by inflation, forcing them to eat less and turn to child labour, the country's central bank has said.


The bank's survey - based on interviews with more than 17,000 people - found that nearly half of the country's poorest had lost money because of inflation.


Households earning less than 375,000 pesos (£63; $75) a month - around the minimum wage - lost an average of 13% of their savings in the past year, it found.


Many said they were eating less, or eating lower-quality food.
Some reported having to send their children to work.
The survey was carried out in October 2021.


"I want to eat three meals a day
but I can't," said one respondent.
"Sometimes I eat only once and that's in the morning.
When I can I eat lunch, otherwise I don't.

A tsunami that hit Indonesia’s Sunda Strait has cost the country’s stock market more than $650m in wiped-out value, as the death toll across western Java and southern Sumatra rose to nearly 400.


The disaster, which has caused widespread destruction across Indonesia’s main island of Java, hit the stock market as it came after the market close on Monday.


“There could be some downward pressure on the index in the short term, but we don’t expect a significant impact beyond that,” said Muhammad Dimyati, chief strategist at Bahana Securities in Jakarta.


The tsunami, which struck the Indonesian coast without warning, washed away hundreds of buildings and killed at least 372 people.


The disaster, coming ahead of the Christmas shopping season, has also hit retail, tourism and other sectors.


“Obviously, the retail sector will be affected by the disaster,” said Ivan Tan, a fixed-income analyst at PT Bank Maybank Indonesia.


“We expect big-ticket items, such as motorbikes and cars, to be affected as consumers rethink their spending plans,” he said.


The tsunami has dealt a blow to the rupiah, which has been under pressure because of the Federal Reserve’s tightening cycle and the strong dollar.


It came after the Indonesian central bank decided to leave interest rates unchanged at its final policy meeting of the year on Wednesday, a decision some investors said was surprising.


“The central bank will probably maintain a hawkish stance for the rest of the year given the Fed’s rate hike trajectory next year and the pressure on the rupiah,” said Antonio Chew, an economist at Bank of Singapore.

Focus turns to implementation of accord after weeks of tense negotiations

Decisions on when and how Turkey's customs union with the European Union will be updated have been put off until March, according to a joint statement agreed by Brussels and Ankara.


Following weeks of tense negotiations, European Union leaders and Turkish Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu agreed a deal in Brussels on Friday to halt the flow of refugees into Europe.


The statement, released early on Saturday, said the customs union would be "modernised" to take account of Turkey's various trade agreements with third countries.


However, the text made no mention of an emergency brake that Turkey had sought, which would allow it to re-impose tariffs on EU imports if it felt the deal was not being honoured.


The issue of the customs union - which removes tariffs on goods travelling between the EU and Turkey - had been one of the key sticking points in the talks.


Turkey wanted to retain the right to impose its own tariffs on imports from Europe if the EU did not allow it to upgrade its customs union agreement. 


The joint statement said the EU and Turkey had agreed to "re-energise" their relations and gradually deepen their political dialogue.


It also said the EU would step up financial and technical assistance to help Turkey cope with the nearly three million refugees it is hosting, most of them Syrians.


The assistance would be worth €3bn ($3.4bn) over the next two years and would be released in stages, subject to progress on the refugee issue.


The statement also made reference to the "sensitive issue" of refugees being returned to Turkey from the EU, saying this would be done "in accordance with internationally accepted norms and standards".

Councils will be able to increase council tax by 5% without a vote from parliament, after the government dropped a clause from the Levelling Up Bill.


The change would save local authorities about £3bn in the next five years, ministers say.


But Labour, the Liberal Democrats and some Tory MPs criticised the move, saying it would hit poorer households.

South Africa scored three tries to Ireland's two but wasted too many chances in an error-strewn match.


Ireland took the lead when centre Bundee Aki went over in the left corner after a brilliant passing move.


The Springboks hit back with an equalising try from winger Kurt-Lee Arendse, who intercepted a pass from Ireland captain Johnny Sexton.


South Africa edged ahead when scrum-half Faf de Klerk dived over after a series of picks and goes by the forwards.


The visitors went further ahead when Eben Etzebeth drove over from a line-out after the hooter had sounded for half-time.


Ireland came out fighting in the second half with flanker Will Connors scoring after a series of offloads by the forwards.


They scored a second try when replacement flanker Peter O'Mahony drove over from a line-out to tie the scores.


South Africa went back in front when Sexton's cross-field kick was caught and touched down by Arendse.


Ireland hit back again when replacement centre Shane Daly scored in the right corner after a brilliant run by fellow replacement Jamie Osborne.


But South Africa secured the win with a penalty from Handre Pollard with two minutes left.

The former England captain took rugby's greatest prize at the sport's highest level but remained his own most demanding critic throughout a glittering career. 


A World Cup winner, a Grand Slam champion and a two-time Lions tourist, Lawrence Dallaglio won everything there was to win in rugby union, yet still described himself as "a bitterly disappointed sportsman".


Even in retirement, the most ferocious of forwards remained his own most demanding critic.
"I expect a lot more of myself than anybody else could," Dallaglio said shortly after ending his international career in 2002.
"I am hard on myself because I want to be the best, and I never thought I was one of the best players in the world.
"

It was typical of Dallaglio's self-effacing nature that, even as he was announced as an inductee into the World Rugby Hall of Fame in 2021, he was quick to praise those he had played with and against.


Speaking to the BBC after receiving the honour, Dallaglio said: "There are obviously a lot of great players that haven't been inducted into the Hall of Fame.
It was probably more emotional than I thought it was going to be, partly because you look at all the great players that have been inducted, and it is a very select group.


"When you look at the players I was lucky enough to play with and against, the calibre of player is absolutely phenomenal.
I am very proud to be part of that group.

text:
Bono, The Edge, Adam Clayton, and Larry Mullen Jr. have been elected to the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame class of 2023.


The announcement caps a year in which the quartet celebrated the 50th anniversary of the release of their debut album, Boy.
Although they have been eligible for induction since 2005, this is the first time the members of U2 have received enough votes for induction into the hall.


They will be inducted during an April ceremony in Los Angeles. 


Punk legends the Ramones, soul singer Roberta Flack, and folk-rock duo Simon & Garfunkel are also among the inductees. 


Eligibility for the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame requires artists to have released a commercial recording at least 25 years prior.
Fans are able to contribute to the selection process, with this year marking the first time that voting was open to fans online. 


More than 650,000 fans cast votes, which counted as a single vote among the more than 1,000 general ballot voters.

What do you think about them finally being inducted into the rock Hall of Fame?

The blogs, which include 9to5Mac, MacRumors, and Apple Insider, have historically maintained a policy of protecting their sources, but Apple's demands could put that policy to the test.


The blogs were contacted by Apple's legal team in recent weeks, according to reports from multiple outlets.
The company demanded that the blogs reveal their sources for specific stories, or provide information on how those stories were obtained.
In some cases, Apple also asked for advance notice of future stories. 


The blogs have historically been critical of Apple, often reporting on leaks and rumors about the company's products and plans.
It is not clear why Apple has chosen to target these specific outlets, or what the company hopes to gain from this effort. 


Some media lawyers have suggested that the letters from Apple are legally sound, and that the blogs could be held in contempt of court if they do not comply.
However, others have argued that the letters are a form of intimidation, and that the blogs should resist the pressure to reveal their sources.


It remains to be seen how this situation will play out, but it is clear that Apple's actions have shaken up the blogosphere and raised important questions about the role of the media in the age of leaks and rumors.

Ford has become a major player in the automotive financing market in the US, where it operates through its Ford Motor Credit subsidiary, allowing it to benefit from the growing popularity of used vehicles.


Ford Credit, which reported a profit of $1.7bn in the third quarter of 2022, makes more money from financing than it does from selling cars.
The division’s pretax profit margin reached a record of 18.4% in the third quarter, while the automotive unit’s margin, including trucks and SUVs, was 13.3%.


The strong performance has helped Ford’s overall profitability, as the company has managed to keep prices high despite declining sales volume.
Moreover, Ford has benefited from the strong used car market, which has boosted its financing division.


“Ford Credit is off to a tremendous start this year,” said John Lawler, Ford’s chief financial officer.
“These results are testament to our disciplined approach to managing the business, meeting customers’ needs with a variety of financing products and services, and delivering exceptional customer experiences.”


About 80% of Ford’s US sales are financed by Ford Credit, which offers a range of products, including loans, leases, and balloon payments.
It also offers a line of credit for customers who are struggling to make their monthly payments.
In addition, the subsidiary provides wholesale financing to Ford dealers, helping them to buy and maintain their inventory.

The US has been accused of holding up a £1.6bn ($2bn) package of aid for tsunami-hit Indonesia and Thailand.


The package - mainly from the UK, Japan and Australia - was due to be distributed at a donors' meeting in Bali on Tuesday.


But the US wanted the package to include debt relief, correspondents say.
The US denied this.


The UK's International Development Secretary, Hilary Benn, said if the US did block the aid, it would be "completely unacceptable".


The massive Boxing Day tsunami last year killed about 220,000 people in 14 countries.


The UK has already given £400m in aid to the affected countries since the disaster.


And earlier this year, Gordon Brown announced that £1.6bn of debt would be written off by international creditors for the countries affected by the tsunami.


These include Indonesia, Thailand, Sri Lanka, India and Maldives.
The debt relief will be implemented over 10 years.

text:
The Government has announced the most significant changes to child access laws in decades, which supporters say will protect thousands of children from "abusive" parents.


Currently, the law says children should have contact with both parents after a separation, unless it is harmful to do so.


The new law will introduce a "primary carer" label for the parent who looks after the day-to-day care of the children.


The other parent will retain the right to contact, but it will be balanced against the right of the primary carer to protect the child from "intense or predatory" contact that could cause them harm.


The Government says the changes, which will be enshrined in law, will stop parents from using children as "pawns" during divorce proceedings.


Lord Wolfson, the minister for family support, said the reforms recognised that "children thrive best when they have both parents involved in their lives".


But shadow justice secretary Stephen Kinnock said the Government was "significantly weakening" the safeguarding of children.


He added that the Government had "totally failed to justify" the removal of the "proven framework" of the current law.


The announcement was also criticised by campaigners, with some warning the changes could put children at risk of abuse.


Rosie Canning, from charity Family Action, said the plans appeared to be based on the "misconception" that child abuse only happens when parents are divorced.

Barcelona icon Samuel Eto'o has revealed that the club were close to re-signing Arjen Robben from Bayern Munich in 2014, but the deal fell through after then-president Sandro Rosell refused to increase Robben's salary.
It came as a shock that Barcelona were interested in Robben, who had been a long-time servant of their great rivals Real Madrid between 2004 and 2007.
The Dutchman had been keen on a return to Spain, and Barcelona were prepared to make his wish come true.


"When I was at Barcelona, they told me that they were close to signing Arjen Robben," Eto'o told ESPN FC.
"We even talked with him about it but in the end, it did not happen."
When asked why the move fell through, Eto'o replied: "The then-president Sandro Rosell did not want to pay the asking price for him."
Rosell resigned in January 2014 following a scandal where he was found to have oversold the club's television rights, with Barcelona announcing that they would not be renewing his contract.


Despite never playing for Barcelona, Robben still had a successful career at the top level.
He lifted the Bundesliga title eight times in his time at Bayern Munich, along with the DFB-Pokal and the Champions League.
The winger also played a crucial role in the Netherlands' run to the World Cup final in 2010.

The interactive search engine Ask Jeeves is set to make a comeback later this year, as the company behind it hopes to capitalise on the growing popularity of voice-activated technology.


The UK-based firm said Ask Jeeves would be "voice-first", with a focus on answering search queries via smart speakers and other internet-connected devices.


It is the latest attempt to revive the brand, which has lain dormant since being sold to the US tech company IAC in 2010.


The new owners said they wanted to "revive and update" the well-known brand, which first launched as a pioneering search engine more than two decades ago.


At the time, it was known for its use of natural language processing, which allowed users to pose questions in normal English, with results drawn from a range of sources, rather than a list of blue links.


The new version will be "a voice-led, AI-powered discovery experience", according to the company, which said it would draw on the original features that made Ask Jeeves popular.


"We're going to bring back the original Ask Jeeves experience, but update it for today's users and for the modern era," said Doug Scott, co-founder and chief executive of Ask.com, which is owned by IAC.


"We believe in a world where asking questions is the easiest way to get things done and we're going to lead in that world."


The company said Ask Jeeves would launch in the US this year, with a global roll-out planned for 2024.


The announcement reflects the growing popularity of voice-activated technology, with sales of smart speakers such as Amazon's Echo and Google's Nest rising steadily over the past five years.

Gaming on smartphones has taken off in the last few years as devices have improved and more people have gotten used to the idea of gaming in casual situations.
This has also given rise to a class of games that are more accessible, and in many cases, more casual than the current offerings of console and PC gaming.
This has given rise to a phenomenon that is set to take off in the next few years as more people get access to smartphones and other mobile devices: casual gaming.


For those who haven’t been following the latest trends in technology, casual gaming is a type of gaming that is typically done on mobile devices such as smartphones and tablets.
These games are often designed to be easy to pick up and play, and can be enjoyed in short bursts of time, such as while waiting for a bus or during a lunch break.
They are often free to play, and many of them offer in-app purchases that allow players to enhance their gameplay experience.


The popularity of casual gaming has been growing steadily in recent years, and there are now many different genres of casual games available.
Some of the most popular genres include puzzle games, word games, and strategy games.
These games are often designed to be challenging, but not so difficult that they are frustrating to play.
This makes them perfect for people who want to relax and unwind after a long day, or for people who want to keep their minds sharp while having fun.

The US broadband market is heating up as competition increases and new entrants enter the market.


The country's largest broadband providers have been expanding their networks and improving their speeds, while new players have been entering the market with innovative offerings.


The biggest news in the US broadband market has been the launch of 5G home internet services.
These services offer speeds up to 1 gigabit per second, which is significantly faster than the average home broadband connection.


AT&T and Verizon have both launched 5G home internet services in select markets, and T-Mobile has plans to launch a similar service in the coming months.


While 5G home internet is still in its early stages, it has the potential to revolutionize the US broadband market.
It could provide much-needed competition to the country's largest providers, and it could also help to bridge the digital divide by providing high-speed internet access to rural and underserved areas.


In addition to 5G home internet, the US broadband market has also seen the launch of new fiber-optic networks from providers like Google and Verizon.
These networks offer speeds up to 2 gigabits per second, which is even faster than 5G home internet.


Google has been expanding its fiber-optic network in select cities across the US, while Verizon has been rolling out its fiber-optic network in the Northeast.

The former chancellor has made a string of claims about the budget, after allies of Rishi Sunak rejected his analysis.


Describing the budget as "average", "thin" and offering "very little", Jeremy Hunt said the measures announced by the current chancellor did not "even scratch the surface" of what was needed.


The Conservative party's annual conference in Birmingham will begin on Sunday, with the party in the midst of an internal row over taxation. 


Mr Hunt, who is the official Conservative candidate for the upcoming by-election in Tiverton and Honiton, said he agreed with "a lot" of what Mr Sunak had done but "it wasn't a course for growth". 


He added that while the decision to increase benefits by inflation next year rather than the rate of inflation plus 1% represented "movement", it "wasn't as much movement as people hoped".


"I think people felt there was a gap between the rhetoric and the reality," he told the BBC's Newsnight programme. 


But Mr Sunak's allies pushed back on Mr Hunt's analysis, saying he had left the Conservatives in a mess after "12 years of stagnation".


Lord Bilimoria, the chancellor's ally in the House of Lords, said: "The reality is that this is a budget which is trying to take decisions to fix the economic mess that the previous chancellor left us in.
"

He told the PA news agency: "Taxes are too high, growth is too low, and we're holding the British public to ransom.
That's not a recipe for economic success.

Britain's biggest peace protest, which brought central London to a standstill and led to more than 1,700 arrests, has failed to get police to reimburse its massive £24m bill.


Demonstrators brought UK's capital to a standstill in 2019. 


The Metropolitan Police applied for the money, arguing the Extinction Rebellion (XR) protest was illegal, but this was rejected by a judge.


The force has 14 days to decide whether to appeal.


XR activists brought London to a standstill for 11 days in October 2019.
They targeted sites including Waterloo Bridge, Parliament Square and Oxford Circus.


The demonstration forced the Met to draft in officers from across the country, at an estimated cost of £24 million.

Scotland boss Steve Clarke is hopeful Billy Gilmour and John Souttar will recover from injury in time for their crucial World Cup play-off final against Ukraine.
The Scots have been dealt an injury blow with the news that captain Andy Robertson will be out of action for up to eight weeks with a hamstring problem.
Left-back Robertson had surgery on the injury this week and will miss the visit of Ukraine on Wednesday.


Clarke does not yet know if Chelsea's Gilmour and Rangers man Souttar will be available after both picked up injuries while on club duty.
"We are hoping that John and Billy are available," Clarke said.
"They have both come back from their clubs with injury concerns.
We are assessing them on a daily basis.
Hopefully they will be available but I won't know that until later in the week." 


Scotland face Ukraine in their World Cup play-off final at Hampden Park on Wednesday.
The winner of the tie will reach this year's tournament in Qatar, with the losers going into the playoffs for the 2024 Euros.

Former British Prime Minister Tony Blair and his successor Gordon Brown have agreed to "draw a line under" their longstanding rift, which has been a source of tension for the Labour Party, according to a spokesperson for Mr. Blair.
The spokesperson confirmed that Mr. Blair had phoned Mr. Brown "out of courtesy" to inform him that he was donating a large sum of money from his personal fortune to the Labour Party.


The donation, which is reported to be around £15,000 ($18,400), is intended to help fund the Labour Party's campaign for the upcoming local elections in England.
It will also be used to support the leadership of current party leader Sir Keir Starmer.


In a statement, Mr. Blair said he believed that Labour was "back on its feet" under Sir Keir's leadership and that the party's prospects in the local elections were "looking strong".
He added that he hoped his donation would "help to contribute to the campaign".


The announcement comes after a lengthy and sometimes bitter public feud between Mr. Blair and Mr. Brown.
The two men have been involved in a longstanding dispute over who was responsible for the financial crisis that occurred under Mr. Brown's watch as Prime Minister.


In a recent BBC documentary, Mr. Blair accused Mr. Brown of "betrayal" for his handling of the financial crisis.
He claimed that Mr. Brown had agreed to a secret deal with the banks to waive regulations in the lead-up to the crisis.
