text:
Daniel Robinson has swapped rugby league for rugby union and is aiming for success with Newcastle Falcons.
The BBC highlights the key points from his interview with BBC Look North.


At the age of 16, Daniel Robinson decided he wanted to be a professional rugby player.


It was a decision which took him on a journey - via London, Newcastle and Australia - which has led to him achieving his dream.


Now 25, the full-back has made it back to his home city with Newcastle Falcons after seven years in rugby league with London Broncos and Newcastle Knights in Australia.


"When I made the choice at 16 it was to become a pro rugby player no matter what standard that was," he said.


"I've gone through a lot of sacrifices, a lot of things you miss out on through the season, especially growing up in London with no family up here, but it was all worth it."

It has been an eventful journey for Robinson since making his debut for the London Broncos in the Championship seven years ago.


He has experienced promotion to the Super League and subsequent relegation back to the Championship, as well as winning the League Leaders' Shield with the Broncos in 2018.


But it was not all plain sailing for the now 25-year-old, who admits he has had to adapt to different styles of rugby and learn how to deal with being dropped from teams.


"It was a tough start, I was 18 and straight away I was playing men's rugby, training full-time, and the physicality of it and the speed of the game was a step up," he said.

It was a decision which took him on a journey - via London, Newcastle and Australia - which has led to him achieving his dream.


Now 25, the full-back has made it back to his home city with Newcastle Falcons after seven years in rugby league with London Broncos and Newcastle Knights in Australia.


"When I made the choice at 16 it was to become a pro rugby player no matter what standard that was," he said.


"I've gone through a lot of sacrifices, a lot of things you miss out on through the season, especially growing up in London with no family up here, but it was all worth it."

It has been an eventful journey for Robinson since making his debut for the London Broncos in the Championship seven years ago.


He has experienced promotion to the Super League and subsequent relegation back to the Championship, as well as winning the League Leaders' Shield with the Broncos in 2018.


But it was not all plain sailing for the now 25-year-old, who admits he has had to adapt to different styles of rugby and learn how to deal with being dropped from teams.


"It was a tough start, I was 18 and straight away I was playing men's rugby, training full-time, and the physicality of it and the speed of the game was a step up," he said.

Apple introduced a new, cheaper iPod model on Monday, marking the first addition to the iPod product line in two and a half years.
The new iPod classic, available in 40GB and 80GB sizes, joins the iPod nano and iPod shuffle in the company's digital music player lineup.
"We're excited to bring the total iPod family to three great products," said Greg Joswiak, Apple's vice president of hardware product marketing. 


The new iPod classic gives customers around the world another option for enjoying their entire digital music collections, in addition to the market-leading iPod nano and iPod shuffle.
Over 55 million iPods have been sold to date.
"Customers are going to love the new iPod classic -- it's an incredible all-in-one digital music player with all the passion and all the heritage of the entire iPod family," Joswiak said.


The new iPod classic retains the original iPod's familiar scroll wheel and intuitive navigation.
The larger, 80GB model holds up to 40,000 songs, or 200 hours of video, as well as thousands of photos.
The 40GB model holds up to 20,000 songs or 100 hours of video, along with thousands of photos.


Both models offer audio controls for playing songs and podcasts, a Cover Flow™ viewing mode that allows users to scroll through album art and select an album by its cover, and the ability to easily create and edit playlists on the go.

The spread of false information online about Covid-19 has been blamed for the rise in cases in some parts of the world.


Social media platforms have been criticised for not doing enough to stop the spread of misinformation.


UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson said on Wednesday that too many people had "been taken in by lies" spread online.


And the World Health Organization (WHO) has repeatedly urged social media firms to act.


Earlier this year, the WHO estimated that a third of the world's population had accessed misinformation about the virus on social media.


In July, Twitter and Facebook announced measures to limit the spread of false information.


And last week, Google introduced a fact check feature in its search results.


But researchers say false information is spreading further online, partly fuelled by websites in Russia and Brazil.


Cyber experts have found a network of hundreds of fake Instagram and Facebook accounts based in Russia that have been posting misinformation about the pandemic.


And Brazilian researchers have traced false claims on WhatsApp to two popular websites there.

The people of Britain have voted to leave the European Union, in a historic referendum that has divided the nation.


The final results showed that 51.9% of voters opted to leave the EU, against 48.1% who voted to remain.


The UK is the first country to leave the EU, which was originally created as a way to foster economic cooperation and integration among its members.


The decision to leave has raised concerns about the future of the UK's economy and its relationship with other EU members.
The prime minister has stated that the UK will continue to trade with the EU, but it is unclear how this will affect the economy.


The leave campaign argued that the UK should take back control of its borders and its laws, and that leaving the EU would save the country money.
However, the remain campaign argued that the UK should stay in the EU to protect its economy and its standing in the world.


The results of the referendum have been met with both celebration and disappointment.
The leave campaign has claimed a victory for democracy, while the remain campaign has stated that the UK has taken a step back from the rest of Europe.


It is unclear what the future holds for the UK, but one thing is certain: the country has taken a step into uncharted territory.

A trial with a cream containing cannabinoids is due to start soon.
The aim is to improve the appearance of skin within 12 weeks. 


The biotechnology firm has been researching the use of cannabinoids in medicine for more than a decade.
The company has developed more than 100 cannabinoid products and has licensed these to more than 10 countries.
Its products are already available in pharmacies in the UK. 


The firm has recently started researching the effects of cannabinoids in the skin.
It believes the ingredients can help to reduce the appearance of wrinkles and improve the texture of the skin.

The NHS waiting time target has been reduced from 18 weeks to 12 weeks.
The change comes as hospitals struggle to clear a backlog of patients resulting from the pandemic.
Ministers say the new target will help speed up access to treatment for patients.
But health experts have warned it will lead to a rise in operations with higher rates of post-operative complications.
The new target, due to come into force in 2024, will only apply to England.
Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland may set their own targets. 


Currently, NHS patients in England have a legal right to begin hospital treatment within 18 weeks of a referral from their GP.
That target will remain in place until the new standard comes into force.
But exactly how the new target will work remains to be seen.


Ministers say the plans will speed up patients' access to surgery.

Glastonbury fans will be able to buy ID cards recognising their vaccination status ahead of this year's festival.


Organisers of the event said the move, for the return of the festival after two years, would offer "a more seamless entry experience".


The cards will indicate whether the bearer has had a negative lateral flow or PCR test in the last 24 or 48 hours, or is fully vaccinated.


Glastonbury 2022, which will feature headline acts including Elton John, Billie Eilish and Kendrick Lamar, gets under way on 22 June.


In a statement issued on the festival's website, organisers said they were confident this year's event would go ahead, after being cancelled in 2020 and 2021 because of the coronavirus pandemic.


They said they were "working closely" with the government and local authorities to make this year's festival safe, "including the requirement for a negative LFT (lateral flow test) prior to arrival".


"There will also be the option of demonstrating proof of two vaccinations in the last 180 days," the statement added.


The NHS Covid Pass, which can be accessed through the NHS app, will change to allow people to demonstrate their vaccination status or test results.


Those who do not have access to the app, for example people without smartphones, will be able to order a paper NHS Covid Pass letter.


Glastonbury organisers said they were aware bearing "proof" of vaccination status or test results "may be tricky" for some people.

Actor and politician Arnold Schwarzenegger has been congratulated on his Oscar win by leaders and fellow celebrities around the world.
The bodybuilder-turned-actor won his first ever Oscar, for best-supporting actor, for his role in “Total Recall” at the 85th Academy Awards.
The 67-year-old star received a standing ovation as he walked to the stage to collect his award.
He previously received 11 nominations for best-leading actor, best-supporting actor, best picture and best director.


Schwarzenegger called his win a “dream come true” and thanked his family, friends and fans in his acceptance speech. 


“I never thought I’d be standing here,” he said.
“I want to thank everyone who worked with me, everyone who believed in me and especially the fans.”

Leaders and celebrities took to social media to congratulate the star on his historic win.
Leader of the Conservative Party Rishi Sunak wrote on Twitter: “Congratulations to @Schwarzenegger on winning his first ever Oscar.
His performance in ‘Total Recall’ was unforgettable.” 


Actor and Schwarzenegger’s fellow bodybuilder Dwayne Johnson also took to social media, writing: “Schwarzenegger has just won an Oscar for best supporting actor… epic moment for the dude.

Former Chelsea midfielder Michael Essien has told the BBC that he expects Ben Chilwell to miss the rest of the season through injury.


The left-back, who has been ever-present for Chelsea this season, was injured during the 2-0 win over Juventus in the Champions League last-16 first leg on Tuesday.


Chilwell, 25, was taken off on a stretcher midway through the second half after appearing to twist his knee.


"When you see him leaving the pitch, you know it's something serious," said Essien, who won the Champions League and the Premier League with Chelsea.


"From the way he was walking, it seemed like something was not right.
I hope he is going to be back soon but, with the way it looks, he might be out for the season, which is a big blow for him and for the team.
"

Chilwell has made 29 appearances for Chelsea this season, with manager Thomas Tuchel relying on the England international as his first-choice left-back.


He has been ever-present in the Premier League this season, starting in each of the last 16 matches, and has also played in all but one of the Champions League and domestic cup games.


Chilwell's injury could see Marcos Alonso regain his place in the side after the Spain left-back has had to be content with being a substitute since the start of the season.


Alonso, who has been with Chelsea since 2016, started the first four games of the season but has not been in the starting line-up since a 1-1 draw at Aston Villa on 7 August.

Ireland captain Brian O'Driscoll has been ruled out of Sunday's Six Nations match against Scotland in Edinburgh with a hamstring injury.


The 33-year-old centre, who has scored 46 tries in 128 Tests, injured his hamstring in training on Tuesday.


Ireland coach Joe Schmidt said he was "devastated" for O'Driscoll, who has been ever-present in his squad during the current campaign.


"To rule him out this close to kick-off is disappointing for everyone, but injuries are part and parcel of the game," said Schmidt.


"Hopefully Brian will be back to full fitness sooner rather than later.
In the meantime, it offers an opportunity for someone else.
"

A statement from the Irish Rugby Football Union on Thursday read: "Brian O'Driscoll suffered a hamstring injury in training yesterday
[Tuesday] and subsequent scans have shown that he will be out of action for up to four weeks.


"No replacement will be called up by Ireland ahead of Sunday's Six Nations clash with Scotland at Murrayfield.
"

O'Driscoll, who has scored five tries in his last seven Tests, will miss the visit to Scotland as well as the matches against Italy and England.

Liverpool manager Jürgen Klopp has laughed off suggestions that Steven Gerrard could replace him at Anfield.


The former England midfielder has overseen Rangers' first Scottish Premiership title for a decade after they beat Livingston on Saturday.


That victory capped a season in which Gerrard has overseen impressive wins over the likes of Celtic, Porto and Bayer Leverkusen.


But he would not be drawn on speculation he could return to his former club to replace Klopp, whose side were pipped to the Premier League title by Manchester City.


"Oh come on, really?"
Klopp said at a news conference before Liverpool's trip to face Southampton in the Premier League on Tuesday.


"How can I deal with that?
I have nothing to say about that.
I would say congratulations to Stevie for winning the league in Scotland.
"

Gerrard won the Champions League, the Uefa Super Cup and the Club World Cup during his time at Liverpool but never managed to win the Premier League during his 17-year playing career at Anfield.

Small firms across the UK are reporting higher costs and struggling to pass these on to customers, a survey has indicated.
The Forum of Private Business said its research showed inflation was the biggest challenge for small and medium-sized companies.
Forum spokesman Toby Marshall said many were "struggling to manage" increases in the cost of energy, fuel and raw materials.
The forum's research showed 42% of firms had seen their energy bills rise in the past three months, while 36% had been hit by higher fuel costs.


Mr Marshall said: "Unfortunately, rising costs are now a fact of life for many small businesses.
"This is a particular challenge for those who have barely recovered from the economic impacts of the pandemic and are still trying to get back on their feet.
This comes amid expectations that the cost of living in the UK is set to rise further, with the price of energy expected to jump by as much as 50% in April.


About a third of the firms had put up their prices in the past three months, the research indicated.
Of these, about 60% managed to pass on all or most of the increased costs to customers, while the rest absorbed the rises.
The monthly survey by the forum is based on the responses of about 1,000 of its members.

The mobile games market is burgeoning with new titles published daily.
The two largest app stores, the Apple App Store and Google Play, offer roughly 7 million and 5 million titles, respectively, with mobile games consistently occupying the top spots in terms of downloads and revenue.
Even the most basic smartphones are capable of running a wide range of games, from simple puzzles to complex 3D experiences.
As a result, the audience for mobile games has expanded to include a wide range of ages, genders, and demographics. 


While mobile games were once considered a lesser form of gaming, this perception has begun to change as the quality and depth of these games continues to improve.
Many mobile games offer a comparable experience to that of traditional video games, with intricate storylines, high-quality graphics, and immersive gameplay.
Even the most casual mobile games can provide a satisfying and engaging experience.
In addition, the social aspect of mobile gaming, through the ability to play with friends or strangers, has helped to increase its popularity. 


The success of the mobile games market has also led to the development of new technologies and innovations.
For example, the use of augmented reality in mobile games has become increasingly popular, allowing players to interact with virtual objects in the real world.

The EU parliament has once again delayed the vote on the software patent directive, amid intense lobbying from both sides of the debate.
The latest delay comes after a narrow victory for the parliament's pro-patent camp last month, when a draft law written by German Christian Democrat MEP Axel Voss was amended in a way that satisfied many of the opponents who had previously fought against it.


The original draft directive, written in 2017, would have required member states to offer patent protection for computer-implemented inventions, including software.
After 18 months of debate, Voss's draft was approved by the European Parliament's legal affairs committee in June this year, but in October a deal was struck that limited the scope of the legislation to cover only "computer-implemented inventions which make a technical contribution".


The deal was seen as a victory for medium and small-sized software developers, who argued that the original directive would have put them at risk of lawsuits from larger companies.
However, the agreement was not enough to win over all opponents, and the vote was delayed for a second time to allow for further negotiations.


Speaking after the decision was taken to delay the vote, Voss said he was "disappointed" that the parliament had not voted on his revised draft, but added that he wanted to give his negotiators time to convince the opponents that the legislation will not harm software developers.
"We want to find a good solution for all sides and I think we will achieve this," he said.


The latest delay is a blow to the European Commission, which has made the software patent directive a priority and has been pushing for it to be approved before the EU parliament's summer recess.
The commission originally proposed the legislation in 2017, and has been working on it ever since.

Roger Federer claimed a historic crown in Dubai on Friday as the legendary Swiss star won his maiden title in the desert.


The world's most successful player had lost three previous finals in Dubai but defeated Felix Auger-Aliassime of Canada 7-6 (7-1), 6-3 to clinch the title.


It was Federer's very first tournament win in over a year and without a doubt one of the most special.
In an on-court interview after the match, Federer said "This is a dream come true.
I am happy for me, and I hope Dubai is happy as well.
This is just unforgettable.
"

With Novak Djokovic being deported from Australia earlier this year and Rafael Nadal missing from Dubai through injury, the 19-time grand slam champion had extra motivation.


Speaking on court, Federer said "There is more pressure since Novak isn't here and Rafa is hurt.
I know everybody is looking at me, maybe going, 'Okay, if Novak isn't there, maybe Roger can still do it.'


"But I think everybody was expecting me to maybe go far in this tournament, maybe even win the tournament, because of the situation.

By.
BBC NEWS, NAIROBI. 


Kenya's athletics governing body have lifted the suspension of former Olympic champion Asbel Kiprop and 800m runner Eunice Sum after being cleared of doping violations.


Kiprop, who won 1,500m gold in Beijing in 2008, and Sum had been suspended after being accused of breaches of doping rules. 


The Athletics Kenya (AK) disciplinary committee cleared the athletes of any wrongdoing on Monday. 


Both athletes have consistently denied doping allegations. 


Sum, who won the 2013 world title in the 800m, had been suspended in April 2019, with Kiprop suspended two months later.


The 30-year-old Sum has not competed since the 2019 World Championships in Doha, where she failed to qualify for the 800m final.


During her hearing, she told the disciplinary committee that her failed tests were due to her consuming traditional medicine to treat a stomach illness. 


Former 1,500m world champion Kiprop, 32, failed to qualify for the 2016 Olympics in Rio following allegations of doping.

The ruins of Pompeii, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, have received a digital makeover.
The project, known as "Pompeii Virtual", is a collaboration between the Ministry of Culture, the Superintendence of Pompeii, and the telecommunications company TIM.
It involves the use of advanced digital technologies to create a virtual reconstruction of the ancient city.
 

The project utilizes holograms, augmented reality, and other interactive technologies to create a digital representation of Pompeii.
This includes the creation of a digital map of the city, which allows users to explore the ruins in a way that is not possible with traditional methods.
The map also includes detailed information about the city's history and architecture.


"Pompeii Virtual" also includes the creation of a digital museum, which will display artifacts and objects found in the ruins.
The museum will use holograms and other interactive technologies to bring the artifacts to life.


The project has been met with mixed reactions from the public.
Some have welcomed the addition of new technology to the ruins, while others have expressed concern about the potential impact on the site's historic integrity.

A blind student from Bristol, UK, says he "hears in colour" after receiving a bionic eye.
Tom Williams, 25, has only ever seen shadows and shapes – but now, after receiving the implant, he can identify colours in food and on clothes.
Williams lost his sight gradually as a result of a genetic condition and had the implant 18 months ago.
"I knew colours existed, but until you experience it for yourself, you don't believe it," he said.
"When I saw red for the first time it was amazing – it was like I'd seen it before, but I hadn't, not in that way.
It's a truly wonderful experience.
"

The bionic eye works by stimulating Williams' retina with pulses of electricity.
It bypasses the part of the eye that doesn't work and sends signals to the brain.
The colours appear in the mind's eye as waves of noise, which he can then interpret.
Williams, who studies psychology at the University of Bristol, hopes to become a mental health nurse after graduation.

"When I saw red for the first time it was amazing – it was like I'd seen it before, but I hadn't, not in that way.
It's a truly wonderful experience.
"

The bionic eye works by stimulating Williams' retina with pulses of electricity.
It bypasses the part of the eye that doesn't work and sends signals to the brain.
The colours appear in the mind's eye as waves of noise, which he can then interpret.
Williams, who studies psychology at the University of Bristol, hopes to become a mental health nurse after graduation.

The number of jobs added to the US economy rose above expectations in the first week of 2023, according to new data.
The labor market showed promise as the week closed on February 19, with the addition of 479,000 jobs, compared to the 350,000 estimates.
The figures suggest that the US economy is on a steady path to recovery from its shortest recession on record, caused by the pandemic and subsequent lockdowns. 


The hospitality industry saw a particular boost, reflecting the renewed consumer demand following the lifting of restrictions.
Hotels and restaurants added 146,000 jobs, bringing the total to pre-pandemic levels.
Meanwhile, professional and business services contributed to a gain of 100,000, with employment in the sector now surpassing its February 2020 level. 


The labor market participation rate remained unchanged at 62.4 percent, with the unemployment rate holding steady at 3.8 percent.
These figures indicate a tight labor market, marked by a shortage of available workers despite the robust job growth.
The data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed a steady trend of job growth over the past year. 


In the past three months, the US has added an average of 550,000 jobs per month.

Matteo Renzi, the former prime minister of Italy, is poised to become the new chief of Fiat Chrysler following a board meeting on Saturday.
The 51-year-old is expected to take on the role of chairman, effective immediately. 


Renzi is set to take over the struggling car manufacturer, which has been struggling to adapt to the industry's shift towards electric vehicles.
This comes after Fiat's current CEO, Sergio Marchionne, died last year. 


The company has been without a permanent CEO since Marchionne's death, with the board of directors ultimately deciding on Renzi's appointment.
The decision has been criticized by some, who argue that Renzi's political background could potentially interfere with his ability to lead the company. 


However, others argue that Renzi's political experience and connections could help to revitalize Fiat's business.
Despite the criticism, Renzi's appointment is expected to be confirmed at the board meeting on Saturday. 


Matteo Renzi began his political career as a member of the Democratic Party, becoming the mayor of Florence in 2009.
In 2014, he was elected as the prime minister of Italy, a position he held until 2016.

The future of television is in the hands of viewers, with the rise of video-on-demand, streaming services, and binge-watching.
The BBC has launched its own streaming service, BBC iPlayer, which has revolutionized the way viewers watch TV.
Instead of relying on traditional TV schedules, viewers can now watch programs at their own convenience, on their own devices.


This shift in viewing habits has led to the rise of "binge-watching," where viewers watch multiple episodes of a show in one sitting.
This has resulted in a more immersive and engaging experience for viewers, who can now become fully absorbed in a show's storyline and characters.


However, this new way of watching TV has also led to some concerns.
Some viewers have complained about the "binge-watching" phenomenon, saying it leads to a lack of diversity in programming and a decline in the quality of shows.


The BBC has responded to these concerns by launching a new campaign, "TV Future in the Hands of Viewers," which aims to encourage viewers to take control of their TV experience and make the most of the new opportunities available.
The campaign includes a range of initiatives, such as the launch of a new streaming service, BBC iPlayer, and the creation of a new "binge-watching" section on the BBC website.


The BBC's move towards a more viewer-focused approach is a clear indication of the changing landscape of television.

"We have to work on our communication when we are in possession.

The move is an effort to reduce the state's severe prison overpopulation.


Under the proposed law, people who have served their sentence would be able to avoid prosecution by legally registering the weapons.


Governor Kemp said the bill, which will be introduced in the state legislature next year, would give people with criminal records a "second chance".


He said the current policy of prosecuting people who have served their initial sentence was unfair.


"I think that's the fair thing to do," he told ABC's Good Morning America on Thursday.
"And again, we're going to work with the general assembly, if they're going to act on it, but I think it's the right thing to do.
"

The proposal has been criticised by Democratic representatives in the state, who said it would endanger the public by allowing people to own guns illegally.


"Governor Kemp's dangerous and irresponsible plan to allow felons to legally possess firearms without a permit is unacceptable," said State House Minority Leader James Beverly on Friday.


"One of the main priorities of our state should be to keep guns out of the hands of criminals, not give them a free pass to ignore the law and endanger our communities.

The BBC has learned that a UK-based company linked to the country's opposition has been occupying a beach in Venezuela's capital, Caracas. 


Video footage obtained by the BBC shows lorries belonging to the company, Beach Boys, on Las Delicias beach. 


And pictures sent to the BBC by a Beach Boys employee show rows of sun loungers and parasols on the same beach. 


But the company, which runs a beach club in neighbouring Colombia, said it has never operated in Venezuela. 


"We have never had any relationship with Venezuela," Beach Boys director Tom Laffey said. 


It comes as Venezuela's government and opposition have been locked in a bitter dispute over President Nicolás Maduro's plans to rewrite the constitution. 


The Beach Boys' presence in Venezuela is being investigated by prosecutors in the city of Maracay. 


But the company's activities are banned in Colombia, where the beaches are considered public territory. 


The Colombian Foreign Ministry said it was "surprised" at the Beach Boys' presence in Venezuela and that it was contacting the company. 


"The ministry will not allow the exporting of the violence that has been experienced in Colombia to another country," it said in a statement.

China has kept a tight rein on credit in the last few months, with total social financing falling significantly compared to last year.
Experts say the government is cautious about stoking inflation, and does not want to add to problems with the country's property sector.
But economists say local governments and businesses are starved of cash, and China's economy is paying the price.
The decline in social financing has been consistent despite four interest rate cuts since last year.
In September, total social financing was down 22% from a year earlier, at 1.35 trillion yuan ($203 billion).
Meanwhile, M2, a broad measure of money supply, is growing at its slowest pace in nearly three decades. 


China's economy is already suffering its slowest growth rate in nearly half a century.
In the third quarter, GDP increased by 3.9% year-on-year, down from 7.9% in the same period the previous year.
And the latest data suggests the economy is slowing further, with retail sales growing 2.5% in September from a year earlier, down from 8.5% in March.
Meanwhile, industrial output grew by just 3.1% year on-year in September, down from 6.3% in March.

JPMorgan Chase has admitted that two of its predecessor firms benefited from slavery in the 19th century.
The bank said its ownership structure was "consistent with" that of slave owners, in a statement accompanying its annual report.
It comes after criticism from a UK-based campaign group, Spotlight on Slavery.
The organisation had called for banks to investigate their historical links to slavery.
Spotlight on Slavery's director, Christopher Brown, said the admission by JPMorgan was a significant step forward.
"There are still thousands of people around the world who are impacted by the legacy of slavery, so it is crucial that financial institutions like JPMorgan Chase take responsibility for helping to address the systemic economic inequalities which are still present today," he added.


The bank did not specify whether it would offer compensation.
It did, however, announce plans to allocate $350m towards a programme of initiatives addressing "systemic economic inequality" and "the legacy of slavery".
These will include funding job training, education and entrepreneurship among communities of colour. 


The admission comes after increasing scrutiny of banks' historic ties to the slave trade.

MetLife, the largest life insurer in the United States, has agreed to buy the life insurance division of Citigroup for about $12.5 billion in cash.
The deal will allow MetLife to expand its consumer finance business and provide Citigroup with much-needed capital. 


MetLife will acquire Citigroup's retail life insurance and annuity businesses, which operate in 52 countries and serve about 9 million customers.
The deal does not include Citigroup's institutional retirement businesses or life reinsurance operations. 


The acquisition is expected to close by the end of 2023, pending regulatory approval.
MetLife said it does not expect the deal to have a material impact on its earnings per share in the first year after closing. 


Under the terms of the deal, MetLife will pay $2.5 billion in cash and issue about 157 million new shares to Citigroup.
The transaction is expected to reduce MetLife's common equity tier 1 capital ratio by about 170 basis points, the company said in a statement. 


MetLife also said it plans to cut about $1.3 billion in annual expenses from the acquisition, with about $870 million of those coming from eliminating duplicate and overlapping expenses between the two companies. 


Citigroup's life insurance division, known as Citigroup Life, had about $136 billion in total assets as of March 31, 2022.

Microsoft has moved to intensify its anti-piracy efforts by introducing a new tool that prevents the unauthorised pre-installation of Windows 11 on computers.
The company emphasised that it is prioritizing security and customer experience rather than device performance in this change.


The new tool, known as the Hardware Compatibility List (HCL), serves as a database that lists all the authorized PCs capable of running Windows 11.
The database includes information such as the manufacturer, model name, and serial number of the devices.


According to Microsoft, the HCL aims to ensure that Windows 11 is only installed on compatible devices, reducing the risk of hardware malfunctions and security issues that can arise from unauthorized modifications.
It believes that this measure is necessary to provide customers with a smooth and secure experience.


The HCL is a follow-up to Microsoft's Windows Genuine Validation (WGV) tool, which was launched in 2019.
The WGV tool was designed to detect fraudulent or unauthorized Windows licenses and prevent them from being used.
The HCL builds on this initiative by ensuring that only genuine devices can run Windows 11.


Microsoft has emphasized that the HCL is just one aspect of its broader anti-piracy strategy, which includes a range of measures such as Windows Update, Windows Defender, and the Microsoft Store.

It believes that this measure is necessary to provide customers with a smooth and secure experience.


The HCL is a follow-up to Microsoft's Windows Genuine Validation (WGV) tool, which was launched in 2019.
The WGV tool was designed to detect fraudulent or unauthorized Windows licenses and prevent them from being used.
The HCL builds on this initiative by ensuring that only genuine devices can run Windows 11.

The BBC has learned that tens of billions of euros earmarked for helping the EU's economic recovery from the Covid pandemic have been lost to fraud.
The scale of fraud and corruption risks derailing the EU's goal of a sustainable and inclusive recovery, and is also depriving citizens of much-needed support, according to a new report by Europol.
The report calls on the EU to tighten up controls and to increase efforts to fight fraud.
It warns that criminals are exploiting weaknesses in the EU's financial controls to steal funds on an "unprecedented" scale.
The report's author, Europol's executive director, Catherine De Bolle, is calling on the EU to tighten up controls and increase efforts to fight fraud. 


"The European Commission, alongside member states, need to improve the overall control environment to prevent fraud, accelerate investigations and recover the proceeds of crime in order to make the EU budget more fraud resistant and future budgets harder to steal," she said.
The call comes after the publication of a study by the European Court of Auditors, which found that weak controls and errors had led to possible fraud in projects worth €42bn (£36bn) - around 4% of the total value of projects funded by the EU's seven-year budget between 2014 and 2020. 


The audit found evidence of fraud in all of the EU's member states, with a particular concentration in Hungary, Italy and Bulgaria.
It also revealed that the European Commission did not perform any checks on projects in member states deemed to be at high risk of fraud.
The commission has welcomed the report, saying it takes the issue of fraud very seriously.

Once revered as a pioneer of personal computing, the Commodore brand now lives on through a quirky Canadian startup that is seeking to revive its legacy.


The company that once brought the world the Commodore 64 has been resuscitated multiple times by different owners since its original bankruptcy in 1994.


The most recent iteration is Toronto-based Commodore International Ltd., owned by former rock star and current businessman, Andy Ashfield.


Since acquiring the rights to the Commodore brand in 2020, Ashfield has been trying to breathe new life into the company by developing a line of modern PCs and laptops bearing the iconic name.


The most recent product announced by Commodore is the Commodore Extreme, a high-end gaming PC that starts at $2,495.
It boasts some serious specs, including up to a 18-core Intel i9 processor, an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 graphics card, and up to 64GB of RAM.


The Commodore Extreme is certainly not cheap, but it is a powerful machine designed for gamers who need a lot of power under the hood.


Whether Commodore can succeed in its latest rebirth remains to be seen.
The company has a long road ahead of it if it wants to recapture even a fraction of the success it found in the 1980s. 


It faces stiff competition from established players like Dell, HP, and Apple, not to mention a bevy of other gaming PC manufacturers like Alienware and Razer.

Sales and prices of homes in Britain have fallen for the first time since the pandemic began, industry figures show.
The price of a typical UK property fell by 0.9% in September, compared with a 0.4% rise in August, according to building society Nationwide.
It said the market had "lost some momentum" as lenders worried about the economic headwinds facing the country.
The number of mortgages approved for house purchases fell to their lowest level since April 2021, according to banking body UK Finance.
It does not expect the market to return to record levels seen earlier this year.
The trend is the same in London, where prices have fallen by 1.2% in September, compared with a 0.5% rise in August, according to the Nationwide figures.
The capital saw the biggest fall in activity, with the number of mortgages approved for house purchases in London dropping to its lowest level since December 2000.
Activity has slowed despite the government's recent decision to pause the imposition of a 1.25% tax on the value of people's homes in England that would have come into effect next month.
From next year, people buying a property in England worth more than £250,000 will have to pay an extra 2% in stamp duty, on top of the 3% they already pay.
But the tax holiday on the first £250,000 of any property purchase in England, which was due to end on 30 September, will continue until March next year.

Music on the move is challenging the "iPod age" with the rapid rise of streaming services and subscription platforms.
A transformation boosted by the pandemic is supercharging the 15-year decline of digital downloads and transforming how we listen as we walk, cycle or drive.


Mobile music streaming increased by 26% in the second half of 2020 according to the IFPI, the organisation that represents the global recorded music industry.
At the same time, downloads declined by 8%.


"Even before the pandemic, mobile listening was growing and fast becoming the most important channel for audio consumption," says Mark Mulligan, a music industry analyst and founder of MIDiA Research.


"Then, in 2020, we saw mobile listening skyrocket.
It was the ultimate lockdown trend.
Instead of being at home where we might listen on desktop or smart speaker, we were all outside, walking and listening on mobile.
"


The figures confirm a seismic shift in how we consume music.

Apple's Mac mini has always been a bit of an outsider in the company's desktop line-up.
While the iMac and Mac Studio have always been sleek all-in-ones and the Power Mac was a powerful workstation, the mini has long been the only desktop Mac that required buyers to bring their own display, keyboard, and mouse.
Yesterday, Apple updated the Mac mini for the first time in three years, and while the aesthetics are still unchanged, the new M2-powered model includes some impressive internal upgrades.


When the M1 Mac mini was announced, it offered impressive performance thanks to Apple's first ARM-based processor.
However, it had some downsides, with the lack of USB4 / Thunderbolt 4 ports being a major disappointment.
The new M2 model fixes that, offering two Thunderbolt 4 ports, an upgraded HDMI 2.1 port, and a Gigabit Ethernet port, with a 3.5mm headphone jack also included.
Combined with the impressive performance gains offered by the M2, and the new Mac mini has the potential to be a great compact desktop for both consumers and professionals.


While the M2 Mac mini's single M2 processor is impressive, the new Mac Studio is what really has us excited.
Available with either an M1 Max or M1 Pro processor, the Mac Studio offers incredible performance in a compact design.
It's aimed at professionals, but with a starting price of $1,999 it's also much more affordable than the $5,999 Mac Pro.

Around midnight on Wednesday, a car pulled up outside the house of Sir Keir Starmer, Labour leader, in Camden, north London.
Daniel Kawczynski, a Conservative MP since 2005, got out and knocked on the door.
Starmer was in bed, but his wife, Victoria, answered, and invited the MP in.
He refused the offer of food and drink, and instead they sat in the kitchen, chatting.


Kawczynski had told his wife he was visiting a friend for "a drink and a chat", but in fact, he was moving MPs from the Conservative party to Labour.
It is a remarkable act of political rebellion – and an indication of the turmoil in the Tory party following the election of Boris Johnson as leader.


For years, Kawczynski had been a loyal Conservative, first as a member of the European Parliament, then as a member of the Polish community in Britain.
He was a strong supporter of Brexit and repeatedly attacked Labour as "the party of open borders".


But he became increasingly frustrated during the Tory leadership contest, as candidates veered to the right.
Michael Gove, who ultimately came third, promised to lead the party out of the European Convention on Human Rights; Johnson gave only a qualified commitment to the Northern Irish backstop.

Lawyer attacks anti-terror laws

A leading human rights lawyer has launched a scathing attack on the government's anti-terror legislation, describing it as "oppressive" and "unjust".


Ramby de Mello, who has represented a string of high-profile clients including Julian Assange and Wikileaks, accused the government of using the threat of terrorism to introduce laws that are "undemocratic and unlawful".


The government has said the legislation is necessary to protect the public from the threat of terrorism.


But Mr de Mello, who is the founder of the International Rights Advocate Group, argued that the laws were being used to restrict freedom of expression and freedom of association.


"The government is using the threat of terrorism as a pretext to introduce laws that are unjust and oppressive," he said.


"This is a classic example of using a sledgehammer to crack a nut.
It is clear that the government is more interested in curbing dissent than in protecting the public from terrorism."


Mr de Mello said the government's attempts to crack down on terrorism were "worrying" and could have a "chilling effect" on freedom of speech.


"The government should be careful not to impose restrictions that are unnecessary and disproportionate," he said.


"The right to freedom of expression and association is a fundamental human right that should not be restricted except in exceptional circumstances."

text:
When Doom 3 was released in 2004, it accelerated the first-person shooter's rise to prominence.
To celebrate the game's 20th anniversary, it's finally getting the sequel it deserves.


Id Software's seminal shooter took the horror genre to a new level - and sped up the then-nascent FPS genre's ascent to the top of the gaming pile.
It's since been ported to just about every platform under the sun and is now being celebrated with a special 20th-anniversary edition, along with a fourth sequel in the series.


Doom 3: Resurrection of Evil is a revamped version of the third game in the franchise, adding a new chapter and updating the 2004 original game with a fresh coat of paint.
And following in the footsteps of Doom (2016), it adds multiplayer too.


The first is a revamped version of Doom 3's BFG Edition, which adds the "Lost Mission" - a brand-new chapter to the campaign, which was originally created for Doom 3's console release but never made it to PC.


It pits you, the sole survivor of the UAC facility on Mars, against the demons of Hell, and this time they're also bringing some zombies for good measure.
The Lost Mission stars David Ashby, a member of the original Doom 3 development team, and has been slightly retooled for this new release.


The second is a spruced-up version of the base game, giving it a fresh coat of paint for 2022.

Then, votes are cast by national jurors and, occasionally, a public tele-vote.

Arsène Wenger admitted he was "disappointed" as Arsenal's hopes of qualifying for the Champions League suffered a significant blow with a 2-1 home defeat against Newcastle.


The Gunners came into the game in need of victory after back-to-back defeats against Manchester United and Everton had derailed their top-four challenge.


But they were unable to find a way past a Magpies side who had not won away from home all season and had not even managed a goal on their travels.


All the goals came in the first half as Jonjo Shelvey's long-range strike and a goal from former Arsenal midfielder Mohamed Elneny meant Newcastle led at the break.


Saka pulled one back with a wonderful strike late on, but it was not enough for the home side.


Wenger said: "I am disappointed because we lost at home.
We made it difficult for ourselves.
We were not ruthless enough in the first half – we always wanted to score the second goal and in the end it came too late.


"We were not efficient enough in the first half – we had plenty of shots but too many were from distance and we did not threaten their goalkeeper enough.
In the second half we had less chances and they had some counter-attacks."

It could crush them, literally.
Traditional DVDs could meet their demise if the movie industry decides to go all-in on high-definition formats.
In 2015, Blu-ray discs accounted for more than half of the $6.2 billion in sales of physical video entertainment, according to the Digital Entertainment Group.
DVD sales, meanwhile, dropped by more than 20 percent.
The numbers indicate that Blu-ray, which can store far more data than a DVD, is quickly becoming the preferred way for people to buy physical copies of movies and TV shows.
But it isn't just consumer preference that could kill the DVD.
Warner Bros., which has sold DVDs for two decades, says it may stop pressing DVDs altogether in the near future.
The company says it wouldn't spend the money to upgrade its DVD production infrastructure — a costly endeavor — when it could funnel that money into the development of 4K, high-definition video.
4K, which offers four times the resolution of standard high-definition video, could give Blu-ray a run for its money.
Streaming 4K video over the internet has already become a reality, and the format of physical 4K video discs is currently under debate by the Blu-ray Disc Association and the DVD Forum, a group representing the interests of DVD manufacturers.

The former Labour prime minister, Tony Blair, has said he is "up for it" when asked if he would consider a return to politics, in an interview to mark the 25th anniversary of his landslide victory in the 1997 general election.


Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Mr Blair said he was "ready to help" his party, but added that Labour should be "under new leadership".


The former prime minister said another Labour victory in 2024 would be "very difficult" but the party could win if it "gets its act together".


He also said the UK was "better off" in the EU and that Brexit had been a "mistake".


Mr Blair served as prime minister from 1997 to 2007, winning three consecutive general elections.


But he was heavily criticised for his decision to take the UK into war in Iraq, and he eventually announced his resignation and left office in June 2007.


His interview was released to mark the 25th anniversary of his election victory in 1997, which saw Labour win 418 seats - giving them a majority of 167 - with Mr Blair as leader.


Speaking about the possibility of a return to politics, Mr Blair said: "I'm up for it - but let's wait and see."


Asked if that meant he would consider a return to politics, he said: "Yeah, I would.
I'm ready to help in any way I can.

The former England striker says gamers should "not be afraid" of the freshly-announced sequel to 2018's Kashmir.
In a startling move, football icon and gaming enthusiast, Harry Kane, has come out in strong support of EA Sports' decision to release a sequel to the much-maligned Kashmir game.
Speaking exclusively to the BBC, the former England striker said he believes that gamers should "not be afraid" of the freshly-announced Kashmir 2 and instead, "embrace the opportunity to play it".


Kane, who is renowned for his passion for video games, went on to say: "I vividly recall the original Kashmir getting a lot of negative attention at the time of its release.
However, as a gamer, I believe that we should not be afraid of exploring new ideas and experiences within the medium."
The Tottenham Hotspur striker has been widely recognised in the gaming community for his impressive performance during the recent FIFA 22 World Cup tournament, where he carried his club side to the final before narrowly losing to Manchester City manager, Pep Guardiola.


Kane believes that the gaming community should embrace the creativity and innovation that Kashmir 2 will bring to the football gaming genre.
"I'm sure that EA Sports has learned from the feedback received for the original game and will deliver an even better experience for gamers this time around."
He applauded the gaming community for their continued support of the series and urged them to continue to provide valuable feedback to developers in order to further enhance the gaming experience. 


When asked if he had any involvement in the development of the game, Kane laughed and stated, "I may know a thing or two about football, but creating video games is a skill that deserves the utmost respect and admiration.

Britons have been making the most of a four-day weekend to go Christmas shopping, despite concerns over the cost of living.


Black Friday was nominally a week ago, but many retailers have extended their sales.


The BBC's Katie Hope was among the throng in London's West End on Saturday.


"Oxford Street was heaving with people stocking up for the festive season," she said.
"It was busy even by pre-pandemic standards - queues snaked round the block at some of the bigger stores."


Kate Gibbs, from Gloucester, was among those making the most of the sales.
She had been up since 05:00 on Saturday morning, and had already been to several shops.


"We're just getting into the Christmas spirit," she said.
"The sales are too good to miss - we've saved a lot of money today.
"

However, not all were enthusiastic.

The BBC has learned that some of the world's leading financial institutions have been hit by a major security breach.


Sources have told the BBC that the US bank, JPMorgan, and the Bank of New York Mellon were both affected by the breach, which was identified in August.


It is believed the hackers were able to install malicious software on the banks' computers, allowing them to spy on the institutions.


The attackers are thought to have been based in Russia, although this has not been confirmed.


The breach is believed to have been discovered when the banks noticed that some of their computers had started to communicate with IP addresses in Russia.


When they investigated, they found that the malicious software had been installed on their computers, and they were able to remove it.


The banks have not commented on the breach, but a spokesperson for JPMorgan said: "We have multiple layers of protection and we are confident in the integrity of our controls."

The Bank of New York Mellon said: "We maintain a robust, multi-layered security protocol and routinely monitor our systems for signs of trouble."


"When issues are identified, we take appropriate actions to address them and mitigate risk.
"

It is not clear how many computers were affected, but sources have told the BBC that the number was significant.


This is not the first time that banks have been targeted by hackers.

Britain's Tim Henman finally won his battle with rival Greg Rusedski as he reached the quarter-finals of the Nasdaq-100 Open in Miami.

The Briton has lost the last six times they have met, including two five-set matches at Grand Slam events.

But Henman earned a straight-set victory 6-3 7-6 against the Canadian in Florida.

And the 30-year-old admitted his relief at finally getting one over on his friend of 15 years.

"It's been a long time coming, I'm very happy," said the world number 48, who faces Russia's Marat Safin next.

"To beat Greg you have to play very solid and take your chances when they come along and I was able to do that today."


Rusedski, ranked nine places higher than his rival at 29 in the world, made a confident start to the match but could not maintain his early advantage.

And Henman, who has never beaten his rival on a hard court, took full advantage to win in one hour and 42 minutes.


"I played well today," added Henman.
"I executed my game plan well and played smart tennis.

The French suitor, Xavier Rolet, presented himself as a "true lover" of the London Stock Exchange as he wooed shareholders with promises of billions of extra pounds in revenue and a leap forward for the UK's financial standing.


The 57-year-old finished his presentation to investors at the London Stock Exchange's (LSE) annual meeting with a question and answer session that was at times tense.


"I'm confident that we have the right plan, the right strategy to deliver and achieve that £5bn vision," he said.


But several shareholders stood up and voiced their concerns, interrupting Mr Rolet as he tried to answer questions put to him by the chairman, Donald Brydon.


One shareholder asked if Mr Rolet planned to move the LSE's headquarters to Paris, to which he replied: "No, no, no.
This is not the plan.
"

Another shareholder accused him of "being vague" on the details of his strategy, before adding: "I am not convinced at all by you.
"

When another investor asked if he had visited the London Stock Exchange, Mr Rolet replied: "I spend most of my time in the office right next door to you.
"

The LSE's chief financial officer, Scott Evans, jumped in to clarify that Mr Rolet had in fact spent "a lot of time in this actual room".


In his opening remarks, Mr Rolet he had "profound respect" for the LSE and its history and traditions.

The lawsuit comes as Argentina is facing an economic crisis, with high inflation and a weakening currency.
The government has been looking to cut costs and has been negotiating with Suez to lower its water prices.


Suez has been operating in Argentina for over 100 years and provides water to many cities and towns in the country.
It is one of the largest water companies in the world and is known for its controversial pricing practices.


The company has been accused of overcharging for water in other countries as well, including Brazil, Spain, and Portugal.

The stars shone on the Bafta red carpet in London on Sunday, with many of those attending opting for shimmering, sparkling and downright glamorous outfits.


Forbes had ranked the best-dressed celebrities on the red carpet, with Emma Thompson coming out on top.
The "Love Actually" star wore a dazzling, silver-colored dress with a matching jacket and trousers, all designed by Valentino.


With her were other stylish stars, such as "The Crown" star Olivia Colman, who donned an elegant black dress with a plunging neckline designed by Stella McCartney.
"Game of Thrones" star Emilia Clarke wore a stunning red gown with a revealing back detail, created by Balmain.


Many of the men also brought their style A-game.
"The Batman" star Robert Pattinson looked dapper in a classic black and white tux, while "Peaky Blinders" actor Tom Hardy went for a more casual look in a blue suit and white shirt.


The ceremony itself was a night of celebration, with many of the winners giving heartfelt speeches.
"Black Panther" star Letitia Wright, who won the EE Rising Star Award, used her platform to encourage young people to follow their dreams.


Overall, the Bafta red carpet was a glittering, glamorous event, with stars from across the globe turning out in style to celebrate the best in film and television.

The strong dollar, which makes American products more expensive abroad, also contributed to the widening of the trade gap.
For 2005, the trade deficit is expected to remain wide, as the US economy continues to expand and import demand remains strong.

The trade gap reflected a widening in the deficit with China, which hit a record $124.4 billion in 2004.
The deficit with Japan also hit a record, rising to $91.8 billion.
The only bright spot in the trade picture was a narrowing of the deficit with Europe, which declined to $142.6 billion.


The strong trade deficit has led to concerns about the US current account deficit, which hit a record $425.6 billion in the third quarter of 2004.

The UK government has been accused of “playing with people’s lives” by refusing to relax the immigration rules for the partners of essential workers.
Campaigners marched through London on Saturday demanding that ministers extend the visa allocation for healthcare workers and other vital staff to the EU and beyond.
Families from the EU, the Caribbean and Africa are being affected by the government’s policy, which they say is discriminatory.
Currently, only NHS workers are eligible to receive visas for their spouses and partners.
But NHS workers have been leaving the health service in droves, saying they cannot afford to live on their salaries while paying for expensive accommodation and for visas for their loved ones. 


It is estimated that every minute, somewhere in the UK, a person is being refused a visa for a spouse or relative who works in the health service.
The campaign group Doctors of the World, which organised the march, said many healthcare workers were relying on food banks and were unable to pay their bills.
It is calling on the government to extend the health and care visa to the partners and children of all who work in the sector.
The group Soapsuds, which is made up of NHS workers, also took part in the demonstration.
Parveen Adams, a medical radiographer at London’s St Thomas’ hospital, said she was forced to move her family back to the Netherlands, missing her children’s exams.

The pound also gained ground, rising to $1.3692.


Markets have been weighing the chances of the Fed raising interest rates at its meeting next week.
Some policymakers have pushed for a more aggressive response to inflation, but others have warned that a hike could slow economic growth.


The euro has been gaining ground versus the dollar since the European Central Bank announced a more hawkish stance last week.
The ECB said it would be "patient" in its approach to raising rates, but added that it would "not hesitate" to act if inflationary pressures increased.


The dollar's decline has also been driven by weakness in the Japanese yen and the British pound.
The yen has been hurt by a weaker economy and lower interest rates, while the pound has been pressured by concerns about the UK's economic outlook.


The dollar's slide has been a significant trend in the past year, as concerns about the Fed's response to inflation and the US's growing debt have weighed on the currency.

Mortgage lenders in the UK have seen a rise in the number of home loan approvals again.
The increase comes after a brief period of decline in September, caused by the closure of the government's Help to Buy program.


The number of mortgages approved for house purchases climbed to 71,000 in October, up from 68,000 in September, according to the latest figures from the Bank of England.
This is the highest level since March 2022.


The data also showed that the value of mortgages approved for house purchases rose to £12.7bn, up from £12.4bn in September.
This is the highest since July 2022.


Mortgage rates have been rising in recent months, as the Bank of England has raised interest rates to combat rising inflation.
However, the housing market has remained resilient, with demand for mortgages still strong.


The Bank of England's data also showed that the number of mortgages approved for remortgaging climbed to 46,000, up from 45,000 in September.
The value of these mortgages rose to £9.6bn, up from £9.3bn in September.

Tennis: Britain's Tim Henman has withdrawn from next month's Australian Open because of injury, allowing Romanian Andrei Pavel to take his place in the main draw.


The ATP international committee has confirmed that the 18-year-old, who reached the quarter-finals of last week's Adelaide International, will take the wildcard entry.


Pavel, who moved to London as a refugee when he was 11, is ranked 96th in the world.


He will now face
either American Taylor Dent or Argentina's Martin Vassallo Arguello in the first round of the season's first Grand Slam in Melbourne, which starts on 16 January.


British number two
Greg Rusedski is hoping to finalise his schedule in the next few days.


The 31-year-old Canadian-born player has been selected to play in the Sydney International, which begins on 10 January, as part of his build-up to the Australian Open.


His place in Sydney was confirmed after Swiss world number seven Roger Federer withdrew because of a knee injury.


British number one Andrew Murray will also play in Sydney as he steps up his preparations for the Australian Open.

China has blocked the Google news site, according to a report in The New York Times.
The move comes as Beijing continues to tighten controls over information and the internet, including recent regulations that have slowed down internet traffic in the country. 


The block on Google news was first reported by GreatFire.org, a China-based organization that tracks blocked websites in the country.
The group said that Google news had been intermittently accessible since September, but was now completely blocked. 


A Google spokesperson confirmed the block, telling the Times that the company was "deeply concerned" about the disruption of service and that it was working to restore access. 


The block on Google news comes as Google and other foreign companies have come under increased pressure in China.
In August, Google announced that it would no longer provide data on requests from Chinese authorities for removal of content from its services, such as search and news. 


Google has had a difficult relationship with China for years, with the country blocking its search engine and other services in 2010.
The company has been trying to re-enter the Chinese market, but has faced challenges from local competitors and strict government regulations. 


The block on Google news is a sign that Beijing is continuing to tighten its controls over the internet and information, and that foreign companies will face increasing challenges in operating in the country.

England captain Ben Stokes and assistant coach Paul Collingwood are both hopeful that batter Ollie Pope will be available for selection for the third Test against Australia, starting in Sydney on January 5.


Pope, who scored a century in the drawn second Test in Melbourne, suffered a blow to the jaw after being struck by a short ball from Australia opener Cameron Bancroft in the nets on Wednesday.


While the 23-year-old trained outdoors on Friday, he did so with a protective mask over his face and will have to pass a number of concussion tests to be given the all-clear to play.


“Ollie is a pretty tough
so and so – comes from a pretty tough background, so him getting hit by a ball is about as likely as getting hit by lightning I think,” said Stokes.


“I’d like to think he’s available for selection.
It’s a wait and see with Ollie.
There’s bits and pieces of protocols that he needs to go through to get cleared for next week.


“Obviously we’ll make sure that he’s absolutely fine to play.
Look at the second innings of this Test, him and Rooty were fantastic in what they did and that gives us a great chance of winning the game.”

The former bosses of the failed telecoms firm WorldCom received $54m in payouts despite the company being accused of fraud.
Documents seen by the BBC show that the seven executives received the payments despite knowing the firm was in trouble.
They were aware that WorldCom had used fraudulent accounting to inflate profits.
WorldCom's internal audit committee approved the payments nine days before the company filed for bankruptcy.
At the time of the payout, the committee was headed by WorldCom's then-CEO Bernie Ebbers.
Mr. Ebbers, who has since been convicted of fraud, received $9.5m. It is believed the other six executives received between $4m and $7m each. 


They were:
- John Sidgmore, who became WorldCom's CEO after Mr. Ebbers
- Scott Sullivan, who was the chief financial officer
- David Myers, the controller of expense reporting
- Darcy Mott, the general counsel
- Philip Anschutz, the company's largest shareholder at the time
- Michael Capellas, who took over as CEO after Mr. Sidgmore

WorldCom's bankruptcy is considered one of the largest financial scandals in history.
The firm, which was founded in 1983, filed for bankruptcy in 2002 with $107bn in debt.
The case involved a long list of prominent executives and celebrities, including former US President Bill Clinton.


Former New York Attorney General, Eliot Spitzer, described the WorldCom fraud as "the most pervasive and significant fraud in the history of the securities markets".

The UK government has declined to issue a formal apology for the country's colonial past, sparking a heated debate about the nation's historical legacy.
Critics argue that an apology is necessary to acknowledge the harm caused by British colonialism, while others maintain that such a move would be anachronistic and unhelpful.


The issue was brought to the fore after a group of MPs and campaigners called for a formal apology for the atrocities committed during the British Empire.
They argue that the UK has a moral obligation to confront its past and make amends for the suffering caused by colonial rule.


However, a government spokesperson stated that while the UK acknowledges its colonial history, it does not believe an apology is the appropriate course of action.
"We recognise that Britain's past has episodes of both pride and shame," the spokesperson said.
"We are committed to facing our history honestly, but we do not believe that issuing a blanket apology for Britain's colonial past is the right approach.
"

The spokesperson added that the UK is focused on building a "forward-looking relationship" with its former colonies, based on "mutual respect, understanding, and cooperation."


The decision has been met with mixed reactions.
Some argue that an apology would be a symbolic gesture of reconciliation, helping to heal historical wounds.

Companies such as CRH, Ryanair, and Kerry Group have seen significant increases in their share prices.

Ireland's robust economic growth, which has outpaced many of its European counterparts, has played a key role.
The country's GDP grew by 5.5% in 2021, according to the Central Statistics Office, well above the Eurozone average.


In addition, Ireland's successful handling of the Covid-19 pandemic and the subsequent economic recovery have boosted investor confidence.

The United States trade deficit soared to an all-time high of $617.7 billion in 2004, according to figures released by the Commerce Department.
This marks a significant increase of 24.4% from the previous year, reflecting the rapidly growing cost of foreign oil and America's insatiable appetite for imported goods.


The deficit in goods and services was up from a $496.5 billion imbalance in 2003.
It has been the fourth consecutive year that America's trade deficit has set a record.
The new report underscored that the United States was far from achieving President Bush's pledge to cut the deficit in half over five years.


The trade gap with China rose to $162 billion, the highest imbalance ever recorded with any country.
Meanwhile, the deficit with the European Union hit a record $109.4 billion.


Economists have warned that the soaring trade deficit could put downward pressure on the dollar and trigger higher interest rates.
Both of these factors could potentially slow down the US economy.


The Bush administration, however, maintains that the soaring deficits are not a cause for concern.

text:
The Conservative Party has unveiled its plans for policing in the UK, promising a significant increase in police numbers and a renewed focus on tackling violent crime.
The proposals, which form part of the party's manifesto for the upcoming general election, have been met with a mixed response from experts and the public.


The Tories have pledged to recruit an additional 20,000 police officers over the next three years, reversing the cuts made to the police force since 2010.
This would bring the total number of officers in England and Wales to just over 140,000, the highest level in a decade.


Home Secretary Priti Patel said the move was necessary to "keep our streets safe" and "restore public confidence" in the police.
She also highlighted the party's commitment to giving police more powers to stop and search suspects, a controversial measure that has been criticised for disproportionately targeting ethnic minorities.


In addition to boosting police numbers, the Conservatives have outlined plans to increase prison sentences for serious crimes and invest more in crime prevention initiatives.
They have also promised to create a new national cyber crime force to tackle online threats and fraud.


However, critics have questioned whether the Tories' plans go far enough in addressing the root causes of crime.
Labour's Shadow Home Secretary, Diane Abbott, accused the Conservatives of "trying to fight crime on the cheap" and called for more investment in community services and youth programmes.

As the deadline for the potential deal between Fiat Chrysler Automobiles (FCA) and General Motors (GM) approaches, both companies are under increasing pressure to finalize negotiations.
The proposed merger, which could potentially reshape the global automotive industry, has been under discussion for several months.

The deal could potentially create the world's largest automaker by volume, surpassing current leaders Toyota and Volkswagen.


However, the merger has faced significant hurdles.
GM has repeatedly rebuffed Fiat Chrysler's advances, with CEO Mary Barra stating that the company is focused on delivering its own strategy.
Despite this, Fiat Chrysler's CEO, Mike Manley, remains optimistic about the potential deal.


"We believe that a merger with GM is the best pathway forward for both companies," Manley said in a recent interview.
"We are confident that we can overcome any obstacles and create a global powerhouse in the automotive industry.
"

The proposed merger comes at a time when the automotive industry is facing significant challenges, including slowing sales, rising costs, and the need to invest in electric and autonomous vehicles.

The leader of the Conservative Party has unveiled a comprehensive spending plan, outlining the party's fiscal strategy for the coming years.
The plan, which prioritises investment in public services, infrastructure, and green initiatives, is being hailed as a blueprint for a post-pandemic economic recovery.


The Tory leader emphasised the need for fiscal responsibility while also acknowledging the necessity of targeted spending to stimulate economic growth.
The plan includes significant investment in the NHS, education, and law enforcement, as well as a commitment to increase spending on infrastructure and green initiatives.


"We recognise the need to balance the books, but we also understand the importance of investing in our public services and infrastructure to ensure a robust recovery from the pandemic," the Tory leader said during the announcement.


The spending plan includes a £20 billion increase in NHS funding over the next four years, a move that the Tory leader said was necessary to ensure the health service can continue to provide high-quality care.
The plan also includes a £14 billion investment in education, with a focus on improving schools in disadvantaged areas.


In addition, the plan outlines a £10 billion investment in law enforcement, aimed at recruiting more police officers and improving community safety.
The Tory leader also announced a £12 billion investment in green initiatives, including renewable energy projects and measures to improve energy efficiency in homes and businesses.


The spending plan has been met with mixed reactions.

Iranian authorities have sentenced a prominent blogger to 14 years in prison on charges of spreading propaganda against the regime, according to local media reports.
The blogger, whose identity has not been disclosed due to safety concerns, is known for his critical views on the Iranian government's policies.


The blogger was reportedly arrested in his home in Tehran by the Revolutionary Guards, an elite branch of the Iranian military, and was later tried in a Revolutionary Court.
These courts are often used for cases involving alleged attempts to overthrow the government.


The charges against the blogger include "spreading propaganda against the system", "insulting the sacred", and "creating public anxiety", according to the Iranian Students News Agency (ISNA).
The blogger's lawyer has denounced the charges as baseless and politically motivated, vowing to appeal the sentence.


This is not the first time Iran has come under scrutiny for its treatment of bloggers and social media activists.
The country has a history of suppressing freedom of speech and has been criticised by international human rights organisations for its harsh treatment of critics.


According to Reporters Without Borders, Iran is one of the world's largest prisons for journalists and netizens.
The organisation has repeatedly called on the Iranian authorities to stop their crackdown on freedom of expression and to release all journalists and bloggers detained unjustly.

Tech giant Microsoft has announced plans to tackle the growing issue of spyware, a type of malicious software that infiltrates computers to gather sensitive information.
The move comes as part of the company's broader strategy to enhance cybersecurity and protect its users from potential threats.


Spyware has become a significant concern for internet users worldwide, with millions of computers infected each year.
It can collect various types of personal information, such as internet surfing habits and user logins, and can also interfere with user control of a computer by installing additional software or redirecting web browsers.


Microsoft's initiative will involve the development of new software tools designed to detect and remove spyware.
The company also plans to educate its users about the risks of spyware and how to protect themselves online.


"Spyware is a serious and growing problem for all computer users," said Brad Smith, Microsoft's Chief Legal Officer.
"We are committed to helping our customers stay safe online, and this initiative is a significant step in that direction."

Microsoft's anti-spyware initiative will be integrated into its existing security services, including Windows Defender and Microsoft Security Essentials.
The company also plans to work closely with law enforcement agencies to track down and prosecute those responsible for creating and distributing spyware.


The move has been welcomed by cybersecurity experts, who have long called for tech companies to take a more proactive role in combating spyware.

Microsoft is developing a new 'safer ID' system, aiming to enhance online security and privacy for its users.
The tech giant is working on a decentralised digital identification system that will give users more control over their personal data.


The new system will be built on blockchain technology, a decentralised and secure method of recording transactions.
This technology is most commonly associated with cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, but Microsoft believes it can be used to create a more secure and private online identification system.


The company's project, known as the Identity Overlay Network (ION), is designed to give users a digital ID that they can use across multiple online platforms.
This ID will be stored on the user's device rather than on a centralised server, reducing the risk of data breaches.


Microsoft's Chief Identity Officer, Alex Simons, explained that the new system is designed to address the increasing concerns about privacy and security in the digital world.
"Each of us needs a digital identity we own, one which securely and privately stores all elements of our digital identity," he said.


The ION system will allow users to verify their identity online without having to share personal information with third parties.
This could be used for anything from proving your age to a website, to verifying your identity for online banking.

The company's project, known as the Identity Overlay Network (ION), is designed to give users a digital ID that they can use across multiple online platforms.
This ID will be stored on the user's device rather than on a centralised server, reducing the risk of data breaches.


Microsoft's Chief Identity Officer, Alex Simons, explained that the new system is designed to address the increasing concerns about privacy and security in the digital world.
"Each of us needs a digital identity we own, one which securely and privately stores all elements of our digital identity," he said.


The ION system will allow users to verify their identity online without having to share personal information with third parties.
This could be used for anything from proving your age to a website, to verifying your identity for online banking.
