It has over 2.4 million processing cores, compared to the TaihuLight's 10.6 million cores.
Despite having fewer cores, Summit is more than twice as powerful, demonstrating the effectiveness of its architecture and the efficiency of its cooling system.

Gold prices have taken a tumble amid concerns that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) may sell a significant portion of its gold reserves.
The precious metal, often seen as a safe haven in times of economic uncertainty, has seen its value decrease by 2% in the last week.


The IMF, which holds around 2,814 tonnes of gold, has been considering a sale as part of a broader strategy to shore up its finances.
However, the potential influx of gold into the market has sparked fears of oversupply, leading to a drop in prices.


"Gold is very sensitive to any suggestion of increased supply," said David Madden, a market analyst at CMC Markets.
"The mere hint that the IMF might sell some of its reserves is enough to spook the market.
"

The IMF's gold reserves are the third-largest in the world, behind the United States and Germany.
Any sale would have to be approved by the majority of its 189 member countries.


The last time the IMF sold some of its gold was in 2010, when it offloaded 403.3 tonnes.
The move was part of a plan to provide low-income countries with additional financial support following the global financial crisis.

The rise of high-quality personal computer (PC) photo printers is posing a significant challenge to professional photo printing services, as more and more consumers opt for the convenience and cost-effectiveness of home printing.


In recent years, the technology behind PC photo printers has advanced significantly.
Today's models can produce images that rival, and in some cases surpass, the quality of those produced by professional photo labs.
This has led to a surge in popularity for home photo printing, with many consumers choosing to invest in their own equipment rather than paying for professional services.


One of the key factors driving this trend is the cost.
While professional photo printing services can charge a premium for their expertise and high-quality materials, PC photo printers are becoming increasingly affordable.
This, coupled with the ongoing cost of ink and paper, often works out cheaper in the long run, particularly for those who print photos regularly.


The convenience of home printing is another major draw.
With a PC photo printer, consumers can print their photos whenever they want, without having to wait for a professional lab to process and deliver them.
This is particularly appealing for those who need their photos in a hurry, or who simply enjoy the flexibility of being able to print at their leisure.

text:
European stock markets have taken a hit following a powerful earthquake in Asia, with investors growing increasingly concerned about the potential economic impact. 


The quake, which measured 7.8 on the Richter scale, struck off the coast of Indonesia, causing widespread damage and disruption.
The tremor was felt in several Asian countries, leading to temporary shutdowns in factories and businesses, and causing significant delays in transportation and logistics.


The FTSE 100 in London fell by 0.6%, while Germany's DAX and France's CAC 40 both dropped by 0.7%.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 index also fell by 0.5%. 


Shares in insurance companies were among the hardest hit, with investors fearing that the cost of the damage could run into billions of dollars.
Companies with significant exposure to the Asian market, such as luxury goods firms and car manufacturers, also saw their share prices fall.


"The earthquake has added another layer of uncertainty to the markets," said Michael Hewson, chief market analyst at CMC Markets.
"There are concerns about the potential impact on supply chains, as well as the cost of the clean-up and reconstruction.
"

Asian markets also suffered, with Japan's Nikkei 225 index falling by 1.2% and Hong Kong's Hang Seng index down by 0.8%.

The global reach of the internet has given rise to a new phenomenon, taking Spanish rap music to an international audience through web radio.
This digital revolution is not only transforming the music industry but also providing a platform for Spanish rap artists to showcase their talent worldwide.


Spanish rap, known for its rhythmic beats and powerful lyrics, has been a significant part of the country's music scene for decades.
However, it was largely confined to Spanish-speaking countries due to language barriers and limited exposure.
Now, with the advent of web radio, these barriers are being broken down, allowing Spanish rap to reach a global audience.


Web radio stations such as Radio Rap Español and Hip Hop en Español have been instrumental in this global expansion.
These stations, accessible from anywhere in the world, play a continuous stream of Spanish rap music, introducing listeners to both established and emerging artists.


One such artist is Madrid-based rapper Kase.
O, who has seen his popularity skyrocket since his music started being played on web radio.
"It's incredible to think that people are listening to my music in places like Japan and Australia," he said.

Residents of Beijing are expressing their frustration over the recent hike in parking fees, which they claim is exacerbating the city's already high cost of living.
The increase, which was implemented by the Beijing Municipal Commission of Transport, has seen hourly parking rates in some areas of the city double.


The new policy, which came into effect on 1st January, has seen the cost of parking in the city centre rise from 10 yuan ($1.50) per hour to 20 yuan ($3).
In the suburbs, the cost has increased from 6 yuan ($0.90) to 10 yuan ($1.50) per hour.
The move is part of a broader strategy by the Beijing government to reduce traffic congestion and air pollution in the city.


However, the decision has sparked outrage among many residents who argue that the increased costs are putting a strain on their finances.
"The cost of living in Beijing is already high, and this just adds to the burden," said Li Wei, a local resident.
"I have to think twice now before taking my car out.
"

Others have pointed out that the increased fees are unlikely to deter car owners from driving, as public transport options are often overcrowded and unreliable.
"The subway is always packed, and buses don't always run on time," said Zhang Wei, another Beijing resident.

Europe is embracing the digital TV lifestyle, with a significant increase in the number of households switching from traditional broadcasting to digital platforms, according to recent reports.
This shift is being driven by a combination of government policies, technological advancements, and changing consumer preferences.


The European Commission has been actively promoting the transition to digital TV, citing improved picture and sound quality, increased channel choices, and the potential for interactive services as key benefits.
The move is also expected to free up valuable spectrum space for other uses, such as mobile broadband.


In countries like the UK, Germany, and France, the switch to digital TV is almost complete, with over 90% of households now receiving digital broadcasts.

Former Prime Ministers Tony Blair and Gordon Brown have come under heavy criticism from Members of Parliament (MPs) over their handling of various issues during their respective tenures.

They argue that the policies implemented by the two leaders have contributed to the current economic and social challenges facing the UK.


Tony Blair, who served as Prime Minister from 1997 to 2007, has been criticised for his role in the Iraq War.
MPs argue that his decision to support the US-led invasion in 2003 was based on flawed intelligence and has led to ongoing instability in the Middle East.
They also accuse him of failing to adequately plan for the aftermath of the war, which has resulted in a power vacuum and the rise of extremist groups.


Gordon Brown, who succeeded Blair in 2007 and served until 2010, has been criticised for his handling of the financial crisis.
MPs argue that his decision to bail out the banks without imposing stricter regulations has led to a culture of impunity in the financial sector.
They also accuse him of failing to implement effective measures to prevent a similar crisis in the future.

British Telecom (BT) has launched a new initiative aimed at combating the growing problem of dialler scams, which have been causing significant financial losses and distress to its customers.


Dialler scams, also known as auto-dialler scams, involve malicious software that takes over a computer's modem and dials premium rate numbers without the user's knowledge.
The scam can result in victims receiving hefty phone bills, often running into hundreds or even thousands of pounds.


BT's new program, named 'Call Protect', is designed to identify and block these scam calls before they reach the customer.
The system uses advanced technology to monitor and analyse call patterns, identifying numbers associated with scams and blocking them automatically.


The telecom giant has also introduced a personal blacklist feature, allowing customers to add specific numbers they wish to block.
This feature is expected to provide an additional layer of protection against unwanted calls.


John Petter, CEO of BT Consumer, said: "We are declaring war on the companies behind these nuisance calls.
With our new technology, we aim to dramatically reduce the number of unwanted calls our customers receive and provide them with greater control over the calls they do want to take.
"

BT's move comes amid growing concern about the scale of the dialler scam problem.

A recent study suggests that casual comments about drinking alcohol can act as a diversion from more serious issues, potentially leading to increased alcohol consumption and related problems. 


The research, conducted by the University of Sheffield, analysed the impact of offhand remarks about drinking on individuals' perceptions and behaviours.
The study found that such comments often trivialise the seriousness of alcohol consumption, acting as a diversion from the potential health risks associated with excessive drinking.


Dr. Sarah Roberts, the lead researcher, said, "Our study shows that casual comments about drinking can create a social environment where excessive alcohol consumption is normalised rather than seen as a problem.
This can divert attention from the serious implications of regular heavy drinking.
"


The study involved 2,000 participants aged 18-65, who were asked about their drinking habits and their perceptions of comments about alcohol made in their social circles.
The results showed a significant correlation between the frequency of such remarks and the participants' own drinking behaviours.


The research also highlighted that these comments often act as a diversion from addressing personal issues.
"People may joke about their heavy drinking to deflect attention from underlying problems such as stress, anxiety or depression," Dr. Roberts added.

In a unique cinematic experience, the Dutch public has been given the opportunity to view the last film ever made by the legendary artist, Vincent Van Gogh.
The film, which was discovered in a private collection and has been painstakingly restored, offers a rare glimpse into the final days of one of the world's most celebrated painters.


The film, titled "The Final Brushstroke", was screened at the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, drawing a crowd of art enthusiasts, historians, and film buffs.
The silent black-and-white film, which runs for just over 15 minutes, was shot by Van Gogh's friend and fellow artist, Émile Bernard, in the summer of 1890, just weeks before Van Gogh's death.


"The Final Brushstroke" captures Van Gogh in his element, painting in the open air in the French village of Auvers-sur-Oise.
The film shows the artist, often considered a tormented genius, in a serene and focused state, completely absorbed in his work.


"This is an extraordinary find," said Adriaan Dönszelmann, the managing director of the Van Gogh Museum.
"It's like a time machine, taking us back to witness Van Gogh's creative process.
It's a poignant reminder of his dedication to his art, even in his final days.
"

The film was found in the collection of a private art collector in France, who wishes to remain anonymous.

A notorious spammer has been hit hard by anti-spam laws, resulting in a hefty fine and a ban from sending unsolicited emails.
The landmark case marks a significant victory for internet users and privacy advocates worldwide.


The spammer, known online as 'Spam King', was found guilty of sending millions of unsolicited emails to internet users, promoting various products and services.
The court ruled that his actions violated anti-spam laws, which are designed to protect internet users from unwanted and intrusive communications.


The 'Spam King' was ordered to pay a fine of £1.5 million, one of the largest penalties ever imposed for spamming.
In addition, he has been banned from sending any unsolicited emails for the next five years.


The case was brought to court by the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), which is responsible for enforcing data protection and electronic communications laws in the UK.
The ICO hailed the ruling as a significant victory in the fight against spam.


"This case sends a clear message to spammers that their actions will not be tolerated," said an ICO spokesperson.
"We will continue to take robust action against those who flout anti-spam laws and invade people's privacy.

Quangos, quasi-autonomous non-governmental organisations, in the UK are facing increasing criticism for their perceived inefficiency and lack of accountability.
Critics argue that these bodies, which are funded by taxpayers but operate independently of the government, are failing to deliver value for money.


There are currently over 1,000 quangos in the UK, costing taxpayers an estimated £90 billion a year.
These bodies cover a wide range of areas, from the Arts Council England to the Youth Justice Board.
They are intended to provide expert advice and services to the government, but there is growing concern that many are not fulfilling their intended roles effectively.


Critics argue that quangos are often unaccountable, with their leaders appointed rather than elected, and their operations lacking transparency.
There have been numerous instances of quangos being criticised for wasteful spending, such as the £500,000 spent on a failed rebranding by the UK Border Agency in 2009.


Furthermore, there is concern that many quangos are duplicating the work of other bodies, leading to unnecessary bureaucracy and inefficiency.
For example, the National Audit Office has identified significant overlap between the roles of the Skills Funding Agency and the Education Funding Agency.


The government has pledged to reduce the number of quangos and improve their accountability.

Jones, a well-known figure in the UK's tech industry, and Conte, a successful Italian businessman, had partnered in 2019 to launch a new digital marketing platform.
However, the venture collapsed in late 2020, leading to significant financial losses for both parties.


The lawsuit alleges that Conte failed to fulfil his contractual obligations, leading to the failure of the business.
Jones is seeking compensation for his financial losses, as well as punitive damages for Conte's alleged breach of contract.


"Mr. Conte's actions have caused significant harm to my client," said Jones' lawyer, Sarah Thompson.
"We are seeking a fair resolution to this matter through the courts."

Conte's legal team has yet to respond to the lawsuit.
However, in a statement released earlier this week, Conte denied any wrongdoing.
"I have always acted in the best interests of the business," he said.

The UK's trade deficit has narrowed significantly as exports have surged, according to the latest figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
The data shows a promising trend for the UK economy, as it continues to recover from the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic.


The trade deficit, the difference between the value of the goods and services a country imports and those it exports, fell to £1.4bn in July, down from £5.2bn in June.
This is the smallest trade gap since February 2020, before the pandemic hit the UK.


The ONS attributed the narrowing of the trade gap to a rise in exports, particularly in machinery and transport equipment, which increased by £800m. There was also a significant rise in exports of chemicals and manufactured goods.


The increase in exports suggests that UK businesses are finding success in international markets, despite the ongoing challenges posed by the pandemic and Brexit.
The figures also indicate a rebound in global demand for UK goods and services.


However, while the export figures are encouraging, imports also fell by £2.9bn, suggesting that domestic demand may be weakening.
This could be due to a number of factors, including supply chain disruptions and increased inflation.


Economists have welcomed the narrowing of the trade gap, but have warned that the situation remains volatile.

The government's anti-spam campaign has been temporarily halted due to budget constraints, sparking concerns about the potential increase in cyber threats.


The campaign, which was launched in 2018, aimed to reduce the number of spam emails and messages received by individuals and businesses.
It has been praised for its effectiveness in reducing spam-related cybercrime by 30% in its first year.
However, the recent freeze has raised questions about the future of the campaign and the potential implications for cybersecurity.


The decision to halt the campaign was announced by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), citing a need to reallocate resources amidst the ongoing economic challenges.
The DCMS has not yet provided a timeline for when the campaign will be resumed.


Cybersecurity experts have expressed concern over the decision, warning that it could lead to an increase in spam-related cybercrime.
"The anti-spam campaign has been a crucial tool in combating cyber threats," said Dr. Sarah Clarke, a cybersecurity expert at the University of Cambridge.
"Without it, we could see a significant rise in spam emails, which are often used as a gateway to more serious cyber attacks.
"

Businesses are also worried about the potential impact of the freeze.

Global industrial conglomerate General Electric (GE) has expressed optimism about the state of the global economy, describing it as 'excellent'.
The company's positive outlook comes amid a period of economic recovery following the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic.


GE's CEO, Larry Culp, stated in a recent interview that the company is witnessing a strong rebound in many of its markets, including aviation, healthcare, and renewable energy.
"We're seeing a lot of positive signs in the global economy," Culp said.
"There's a lot of pent-up demand out there, and we're well-positioned to meet it."


The company's aviation sector, which was severely hit by the pandemic as travel restrictions were imposed worldwide, is now seeing a significant recovery.
Culp noted that the increase in air travel, particularly in domestic markets, is driving demand for GE's jet engines and services.


In the healthcare sector, GE is experiencing robust demand for its medical imaging and diagnostic equipment, as hospitals and clinics worldwide continue to deal with the ongoing health crisis.
The company's renewable energy business is also thriving, driven by the global push towards cleaner and more sustainable energy sources.


Culp's positive comments come as GE reported better-than-expected earnings for the second quarter of 2021.

The company has not yet provided specific details about which roles will be affected, but it has confirmed that the cuts will be implemented across all levels of the organisation.

The company has been investing heavily in its digital operations in recent years, as it seeks to attract a younger, more digitally-savvy audience.
However, the transition has been challenging, with the company facing stiff competition from online news outlets and social media platforms.


TMG, which publishes the Daily Telegraph and the Sunday Telegraph, is one of the UK's largest newspaper groups.
The company has been struggling with falling print circulation and a decline in advertising revenues, which has been exacerbated by the economic fallout from the coronavirus pandemic.


In a statement, TMG said: "Like many media organisations, we are facing significant challenges brought about by the changing ways in which our readers are consuming news.

In the wake of recent natural disasters, web logs, or blogs, have emerged as a crucial tool in disaster recovery efforts.
These online platforms are being used to disseminate information, coordinate relief efforts, and even raise funds for those affected.


In the aftermath of a disaster, communication is often disrupted, making it difficult for aid organisations to understand the full extent of the damage or to locate those in need.
Blogs, with their ability to be updated in real-time and accessed from anywhere with an internet connection, are helping to bridge this gap.


One such example is the role blogs played in the aftermath of the devastating earthquake in Haiti in 2010.
Bloggers from around the world used their platforms to share information about the situation on the ground, helping aid organisations to direct their resources more effectively.
They also provided a platform for those affected to share their stories, giving a human face to the tragedy.


In addition to providing information, blogs have also been used to coordinate relief efforts.
In the wake of Hurricane Katrina in 2005, a group of bloggers set up a 'Katrina Help' blog, which served as a hub for information about where help was needed and how people could contribute.
The blog was updated constantly with information about missing persons, aid drop-off points, and fundraising efforts.

The Bayern Munich defender has been serving on the board since 2018, but has decided to step down to focus on his football career.


Boateng, 32, has been a key figure in the DFB, advocating for diversity and inclusion in German football.
His decision to step down comes at a time when the DFB is facing criticism for its handling of racial and social issues.


In a statement, Boateng said, "It has been an honour to serve on the DFB board, but I believe it is time for me to focus on my career on the pitch.
I will continue to use my platform to fight for diversity and inclusion in football.
"

The DFB has yet to announce who will replace Boateng on the board.
The election is scheduled to take place in March.


Boateng's decision to step down has been met with mixed reactions.
Some have praised his commitment to his football career, while others have expressed concern about the loss of his voice on the DFB board.

The UK film industry has experienced a significant decline in production, with a 40% drop reported in 2021, according to the British Film Institute (BFI).
This sharp decrease is largely attributed to the ongoing impact of the Covid-19 pandemic, which has disrupted filming schedules and led to the closure of cinemas nationwide.


The BFI's annual report revealed that only 188 films went into production in the UK last year, compared to 314 in 2020, marking the lowest number since records began.
The total spend on film production also fell by 21% to £1.3bn, down from £1.6bn in 2020.


The pandemic has had a profound impact on the film industry, with social distancing measures and lockdowns forcing many productions to halt or delay filming.
The closure of cinemas has also led to a significant loss of revenue, with many films being released directly to streaming platforms instead.


Despite the challenges, the BFI report highlighted some positive trends.
High-end television production, which includes shows made for streaming platforms like Netflix and Amazon, increased by 11% to a record £2.3bn.
This suggests a shift in consumer behaviour, with more people choosing to watch content at home rather than in cinemas.


The report also noted that the UK film industry is showing signs of recovery.

The shift towards prioritising looks and music is a response to changing consumer demands.
With the basic functionality of smartphones now largely standardised, users are seeking devices that offer a more personalised experience.
This includes a desire for sleek, visually appealing designs and high-quality audio features.


"Smartphones are no longer just communication devices.
They are fashion statements, entertainment centres and much more," says tech analyst, Jason Hope.
"Manufacturers are recognising this and are investing heavily in design and music capabilities.
"

One trend that is gaining traction is the use of premium materials in smartphone construction.
Aluminium, glass and even ceramic are being used to give devices a more luxurious feel.

In a bid to combat cyber-attacks, a new technology that uses 'net fingerprints' is being developed.
This innovative approach aims to identify and neutralise threats before they can cause significant damage.


The technology, developed by cybersecurity firms, uses machine learning algorithms to analyse patterns and behaviours in network traffic.
These patterns, or 'net fingerprints', can then be used to identify potential threats.
The system can detect unusual activity, such as a sudden surge in data requests or an unexpected communication between servers, which could indicate a cyber-attack.


The use of 'net fingerprints' is a significant step forward in the fight against cybercrime.
Traditional methods of cybersecurity often rely on identifying known threats, such as specific malware or viruses.
However, this approach can be ineffective against new or evolving threats.
By analysing network behaviour, the 'net fingerprints' technology can identify and respond to unusual activity, even if the specific threat has not been encountered before.


The technology is also capable of learning and adapting over time.

Unlike the high-pressure, competitive atmosphere of the awards night, the luncheon is a more casual affair.
It's a chance for the nominees to let their hair down, enjoy a meal, and celebrate their nominations with their peers.


This year's nominees, including the likes of Lady Gaga, Will Smith, and Benedict Cumberbatch, will be in attendance.
They will be joined by a host of other stars, directors, and industry professionals, all eager to celebrate the best of cinema in the past year.


The event is also an opportunity for the nominees to participate in the traditional "class photo", where all the nominees gather together for a group shot.
This photo often serves as a memento of the occasion and a testament to the collective talent of the year's nominees.


The luncheon is not just about celebration, however.

Former France rugby coach, Philippe Saint-Andre, has expressed his frustration over the absence of key players from the national team's training camp.
The players, who are currently involved in the Top 14 and European Champions Cup, have been unable to join the rest of the squad due to their club commitments.


Saint-Andre, who coached Les Bleus from 2011 to 2015, has been vocal about the need for the French Rugby Federation (FFR) to prioritise national team duties over club games.
He believes that the absence of these players could potentially harm France's chances in the upcoming Six Nations tournament.


"It's a real shame that we are missing some of our best players at this crucial time," Saint-Andre said.
"The FFR needs to find a solution to this problem.
We cannot continue to let our national team suffer because of club games.
"

The former coach's comments come after several high-profile French players, including Toulouse's Antoine Dupont and Racing 92's Virimi Vakatawa, were unable to join the national team's training camp due to their club commitments.


Saint-Andre's frustration is shared by many in French rugby, who believe that the current system, which allows clubs to hold onto their players during international windows, is detrimental to the national team's success.


"The current system is not working," Saint-Andre continued.

Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) tags, a technology used to track items from clothing to food products, are raising concerns among consumers over privacy and data security.


RFID tags are tiny devices that use radio waves to communicate information.
They are commonly used in retail for inventory management, allowing businesses to track products and assets.
However, the increasing prevalence of these tags has led to growing unease among consumers.


The primary concern centres around the potential misuse of data collected by RFID tags.
While the tags themselves only contain basic information such as product type and price, when combined with personal data from a credit card transaction, a detailed profile of a consumer's purchasing habits can be created.
This information could potentially be exploited by hackers or used for targeted advertising without the consumer's consent.


Moreover, there are fears that RFID tags could be used to track individuals' movements.
While most tags are deactivated at the point of sale, some remain active, leading to concerns that consumers could be tracked without their knowledge or consent.


Privacy advocates argue that consumers should have the right to know when products contain RFID tags and to have them deactivated upon purchase.

After a hiatus from the music industry, British R&B singer and television personality, Jamelia, is making a triumphant return to the top.
The Birmingham-born star, who dominated the UK charts in the early 2000s with hits like "Superstar" and "Thank You", is back in the studio, working on new music that promises to be as soulful and catchy as her previous work.


Jamelia's career took off in 1999 with her debut single, "So High", followed by her first album, "Drama", which was certified Gold in the UK.
Her subsequent albums, "Thank You" and "Walk With Me", were both critically acclaimed and commercially successful, solidifying her status as one of the UK's top R&B artists.


However, in 2007, Jamelia decided to take a break from music to focus on her family and other ventures.
She became a regular on television, appearing on shows like "Loose Women" and "Strictly Come Dancing", and used her platform to speak out on issues close to her heart, such as body positivity and racial equality.


Now, after more than a decade away from the music scene, Jamelia is ready to make her comeback.
She has been teasing fans with snippets of new music on social media, and the response has been overwhelmingly positive.


"I'm so excited to be back in the studio," Jamelia said in a recent interview.
"I've missed making music and I can't wait for everyone to hear what I've been working on."

Jamelia's return to music comes at a time when the UK R&B scene is thriving, with artists like Jorja Smith, Mahalia, and Ella Mai achieving international success.

France has initiated the transition to digital terrestrial television (DTT), marking a significant shift in the country's broadcasting landscape.
This move is part of a broader European Union directive to switch off analogue signals and move towards a fully digital broadcasting system.


The French government has been preparing for this transition for several years, investing heavily in the necessary infrastructure and technology.
The switch to digital terrestrial television will provide viewers with a wider range of channels, improved picture and sound quality, and additional features such as electronic programme guides and interactive services.


The first phase of the switch-over began in the Alsace region, with other regions set to follow in a phased manner over the next two years.
The French broadcasting authority, the Conseil Supérieur de l'Audiovisuel (CSA), has been tasked with overseeing the transition process.


The French government has also put measures in place to ensure that no viewer is left behind in this transition.
Households that do not have the necessary equipment to receive digital signals will be provided with financial assistance to purchase a set-top box or a new television set with a built-in digital tuner.


However, the switch to digital terrestrial television has not been without controversy.
Some critics argue that the government has not done enough to educate the public about the transition and that many households may be caught off guard when their analogue signals are switched off.

Renowned rapper and entrepreneur, Jay-Z, has added another feather to his cap by becoming the boss of a record label.
The hip-hop mogul, whose real name is Shawn Carter, has taken over the reins of Def Jam Recordings, one of the most iconic labels in the music industry.


Jay-Z, who has been in the music industry for over three decades, has been instrumental in shaping the careers of many artists.
His new role as the head of Def Jam Recordings will see him overseeing the label's operations and artist development.


Def Jam Recordings, founded in 1984, has been home to some of the biggest names in hip-hop, including Kanye West, Rihanna, and Public Enemy.
Jay-Z himself was signed to the label in the mid-90s and released several of his most successful albums under its banner.


The rapper's appointment as the label boss is seen as a strategic move by the parent company, Universal Music Group, to leverage his industry experience and connections.
Jay-Z's business acumen is well-documented, with successful ventures in fashion, sports management, and streaming services.


In a statement, Jay-Z expressed his excitement about his new role.
"I look forward to working with the talented team at Def Jam and helping guide the careers of the artists on the roster," he said.

Former Speaker of the House of Commons, Baroness Betty Boothroyd, has called for the House of Lords to have its own speaker.
She believes that this would help to modernise the upper chamber and make it more accountable to the public.


Baroness Boothroyd, who served as Speaker of the House of Commons from 1992 to 2000, said that the Lords needed a speaker who could represent it to the outside world and defend its interests.
She argued that the current arrangement, where the Lord Speaker has limited powers and the House is largely self-regulating, is outdated and lacks transparency.


"The House of Lords is a vital part of our parliamentary democracy," she said.
"But it needs to evolve and adapt to meet the challenges of the 21st century.
A speaker with real authority could help to drive that change.
"

Baroness Boothroyd's comments come amid ongoing debate about the role and size of the House of Lords, which is currently the second largest legislative assembly in the world after the National People's Congress of China.
Critics argue that it is too large, too costly and lacks democratic legitimacy.


The Baroness suggested that a Lords speaker could be elected by members of the House, in the same way that the Speaker of the House of Commons is chosen.

The Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN), the global body that oversees the web's address system, has given the green light for the creation of new internet domain names.
This decision could potentially revolutionise the digital landscape, allowing for a significant expansion in the range of web addresses.


Currently, web addresses end in familiar domain suffixes such as .com, .org, .net, and country codes like .uk or .fr.
However, ICANN's decision will allow companies, organisations, and even cities to apply for their own domain suffixes, such as .google, .bbc, or .london.


ICANN's board voted overwhelmingly in favour of the proposal at a meeting in Singapore.
The decision was hailed as a "historic moment" by ICANN's President and CEO, Rod Beckstrom.
"ICANN has opened the internet's naming system to unleash the global human imagination," he said.


The move is expected to significantly increase the number of generic top-level domains (gTLDs), which currently stands at 22.
The first of these new gTLDs could be live by late 2022 or early 2023.


However, the decision has not been without controversy.

Calls are growing for a televised debate between the leaders of the UK's major political parties ahead of the next general election.
Advocates argue that such a debate would provide a platform for party chiefs to outline their policies and engage directly with the public.


The proposal has been backed by several prominent figures, including former BBC director-general Mark Thompson, who said that a TV debate would "help to re-energise the democratic process".
He added that it would "give voters a chance to see the leaders of the main parties debate the big issues of the day in a live, unscripted setting".


The idea has also been supported by a number of MPs, who believe that a televised debate would increase public engagement in politics.
Labour MP Jess Phillips said: "A TV debate would give people a chance to see what the leaders of the different parties stand for, and to make an informed decision about who they want to vote for."


However, the proposal has also faced opposition.
Some critics argue that a TV debate could turn into a popularity contest, rather than a serious discussion of policy.
Others have raised concerns about the potential for bias in the way the debate is moderated.


The last time a televised debate between party leaders took place was in 2010, when Gordon Brown, David Cameron and Nick Clegg faced off ahead of the general election.

"

Lufthansa is now in talks with its legal team to determine the feasibility of a lawsuit against the German government or the security agencies involved in coordinating the visit.

Several high-profile musicians are joining forces to challenge the bureaucratic red tape that often hinders international artists from performing in the United States.
The group, which includes prominent figures from various music genres, aims to streamline the visa application process for foreign musicians.


The current process for obtaining a visa to perform in the US is often described as complex and time-consuming.
Artists must apply for a specific type of visa, known as a P-1, which is intended for "Internationally Recognized Athletes, Entertainers, and Artists."
The application process can take several months and requires extensive documentation, including proof of international recognition and a consultation from a peer group or labor organization.


The group of musicians advocating for change includes British singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran, American pop star Taylor Swift, and Canadian rapper Drake, among others.
They argue that the current system is not only burdensome for established artists but also discourages emerging talent from seeking opportunities in the US.


"The current process is a significant barrier to entry for many talented artists," said Swift.
"We want to make it easier for musicians from all over the world to share their talent with American audiences.
"

The group is working with legal experts and lobbying firms to propose changes to the current system.

The report suggests that despite a surge in streaming services, the industry is struggling to innovate and adapt to the digital age.


The BVMI's annual report paints a bleak picture of the German music industry, with physical sales continuing to decline and digital sales failing to make up the shortfall.
Despite the popularity of streaming services like Spotify and Apple Music, the report suggests that the industry is failing to capitalise on these platforms.


"The German music industry is in a state of paralysis," said BVMI CEO Florian Drücke.
"We are seeing a lack of innovation and a reluctance to embrace the digital revolution.
This is leading to a 'zombie' state, where the industry is neither dead nor alive.
"

The report also highlights a lack of diversity in the German music scene, with the majority of chart-topping artists being male and from Western countries.
This lack of representation is seen as another factor contributing to the industry's stagnation.


Despite these challenges, the report does highlight some areas of growth.

The proposed legislation, which would allow pubs, clubs, and bars in England and Wales to serve alcohol around the clock, has sparked a heated debate.
Supporters argue that it would boost the hospitality industry and offer more freedom to consumers.
However, the Tories have raised concerns about the potential social and health implications.


Shadow Home Secretary, Oliver Dowden, stated, "While we understand the need to support our hospitality sector, especially after the devastating impact of the pandemic, we must also consider the wider societal effects of such a move.
We fear that 24-hour drinking could lead to an increase in alcohol-related incidents, putting additional pressure on our already stretched emergency services.
"

The Conservatives have also highlighted the potential health risks associated with increased alcohol consumption.
Shadow Health Secretary, Sajid Javid, said, "We know that excessive drinking can lead to a range of health problems, from liver disease to mental health issues.
We need to be promoting responsible drinking, not encouraging a 24-hour drinking culture.
"

The proposed legislation has also been met with opposition from health professionals and charities.

UK gambling regulators are considering a ban on some practices used by casinos in the United States that are deemed to be manipulative and potentially harmful to players.
The move comes amid growing concerns about the impact of these 'tricks' on problem gamblers.


The Gambling Commission, the body responsible for regulating gambling in the UK, is reportedly looking into the use of certain tactics that are common in US casinos but are currently not widespread in the UK.
These include the use of free alcohol to encourage continued gambling, the absence of clocks and windows in casinos to disorientate players and make them lose track of time, and the use of flashing lights and sounds to celebrate even small wins, creating an illusion of winning more often than is actually the case.


The Commission is also said to be considering restrictions on the use of credit cards for gambling, following evidence that this can lead to problem gamblers accruing significant debt. 


"These practices can be highly manipulative and are designed to keep people gambling for longer than they otherwise would," said a spokesperson for the Gambling Commission.

Brazil's unemployment rate has dropped to a record low, according to the latest data from the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE).
The jobless rate fell to 11.2% in the three months to November, down from 11.6% in the previous quarter.


This is the lowest unemployment rate recorded in Brazil since the current series of data began in 2012.
The decline in unemployment is seen as a sign of recovery in Latin America's largest economy, which has been struggling with a recession for the past few years.


The IBGE report also showed that the number of people in employment increased by 785,000 to 94.4 million in the three months to November.
The rise in employment was driven by the creation of jobs in sectors such as construction, agriculture, and services.


The drop in the jobless rate comes as a boost for President Jair Bolsonaro, who has pledged to revive the economy and create jobs.
However, despite the positive figures, many Brazilians are still struggling with underemployment and low wages.


The IBGE data also revealed that the number of underemployed - those working fewer hours than they would like - stood at 27 million, or 23.8% of the workforce.
Meanwhile, the average monthly wage was BRL 2,332 ($445), virtually unchanged from a year earlier.

UK house prices have experienced an unexpected drop during the festive season, according to the latest data from the Nationwide Building Society.
The average price of a home in the UK fell by 0.5% in December, the first monthly decline since June.


The average house price now stands at £229,721, down from £230,630 in November.
Despite the monthly fall, house prices are still 4.8% higher than a year ago, reflecting the strong growth seen in the earlier part of the year.


Nationwide's chief economist, Robert Gardner, said the fall was a surprise, given the strength of the market in recent months.
"The slowdown in December is a little surprising given the strength of the market in recent months, buoyed by the stamp duty holiday and a desire for more space as people work from home," he said.


However, he added that the economic uncertainty caused by the ongoing Covid-19 pandemic and the end of the Brexit transition period could be starting to weigh on the market.
"It may be that the economic uncertainty is starting to take its toll, with the end of the furlough scheme and the Brexit transition period also likely to be factors," he said.


The stamp duty holiday, introduced by the government in July to boost the housing market, is due to end in March.
This has led to a surge in demand, particularly for larger homes, as people look to complete purchases before the deadline.

"

This means that fans could potentially watch their favourite artists perform live, right from the comfort of their own homes.

"Dimitri's experience and knowledge of the game will be invaluable to us," Galthié said.
"He was an exceptional player and we are confident that he will bring the same level of excellence to his coaching role."

The Chancellor of the Exchequer has received a significant boost as the government's adherence to the 'golden rule' of public finance has been confirmed by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).


The golden rule, a fiscal policy principle, stipulates that the government should borrow only to invest and not to fund current spending.
This means that over the economic cycle, the government will borrow only if it is investing in projects that will increase the country's productive potential.


The OBR's latest report indicates that the Chancellor has successfully adhered to this rule, providing a much-needed boost to his credibility.
This comes at a crucial time as the government prepares to unveil its latest budget, with the Chancellor under pressure to demonstrate fiscal responsibility.


The Chancellor's adherence to the golden rule is seen as a sign of prudent economic management.
It suggests that the government is committed to maintaining fiscal discipline, even in the face of significant economic challenges.


The OBR's endorsement is likely to be welcomed by financial markets, which tend to favour stability and predictability in fiscal policy.
It could also help to bolster the government's standing with international investors, who are often wary of governments that borrow to fund current spending.


However, the report also highlighted some areas of concern.

UK companies are investing billions of pounds into their pension schemes in an effort to address the growing deficit and ensure the financial security of their employees in retirement. 


According to a recent report by the Pension Protection Fund (PPF), the total deficit of all UK private sector pension schemes has increased to £160bn.
This has prompted many firms to take action and increase their contributions to their pension funds.


Among the companies leading the way is BT, which has announced plans to pump £2bn into its pension scheme over the next three years.
Similarly, Royal Mail has committed to investing an additional £1.8bn into its pension fund by 2023.


These investments come at a time when many companies are grappling with the financial implications of the Covid-19 pandemic.
However, despite these challenges, firms are recognising the importance of safeguarding their employees' futures.


The PPF's report also highlighted that the number of pension schemes in deficit has risen by 10% over the past year.
This has led to increased pressure on companies to address the shortfall and ensure they can meet their future pension obligations.


Pensions expert, Dr Ros Altmann, said: "It's encouraging to see companies taking their pension responsibilities seriously and investing significant sums to secure their employees' futures.

His performance was hailed as "a return to form" by critics, with many praising his ability to combine action with emotional depth.

"I am incredibly grateful for this recognition," Schwarzenegger said in his acceptance speech.
"I've always believed in pushing boundaries and taking risks in my roles, and it's an honour to have that recognised by the Academy."


The win marks a significant milestone in Schwarzenegger's career, which spans over four decades.

The Secretary General of Amnesty International, Agnes Callamard, has expressed deep concern over the international community's failure to address and prevent conflicts, leading to widespread human rights abuses. 


In an exclusive interview, Callamard criticised the global response to ongoing wars, particularly in regions such as Yemen, Syria, and Myanmar.
She argued that the international community's inability to effectively intervene has resulted in devastating humanitarian crises.


"The world has failed to learn from past mistakes.
We are witnessing the same patterns of violations, the same silence, the same inaction that have characterised other horrific conflicts," Callamard said.


She highlighted the war in Yemen, now in its seventh year, as a prime example of this failure.
Despite widespread reports of human rights abuses and war crimes, including the use of starvation as a weapon of war, the international community has largely failed to take decisive action.


Similarly, in Syria, where the civil war has been raging for over a decade, Callamard noted that the international community's response has been woefully inadequate.
Despite the displacement of millions and the death of hundreds of thousands, there has been little progress towards a resolution.


Callamard also pointed to the situation in Myanmar, where a military coup in February 2021 has led to widespread violence and repression.

The 47-year-old athlete, who has previously won gold at the European Championships and Commonwealth Games, is now focusing her training on the indoor circuit.

Despite her age, she has shown no signs of slowing down, with her recent performances suggesting she still has plenty to offer.


"I love competing and I still feel I have a lot to give," Pavey said.
"I've always enjoyed running indoors and I think it suits my style of running.
I'm really looking forward to the challenge.
"

Pavey's decision to focus on indoor running comes after a successful outdoor season, where she finished in the top 10 in several major races.
Her experience and tactical nous will be invaluable on the indoor circuit, where races are often tightly contested and can be won or lost on the smallest of margins.


The Devon-born athlete's training regime has been adjusted to suit the demands of indoor running.

American R&B superstar, Usher, has emerged as the leading nominee for the upcoming Soul Train Music Awards, underscoring his enduring influence in the soul and R&B genre.


The "Yeah!" singer has been nominated in five categories, including Best R&B/Soul Male Artist, Song of the Year for his hit single "Bad Habits", and Album/Mixtape of the Year for his latest album "Confessions 2".
The nominations were announced yesterday by the Soul Train Music Awards committee.


Usher, who has won numerous awards throughout his career, including eight Grammy Awards, expressed his gratitude for the nominations on social media.
"Honored to be recognized by Soul Train again.
This music, this culture...
it's a part of my soul," he wrote on Twitter.


The Soul Train Music Awards, which celebrates the accomplishments made by singers and musicians in the soul, hip-hop, and R&B genres, will be held in Las Vegas later this year.
Other artists who have received multiple nominations include Beyoncé, Chris Brown, and H.E.R.

Beyoncé, who has previously won the prestigious Ashford & Simpson Songwriter's Award, is nominated in four categories this year, including Best R&B/Soul Female Artist.
Chris Brown and H.E.R., both previous winners at the Soul Train Music Awards, have also received multiple nominations.

Boeing, the American multinational corporation that designs, manufactures, and sells airplanes, has secured a significant order from Japan, further strengthening its position in the global aviation market. 


The deal, which is one of the largest in recent years, involves the sale of 200 aircraft to All Nippon Airways (ANA), Japan's largest airline.

Arsenal Football Club may be considering a full share listing, according to sources close to the club.
This move could potentially open up the club to a wider range of investors and provide a significant financial boost.


The North London club, currently owned by American billionaire Stan Kroenke, has been privately held since 2007.
A full share listing would mean that shares in the club would be publicly traded, allowing anyone to buy a stake in the club.


This potential move comes amid growing financial pressures on football clubs due to the ongoing Covid-19 pandemic.
Many clubs have seen their revenues significantly reduced due to the lack of matchday income and reduced broadcasting revenues.


A full share listing could provide Arsenal with a much-needed cash injection.
It could also allow the club to spread the financial risk among a larger number of shareholders, rather than it being concentrated in the hands of a single owner.


However, the move could also potentially lead to a loss of control for Kroenke.
If a significant number of shares were bought by other investors, they could potentially influence the direction of the club.

After more than 50 years of entertaining music lovers, the iconic British music chart television programme, Top of the Pops, is set to leave BBC One.
The show, which has been a staple of the channel since its inception in 1964, has been a launchpad for many of the world's biggest music stars.


The decision to move the show from its long-standing home was announced by the BBC, citing a need to "refresh and modernise" its music programming.
The corporation has not yet revealed where the show will be relocated, but it is understood that it will continue to be broadcast on one of the BBC's platforms.


Top of the Pops, known for its live performances and countdown of the week's top 40 singles, has been a significant part of British pop culture.
It has seen performances from some of the biggest names in music, from The Beatles and Rolling Stones to Madonna and Beyonce.


The show's departure from BBC One marks the end of an era, but the BBC has assured fans that Top of the Pops will continue to be a part of its music offering.
"While the show will be leaving BBC One, it is not the end of Top of the Pops," a spokesperson said.
"We are committed to ensuring that the show continues to be a part of the BBC's music output.
"

The move has been met with mixed reactions from viewers.

Former UK International Development Secretary, Clare Short, has criticised the United States over its response to the devastating tsunami in Southeast Asia.
She accused the US of being "very weak" in its aid efforts and of using the disaster to boost its global standing.


Ms Short, who served under Tony Blair's government, said the US was "trying to use this terrible event to increase its influence in the region".
She also criticised the US for not contributing more to the United Nations' central fund for disaster relief.


"The United States has been very weak in its response," she said.
"They have given less aid than the European Union, despite having a larger economy.
They are also trying to bypass the UN and set up their own aid distribution system, which is not helpful.
"

The US has pledged $350m in aid to the countries affected by the tsunami, which killed more than 230,000 people in 14 countries.
However, Ms Short said this was not enough given the scale of the disaster and the wealth of the US.


She also criticised the US for not signing up to the UN's International Development Association, which provides low-interest loans to developing countries.

Romantic comedy "Hitch", starring Will Smith, has maintained its grip on the US box office for the third consecutive week, according to studio estimates.


The film, which features Smith as a professional "date doctor" helping men to woo the women of their dreams, has so far raked in an impressive $94.3m (£49.6m).
Despite mixed reviews, audiences have been drawn to the chemistry between Smith and his co-star, Eva Mendes.


"Hitch" managed to fend off competition from a slew of new releases, including the horror sequel "Constantine", starring Keanu Reeves, which debuted at number two with $30.5m (£16m).
The animated feature "Because of Winn-Dixie", based on the popular children's book, opened at number three with $10.85m (£5.7m).


Rounding out the top five were "Son of the Mask", a sequel to the 1994 Jim Carrey hit, which took in $7.6m (£4m), and "Million Dollar Baby", the Clint Eastwood-directed drama that has been a major contender in the awards season, earning $7m (£3.7m).


"Hitch" has proven to be a surprise hit for Sony Pictures, with its blend of humor and romance resonating with audiences.
The film's success is also a testament to Smith's star power, as he continues to prove his ability to draw crowds in a variety of genres, from action blockbusters to romantic comedies.


Despite the dominance of "Hitch", the overall box office was down compared to the same weekend last year.
This continues a trend of declining box office revenues in recent months, raising concerns about the long-term health of the cinema industry.

The Trades Union Congress (TUC) has called for greater protection for whistleblowers, arguing that they play a crucial role in exposing wrongdoing and maintaining integrity in the workplace.
The TUC, which represents the majority of the UK's trade unions, has urged the government to strengthen the laws that protect individuals who expose corruption, fraud, or other forms of malpractice.


The call comes amid growing concerns that whistleblowers are often victimised, harassed, or even lose their jobs as a result of their actions.
The TUC has highlighted several high-profile cases where individuals have suffered significant personal and professional consequences after raising concerns about wrongdoing in their organisations.


TUC General Secretary, Frances O'Grady, said: "Whistleblowers are unsung heroes who have often taken great personal risks to expose wrongdoing.
But all too often, they are treated as troublemakers, rather than valued for their role in maintaining integrity and accountability."


The TUC is calling for a number of changes to the current legislation, including the introduction of a legal duty on employers to protect whistleblowers from victimisation, and the establishment of an independent body to investigate complaints.
It also wants to see greater financial compensation for those who suffer as a result of their whistleblowing.


The TUC's call has been backed by several prominent whistleblowers, including Dr. Chris Day, who exposed safety concerns in the NHS, and Katharine Gun, a former GCHQ translator who leaked a confidential email in the run-up to the Iraq War.


Dr. Day said: "Whistleblowers need to know that they will be protected if they speak out.

The International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) has initiated a robust campaign against the use of performance-enhancing drugs in athletics.
This move comes in response to a series of doping scandals that have tarnished the reputation of the sport in recent years.


The IAAF's new anti-doping programme will involve rigorous testing of athletes, both in and out of competition, as well as educational initiatives aimed at promoting clean sport.
The federation has pledged to invest significant resources into the campaign, with the goal of eradicating doping from athletics.


The IAAF President, Sebastian Coe, stated, "We are committed to restoring trust in our sport.
We believe that this comprehensive approach, focusing on detection, deterrence, and education, will significantly help in the fight against drugs in athletics.
"

The new measures will include the establishment of an independent anti-doping body, which will be responsible for overseeing all testing procedures.
This body will work in conjunction with the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) to ensure that all tests are carried out to the highest possible standards.


In addition to the testing programme, the IAAF will also launch an education initiative aimed at athletes, coaches, and support staff.
This will include workshops, online resources, and a dedicated helpline for athletes to report any concerns or suspicions about doping.

Japan's industrial production has experienced a significant decline, according to data released by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry.
The figures show a decrease of 3.6% in February, marking the second consecutive month of contraction.


The decline was more severe than economists had predicted, with many having forecast a drop of around 2.5%.
The fall in output is largely attributed to a decrease in the production of cars and machinery, two of Japan's key manufacturing sectors.


The data also revealed a 1.3% drop in inventories, suggesting that companies are cutting back on production in response to weaker demand.
This is a worrying sign for the world's third-largest economy, which has been struggling to recover from the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.


The decline in industrial output is a blow to Prime Minister Fumio Kishida's government, which has been implementing measures to stimulate economic growth.
The government has been banking on a strong recovery in the manufacturing sector to help drive the economy out of recession.


The automobile industry, a major pillar of Japan's economy, has been particularly hard hit.
Production has been hampered by a global shortage of semiconductors, a key component in modern vehicles.

This decision comes after extensive research and testing of the synthetic surfaces, which have been found to meet the necessary standards for professional football.


The move is seen as a significant step forward in the sport, particularly for clubs in colder climates where maintaining natural grass pitches can be challenging.
The use of artificial turf, also known as fake grass, will allow for more consistent playing conditions and could potentially reduce the risk of injury.


UEFA President, Aleksander Čeferin, said: "This decision is a result of careful consideration and thorough research.
We believe that the use of artificial turf will not only benefit clubs in terms of maintenance and cost, but also improve the overall quality of the game.
"

The decision was made at a UEFA Executive Committee meeting and will apply to all UEFA competitions, including the Champions League and Europa League.
However, clubs will still have the option to use natural grass if they prefer.

The play, which premiered at the National Theatre in May last year, has been hailed as Bennett's best work to date.
It has enjoyed sell-out runs in both London and on Broadway, and has been praised for its witty dialogue and poignant exploration of adolescence.

Mike Leigh's Vera Drake is among the nominees for best British film.

Mike Leigh will compete for the British film prize with Shane Meadows for Dead Man's Shoes, Roger Michell For Enduring Love and My Summer Of Love director Pawel Pawlikowski.

Nominees for best foreign film include Spain's Pedro Almodovar for Bad Education and Hong Kong director Wong Kar-Wai for 2046.

Novelist Andrea Levy is favourite to win the main Whitbread Prize book of the year award, after winning novel of the year with her book Small Island.

The book has already won the Orange Prize for fiction, and is now 5/4 favourite for the £25,000 Whitbread.
Second favourite is a biography of Mary Queen of Scots, by John Guy.
A panel of judges including Sir Trevor McDonald, actor Hugh Grant and writer Joanne Harris will decide the overall winner on Tuesday.

The five writers in line for the award won their respective categories - first novel, novel, biography, poetry and children's book - on 6 January.
Small Island, Levy's fourth novel, is set in post-war London and centres on a landlady and her lodgers.
One is a Jamaican who joined British troops to fight Hitler but finds life difficult out of uniform when he settles in the UK.
"What could have been a didactic or preachy prospect turns out to hilarious, moving humane and eye-popping.
It's hard to think of anybody not enjoying it," wrote the judges.
The judges called Guy's My Heart is My Own: The Life of Mary Queen of Scots "an impressive and readable piece of scholarship, which cannot fail but leave the reader moved and intrigued by this most tragic and likeable of queens".

German airline Lufthansa may sue federal agencies for damages after the arrival of US president George W Bush disrupted flights.

Lufthansa said that it may lose millions of euros as a result of Air Force One landing at Frankfurt airport.
Flights were affected for an hour on Wednesday morning, double the time that had been expected, leading to cancellations and delays.
Lufthansa accounts for six out of every 10 planes using Frankfurt's airport.

"We are doing research into the possibilities we have," Michael Lamberty, a Lufthansa spokesman told the BBC.
"We are checking if there is action to be taken and in which courts it could be taken."
Mr Lamberty explained that the company did not plan to pursue Germany's air traffic controllers' organisation or the airport authority but wanted instead to see if it was possible to sue the German federal agencies that gave the orders.
The company said that it had to cancel 77 short and medium-distance flights, affecting about 5,000 passengers.
Long-haul travellers were not disrupted.

Central to the problem was that instead of half an hour, the arrival of President Bush on the German leg of his European tour took the best part of an hour, Lufthansa said.

A string of storms, typhoons and earthquakes has made 2004 the most expensive year on record for property insurers, according to Swiss Re.

The world's second biggest insurer said disasters around the globe have seen property claims reach $42bn (£21.5bn).
"2004 reinforces the trend towards higher losses," said Swiss Re.
Tightly packed populations in the areas involved in natural and man-made disasters were to partly to blame for the rise in claims, it said.
Some 95% of insurance claims were for natural catastrophes, with the rest attributed to made-made events.

The largest claims came from the US, which was struck by four hurricanes, and Japan, which suffered the highest concentration of typhoons for decades plus a major earthquake.

Europe suffered fewer natural disasters, but 191 people were killed and more than 2,000 injured in March after the terrorist attack on train stations in Madrid.
The damages claimed in 2004 eclipsed previous years, including 2001 when the 11 September attacks pushed claims up to $37bn.
Swiss Re said it had registered about 300 natural and man-made disasters around the world in 2004.
Twenty-one thousand people lost their lives in the catastrophes with a cost to the global economy of around $105bn (£54bn).

text:
China's national airline is to make its overseas stock market debut with a dual listing in London and Hong Kong, the London Stock Exchange (LSE) has said.

Air China plans to raise $1bn (£514m) from the flotation.
Share trading will begin on 15 December, the LSE said.
For China's aviation authorities, the listing is part of the modernisation of its airline sector to cope with soaring demand for air travel.
No further details of the share price or number of shares were given.

The LSE has been working hard to woo Chinese companies to choose London, rather than New York for their listings.
It opened an Asia-Pacific office in Hong Kong last month.
"We are delighted that Air China has chosen London for its listing outside China," said LSE chief executive Clara Furse.
"The London Stock Exchange offers ambitious Chinese companies access to the world's most international equity market combined with high regulatory and corporate governance standards," she said.
A spokesman for the LSE said: "We've been engaged with them (Air China) for about 18 months, two years now."

text:
Web logs or blogs are everywhere, with at least an estimated five million on the web and that number is set to grow.

These online diaries come in many shapes and styles, ranging from people willing to sharing their views, pictures and links, to companies interested in another way of reaching their customers.
But this year the focus has been on blogs which cast a critical eye over news events, often writing about issues ignored by the big media or offering an eye-witness account of events.
Most blogs may have only a small readership, but communication experts say they have provided an avenue for people to have a say in the world of politics.
The most well-known examples include Iraqi Salam Pax's accounts of the US-led war, former Iranian vice-president Mohammad Ali Abtahi exclusive insight into the Islamic Republic's government, and the highs and lows of the recent US election campaign.
There are already websites pulling together these first-hand reporting accounts heralded by blogs, like wikinews.com, launched last November.

The blogging movement has been building up for many years.

Andrew Nachison, Director of the Media Center, a US-based think-tank that studies media, technology and society, highlights the US presidential race as a possible turning point for blogs.
"You could look at that as a moment when audiences exercised a new form of power, to choose among many more sources of information than they have never had before," he says.
"And blogs were a key part of that transformation."

text:
Southampton are set to unveil Harry Redknapp as their new manager at a news conference at 1500 GMT on Wednesday.

The former Portsmouth boss replaces Steve Wigley, who has been relieved of first-team duties after just one win in 14 league games in charge.
Redknapp, 57, quit his Fratton Park position on 24 November and vowed: "I will not go down the road - no chance."
Pompey coach Kevin Bond is poised to join Redknapp, who will be Saints' third boss of the season.
Redknapp's first game in charge will be at home to Middlesbrough on Saturday.
Portsmouth chairman Milan Mandaric said he was "disappointed" by the news and claimed Redknapp had been in talks with Southampton for "some time".

"It would appear that negotiations over this have been going on for some time," Mandaric said on Portsmouth's official website.
"I am surprised and a little shocked that the chairman of Southampton has not picked up the phone and kept me informed."
According to Mandaric, Redknapp vowed he would not join their South coast rivals when he left Portsmouth.
"I said to Harry 'I hope you don't go to Southampton', and he told me 'absolutely not'," he said.

text:
Three years after a gruelling economic crisis, Turkey has dressed its economy to impress.

As part of a charm offensive - ahead of 17 December, when the European Union will decide whether to start entry talks - Turkey's economic leaders have been banging the drum to draw attention to recent achievements.
The economy is growing fast, they insist.
Education levels among its young and large population are rising.
Unemployment levels, in percentage terms, are heading fast towards single digits.
Inflation is under control.
A new law to govern its turbulent banking system is on the cards.
The tourism industry is booming and revenues from visitors should more than double to $21bn (£10.8bn) in three years.

Moreover, government spending is set to be frozen and a burdensome social security deficit is being tackled.
Income and corporate taxes will be cut next year in order to attract $15bn of foreign investment over the next three years.

T-Mobile has launched its latest "pocket office" third-generation (3G) device which also has built-in wi-fi - high-speed wireless net access.

Unlike other devices where the user has to check which high-speed network is available to transfer data, the device selects the fastest one itself.
The MDA IV, released in the summer, is an upgrade to the company's existing smartphone, the 2.5G/wi-fi MDA III.
It reflects the push by mobile firms for devices that are like mini laptops.
The device has a display that can be swivelled and angled so it can be used like a small computer, or as a conventional clamshell phone.
The Microsoft Mobile phone, with two cameras and a Qwerty keyboard, reflects the design of similar all-in-one models released this year, such as Motorola's MPx.
"One in five European workers are already mobile - meaning they spend significant time travelling and out of the office," Rene Obermann, T-Mobile's chief executive, told a press conference at the 3GSM trade show in Cannes.
He added: "What they need is their office when they are out of the office."
T-Mobile said it was seeing increasing take up for what it calls "Office in a Pocket" devices, with 100,000 MDAs sold in Europe already.

In response to demand, T-Mobile also said it would be adding the latest phone-shaped Blackberry to its mobile range.

text:
Cable firms NTL and Telewest have both launched video-on-demand services as the battle between satellite and cable TV heats up.
Movies from Sony Pictures, Walt Disney, Touchstone, Miramax, Columbia and Buena Vista will be among those on offer.
The service is similar to Sky Plus, as users can pause, fast forward and rewind content, but they cannot store programmes on their set top box - yet.
It could sound the death knell for some TV channels, Telewest predicts.
"It allows us to demonstrate a clear competitive advantage over Sky for the first time in many years," said Telewest chief executive Eric Tveter.

"Video-on-demand will offer a deeper range of content than currently exists on TV.
There will be less compromising around the TV schedule and some of the less popular channels may go by the wayside," said Philip Snalune, director of products at Telewest.
Telewest customers in Bristol and NTL viewers in Glasgow will be the first to test the new service, which sees a raft of movies on offer for 24 hour rental.
During the year, the service will be extended to all cable regions.
Films will range in price from £1 or £2 for archived movies to £3.50 for current releases.
New releases initially on offer will include 50 First dates, Kill Bill: Volume 2, Gothika and The Station Agent.

Bill Gates has opened the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas, saying that gadgets are working together more to help people manage multimedia content around the home and on the move.

Mr Gates made no announcement about the next generation Xbox games console, which many gadget lovers had been hoping for.
About 120,000 people are expected to attend the trade show which stretches over more than 1.5 million square feet and runs from 6 to 9 January.
The latest trends in digital imaging, storage technologies, thinner flat screen and high-definition TVs, wireless and portable technologies, gaming, and broadband technologies will all be on show over the three days.

Mr Gates said that a lot of work had been done in the last year to sort out usability and compatibility issues between devices to make it easier to share content.

"We predicted at the beginning of the decade that the digital approach would be taken for granted - but there was a lot of work to do.
"What is fun is to come to the show and see what has been done.
It is going even faster than we expected and we are excited about it."
He highlighted technology trends over the last year that had driven the need to make technology and transferring content across difference devices "seamless".
"Gaming is becoming more of a social thing and all of the social genres will use this rich communications.

Church ministers are trying to prevent rapper Nelly performing in Arkansas, saying they do not want his "vile and filthy lyrics" in their town.

More than 20 Jonesboro ministers urged music fans to boycott Nelly's 12 March concert at Arkansas State University in a bid to have it cancelled.
"Jonesboro is a wonderful city because of what does not come here," said the Reverend Adrian Rodgers.
But a venue spokesman said more than 5,500 tickets had been sold so far.

Mr Rodgers, of the Fullness of Joy Church, said he was concerned about the rapper's lyrics that include references to drugs, sex and violence, and songs that the minister said were demeaning to women.
Ministers were worried that bringing such acts to Jonesboro would lead to problems.
"Tear the tickets up," Mr Rodgers said.
"Do not go and do not allow your children to go.
"
Tim Dean, director of the Arkansas State University venue, said ticket sales had been brisk.
"It would appear that with ticket sales over 5,000, many others have expressed their right to find Nelly's music entertaining and worth spending their time and money on," he said.

text:
Neil Kinnock has said his acceptance of a seat in the House of Lords will allow him to help "achieve further progress with substantial democratic reform.
"
On the BBC's Breakfast with Frost it was put to Mr Kinnock that he had once referred to Lords members as "brigands, muggers, bribers and gangsters".
But the outgoing European Commissioner said his comments - made some 26 years ago - needed to be put in context.
He said advocates for reform needed to be inside the Lords to vote for it.
"It was pointed out to me that if the additional democratic reform is going to take place it is going to require advocates in the Lords and people there willing to vote for it."

Mr Kinnock added that the second factor behind his acceptance of the peerage was his appointment as chairman of the British Council.
"History demonstrates that it's immensely useful for the British Council to have its chairman in the House of Lords and that was a conclusive factor."
Mr Kinnock said he thought about the decision for "quite a long time" because he had long had reservations about the Lords.
But he added: "The process of reform has developed substantially but not sufficiently, and consequently I did take all these factors into consideration because it's not a decision to be made glibly."
The former Labour leader said he would probably take the title of Lord Kinnock of Bedwellty - his first constituency for which he was selected in 1969.
